How to use this document

The copy describes how FigSumo's calculators work today. Features the copy relies on but the tools do not yet have are listed as developer notes in Appendix B. Fix the items marked 'FIX before publishing' before the pages go live.
Links to /methodology and /privacy point to site pages that are not in the calculator sheet. Create them before launch.

Money, Finance and Tax (109 pages)
401(k) Calculator (2026 Limits)
URL
https://figsumo.com/us/401k-calculator
Title tag
401(k) Calculator 2026: Employer Match & Growth | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Project your 401(k) balance with employer match, salary growth and 2026 IRS contribution limits, including catch-up contributions for ages 50+ and 60–63. (153 chars)
Country
US
Status
rename (301) · tax year 2026 plan-year limits (IRS IR-2025-111)
Body words
1,073 (minimum 1,000)
H1: 401(k) Calculator (2026 Limits)
A 401(k) combines three sources of growth: your own salary deferrals, your employer's match, and investment returns that aren't taxed until withdrawal (traditional) or ever (qualified Roth). This calculator projects the balance at retirement under the 2026 IRS limits. It shows how much comes from the match, and it warns you if your contribution rate is too low to get the full match.
How to use this calculator
1. Current age, retirement age and current 401(k) balance.
2. Annual salary and expected yearly raise.
3. Your contribution as a percent of salary. The calculator caps it at the IRS limit for your age.
4. Employer match formula, for example "100% of the first 4%" or "50% of the first 6%". You can add a second tier.
5. Expected annual return and contribution frequency (per paycheck or annual).
6. Vesting (optional): the percent of employer money you'd keep if you left today.
The formula
Each year y:
Salary_y      = Salary_0 × (1 + raise)^y
Employee_y    = min(contribution % × Salary_y, deferral limit for age)
Match_y       = match rate × min(contribution %, match cap %) × Salary_y
Total_y       = min(Employee_y + Match_y, §415(c) limit) (+ catch-up, which sits outside §415(c))
Balance_(y+1) = Balance_y × (1 + return) + Total_y        (annual mode, contributions at year-end)
In per-paycheck mode, contributions are added each pay period and compounded at the equivalent periodic rate. This gives a slightly higher result than annual mode.
2026 limits (IRS):
Employee elective deferral: $24,500
Catch-up, age 50+: $8,000, for a total of $32,500
Higher catch-up at ages 60–63: $11,250 instead of $8,000, for a total of $35,750
Total annual additions (employee + employer, excluding catch-up): $72,000
Worked examples
Example 1: getting the full match. Age 40, $10,000 balance, $70,000 salary (no raises, to keep the arithmetic clear), 6% contribution, employer matches 100% of the first 4%, 7% annual return, 25 years, annual mode.
Your contribution: 6% × 70,000 = $4,200 a year
Match: 100% × 4% × 70,000 = $2,800 a year
Balance at 65: 10,000 × 1.07^25 + 7,000 × (1.07^25 − 1) / 0.07 = $497,017.59
Without the match, the same plan would reach $319,920.28. The match adds $177,097.31.
Example 2: maximising, and age-based catch-up.
At a $150,000 salary, reaching the 2026 deferral limit of $24,500 takes 24,500 ÷ 150,000 = 16.33% of pay.
At age 61, the limit is 24,500 + 11,250 = $35,750.
Employer contributions count toward the $72,000 total-additions limit. Catch-up contributions are not included in that limit.
Understanding your results
Balance at retirement: split into your contributions, employer contributions and investment growth.
Match left on the table: if your rate is below the match cap, the calculator shows the yearly match you're missing.
Limit warning: shown when your percentage would exceed the deferral limit. Some plans stop deferrals at the limit, which can also stop the match for the rest of the year unless the plan has a "true-up". Ask your plan administrator.
Real value: add inflation to see the balance in today's dollars.
Taxes not deducted: traditional 401(k) withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. Qualified Roth 401(k) withdrawals are tax-free.
The cost of early withdrawal
Taking $20,000 out at age 45 from a traditional 401(k), with a 22% federal marginal rate:
Federal income tax: 22% × 20,000 = $4,400
10% additional tax: $2,000
You keep about $13,600 before any state tax, and lose the future growth on the $20,000.
Exceptions to the 10% additional tax exist, for example separation from service in or after the year you turn 55. Check IRS Topic 558.
Required minimum distributions
You generally must start taking RMDs from traditional 401(k)s and IRAs when you reach age 73. Workplace-plan participants can usually delay until the year they retire, unless they are a 5% owner of the business. Roth 401(k) accounts are no longer subject to lifetime RMDs.
Country notes
US only. Similar accounts elsewhere: Canada's RRSP and group RRSPs; UK workplace pensions under auto-enrolment.
Roth catch-up rule: under SECURE 2.0, if your FICA wages from this employer were over $150,000 in 2025, any catch-up contributions you make in 2026 must be Roth (after-tax) contributions.
Tips and common mistakes
Leaving the match on the table. Contribute at least enough to get the full employer match; it's an immediate return no investment can promise.
Forgetting the vesting schedule. Employer contributions may not be fully yours until you've worked a set number of years.
Over-contributing with two employers. The $24,500 employee limit is per person, not per plan, so add up deferrals at every job.
Ignoring fund fees. An expense ratio difference of 0.5% a year compounds into a large sum over decades.
Cashing out when you change jobs. Roll the balance into the new plan or an IRA to avoid tax and the 10% early-withdrawal penalty.
Frequently asked questions
What is the 401(k) contribution limit for 2026?
$24,500 for employee deferrals. People aged 50 or older can add $8,000, and people aged 60–63 can add $11,250 instead. Total employee plus employer additions are capped at $72,000, not counting catch-up.
Is the employer match included in the $24,500?
No. The $24,500 limit applies only to your own deferrals. Employer contributions count toward the separate $72,000 total limit.
Should I choose traditional or Roth 401(k)?
Traditional lowers your taxable income now. Roth contributions are taxed now, but qualified withdrawals are tax-free. The better choice depends on your current and expected future tax rates. Many people split between the two. This calculator shows the balance for either; tax outcomes are personal.
What happens if I withdraw early?
Distributions before age 59½ are generally subject to income tax plus a 10% additional tax, unless an exception applies. Plan loans and hardship withdrawals follow plan rules.
What does vesting mean?
Your own contributions are always 100% yours. Employer contributions may vest over several years. If you leave before you're fully vested, you forfeit the unvested part.
Why does contribution frequency change the result?
Money invested each paycheck starts growing sooner than money added once a year. Over decades, that adds a little to the balance.

Disclaimer
Projections assume constant returns and the inputs you enter. They are not investment or tax advice. Plan rules (match, vesting, true-ups) vary; check your Summary Plan Description.

Amortization Calculator & Schedule with Extra Payments | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Generate a full amortization schedule for any fixed-rate loan, see interest vs principal each month and test how extra payments shorten the loan. (145 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,053 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Amortization Calculator
An amortization schedule shows, payment by payment, how much of what you pay is interest, how much reduces the balance, and what is still owed. It explains why early payments do so little to shrink a long loan, and why extra payments made early save so much. Enter your loan details to see the full schedule, a yearly summary and the effect of paying extra.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount, interest rate and term: take these from your loan agreement.
2. Start date: the month of your first payment, so the schedule shows real dates.
3. Extra payments (optional): a fixed extra amount each month, an extra amount once a year, or a one-time lump sum in a chosen month.
4. Switch between the monthly schedule, the yearly summary and the balance chart. You can download the schedule as a CSV.
The formula
The regular payment is:
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Then, for each period k:
Interest_k  = Balance_(k−1) × r
Principal_k = PMT − Interest_k (+ any extra payment)
Balance_k   = Balance_(k−1) − Principal_k
P: original loan amount
r: periodic rate (annual rate ÷ 12 for monthly payments)
n: number of payments
The last payment is reduced so the balance ends at exactly zero. Extra payments go straight to principal. This lowers every later interest charge, so the loan ends early, while the scheduled payment stays the same.
Worked examples
Example 1: the first three months of a mortgage. $250,000 at 6% for 30 years. r = 0.005, n = 360, payment $1,498.88.

Month 1 interest is 250,000 × 0.005 = $1,250.00. The rest of the payment, $248.88, reduces the balance. Each month, interest falls a little and principal rises by the same amount.
First-year totals: $14,916.49 of interest, balance $246,929.97. Only about $3,070 of the $17,987 paid in year 1 went to principal.
Principal first exceeds interest in month 223 (year 19).
Total interest over 30 years: $289,595.47.
Example 2: adding $200 a month. The same loan with an extra $200 every month from the start:
Paid off in 267 months instead of 360 (7 years 9 months sooner)
Total interest $203,362.51, a saving of $86,232.96
That saving comes from $53,400 of extra payments (267 × $200). Each dollar paid early saves interest for the rest of the loan.

Example 3: a $30,000 car loan at 6% over 5 years. The payment is $579.98 a month. In the first year, about $1,655.71 of the $6,959.81 paid is interest; in the final year, only about $221.01. Shorter loans shift to principal far faster than mortgages.
Understanding your results
Schedule table: each row is one payment. The interest column falls, the principal column rises, and the balance reaches zero at the end.
Yearly summary: totals for each year. Useful for planning, and in the US for estimating how much mortgage interest you might report if you itemize deductions. Your lender's Form 1098 gives the official figure.
Chart: the balance over time, with cumulative interest and principal. The vertical axis is in your currency; it is not a percentage.
With extra payments: the new payoff date, the interest saved, and the total extra paid.
Country notes
United States: most fixed-rate mortgages and auto loans amortize monthly, as shown here.
Canada: fixed-rate mortgages use semi-annual compounding. The Canadian mortgage calculator produces the correct schedule.
UK: repayment mortgages amortize the same way. Many fixed-rate deals limit penalty-free overpayments, so check your offer before modelling large extra payments.
Tips and common mistakes
Assuming extra payments go to principal automatically. Tell your lender to apply them to principal, and check the next statement.
Comparing loans by payment alone. Look at total interest across the whole schedule.
Forgetting escrow. The schedule covers principal and interest; taxes and insurance are added on top.
Using a rounded rate. 6.49% and 6.5% give slightly different schedules; use the exact note rate.
Frequently asked questions
Why is most of my early payment interest?
Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which is largest at the start. As the balance falls, less of each payment is needed for interest and more goes to principal.
Do extra payments lower my monthly payment?
Usually not. Most lenders keep the payment the same and end the loan earlier. Some offer a "recast" that lowers the payment after a large lump sum, usually for a fee.
Is it better to pay extra monthly or once a year?
For the same total amount, paying earlier saves slightly more interest because it reduces the balance sooner. Either option saves far more than not paying extra.
Does the schedule match my lender's exactly?
It should be within cents if your lender charges interest monthly. Lenders that charge daily interest, or that apply payments on specific dates, may show small differences.
Can I see the schedule for a loan I've already started?
Yes. Enter the current balance, the remaining term and your rate, and set the start date to your next payment.
What does "negative amortization" mean?
It means the payment is smaller than the interest due, so the balance grows. Standard fixed-rate loans don't do this. The calculator warns you if your inputs would cause it.

Annuity Calculator

https://figsumo.com/annuity-calculator
Title tag
Annuity Calculator: Future Value of Regular Deposits | FigSumo (62 chars)
Meta description
Work out what regular deposits into an annuity grow to, with start-of-period or end-of-period timing, compounding choice and a year-by-year table. (146 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,269 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Annuity Calculator
This calculator shows what a series of equal, regular deposits grows to by the end of a set number of years at a steady annual return. That is the "accumulation" phase of an annuity, and the same arithmetic applies to any plan where you pay in a fixed amount each month, quarter or year. Enter the deposit, the return, the number of years and how many deposits you make per year.
How to use this calculator
1. Periodic payment: the amount you pay in each period, before any fees. For a deferred annuity contract this is your scheduled premium; for a savings plan it is your standing order.
2. Annual return: the yearly rate you expect the money to earn, as a percentage. Use a net figure (after the contract's annual charges) if you know it, because fees reduce the rate you actually earn.
3. Years: how long you keep paying in.
4. Payments per year: 12 for monthly, 4 for quarterly, 2 for half-yearly, 1 for annual.
The results show the accumulated value at the end of the final period and the total payments made. The difference between the two is the growth earned.
The formula
The tool uses the future value of an ordinary annuity, which assumes each payment is made at the end of its period:
FV = PMT × ((1 + i)^n − 1) / i
FV: accumulated value at the end
PMT: the periodic payment
i: interest per period = annual return ÷ payments per year
n: number of payments = years × payments per year
Interest compounds once per payment period, so a monthly plan compounds monthly and a quarterly plan compounds quarterly. If the return is 0%, the result is simply PMT × n.
If you pay at the start of each period instead (an "annuity due"), every payment earns one extra period of interest, so the result is FV × (1 + i). The calculator does not have a timing switch at present; multiply by (1 + i) yourself to see the difference.
Worked examples
Example 1: $500 a month for 20 years at 5%
i = 0.05 ÷ 12 = 0.0041667; n = 20 × 12 = 240
FV = 500 × ((1.0041667)^240 − 1) ÷ 0.0041667 = $205,516.83
Total paid in: 500 × 240 = $120,000.00
Growth: $85,516.83
With payments at the start of each month instead, the value would be $206,373.15.
The return assumption matters more than most people expect. The same deposits give $183,387.31 at 4% and $231,020.45 at 6%.
Example 2: $1,500 a quarter for 15 years at 6%
i = 0.06 ÷ 4 = 0.015; n = 15 × 4 = 60
FV = 1,500 × ((1.015)^60 − 1) ÷ 0.015 = $144,321.98
Total paid in: $90,000.00; growth: $54,321.98
Paying the same $6,000 a year as $500 a month (12 payments a year) gives $145,409.36, slightly more, because money paid monthly starts earning sooner and compounds more often.
Understanding your results
Accumulated value is a projection, not a guarantee. It assumes the same return every period. Real returns vary year to year, and with a variable annuity they can be negative.
Total payments made is your own money. Growth is everything above it.
No tax or inflation is applied. In 20 years, prices will probably be higher, so the buying power of the final sum will be lower than its face value. Use the inflation calculator to restate it in today's money.
No contract charges are deducted unless you lower the return to allow for them. Annual fees of 1–2% are common in some annuity products (check your contract's fee table), and over 20 years they make a large difference.
Types of annuity and what this tool models
An annuity contract usually has two phases. In the accumulation phase you pay in, as this calculator models. In the payout (annuitization) phase the insurer converts the balance into income; to model that, use the annuity payout calculator.
Fixed annuity: the insurer credits a stated rate for a period. Your input rate is close to reality for that period.
Variable annuity: the money is invested in sub-accounts, so the return is not known in advance. Treat any rate you enter as an assumption and try a range.
Indexed annuity: credits are linked to a market index with caps or participation rates. The yearly credit can be zero, so a flat input rate is only a rough guide.
Immediate vs deferred: an immediate annuity starts paying out soon after a single premium and has no accumulation phase. This tool is for deferred, regular-premium plans.
Surrender charges often apply if you withdraw money in the first years of a contract. The calculator does not include them.
Country notes
United States: gains inside a deferred annuity are tax-deferred, and withdrawals of earnings before age 59½ can trigger a 10% additional tax as well as ordinary income tax (IRS Publication 575). The SEC and FINRA publish investor guidance on variable and indexed annuities.
Canada: annuities are sold by life insurers. Registered annuities bought with RRSP or RRIF money are taxed as income when paid. Contributions to your plan may be limited by your RRSP room.
United Kingdom: "annuity" usually means the income product bought with a pension pot at retirement. Regular savings into a pension or ISA follow the same growth formula, so this tool still works for those. See the ISA calculator for the annual allowance.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the gross rate when fees are charged. Subtract the annual charge from the expected return.
Mixing up payments per year and years. "Payments per year" is a count (12, 4, 1), not an amount.
Assuming a variable product earns a fixed rate. Run the calculation at a low, middle and high rate to see a range.
Ignoring the payout phase. A large accumulated value does not tell you the income it buys. Annuity payout rates depend on age, interest rates and options such as guarantees.
Frequently asked questions
Does the calculator assume payments at the start or end of each period?
At the end. This is the standard ordinary-annuity convention. If you pay at the start, multiply the result by (1 + annual rate ÷ payments per year).
How often does interest compound?
Once per payment period. A monthly plan compounds monthly; an annual plan compounds annually.
Can I include money I already have in the annuity?
Not directly. Work out the growth of the existing balance separately with the future value calculator and add the two results.
What return should I enter?
For a fixed annuity, the guaranteed rate in the contract. For variable or indexed products there is no single answer, so try a cautious and an optimistic rate and plan around the cautious one.
Is the accumulated value what I can take out?
Not necessarily. Surrender charges, market value adjustments and taxes can reduce what you receive, especially in the early years of a contract.
Why does monthly beat annual for the same yearly total?
Each monthly payment starts earning interest earlier in the year, and monthly compounding adds interest on interest more often.
Does this tell me my retirement income?
No. It gives the balance at the end of saving. Use the annuity payout or retirement calculator to turn a balance into income.

Annuity Payout Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/annuity-payout-calculator
Title tag
Annuity Payout Calculator: Income From a Lump Sum | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description
Find the regular payout a lump sum can fund for a set number of years at a given return, or how long a chosen payout will last. Includes a schedule. (148 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,162 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Annuity Payout Calculator
This calculator turns a lump sum into a level monthly income. Enter the balance you will draw from, the annual return you expect it to earn while it is being paid out, and the number of years the income should last. The result is the fixed monthly amount that runs the balance down to exactly zero at the end of that period.
It suits a retirement pot, an annuity balance at the point you start withdrawals, an inheritance you want to spread out, or any fund you plan to spend evenly.
How to use this calculator
1. Account balance: the amount available on the day payouts start. Take it from your latest annuity, 401(k), IRA, RRSP/RRIF or pension statement, after any tax you must pay on a lump-sum withdrawal.
2. Annual return: the yearly rate the remaining balance earns during the payout years. A lower, cautious figure is sensible because the money is being spent, not left to grow.
3. Payout period (years): how many years the income must last.
The results are the monthly payout (level) and the total paid out over the whole period.
The formula
The payout is the payment on an amortizing balance, like a loan in reverse:
Payout = B × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
B: starting balance
r: monthly return = annual return ÷ 12
n: number of monthly payouts = years × 12
Conventions: payouts are made at the end of each month, and the balance earns interest monthly at r. At 0% return, the payout is simply B ÷ n.
Each month, the balance earns interest and then the payout is taken. In the early years, most of each payment is covered by interest; later, more of it comes from capital.
Worked examples
Example 1: $500,000 over 25 years at 5%
r = 0.05 ÷ 12; n = 300
Payout = 500,000 × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−300) = $2,922.95 a month
Total paid out: $876,885.06, of which $376,885.06 is investment growth earned during the payout years
First month: the balance earns $2,083.33 of interest, so only $839.62 of the first payout comes from capital
Example 2: $250,000 over 20 years at 4%
n = 240, r = 0.04 ÷ 12
Payout = $1,514.95 a month; total $363,588.20
Stretching the same balance to 30 years lowers the payout to $1,193.54
With no growth at all (0%), 20 years of payouts would be $1,041.67 a month
Working the other way: if you take $2,000 a month from $250,000 at 4%, the money lasts about 162.0 months (13.5 years). The calculator does not yet solve for duration; the formula is n = −ln(1 − B × r ÷ payout) ÷ ln(1 + r).
Understanding your results
Monthly payout (level) is constant in dollars. It does not rise with inflation, so its buying power falls each year. At 2.5% inflation, a fixed payment loses about a fifth of its value in nine years.
Total paid out is the sum of all payouts. It is higher than the balance because the unspent part keeps earning.
Steady returns are assumed. Real investments vary. Poor returns in the first years of withdrawals (sequence-of-returns risk) can shorten how long the money lasts even if the average return is as expected.
Before tax. Payouts from pre-tax accounts are usually taxed as income.
Payout options in real annuity contracts
An insurer's annuity quote is not the same calculation. A life annuity pays for as long as you live, however long that is, so the insurer prices it on life expectancy and its own interest rate. Common options:
Life only: the highest income, ending at death.
Life with period certain: payments for life, but at least for a set number of years (e.g. 10) to your beneficiary.
Joint and survivor: payments continue to a spouse or partner, often at a reduced percentage.
Fixed period: income for a set number of years only. This is the case this calculator models.
Lump-sum or systematic withdrawal: you keep control and draw down yourself.
Use this tool to compare a quote against what the same money could pay if you drew it down yourself over a fixed period.
Country notes
United States: distributions from traditional IRAs and 401(k)s are taxed as ordinary income, and required minimum distributions start at age 73 for most people (see the RMD calculator). The non-taxable part of annuity payments bought with after-tax money is set out in IRS Publication 575 and Publication 939.
Canada: RRSPs must be converted (to a RRIF or annuity) by the end of the year you turn 71, and RRIFs have prescribed minimum withdrawals. Registered annuity payments are taxed as income.
United Kingdom: from a defined-contribution pension you can buy an annuity, use flexi-access drawdown or take lump sums. Usually 25% can be taken tax-free, subject to limits; the rest is taxed as income. MoneyHelper (Pension Wise) offers free guidance for people aged 50 and over.
Tips and common mistakes
Using an accumulation-phase return. During payout the money has a shorter horizon; many people hold more cash and bonds, which earn less.
Ignoring inflation. Plan for a payout that can rise, or lower the return to a "real" rate (return minus inflation) to get a payout in today's money.
Forgetting tax. Enter the after-tax balance, or reduce the payout by your expected tax rate.
Setting the period too short. A 65-year-old has a real chance of living past 90. Running out early is worse than leaving money behind.
Frequently asked questions
What does "level" payout mean?
The same dollar amount every month for the whole period. It does not increase with inflation.
Will the balance be exactly zero at the end?
Yes, if the return you entered is earned every month. With real-world returns the end balance will be higher or lower.
How do I get an inflation-adjusted payout?
Enter a real return (expected return minus expected inflation). The payout is then in today's money, and you would raise it each year by inflation.
Is this the same as an insurer's annuity quote?
No. Insurers price lifetime income on life expectancy, interest rates and their costs. This tool models a fixed-period drawdown at the rate you choose.
Can I see how long a set income will last?
Not yet in the tool. The worked example above shows the formula, and the retirement calculator includes a drawdown view.
Does it include fees?
No. Lower the return by your annual fees.

APR Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/apr-calculator
Title tag
APR Calculator: True Cost of a Loan Including Fees | FigSumo (60 chars)
Meta description
Convert a loan's interest rate plus upfront fees into an annual percentage rate (APR) so you can compare offers on a like-for-like basis. (137 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,173 (minimum 1,000)
H1: APR Calculator
The annual percentage rate (APR) folds a loan's upfront fees into its interest rate, so two offers with different fees can be compared on one number. Enter the loan amount, the fees you pay up front, the quoted interest rate and the term. The calculator returns the monthly payment and the APR including fees.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: the amount you borrow and repay, as shown on the loan agreement.
2. Upfront fees: charges you pay to get the loan, such as an origination or arrangement fee, discount points or a broker fee. Include only finance charges, not optional products. On a US mortgage, these are listed in Section A of the Loan Estimate.
3. Nominal interest rate: the yearly rate the lender charges on the balance (sometimes called the note rate).
4. Term (years): the full repayment period.
Results: monthly payment, APR (includes fees) and the nominal rate for comparison.
How the APR is calculated
First the monthly payment is worked out on the full loan amount at the nominal rate:
PMT = L × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
L: loan amount
r: nominal rate ÷ 12
n: term in years × 12
Then the calculator treats the fees as money you never really received. It finds the monthly rate a at which the payments repay only the net amount:
L − Fees = PMT × (1 − (1 + a)^−n) / a
APR = a × 12
There is no algebraic solution for a, so the tool finds it numerically by bisection and displays the APR to two decimal places (the examples below show three). Payments are monthly and made at the end of each month.
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 personal loan, $500 fee, 6.5% for 5 years
PMT = 20,000 at 6.5% over 60 months = $391.32
Net amount received: 20,000 − 500 = $19,500
The rate that links $19,500 to 60 payments of $391.32 gives APR = 7.563%
Total repaid: $23,479.38; total cost of credit including the fee: $3,979.38
A $500 fee adds about one percentage point to a 5-year loan of this size. A competing offer at 7.2% with no fee has an APR of 7.2%, so it is the cheaper loan per dollar you actually receive, even though its payment ($397.91) is higher because you get the full $20,000.
Example 2: $300,000 mortgage, $6,000 in fees, 6.25% for 30 years
PMT = $1,847.15 a month
Net received: $294,000
APR = 6.442% if the loan runs the full 30 years
APR spreads the fee over the whole term. If you sell or refinance after 5 years, the fee is spread over only 60 payments and the effective rate for that period is about 6.736%. That is why a loan with high fees and a low rate suits someone who keeps it a long time, and a no-fee loan suits someone who may move soon.
Understanding your results
APR above the nominal rate means fees are included. The bigger the fees and the shorter the term, the bigger the gap.
APR equals the nominal rate when fees are zero.
APR is not the same as the effective annual rate. APR here is the monthly rate × 12. Compounded monthly, the Example 1 loan has an effective annual rate of 7.83%.
A lender's official APR may differ. In the US, Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) defines which charges count as finance charges, and it varies by loan type. Use the APR on your Loan Estimate or credit agreement for formal comparisons, and this tool to test "what if" scenarios.
Limits of APR
It assumes you keep the loan to the end of the term, which many borrowers don't.
On adjustable-rate loans, the APR is based on assumed future rates, so it is less reliable.
It ignores costs that are not finance charges (for example, title insurance on some loans), even though you pay them.
It doesn't compare loans of different lengths fairly: a longer loan can have a lower APR but a much higher total interest cost. Check the total repaid as well.
Country notes
United States: the Truth in Lending Act and Regulation Z require lenders to disclose APR. The CFPB's Loan Estimate shows it on page 3 for mortgages.
Canada: federally regulated lenders must disclose the annual cost of borrowing, which includes most non-interest charges. Provincial rules cover other lenders.
United Kingdom: credit adverts and agreements must show the APR under the Consumer Credit (Disclosure of Information) rules; mortgage documents show an APRC (annual percentage rate of charge). A "representative APR" only has to be offered to at least 51% of successful applicants, so your own rate can be higher.
Tips and common mistakes
Including the fee in the loan amount twice. If the fee is added to the loan, enter the higher loan amount and the fee; if it is deducted from what you receive, enter the original amount and the fee.
Leaving out discount points. Points are prepaid interest and belong in the fee field.
Comparing APRs on different terms. Compare like-for-like terms, then look at total cost.
Ignoring how long you will keep the loan. Re-run the numbers with the term you expect to keep it.
Frequently asked questions
Why is the APR higher than my interest rate?
Because the fees are treated as extra cost of borrowing. You pay interest on the full amount but receive less, which raises the true rate.
Which fees should I include?
Charges you must pay to get the credit: origination or arrangement fees, points, mortgage broker fees and similar lender charges. Leave out costs you'd pay anyway, such as a home inspection.
Is a lower APR always better?
Not always. A longer loan may show a lower APR but cost more in total interest, and a high-fee loan only delivers its APR if you keep it for the full term.
What is the difference between APR and APY?
APR is a simple yearly rate (monthly rate × 12) used for loans. APY or AER includes compounding and is used for savings. For a loan, the effective annual rate is the APY-style equivalent.
Does the calculator handle fees added to the loan?
Yes, as long as you enter the loan amount including the financed fee and the fee itself. The APR is computed on what you actually receive.
Why does my lender's APR differ slightly?
Lenders follow legal rules on which charges are finance charges and how to handle irregular first periods. Small differences are normal.

Auto Lease Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/auto-lease-calculator
Title tag
Car Lease Calculator: Monthly Payment From Money Factor | FigSumo (65 chars)
Meta description
Estimate a monthly car lease payment from price, residual value, money factor or rate, term, down payment and sales tax. Explains each lease term. (146 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,113 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Auto Lease Calculator
This calculator estimates the monthly payment on a car lease from the negotiated price, the residual value, the money factor, the term and any down payment. It splits the payment into its two parts, depreciation and the rent (finance) charge, so you can see what you are paying for and check a dealer's quote.
How to use this calculator
1. MSRP / capitalized cost: the price the lease is based on. Use the negotiated selling price, not the sticker price, plus any fees rolled into the lease. It appears on the lease worksheet as "gross capitalized cost".
2. Residual value: what the leasing company expects the car to be worth at the end of the lease, in dollars. It is usually quoted as a percentage of MSRP; multiply to get the dollar figure.
3. Money factor: the lease's interest charge in decimal form, for example 0.00125. Ask the dealer for it; it is not always printed on the contract.
4. Lease term (months): commonly 24, 36 or 39 months.
5. Down payment: cash, rebates or trade-in equity that reduce the capitalized cost.
The results show the estimated monthly lease payment, the implied APR (money factor × 2,400) and the total of monthly payments.
The formula
A lease payment (before tax) has two parts:
Net cap cost   = Capitalized cost − Down payment
Depreciation   = (Net cap cost − Residual) ÷ Term
Rent charge    = (Net cap cost + Residual) × Money factor
Payment        = Depreciation + Rent charge
Depreciation is the part of the car's value you use up, spread evenly over the term.
Rent charge is the finance cost. Adding net cap cost and residual and multiplying by the money factor is the standard shortcut for the average balance times a monthly rate.
Money factor ≈ APR ÷ 2,400. So a money factor of 0.00125 is roughly a 3% APR.
Worked examples
Example 1: $38,000 car, $22,000 residual, 36 months, $2,000 down
Net cap cost = 38,000 − 2,000 = $36,000
Depreciation = (36,000 − 22,000) ÷ 36 = $388.89
Rent charge = (36,000 + 22,000) × 0.00125 = $72.50
Payment = $461.39 a month before tax
Implied APR: 0.00125 × 2,400 = 3.00%
36 payments total $16,610.00; with the $2,000 down payment, $18,610.00 for three years of use
Example 2: $45,000 car, 55% residual, 39 months, money factor 0.0021, nothing down
Residual = 55% × 45,000 = $24,750
Depreciation = (45,000 − 24,750) ÷ 39 = $519.23
Rent charge = (45,000 + 24,750) × 0.0021 = $146.47
Payment = $665.71 before tax (implied APR 5.04%)
With an 8% sales tax on each payment (a common US approach), add $53.26 for a total of $718.96
Understanding your results
Monthly payment excludes sales tax, registration and insurance. Add tax at your local rate.
Implied APR helps you compare the lease's finance cost with a loan. A dealer quoting a payment without the money factor can hide a high rate inside it.
Total of monthly payments is what you pay for the use of the car, excluding the down payment and fees. At the end you return the car, or buy it for the residual value.
A high residual lowers the payment because you use up less value. A low money factor lowers the rent charge.
Lease vs buy
Leasing usually means lower monthly payments than a loan on the same car, because you only pay for the depreciation during the term plus the rent charge. But you own nothing at the end, and mileage limits and wear charges apply. If you keep cars for many years, buying (see the auto loan calculator) usually costs less overall. Leasing can suit drivers who want a new car every few years and drive a predictable number of miles.
Ending a lease early is often expensive: you may owe the remaining payments or the difference between the payoff amount and the car's value, plus an early termination fee. Read the early-termination section of the contract before signing.
Country notes
United States: most states tax each monthly payment rather than the full price; a few tax the full cost up front [VERIFY your state's rule with its revenue department]. The CFPB and FTC publish consumer guides to vehicle leasing, and federal Regulation M requires lease disclosures.
Canada: GST/HST (and PST/QST where applicable) is charged on lease payments. Leases often quote a "lease rate" as an annual percentage instead of a money factor; divide by 2,400 to convert.
United Kingdom: the closest products are personal contract hire (PCH), where you never own the car, and PCP finance, which has an optional final "balloon" payment. UK PCH prices usually include VAT. Use this calculator as a guide only; UK quotes often state an initial rental of several months' payments.
Tips and common mistakes
Negotiate the price, not the payment. The capitalized cost is negotiable just like a purchase price.
Check the money factor against the lender's base rate for your credit tier.
Watch for rolled-in extras. Acquisition fees, add-on products and negative equity raise the cap cost.
Pick a realistic mileage allowance. Excess-mile charges (often quoted per mile) can cost more than a higher allowance.
Large down payments are risky. If the car is written off early, the down payment is usually lost; gap coverage typically protects the lender's balance, not your cash.
Frequently asked questions
What is a money factor?
The lease equivalent of an interest rate, written as a small decimal. Multiply it by 2,400 to get an approximate APR.
How do I find the residual value?
The leasing company sets it, usually as a percentage of MSRP for a given term and mileage. Ask the dealer, then multiply by the MSRP to enter it in dollars.
Does a down payment lower the payment?
Yes. It reduces the net capitalized cost, which lowers both the depreciation and the rent charge.
Does the result include sales tax?
No. Multiply the payment by your local tax rate and add it, or check how your state or province taxes leases.
Why is my dealer's payment higher?
Common reasons: a higher cap cost (fees or add-ons), a higher money factor, sales tax, or a lower residual than you assumed.
Can I buy the car at the end?
Most leases include a purchase option at the residual value plus any purchase fee. Compare it with the car's market value at the time.

Auto Loan Calculator with Sales Tax, Trade-In & Fees | FigSumo (62 chars)

Estimate your car payment including sales tax, fees, down payment and trade-in, and compare loan terms or a cash rebate against low-APR financing. (146 chars)

H1: Auto Loan Calculator
The sticker price is only the starting point. Sales tax, dealer and registration fees, your trade-in and any money still owed on it all change the amount you finance. This calculator works out the amount financed first, then the monthly payment and total interest. It can also show whether a cash rebate or a low promotional APR saves more.
How to use this calculator
1. Vehicle price: the negotiated price, not the MSRP.
2. Cash incentives/rebate: money the manufacturer takes off the price.
3. Down payment: the cash you put in.
4. Trade-in value and amount owed: if you owe more than the trade-in is worth (negative equity), the difference is added to the loan.
5. Sales tax rate and fees: enter your combined state and local rate, plus title, registration and documentation fees. Choose whether they are paid upfront or financed.
6. Interest rate (APR) and term: usually 36–84 months.
The formula
Amount financed. When tax and fees are financed:
Amount financed = Price − Rebate − Down payment − (Trade-in value − Amount owed) + Sales tax + Fees
Sales tax. States differ on what is taxed:
Sales tax = Tax rate × taxable amount
In many states, the taxable amount is the price minus the trade-in value. Some states tax the full price, and some states treat rebates differently. The calculator lets you pick the rule; check your state's revenue department.
Monthly payment:
PMT = A × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
A: amount financed
r: APR ÷ 12
n: term in months
Total interest = PMT × n − A.
Worked examples
Example 1: choosing a term. Price $35,000, sales tax 6% on the full price ($2,100), $5,000 down, no trade-in, no fees, APR 6.9%.
Amount financed: 35,000 + 2,100 − 5,000 = $32,100
60 months: r = 0.00575 → $634.11 a month, total interest $5,946.30
72 months: $545.73 a month, total interest $7,192.78
The 72-month loan lowers the payment by $88.38 but costs $1,246.48 more interest. It also keeps you in debt a year longer, during the period when the car is losing value fastest. In the first month of the 60-month loan, $184.58 of the payment is interest.
Example 2: $2,000 rebate or 0.9% APR? Same car and down payment, 60 months. The dealer offers either a $2,000 cash rebate with your 6.9% bank loan, or 0.9% manufacturer financing with no rebate. Tax is assumed on the full $35,000 in both cases.
Rebate: financed $30,100 at 6.9% → $594.60 a month, $35,675.82 in total payments
0.9% APR: financed $32,100 at 0.9% → $547.33 a month, $32,839.70 in total payments
The low APR wins by about $2,836 over the loan. With a smaller rate gap, or a larger rebate, the answer can flip, which is why the comparison mode runs both options with your numbers.
Dealer financing, bank loans or cash?
Dealer-arranged financing is convenient and sometimes carries manufacturer promotions, such as Example 2's 0.9% APR. The dealer may also be able to mark up the rate it obtains from the lender.
Direct loans from a bank or credit union let you shop for a rate before you visit the dealer, and give you something to compare the dealer's offer with.
Paying cash avoids interest entirely but ties up savings. Compare the interest cost shown here with what that cash would earn, and keep an emergency fund.
Whichever you choose, negotiate the vehicle price separately from the financing and the trade-in, so that a low payment doesn't hide a higher total cost.
Understanding your results
Amount financed is the real loan size. If it is larger than the car's value (because of negative equity, financed fees or tax), you start the loan "upside down".
Monthly payment covers principal and interest only. Insurance, fuel and maintenance are extra.
Total cost = down payment + all payments + any tax and fees paid upfront.
Term comparison table: the same loan at 36, 48, 60, 72 and 84 months, so you can see the trade-off between payment and interest at a glance.
Country notes
United States: sales tax rules and rates are set by states and localities. Dealers must give you a Truth in Lending disclosure showing the APR, the finance charge and the amount financed. Compare it with this estimate.
Canada: GST/HST and provincial sales tax apply to vehicle purchases, and the rules differ by province. Enter your combined rate.
UK: car finance is often hire purchase (HP) or personal contract purchase (PCP) rather than a simple loan. PCP has a large final "balloon" payment, so this calculator only models HP or a personal loan.
Tips and common mistakes
Negotiating the monthly payment instead of the price. A longer term can make a higher price look affordable.
Rolling negative equity into the new loan. You'll start owing more than the car is worth.
Skipping preapproval. A bank or credit union offer gives you a rate to compare with the dealer's.
Forgetting tax, title and fees. They can add several percent to the amount you finance.
Buying add-ons you don't need. Extended warranties and gap cover are optional and can be bought elsewhere.
Frequently asked questions
Is it better to finance sales tax and fees or pay them upfront?
Paying upfront avoids interest on them. Financing them keeps more cash in hand but raises the amount financed and the interest. On a 6.9%, 60-month loan, every $1,000 financed adds about $185 of interest.
How does a trade-in affect the payment?
Positive equity (the trade-in is worth more than you owe) works like a down payment. Negative equity is added to the new loan. In many states, the trade-in value also lowers the taxable price.
What loan term should I choose?
Shorter terms cost less interest and build equity faster. Longer terms lower the payment but increase total interest and the risk of owing more than the car is worth. The comparison table shows the cost of each option.
Why is the dealer's payment higher than this?
Check whether the dealer added fees, an extended warranty, GAP insurance or other products to the amount financed. Ask for an itemised breakdown and compare it with the amount financed here.
Does my credit score matter?
Yes. Lenders set the APR based on credit and other factors. Get a pre-approval from a bank or credit union so you have a rate to compare with the dealer's offer.
Rebate or low APR: which is better?
It depends on the size of the rebate, the rate gap and the term. Run both options in comparison mode. Example 2 shows one case where the low APR wins.

Title tag
Average Return Calculator: Arithmetic vs CAGR | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Calculate the average annual return of an investment from yearly returns or start and end values. Shows arithmetic mean and compound annual growth rate. (152 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,045 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Average Return Calculator
This calculator takes a series of yearly returns and gives you two averages: the geometric average (also called the compound annual growth rate, or CAGR) and the simple arithmetic average. The geometric figure is the one that tells you how fast your money actually grew. Enter each year's return as a percentage, separated by commas.
How to use this calculator
1. Annual returns (comma-separated %): type each period's return in order, for example 10, -5, 8, 12, 6. Use a minus sign for losses. Your fund factsheet, brokerage statement or pension annual statement lists calendar-year returns.
The tool ignores anything that is not a number, so a stray space is fine. It returns the geometric average (CAGR), the arithmetic average and the number of periods it read.
The periods don't have to be years. If you enter monthly returns, the result is an average monthly return.
The formula
Each return is turned into a growth factor (1 + r). The factors are multiplied together and the n-th root is taken:
Geometric average = ((1 + r1) × (1 + r2) × … × (1 + rn))^(1/n) − 1
Arithmetic average = (r1 + r2 + … + rn) ÷ n
Cumulative return  = (1 + r1) × … × (1 + rn) − 1
r1 … rn: the returns for each period, as decimals (10% = 0.10)
n: the number of periods
The geometric average is the constant yearly rate that would have produced the same end value. The arithmetic average is just the mean of the numbers, which ignores compounding.
Worked examples
Example 1: five years of returns
Returns: 10%, −5%, 8%, 12%, 6%.
Product of growth factors: 1.10 × 0.95 × 1.08 × 1.12 × 1.06 = 1.340 (cumulative return 33.99%)
Geometric average = 1.340^(1/5) − 1 = 6.03%
Arithmetic average = (10 − 5 + 8 + 12 + 6) ÷ 5 = 6.20%
$10,000 invested would have grown to $13,398.74. Growing at the geometric average for five years gives the same figure ($13,398.74). Growing at the arithmetic average would overstate it.
Example 2: why the two averages can disagree sharply
Returns: +50% then −50%.
Arithmetic average: 0.00%
Geometric average: -13.40%
$100 becomes $150, then $75. You lost a quarter of your money, yet the arithmetic average says you broke even. Only the geometric average reflects that.
A more volatile five-year run (25%, −20%, 30%, −15%, 18%) gives an arithmetic average of 7.60% but a geometric average of only 5.45%. The gap of 2.15 percentage points is the cost of volatility.
Understanding your results
Geometric average (CAGR) is the right figure for "what did I actually earn per year?" and for projecting a lump sum forward with the compound interest calculator.
Arithmetic average is always equal to or higher than the geometric average. It is the better estimate of a single typical year's expected return, which is why some statistical models use it, but it overstates long-run growth.
The bigger the swings, the bigger the gap. A rough rule: geometric ≈ arithmetic − (variance ÷ 2).
These are time-weighted returns. They measure the investment's performance, not your personal result if you added or withdrew money along the way. For that, use a money-weighted return, such as the IRR calculator.
Common uses
Comparing funds. Fund factsheets usually show annualized (geometric) returns over 1, 3, 5 and 10 years. Enter the calendar-year returns here to check them.
Checking a sales claim. An "average return of 10%" may be arithmetic. Ask which average is meant.
Real returns. Subtract inflation year by year first (or use (1 + nominal) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1) to get a real geometric average. The inflation calculator helps with the inflation figures.
Annualizing a total return
If you only know the total return over several years, you can still get the yearly figure. A fund that turned $10,000 into $14,000 over 6 years has a cumulative return of 40%. Its annualized return is 1.40^(1/6) − 1 = about 5.77% a year. To check a single figure in this calculator, enter that rate six times; the geometric average will match.
Country notes
The maths is the same everywhere. In the US, SEC rules require mutual fund advertisements that quote performance to show standardized average annual total returns over 1, 5 and 10 years. In the UK, FCA rules require past performance to cover up to the previous five complete 12-month periods and to carry a warning that it is not a reliable guide to future returns [VERIFY exact COBS 4.6 wording]. Canadian fund facts documents show year-by-year returns and an average return figure.
Tips and common mistakes
Enter percentages, not decimals. Type 8 for 8%, not 0.08.
Keep periods consistent. Don't mix monthly and annual returns in one list.
Include fees. Use returns after fund charges if you want the return you actually received.
Order doesn't matter for the averages, but it matters a great deal if you are adding or withdrawing money.
A −100% year wipes out the investment; the geometric average then shows −100%.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between geometric and arithmetic average return?
The geometric average accounts for compounding and gives the steady rate that produces the same final value. The arithmetic average is a plain mean that ignores compounding, so it overstates growth when returns vary.
Is CAGR the same as the geometric average?
Yes, when each period is one year. CAGR is the geometric average annual growth rate.
Can I enter monthly returns?
Yes. The result is then an average monthly return. To annualize it, use (1 + monthly)^12 − 1.
Why is my fund's "average return" different from my own return?
The fund's figure is time-weighted. If you invested more before a bad year or less before a good year, your money-weighted return differs.
How many years of data should I use?
As many as you have, ideally covering a full market cycle. Short periods are dominated by one or two years.
What does a negative geometric average mean?
That the investment lost value overall across the periods entered.

H1: Boat Loan Calculator
Use this calculator to estimate the monthly payment, total interest and payoff pattern of a loan to buy a boat, personal watercraft or other recreational vessel. Enter the amount you will borrow, the interest rate and the term in years and months. It returns the payment, the total of all payments and an amortization chart showing how the balance falls.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: the amount you will finance. Work it out as purchase price + any taxes and fees you finance − down payment − trade-in value. Lenders commonly ask for a down payment on boat loans [VERIFY typical percentage with lenders; it varies].
2. Interest rate: the annual rate on the loan offer. If you have the APR from a disclosure, using it gives a cost closer to reality.
3. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): the repayment period. Enter 10 years and 6 months as 10 and 6. Boat loans often run longer than car loans; terms of 10 to 20 years are common for larger boats.
Results: monthly payment, total of payments, total interest paid and the rate used, plus a chart of the balance, cumulative interest and cumulative payments over time.
The formula
The payment is a standard fixed-rate amortizing payment:
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
P: loan amount
r: monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12
n: total months = years × 12 + months
Each month, interest is charged on the remaining balance (balance × r) and the rest of the payment reduces the balance. Total interest = PMT × n − P.
Worked examples
Example 1: $30,000 over 5 years at 7.5%
r = 0.075 ÷ 12 = 0.00625; n = 60
PMT = $601.14 a month
Total of 60 payments: $36,068.31; total interest: $6,068.31
The first payment is $187.50 interest and $413.64 principal
Example 2: $85,000 boat, 15% down, 8.25% for 15 years vs 10 years
Loan amount: 85,000 × 0.85 = $72,250.00
15 years (180 months): $700.93 a month, total interest $53,916.75
10 years (120 months): $886.17 a month, total interest $34,089.83
Choosing the shorter term saves $19,826.93 of interest, at the cost of a higher monthly payment
Understanding your results
Monthly payment covers principal and interest only. It does not include insurance, mooring or storage, which can be significant.
Total interest paid is the cost of borrowing over the full term. Long terms cut the payment but raise this figure sharply.
The chart shows the balance falling slowly at first, because early payments are mostly interest, then faster later. Boats lose value, and on a long loan the balance can exceed the boat's resale value for years.
The real cost of owning a boat
The loan is only part of the budget. Typical ongoing costs include:
Insurance, often required by the lender.
Mooring, slip or dry storage, plus winter storage in cold climates.
Maintenance, including engine servicing, antifouling, and winterizing.
Fuel, which for a powerboat can be large; use the fuel cost calculator for an estimate.
Registration, licensing and safety equipment, which vary by state, province or country.
Trailer and towing vehicle for trailerable boats.
Add these to the payment in the budget calculator to see whether the full cost fits.
Paying cash vs financing
Financing keeps savings available for emergencies but costs interest. Paying cash avoids interest but ties up money that could earn a return elsewhere. A simple comparison: if your savings earn less after tax than the loan rate, paying cash (or a bigger down payment) usually costs less overall. Keep an emergency fund either way, because boats bring surprise repair bills.
Country notes
United States: a boat with a galley, sleeping berth and toilet can qualify as a second home, in which case loan interest may be deductible as qualified mortgage interest if you itemize (IRS Publication 936). Sales tax and registration are set by each state.
Canada: pleasure craft with engines of 10 hp (7.5 kW) or more must be licensed with Transport Canada, and operators need proof of competency. Sales tax (GST/HST and any PST) applies to the purchase.
United Kingdom: marine finance is usually an unsecured personal loan or a secured marine mortgage. Boats on many inland waterways need a licence (for example from the Canal & River Trust), and VAT status matters when buying a used boat.
Tips and common mistakes
Compare the APR, not just the rate, if there are lender fees.
Don't stretch the term to afford a bigger boat. You pay more interest on a depreciating asset.
Check prepayment terms. Some marine loans charge for early payoff.
Get a marine survey on used boats before committing to a loan; many lenders require one for larger vessels.
Budget for running costs, not just the payment.
Frequently asked questions
How long can a boat loan last?
It depends on the lender, the amount and the boat's age. Small loans may run a few years; loans on large new boats can run 15 to 20 years.
Is a boat loan secured?
Often, yes: the boat is the collateral. Secured loans usually carry lower rates than unsecured personal loans.
Can I enter the term in months only?
Yes. Leave years at 0 and enter the months, or combine both fields.
Does the payment include insurance or taxes?
No. The result covers principal and interest only.
Will paying extra each month help?
Yes, if the lender applies it to principal. It shortens the loan and cuts total interest. Use the amortization calculator to model extra payments.
Is boat loan interest tax-deductible?
In the US it can be, if the boat qualifies as a second home and you itemize; see IRS Publication 936. In Canada and the UK, interest on a personal boat loan is generally not deductible.

Title tag
Bond Price & Yield Calculator | FigSumo (39 chars)
Meta description
Price a bond from face value, coupon rate, yield and years to maturity, or solve for yield to maturity. Shows coupon cash flows and current yield. (146 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,072 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Bond Calculator
This calculator prices a fixed-rate bond: it tells you what a bond is worth today given its face value, coupon rate, years to maturity and the yield the market demands. It also shows the yearly coupon in dollars and the current yield. Use it to check a quote from a broker, to see why bond prices fall when rates rise, or to compare a bond with a CD or savings account.
How to use this calculator
1. Face value: the amount repaid at maturity, also called par or principal. Most bonds have a face value of $1,000 (or £100 for UK gilts).
2. Annual coupon rate: the interest the bond pays each year as a percentage of face value, as stated in the bond's terms.
3. Years to maturity: whole years until the bond repays its face value.
4. Yield to maturity: the annual return the market requires on a bond like this one. Take it from a broker's quote screen or a published yield for similar bonds.
Results: estimated bond price, annual coupon payment and current yield.
The formula
A bond's price is the present value of every payment it will make, discounted at the yield to maturity:
Price = Σ (C ÷ (1 + y)^t) for t = 1 … N  +  F ÷ (1 + y)^N
C = F × coupon rate
Current yield = C ÷ Price
F: face value
C: annual coupon payment
y: yield to maturity as a decimal
N: years to maturity
t: year number of each coupon
The calculator assumes one coupon per year, paid at the end of each year, and prices the bond on a coupon date, so there is no accrued interest. Years are treated as whole numbers.
Worked examples
Example 1: 4% coupon, 10 years, market yield 5%
C = 4% × 1,000 = $40.00 a year
Present value of the ten coupons: $308.87
Present value of the $1,000 repayment: 1,000 ÷ 1.05^10 = $613.91
Price = $922.78
Current yield = 40 ÷ $922.78 = 4.33%
The bond sells below par (at a discount) because its 4% coupon is less than the 5% the market wants. The buyer makes up the difference by receiving $1,000 at maturity for less than $1,000 today.
Example 2: 6% coupon, 5 years, how price moves with yield
At a 4.5% yield: $1,065.85 (a premium, because the coupon beats the market rate); current yield 5.63%
At 3.5%: $1,112.88
At 5.5%: $1,021.35
As yields go up, the price goes down, and vice versa.
Understanding your results
Price above face value (premium): coupon rate > yield.
Price below face value (discount): coupon rate < yield.
Price equal to face value (par): coupon rate = yield.
Current yield is only the coupon income relative to price. It ignores the gain or loss as the price moves back to par at maturity, so yield to maturity is the fuller measure.
Interest-rate risk
The longer the maturity, the more the price moves when yields change. A 4% bond moving from a 5% to a 6% yield drops from $922.78 to $852.80 (-7.6%) with 10 years left, but from $846.28 to $724.70 (-14.4%) with 30 years left. This sensitivity is measured by duration.
Semi-annual coupons
Most US Treasury notes and bonds, many corporate bonds and UK gilts pay coupons twice a year. To price those, halve the coupon and the yield and double the number of periods. The Example 1 bond priced with semi-annual payments is $922.05, slightly different from the annual-coupon figure. The calculator currently uses annual coupons, so treat its result as an approximation for semi-annual bonds.
Clean and dirty price
Between coupon dates, the seller is owed interest that has built up since the last coupon (accrued interest). The clean price is the quoted price without it; the dirty price is what you actually pay, including it. This calculator prices on a coupon date, so clean and dirty are the same.
Country notes
United States: Treasury securities are bought through TreasuryDirect or a broker. Interest on Treasuries is exempt from state and local income tax but taxable federally; municipal bond interest is often exempt from federal tax.
Canada: Government of Canada bonds pay semi-annual coupons. Interest is fully taxable as income outside registered accounts such as an RRSP or TFSA.
United Kingdom: gilts are quoted per £100 nominal and pay semi-annually. Gains on gilts are exempt from Capital Gains Tax, though coupons are taxable income outside an ISA or pension.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing up coupon and yield. The coupon is fixed by the bond; the yield is set by the market.
Using a percentage of par as the face value. Enter dollars (1,000), not 100, unless you want the price per 100 of face.
Forgetting credit risk. A high yield often means a higher chance of default. Ratings and spreads matter.
Ignoring call features. Callable bonds may be repaid early, so yield to call can matter more than yield to maturity.
Frequently asked questions
Why does a bond's price fall when interest rates rise?
Its coupon is fixed. When new bonds pay more, investors will only buy the old bond at a lower price that gives them the market yield.
What is the difference between coupon rate and yield to maturity?
The coupon rate sets the cash interest as a percentage of face value. Yield to maturity is the total annual return if you buy at today's price and hold to maturity, including the move back to par.
What is current yield?
Annual coupon ÷ current price. It is a quick income measure that ignores the gain or loss at maturity.
Does the calculator handle zero-coupon bonds?
Yes. Set the coupon rate to 0 and the price is the face value discounted at the yield.
Can I find the yield if I know the price?
Not directly yet. Try different yields until the price matches; the yield that gives your price is the YTM.
Is the price the same as the amount I'd pay?
Close, but brokers add commissions or spreads, and between coupon dates you also pay accrued interest.

Break-Even Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/break-even-calculator
Title tag
Break-Even Point Calculator | FigSumo (37 chars)
Meta description

H1: Break-Even Calculator
The break-even point is the sales level at which revenue exactly covers costs, so you make neither a profit nor a loss. Knowing it tells you how many units you must sell before a product, shop or project starts to make money, and how sensitive that is to price and costs. This calculator works out break-even units and revenue, the sales needed for a target profit, and your margin of safety.
How to use this calculator
1. Fixed costs: costs that don't change with sales volume over the period, such as rent, salaries, insurance, software and loan payments. Use one period consistently (a month or a year).
2. Price per unit: what you charge, excluding sales tax or VAT.
3. Variable cost per unit: costs that rise with each sale, such as materials, packaging, shipping, card fees and sales commission.
4. Target profit (optional): the profit you want for the period.
5. Expected sales (optional): to calculate the margin of safety.
Results: contribution margin per unit, contribution margin ratio, break-even units, break-even revenue, units for target profit and margin of safety.
The formulas
Contribution margin (CM) = Price − Variable cost per unit
CM ratio = CM ÷ Price
Break-even units = Fixed costs ÷ CM
Break-even revenue = Fixed costs ÷ CM ratio
Units for target profit = (Fixed costs + Target profit) ÷ CM
Margin of safety = (Expected sales − Break-even sales) ÷ Expected sales
Round break-even units up to the next whole unit: selling a fraction of a unit isn't possible.
Worked examples
Example 1: a small product business
Fixed costs $12,000 a month; price $50; variable cost $20.
CM = $30 a unit; CM ratio 60%
Break-even = 12,000 ÷ 30 = 400 units a month
Break-even revenue = $20,000.00
To make $6,000 profit: (12,000 + 6,000) ÷ 30 = 600 units
If you expect to sell 600 units, the margin of safety is 200 units, or 33.33%: sales could fall that much before you make a loss.
Example 2: what if price or costs change?
Cut the price to $45: CM falls to $25 and break-even rises to 480.00, so 480 units.
Variable cost rises to $24: CM $26, break-even 461.54, so 462 units.
A small change in contribution margin moves the break-even point a lot. That's why discounting can be expensive.
Example 3: service business using revenue
A consultancy has $12,000 of monthly fixed costs and a 60% contribution margin ratio (40% of each sale goes on direct costs). Break-even revenue = 12,000 ÷ 0.6 = $20,000.00 a month.
Operating leverage
Above break-even, every extra unit adds its full contribution margin to profit. At 600 units, Example 1 makes $6,000.00; at 660 units (10% more), it makes $7,800.00, a 30% jump in profit from a 10% rise in sales. High fixed costs magnify both gains and losses.
Understanding your results
Break-even is a planning tool. It assumes price and variable cost per unit stay constant, which may not hold with volume discounts or price changes.
Multiple products: use a weighted-average contribution margin based on your sales mix.
Cash vs profit: break-even here is accounting profit. Cash flow also depends on timing of payments, stock purchases and loan principal.
Taxes: the target profit is before income tax. To hit an after-tax target, divide it by (1 − tax rate) first.
Choosing what's fixed and what's variable
Some costs are mixed. A phone plan with a base fee plus usage, or staff paid a salary plus overtime, have fixed and variable parts. Split them as best you can. Over a long enough horizon, most costs become variable, so match the period to the decision you're making.
Tips and common mistakes
Leaving card fees, shipping or commission out of variable costs.
Mixing periods, such as annual fixed costs with monthly unit sales.
Using a price that includes VAT or sales tax.
Forgetting the owner's pay in fixed costs, which makes the business look profitable when it isn't.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate the break-even point?
Divide fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit (price minus variable cost).
What is contribution margin?
The amount each sale contributes toward fixed costs and profit: price minus variable cost.
What is break-even revenue?
The sales value needed to cover all costs: fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio.
What if my variable cost is higher than my price?
You can never break even; each sale increases the loss. Raise the price or cut costs.
What is margin of safety?
How far sales can fall before you reach break-even, as a percentage of expected sales.
How is break-even different from payback period?
Break-even is about sales volume in a period; payback is about how long it takes to recover an upfront investment. See the payback period calculator.

Monthly Budget Calculator | FigSumo (35 chars)

H1: Budget Calculator
This budget calculator shows whether your monthly take-home pay covers your main spending and a savings goal, and how much is left over (or missing) at the end of the month. Enter your income and five spending lines. It totals what you have planned to spend and save, gives the monthly surplus or deficit, and works out your planned savings rate.
How to use this calculator
1. Monthly income: your take-home pay after tax and payroll deductions, plus any regular income such as benefits or a side job. Use your payslip's net pay, or the paycheck calculator if you only know your salary. If you're paid weekly, multiply weekly pay by 52 and divide by 12; don't just multiply by 4.
2. Housing: rent or mortgage payment, plus property tax, home insurance, service charges and utilities if you want them included here.
3. Transportation: car payment, insurance, fuel, parking, transit passes.
4. Food: groceries plus eating out.
5. Other expenses: everything else, such as phone, internet, subscriptions, childcare, debt payments, clothing, health costs, gifts.
6. Savings goal: the amount you want to put aside each month, including retirement contributions you make from take-home pay.
Results: total planned outflows, monthly surplus / deficit and savings rate.
The formula
Total planned outflows = Housing + Transportation + Food + Other + Savings goal
Surplus (or deficit)   = Monthly income − Total planned outflows
Savings rate           = Savings goal ÷ Monthly income × 100
A positive surplus is unallocated money. A negative figure (a deficit) means the plan spends and saves more than you earn. The savings rate counts only the savings goal you entered, not the surplus.
Worked examples
Example 1: income $6,500
Housing $1,800, transportation $500, food $700, other $900, savings $500.
Outflows = 1,800 + 500 + 700 + 900 + 500 = $4,400.00
Surplus = 6,500 − 4,400 = $2,100.00
Savings rate = 500 ÷ 6,500 = 7.7%
The plan leaves a large unallocated surplus. If all of it were saved too, the savings rate would be 40.0%. In practice, a surplus this large usually means some spending is missing from the plan, so check your bank statements before counting on it.
Example 2: income $3,900
Housing $1,450, transportation $380, food $520, other $650, savings $300.
Outflows = $3,300.00; surplus $600.00
Savings rate 7.7%; housing takes 37.2% of income
Housing above about 30% of income is a common warning sign; it leaves less room for everything else.
Understanding your results
Surplus: money with no job yet. Give it one (extra savings, debt payments, a sinking fund for irregular bills) or it tends to get spent.
Deficit: the plan doesn't balance. Cut a line, raise income, or lower the savings goal temporarily. Don't cover a deficit with credit cards; interest makes the gap grow.
Savings rate: the share of take-home pay you plan to save. Higher rates build an emergency fund and retirement savings faster.
A simple framework: 50/30/20
One popular starting point splits take-home pay into 50% needs (housing, basic food, transport, minimum debt payments), 30% wants and 20% savings and extra debt repayment. On $3,900 that is $1,950.00 for needs, $1,170.00 for wants and $780.00 for saving. It is a guide, not a rule: in high-cost cities, housing alone can exceed 50%.
Building a budget that holds up
Start from real spending. Download two or three months of bank and card statements and sort them into the five lines.
Spread irregular costs. Divide annual bills (car insurance, holidays, gifts, subscriptions) by 12 and include them in "Other".
Pay yourself first. Set up an automatic transfer for the savings goal on payday.
Build an emergency fund. A common target is three to six months of essential spending. Use the savings calculator to see how long it will take.
Tackle expensive debt. If "Other" includes card payments, the debt payoff calculator shows how much faster extra payments clear it.
Review monthly. Budgets fail when they stop matching reality.
Country notes
United States: the CFPB publishes free budgeting worksheets. Employer 401(k) contributions are taken before take-home pay, so don't count them twice in the savings line.
Canada: the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada offers a free budget planner. TFSA and RRSP contributions made from your bank account belong in the savings line.
United Kingdom: MoneyHelper has a free budget planner. Council Tax belongs in housing; workplace pension contributions are already deducted from net pay.
Tips and common mistakes
Using gross salary. Budget from take-home pay.
Forgetting small recurring charges. Subscriptions add up quickly.
Leaving no slack. Budget a small "miscellaneous" amount in Other so surprises don't break the plan.
Being too strict. A budget with no room for wants is hard to keep.
Frequently asked questions
Should I use gross or net income?
Net (take-home) income. Taxes and payroll deductions are taken before you can spend the money.
What counts as housing?
Rent or mortgage at minimum. Many people also include property tax, insurance, utilities and service charges so the line shows the full cost of the home.
How much should I save each month?
There is no single answer. Common guides suggest about 20% of take-home pay, but start with what you can sustain and build up.
What if I have a deficit?
Look first at the largest flexible lines (food, transportation, other), then consider whether housing is sustainable. Avoid filling the gap with high-interest borrowing.
Does the savings rate include my surplus?
No. It uses only the savings goal you entered. Move the surplus into the savings line if you plan to save it.
How do I handle irregular income?
Budget on a cautious month's income, and put anything above it into savings or a buffer account.

Business Loan Calculator: Payment, Interest & APR | FigSumo (59 chars)
