H1: Business Loan Calculator
Use this calculator to estimate the payments on a term loan for a business: equipment finance, a bank term loan, an SBA-backed loan in the US or a government-backed loan elsewhere. Enter the amount, interest rate and term. You get the monthly payment, the total you will repay, the total interest and a chart of how the balance falls over time.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: the principal you will borrow. If the lender deducts a fee from the funds, still enter the full amount borrowed (see the APR note below).
2. Interest rate: the annual rate on the term sheet or offer letter. For a variable-rate loan, enter today's rate and re-run at a higher one to test affordability.
3. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): the repayment period. Equipment loans often match the asset's useful life; working-capital loans tend to be shorter.
Results: monthly payment, total of payments, total interest paid, the rate used, and an amortization chart.
The formula
The calculator assumes a fixed-rate loan repaid in equal monthly instalments:
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
P: loan amount
r: annual interest rate ÷ 12
n: years × 12 + months
Interest each month = remaining balance × r. The rest of the payment repays principal. Total interest = PMT × n − P.
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 over 5 years at 7.5%
n = 60, r = 0.075 ÷ 12
PMT = $400.76
Total of payments $24,045.54; total interest $4,045.54
Example 2: $150,000 equipment loan at 9.25% for 10 years, with a 3% fee
n = 120, r = 0.0925 ÷ 12
PMT = $1,920.49 a month; total repaid $230,458.90; interest $80,458.90
If the lender deducts a 3% fee ($4,500.00) from the funds, the effective APR is about 9.97%. The APR calculator does this conversion.
Can the business afford it? Lenders often look at the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR): cash available for debt service ÷ debt payments. If the business generates $2,400 a month of operating cash flow before debt payments, DSCR = 2,400 ÷ $1,920.49 = 1.25. Many lenders want to see comfortably more than 1.0; the required level varies by lender and loan type.
Understanding your results
Monthly payment is principal and interest. It excludes fees, insurance required by the lender, and any personal guarantee costs.
Total interest is the full cost of borrowing over the term if you make every scheduled payment. Prepayment can reduce it, unless the loan has a prepayment penalty.
The chart shows the balance falling slowly at first and faster later, because early payments are mostly interest.
Other types of business finance
Not all business funding is a fixed monthly term loan, and the calculator only models that type.
Line of credit: draw and repay as needed; interest only on what you use. Payments vary.
Merchant cash advance and short-term loans: often priced with a factor rate rather than an interest rate. For example, $50,000 at a factor of 1.25 means repaying $62,500.00. Spread over 12 equal monthly payments of $5,208.33, that equals an APR of roughly 43.3%. Convert factor rates before comparing offers.
Invoice financing: borrowing against unpaid invoices, priced as a percentage of invoice value.
Asset finance and leasing: the equipment is the security; payment profiles can include a balloon.
Country notes
United States: the SBA guarantees loans made by participating lenders, including 7(a) and 504 loans, with maximum rates and fees set by SBA rules [VERIFY current SBA maximum rates and guarantee fees on sba.gov]. Business loan interest is generally deductible as a business expense, subject to the business interest limitation for larger businesses (section 163(j), reported on IRS Form 8990).
Canada: the Canada Small Business Financing Program shares lending risk with banks for loans to buy equipment, property and improvements; BDC is a federal Crown corporation lending to small businesses.
United Kingdom: the British Business Bank runs government-backed schemes delivered through accredited lenders, such as the Growth Guarantee Scheme [VERIFY scheme name and status]. Business loans are not covered by the Consumer Credit Act in most cases, so protections are fewer than for personal loans.
Tips and common mistakes
Match the term to the asset. Don't finance a short-lived asset over a long term.
Ask for the APR or total cost of credit, not just the rate, especially with fees or factor rates.
Check prepayment terms and personal guarantees before you sign.
Stress-test the payment. Re-run with a rate two or three points higher, and with lower revenue.
Keep the cash buffer. Paying a large down payment can leave the business short of working capital.
Frequently asked questions
What interest rate should I expect on a business loan?
It depends on the lender, the business's trading history, credit and collateral, and the type of loan. Get several quotes and compare APRs.
Does the result include fees?
No. Enter fees in the APR calculator to see their effect on the true cost.
Can I model a variable-rate loan?
Only one rate at a time. Run the calculator at the current rate and at higher rates to see a range.
How do I convert a factor rate to an APR?
Multiply the amount by the factor rate to get total repayment, then use the APR calculator with the actual payment schedule. Factor-rate products often have very high APRs because the term is short.
Is business loan interest tax-deductible?
Interest on money used for business purposes is usually deductible against business income in the US, Canada and the UK, subject to each country's rules. Check with an accountant.
What is a balloon payment?
A large final payment that repays the remaining balance. This calculator assumes a fully amortizing loan with no balloon.

Buy-to-Let Mortgage Calculator: Rental Cover & Payments | FigSumo (65 chars)
Meta description
Estimate buy-to-let interest-only payments, rental cover ratio and maximum loan from rent and stressed rate. Lender criteria vary. (130 chars)

H1: Buy-to-Let Mortgage Calculator
Buy-to-let mortgages are assessed mainly on the rent the property will earn rather than your salary. Lenders apply a rental cover test (the interest coverage ratio, or ICR) at a stressed interest rate to decide how much you can borrow. This calculator works out your loan, loan-to-value, monthly payment on interest-only or repayment terms, and the maximum loan the rent supports under the ICR test you enter.
How to use this calculator
1. Property value or purchase price.
2. Deposit: typically at least 25% for buy-to-let.
3. Interest rate and term.
4. Repayment type: interest-only (most common for buy-to-let) or capital repayment.
5. Expected monthly rent: from local letting agents or comparable listings.
6. Lender ICR (%) and stress rate (%): these vary by lender and product. 125% is common for basic-rate taxpayers and limited companies; 145% for higher-rate taxpayers. Stress rates are often around 5% to 5.5%, or the pay rate for five-year fixes [VERIFY with your lender or broker].
Results: loan, LTV, monthly payment, maximum loan by rental cover, a pass/fail check and the gross rental yield.
How it works
Loan = Value − Deposit
Interest-only payment = Loan × Rate ÷ 12
Repayment payment = Loan × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Maximum loan (rental cover) = Annual rent ÷ (ICR × Stress rate)
Gross yield = Annual rent ÷ Value
The lender will lend the lower of the LTV limit and the rental-cover limit.
Worked examples
Example 1: £300,000 property, 25% deposit, £1,500 rent
Loan = £225,000.00 (75% LTV)
Interest-only at 4.8%: £900.00 a month
Capital repayment over 25 years: £1,289.24 a month
Rental cover at 145% and 5.5%: maximum loan = 18,000 ÷ (1.45 × 0.055) = £225,705.33. The loan passes, just.
The test needs rent of at least £1,495.31 a month for this loan.
Gross yield: 6.00%
At a 125% ICR (for example, a limited company or basic-rate taxpayer), the same rent supports up to £261,818.18.
Example 2: how much rent for a £250,000 loan?
At 145% and 5.5%: 250,000 × 1.45 × 0.055 ÷ 12 = £1,661.46 a month.
Example 3: tax on the rental profit (individual landlord)
Rent £18,000 a year, letting and maintenance costs £2,700, mortgage interest £10,800, higher-rate taxpayer:
Taxable rental profit (interest not deductible): £15,300.00
Tax at 40% less a 20% credit on the interest (£2,160.00): £3,960.00
Cash left after tax: £540.00
Through a limited company, mortgage interest is deductible and profit is taxed at Corporation Tax rates (19% on profits up to £50,000: £855.00 here), but extracting the money as dividends adds personal tax. Get advice before choosing a structure.
Example 4: the basic-rate ICR
For a basic-rate taxpayer or a limited company at a 125% ICR and the same 5.5% stress rate, a £250,000 loan needs rent of 250,000 × 1.25 × 0.055 ÷ 12 = £1,432.29 a month, £229.17 less than at 145%.
Example 5: gross and net yield
Example 1's property at £300,000 with £1,500 a month rent has a gross yield of 18,000 ÷ 300,000 = 6.00%. After £10,800 of mortgage interest and £2,400 of other costs, the pre-tax profit is £4,800. On the £75,000 deposit, that's a return of 6.40% before tax, stamp duty and fees, and before any change in the property's value.
Understanding your results
Rental cover is often the binding limit, especially in high-price, low-yield areas.
Interest-only means the loan isn't repaid. You need a plan to clear it at the end of the term, usually by selling.
Fees: buy-to-let products often have arrangement fees of 1% to 3% of the loan; adding them to the loan affects the rental cover test.
Voids and costs: the ICR test ignores your other costs. Use the rental property calculator for cash flow.
Costs and rules for landlords
Stamp Duty: in England and Northern Ireland, additional properties carry a 5% surcharge on top of standard SDLT rates. Scotland adds an 8% Additional Dwelling Supplement and Wales has higher LTT rates; see the LTT calculator.
Section 24: individual landlords can't deduct mortgage interest; they get a basic-rate tax credit instead.
Capital Gains Tax applies when you sell, at 18% or 24% on residential property gains; see the CGT calculator.
Regulation: most buy-to-let mortgages aren't regulated by the FCA, except "consumer buy-to-let" (for example, letting a former home). Landlords must meet safety, deposit protection and licensing rules.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the pay rate instead of the stress rate in the ICR test.
Forgetting the higher ICR for higher-rate taxpayers.
Assuming rent will rise to cover a rate increase at remortgage.
Ignoring the tax change that removed mortgage interest deductions for individuals.
Notes for US and Canadian readers
US: investors often use conventional investment-property mortgages with 15% to 25% down, or "DSCR" loans sized on rental income, a similar idea to the UK rental cover test. Mortgage interest on rentals is deductible against rental income.
Canada: a rental property that you won't live in normally needs at least 20% down, because CMHC insurance is generally limited to owner-occupied homes of up to four units. Lenders often count only part of the expected rent toward qualifying [VERIFY lender policy].
Frequently asked questions
How much deposit do I need for buy-to-let?
Usually at least 25%, although some lenders accept 20% or less at higher rates.
What is the ICR?
The interest coverage ratio: the rent must cover the stressed interest cost by a set percentage, often 125% or 145%.
Can I get an interest-only buy-to-let mortgage?
Yes, most buy-to-let mortgages are interest-only.
Is my salary relevant?
Some lenders require a minimum personal income, often around £25,000, and may use it to top up a rental shortfall.
Should I buy through a limited company?
It can suit higher-rate taxpayers with several properties, but costs, rates and extraction taxes differ. Take advice.
What yield is good for buy-to-let?
Gross yields vary widely by region; compare net yield after costs, not just gross.

Canada Capital Gains Tax Calculator 2026 | FigSumo (50 chars)
Meta description
Estimate tax on a capital gain in Canada from the gain, the inclusion rate for the year and your combined federal and provincial marginal rate. (143 chars)

H1: Canada Capital Gains Tax Calculator
In Canada, only half of a capital gain is taxable. When you sell shares, a cottage, a rental property or other capital property for more than its adjusted cost base, you add 50% of the gain (the taxable capital gain) to your income and pay tax at your normal federal and provincial rates. This calculator estimates the gain, the taxable portion and the extra tax it adds to your 2026 return.
How to use this calculator
1. Province or territory of residence on 31 December.
2. Other taxable income: employment, pension, interest and other income for the year.
3. Proceeds of disposition: the sale price (or fair market value for gifts and deemed dispositions).
4. Adjusted cost base (ACB): what you paid, plus costs to acquire and capital improvements.
5. Outlays and expenses: commissions, legal fees and other selling costs.
6. Capital losses: current-year losses and net capital losses carried forward.
Results: capital gain, taxable capital gain, incremental federal and provincial tax, and the effective tax rate on the gain.
How it works
Capital gain = Proceeds − ACB − Outlays and expenses
Taxable capital gain = Capital gain × 50%
Tax on gain = Tax(Other income + Taxable gain) − Tax(Other income)
The inclusion rate stays at one-half: the proposal to raise it to two-thirds was cancelled on 21 March 2025. Because the taxable gain is added to your income, the tax depends on your marginal rate, which varies by province and income (including surtaxes and health premiums in Ontario).
Capital losses: half of a capital loss is an allowable capital loss. It can only offset taxable capital gains, not other income. Unused net capital losses can be carried back three years or forward indefinitely.
Worked examples
Example 1: selling shares in Alberta
Other income $75,000. You sell shares for $30,000 with an ACB of $9,500 and $500 of commissions.
Capital gain = $20,000.00; taxable capital gain = $10,000.00
Your income rises from $75,000 to $85,000. In 2026, that range is taxed at 20.5% federally and 10% in Alberta, a 30.5% combined marginal rate.
Tax on the gain = $3,050.00, an effective rate of 15.25% on the whole gain.
Example 2: working out the ACB
You bought 50 shares at $20 ($20 commission) and later 60 shares at $25 ($10 commission). Your ACB per share is the total cost ÷ total shares = $23.00. Canada uses this average cost method for identical properties, so each sale uses the average, not the price of a specific lot.
Example 3: a cottage held for 10 years
You owned a cottage and a city home for 10 years and designate the cottage as your principal residence for 6 of those years. The exempt share of a $300,000 gain is (6 + 1) ÷ 10, or $210,000.00. The remaining $90,000.00 is a capital gain, so $45,000.00 is taxable. A family can designate only one principal residence per year.
Losses
A $4,000 capital loss gives an allowable capital loss of $2,000.00, which reduces taxable capital gains this year, in the previous three years, or in future years.
Exemptions and sheltered accounts
Principal residence exemption: gains on your home are generally exempt for years you designate it as your principal residence. You must report the sale on Schedule 3 even if it's fully exempt.
TFSA, RRSP, RRIF and FHSA: gains inside these accounts aren't capital gains for tax purposes. See the TFSA calculator.
Lifetime capital gains exemption: qualified small business corporation shares and qualified farm or fishing property can be eligible for an exemption of up to $1.25 million of gains [VERIFY current limit]. Large exempt gains can trigger alternative minimum tax.
Gifts of listed securities to charity: the taxable gain is generally nil.
Deemed dispositions
You can owe tax without selling: when you give property to someone other than your spouse, change a property's use (for example, a home becomes a rental), emigrate, or at death (with a rollover to a surviving spouse).
Understanding your results
Incremental tax is the difference between your tax with and without the gain, which captures bracket changes.
Instalments: a large gain may mean you need to pay tax by instalments next year.
Reporting: report dispositions on Schedule 3 of your T1 return; brokers issue T5008 slips but they don't always show the correct ACB.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the T5008 cost without checking it against your records.
Superficial loss rule: a loss is denied if you or an affiliated person buy the same property within 30 days before or after the sale and still hold it 30 days later.
Forgetting reinvested distributions that increase ACB, which makes you pay tax twice.
Assuming the principal residence exemption is automatic. You must report the sale and designate.
Frequently asked questions
What is the capital gains inclusion rate in Canada?
50%. The proposed increase to two-thirds was cancelled.
How much tax will I pay on a capital gain?
Half the gain is added to income and taxed at your marginal rate, so the effective rate is roughly half your marginal rate.
Is the sale of my home taxable?
Usually not, if it was your principal residence for every year you owned it. You still report it.
Can capital losses reduce my salary income?
No, except in the year of death and the year before. They offset taxable capital gains.
What is the adjusted cost base?
Your cost, including acquisition costs and improvements, averaged across identical properties.
Are capital gains in a TFSA taxable?
No.

Canada Take-Home Pay Calculator 2026: CPP, EI & Tax | FigSumo (61 chars)
Meta description
Estimate 2026 take-home pay in Canada after federal and provincial income tax, CPP, CPP2 and EI, by province and pay frequency. (127 chars)

new · tax year 2026 calendar year (CRA payroll values effective 1 Jan 2026)

1,052 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Canada Take-Home Pay Calculator (2026)
In Canada, your employer takes four things off each paycheque: federal income tax, provincial or territorial income tax, Canada Pension Plan (CPP) contributions and Employment Insurance (EI) premiums. Above a certain level of earnings there is also a second CPP contribution, CPP2. This calculator applies the 2026 CRA figures for your province and shows your net pay for the year and for each pay period.
How to use this calculator
1. Province or territory of employment. Quebec is not supported yet, because it uses QPP, QPIP and its own provincial tax.
2. Gross annual salary, or an hourly rate with hours.
3. Pay frequency: weekly, bi-weekly, semi-monthly or monthly.
4. Deductions (optional): RRSP contributions made through payroll and union dues. Both reduce taxable income.
5. Results show each deduction for the year and per pay, with your net pay.
The formula
CPP (employee), 2026:
CPP  = 5.95% × (min(earnings, $74,600) − $3,500)      → maximum $4,230.45
CPP2 = 4%    × (min(earnings, $85,000) − $74,600)     → maximum $416.00
The 5.95% is made up of 4.95% "base" and 1% "first additional". The base part earns a non-refundable credit. The enhanced 1% and all of CPP2 are deducted from income instead.
EI (outside Quebec), 2026:
EI = 1.63% × min(insurable earnings, $68,900)          → maximum $1,123.07
Income tax:
Taxable income = salary − enhanced CPP − CPP2 − RRSP − union dues
Federal tax    = federal brackets(taxable) − 14% × (BPA $16,452 + CPP base + EI + Canada employment amount $1,501)
Provincial tax = provincial brackets(taxable) − lowest provincial rate × (provincial BPA + CPP base + EI)
                 + any provincial surtax or premium (e.g., Ontario surtax and Ontario Health Premium)
Net pay        = salary − CPP − CPP2 − EI − federal tax − provincial tax − other deductions
2026 federal brackets: 14% to $58,523 · 20.5% to $117,045 · 26% to $181,440 · 29% to $258,482 · 33% above. The federal basic personal amount is $16,452, reduced gradually to $14,829 for net income between $181,440 and $258,482.
Ontario 2026: 5.05% to $53,891 · 9.15% to $107,785 · 11.16% to $150,000 · 12.16% to $220,000 · 13.16% above. Basic personal amount $12,989. Surtax: 20% of basic Ontario tax over $5,818, plus 36% over $7,446. The Ontario Health Premium is up to $900 a year.
Worked examples
Example 1: Ontario, $75,000 salary, no other deductions.
CPP: 5.95% × (74,600 − 3,500) = $4,230.45. Base part $3,519.45; enhanced part $711.00.
CPP2: 4% × (75,000 − 74,600) = $16.00
EI: 1.63% × 68,900 = $1,123.07
Taxable income: 75,000 − 711 − 16 = $74,273
Federal: brackets give $11,421.97. Credits: 14% × (16,452 + 3,519.45 + 1,123.07 + 1,501) = $3,163.37. Federal tax $8,258.60
Ontario: brackets give $4,586.45. Credits: 5.05% × (12,989 + 3,519.45 + 1,123.07) = $890.39. Basic Ontario tax $3,696.06, which is under $5,818, so there is no surtax. Health Premium $750. Ontario total $4,446.06
Net pay: $56,925.82 a year, or $4,743.82 a month, or about $2,189.45 bi-weekly
Total deductions are $18,074.18, which is 24.1% of gross pay.
Example 2: Ontario, $120,000 salary.
CPP $4,230.45 · CPP2 at the maximum, $416 · EI $1,123.07
Taxable income $118,873; federal tax $17,502.14
Basic Ontario tax $7,999.83 → surtax $635.74 → plus OHP $750 → Ontario total $9,385.57
Net pay: $87,342.77 a year, or $7,278.56 a month
At this income, the Ontario surtax adds about 8% to basic Ontario tax.
Understanding your results
CPP and EI stop for the year once you reach the maximums. This often happens in the autumn for higher earners, and your later paycheques rise.
Per-pay figures are annual amounts divided evenly. Payroll software uses CRA's formulas each period, so individual paycheques can differ slightly.
Your tax return reconciles everything. Credits such as tuition, medical expenses or donations can change the final result.
Marginal rate: in Example 1, the next dollar is taxed at 20.5% federal + 9.15% Ontario = 29.65% (before CPP and EI).
Country notes
Provinces: every province and territory has its own brackets and basic personal amount. The calculator uses the CRA's 2026 table for each one. Surtaxes and premiums currently apply in Ontario. Other provincial credits and reductions are flagged where they apply.
Quebec: not supported yet. Quebec residents contribute to QPP instead of CPP, pay QPIP premiums, pay a lower EI rate and file a separate provincial return with Revenu Québec.
United States / UK: see the US paycheck calculator and the UK take-home pay calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting provincial tax. It varies a lot by province.
Ignoring CPP and EI maximums. Deductions stop once you reach them, so later paycheques rise.
Comparing salaries across provinces without tax. The same gross pay gives different net pay.
Leaving out benefits deductions such as group insurance or pension contributions.
Frequently asked questions
What is CPP2?
It is a second CPP contribution, at 4% on earnings between the year's maximum pensionable earnings ($74,600) and the year's additional maximum ($85,000) in 2026. It funds a higher CPP pension later. The maximum employee contribution in 2026 is $416.
Why is part of CPP a deduction and part a credit?
Base contributions (4.95%) earn a non-refundable tax credit. Enhanced contributions (the extra 1% and CPP2) are deducted from income, which gives more tax relief to higher earners.
Does an RRSP contribution increase my take-home pay?
If it is deducted through payroll, your employer can reduce the tax withheld right away. Personal contributions are deducted on your tax return and usually produce a refund instead. The RRSP calculator estimates that refund.
What is the Ontario Health Premium?
It's an amount added to Ontario income tax, based on taxable income. It is $0 up to $20,000 and rises in steps to a maximum of $900 above $200,600.
Why is my EI deduction different?
If you work in Quebec, the EI rate is lower because QPIP covers parental benefits. Some employment is not insurable. Your employer's payroll determines this.
Does this include the Canada Workers Benefit or GST/HST credit?
No. Those are paid through the tax return or by separate payments. They are not part of payroll deductions.

H1: Canadian Income Tax Calculator (2026)
Every Canadian taxpayer outside Quebec pays two income taxes, calculated on the same T1 return: federal tax and provincial or territorial tax. Each has its own brackets and its own non-refundable credits. This calculator works out both for 2026 using CRA-published rates. It shows the tax at each step, your average rate and the marginal rate that applies to your next dollar.
How to use this calculator
1. Province or territory where you lived on 31 December 2026.
2. Employment income and other income (interest, rental, self-employment net income).
3. Deductions: RRSP contributions, union dues and similar.
4. CPP and EI: calculated automatically from employment income. If you are self-employed, you pay both the employee and employer shares of CPP, and the calculator uses those rules.
5. Results show federal tax, provincial tax, the total, the average rate and the marginal rate.
The formula
Taxable income   = total income − deductions (RRSP, enhanced CPP, CPP2, union dues…)
Federal tax      = federal brackets(taxable income) − 14% × federal credit amounts
Provincial tax   = provincial brackets(taxable income) − lowest provincial rate × provincial credit amounts
                   (+ surtax / health premium where applicable)
Average rate     = (federal + provincial tax) ÷ total income
2026 federal brackets and credits. CRA rates: 14% on the first $58,523 · 20.5% to $117,045 · 26% to $181,440 · 29% to $258,482 · 33% above.
Federal credit amounts:
Basic personal amount: $16,452, reducing to $14,829 between $181,440 and $258,482 of net income
Canada employment amount: up to $1,501
CPP base contributions and EI premiums
All credits are claimed at the lowest rate, 14%.

Provincial basic personal amounts, surtaxes and low-income reductions differ by province. The calculator applies each one from the CRA's 2026 payroll tables (T4032).
Worked examples

Ontario: basic tax $7,999.83, surtax $635.74, Health Premium $750 → $9,385.57
Total income tax ≈ $26,887.71, an average rate of about 22.4%
Marginal rate on the next dollar: 26% federal + 11.16% Ontario, plus the 20% + 36% surtax on the Ontario portion ≈ 43.4%
Example 2: Ontario, $75,000 employment income.
Taxable income $74,273 (after $711 enhanced CPP and $16 CPP2)
Federal tax $8,258.60 · Ontario tax $4,446.06, including the $750 Health Premium and no surtax
Total income tax $12,704.65, an average rate of 16.9%
Marginal rate: 20.5% + 9.15% = 29.65%
Understanding your results
Average rate: your total tax as a share of income. This is what you pay overall.
Marginal rate: what you'd pay on an extra dollar. Use it to value an RRSP contribution: at a 29.65% marginal rate, a $1,000 RRSP deduction saves about $296.50.
Refund or balance owing depends on what was withheld at source. Compare the total with box 22 of your T4.
Not included: most non-refundable credits beyond the basic ones (tuition, medical, donations, disability), dividend tax credits, capital gains, OAS clawback, and refundable benefits.
Country notes
Quebec: residents file a separate provincial return with Revenu Québec and receive a federal abatement. Not supported yet.
Capital gains: half of a capital gain is included in income. A proposed increase to two-thirds was cancelled in March 2025. A dedicated capital gains calculator is planned.
For the US or UK, see the US income tax calculator and the UK income tax calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Applying your top rate to all income. Canadian brackets are marginal, federally and provincially.
Forgetting non-refundable credits. The basic personal amount and CPP/EI credits reduce tax.
Overlooking RRSP deductions. Contributions lower taxable income.
Using the wrong province. Your province of residence on 31 December applies for the whole year.
Frequently asked questions
Which province's rates apply to me?
Generally, the province or territory where you lived on 31 December of the tax year, even if you moved during the year.
What is the federal basic personal amount for 2026?
$16,452. It is reduced gradually for net income above $181,440, to a minimum of $14,829 at $258,482 and above.
Why are credits calculated at 14%?
Federal non-refundable credits are worth the lowest federal rate multiplied by the credit amount. For 2026 that rate is 14%.
What's the difference between my marginal and average rate?
The average rate is total tax ÷ income. The marginal rate applies to your next dollar, and it is higher because of progressive brackets and Ontario's surtax.
Does this include CPP and EI?
CPP and EI are calculated because they generate credits and deductions. They are payroll contributions, not income tax, so they are shown separately. Your total payroll deductions are on the take-home pay calculator.
How does an RRSP contribution change my tax?
It is deducted from income, so it saves tax at your marginal rate, up to your deduction limit. The 2026 RRSP dollar limit is $33,810, but your own limit is on your notice of assessment.

Canada Mortgage Affordability Calculator (Stress Test) | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Estimate how much home you can afford in Canada using GDS/TDS ratios and the minimum qualifying rate stress test. (113 chars)
Country
CA
Status
new · tax year 2026
Body words
1,012 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Canadian Mortgage Affordability Calculator
How much mortgage can you qualify for in Canada? Lenders check two ratios, gross debt service (GDS) and total debt service (TDS), and they test them at a stress-test rate above your actual mortgage rate. This calculator applies those rules to your income and costs and shows the maximum monthly payment, the maximum mortgage and an estimated maximum purchase price for your down payment.
How to use this calculator
1. Gross annual household income: before tax, for everyone on the mortgage.
2. Monthly debt payments: car loans, student loans, lines of credit, and credit card minimums (lenders often use 3% of card balances).
3. Property tax (annual) and heating (monthly): estimates for the home you're looking at.
4. Condo fees (monthly): if applicable.
5. Down payment: cash you'll put down.
6. Mortgage rate: the contract rate you've been offered.
7. Amortization: 25 years, or 30 where eligible.
Results: qualifying rate, maximum monthly mortgage payment (the lower of the GDS and TDS limits), maximum mortgage, estimated maximum price, and the payment at your contract rate.
How it works
Ratios (CMHC guideline limits [VERIFY]):
GDS = (Mortgage payment + Property tax + Heating + 50% of condo fees) ÷ Gross monthly income ≤ 39%
TDS = (GDS costs + All other debt payments) ÷ Gross monthly income ≤ 44%
Stress test: you must qualify at the minimum qualifying rate, the higher of your contract rate plus 2 percentage points or 5.25%. This applies to insured and uninsured mortgages at federally regulated lenders.
Maximum mortgage: the present value of the maximum payment at the qualifying rate over the amortization. Canadian fixed-rate mortgages compound semi-annually by law, so the monthly rate is (1 + rate ÷ 2)^(1/6) − 1.
Worked example
Household income $120,000 ($10,000 a month); property tax $4,800 a year ($400 a month); heating $100 a month; car payment $500 a month; contract rate 4.5% over 25 years.
1. Qualifying rate = max(4.5% + 2%, 5.25%) = 6.5%
2. GDS limit: 39% × 10,000 = $3,900.00 − 400 − 100 = $3,400.00 for the mortgage
3. TDS limit: 44% × 10,000 = $4,400.00 − 400 − 100 − 500 = $3,400.00
4. Maximum payment = $3,400.00 (both limits are equal here)
5. Maximum mortgage at 6.5% over 25 years = $507,596.19
6. Your actual payment at 4.5% would be $2,809.41
Maximum price:
With 20% down, the price could be up to $634,495.23 (down payment $126,899.05).
With $60,000 down, the insured mortgage including a 3.10% CMHC premium can't exceed $507,596.19, so the base loan is $492,333.84 (premium $15,262.35) and the maximum price is about $552,333.84 (LTV 89.1%). The minimum down payment at that price is $30,233.38, so $60,000 is enough.
Effect of more debt: with $1,100 a month of other debts instead of $500, the TDS limit drops to $2,800.00 and the maximum mortgage to $418,020.39. Paying off a car loan before applying can raise what you qualify for.
A 30-year amortization at the same payment would allow $542,782.06, where eligible.
Understanding your results
This is a maximum, not a recommendation. Lenders may approve less based on credit score, employment history and their own policies.
The stress test is the binding constraint for most buyers. It reduces borrowing power by about a fifth compared with qualifying at the contract rate.
Cash to close: budget for land transfer tax, legal fees, inspection and adjustments (often 1.5% to 4% of the price). See the land transfer tax calculator.
Down payment under 20% means CMHC or private mortgage insurance, a price cap of $1.5 million and a minimum down payment of 5% on the first $500,000 and 10% on the rest. See the CMHC insurance calculator.
Ways to increase what you can afford
Pay down or close high-payment debts before applying.
Save a larger down payment, using the FHSA and RRSP Home Buyers' Plan (FHSA calculator).
Add a co-borrower with income.
Choose a home with lower property tax or condo fees.
Tips and common mistakes
Using net income. Lenders use gross income.
Forgetting heating costs and condo fees in GDS.
Qualifying at your contract rate. The stress test applies.
Spending to the limit. Leave room for maintenance, rate changes at renewal and savings.
Before you apply
Pull your credit report from Equifax and TransUnion and correct any errors, because your score affects both approval and rate. Keep your employment stable through closing, and avoid new car loans or credit cards that would raise your debt ratios. If you're self-employed, lenders usually want two years of Notices of Assessment. A pre-approval can hold a rate for 90 to 120 days, which protects you if rates rise while you house-hunt. [VERIFY]
Frequently asked questions
What is the mortgage stress test?
A rule requiring you to qualify at the higher of your contract rate plus 2 points or 5.25%.
What GDS and TDS ratios do lenders use?
CMHC's limits are 39% GDS and 44% TDS [VERIFY]; some lenders use different limits for uninsured mortgages.
How much house can I afford on $100,000 a year?
It depends on debts, property tax, rate and down payment. Enter your figures; with no other debts, low property tax and a 4.5% contract rate, a maximum mortgage in the mid-$400,000s is typical.
Does the stress test apply at renewal?
Not if you renew with your current lender. Switching lenders at renewal for an uninsured mortgage generally no longer requires re-qualifying under the stress test [VERIFY].
Why does Canada use semi-annual compounding?
The Interest Act requires fixed-rate mortgage rates to be stated as calculated yearly or half-yearly, not in advance, and lenders quote semi-annual compounding.
Do lenders count child support or rental income?
Often, with documentation; policies vary.

Canadian Mortgage Calculator

https://figsumo.com/ca/mortgage-calculator
Title tag
Canadian Mortgage Calculator with CMHC Insurance | FigSumo (58 chars)
Meta description
Calculate Canadian mortgage payments with semi-annual compounding, CMHC insurance, minimum down payment rules and monthly, bi-weekly or accelerated payments. (157 chars)
Country
CA
Status
rename (301)
Body words
1,218 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Canadian Mortgage Calculator
Canadian mortgages follow rules that most US-built calculators ignore. Fixed rates are compounded semi-annually rather than monthly. Down payments under 20% require mortgage default insurance, and the premium is usually added to the loan. Lenders offer accelerated payment schedules that shorten the amortization. This calculator applies all three, so the payment you see is close to what a Canadian lender would quote.
How to use this calculator
1. Purchase price and down payment. The calculator checks your down payment against the federal minimum and warns you if it is too low.
2. Mortgage default insurance. If the down payment is under 20%, it looks up the CMHC premium rate for your loan-to-value and adds the premium to the mortgage. You can switch this off to see the uninsured figure.
3. Interest rate, term and amortization. The term is how long the rate is locked, often 5 years. The amortization is the total payoff period, for example 25 or 30 years. The payment is based on amortization.
4. Payment frequency. Choose monthly, semi-monthly, bi-weekly, weekly, accelerated bi-weekly or accelerated weekly.
5. Property tax and condo fees (optional) give a full monthly housing cost.
The formula
Step 1: convert the quoted rate to a periodic rate. Canada's Interest Act requires a blended-payment mortgage to state the rate "calculated yearly or half-yearly, not in advance." For fixed-rate mortgages that is normally half-yearly (semi-annual) compounding. The rate per payment period is:
r = (1 + i/2)^(2/k) − 1
i: quoted annual rate (5% → 0.05)
k: payments per year (12 monthly, 24 semi-monthly, 26 bi-weekly, 52 weekly)
Step 2: the standard payment formula.
PMT = L × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−N)
L: mortgage amount including any insurance premium
N: amortization years × k
Accelerated bi-weekly is the monthly payment ÷ 2, paid every two weeks. Twenty-six half-payments make 13 monthly payments a year instead of 12, so the loan is paid off sooner.
Minimum down payment (FCAC):
Up to $500,000: 5%
$500,000 to under $1.5 million: 5% of the first $500,000 plus 10% of the rest
$1.5 million or more: 20%
CMHC premium, as a % of the loan, by loan-to-value (LTV):
LTV
Premium
up to 65%
0.60%
65.01–75%
1.70%
75.01–80%
2.40%
80.01–85%
2.80%
85.01–90%
3.10%
90.01–95%
4.00%
90.01–95%, non-traditional down payment
4.50%
Worked examples
Example 1: $500,000 home, 10% down, 5%, 25 years, monthly.
Down payment $50,000. The minimum for $500,000 is 5% = $25,000, so this qualifies.
Base loan $450,000; LTV 90%, so the premium rate is 3.10%: $450,000 × 0.031 = $13,950
Insured mortgage L = $463,950
r = (1.025)^(1/6) − 1 = 0.0041239
N = 300
Monthly payment: $2,698.36
Total interest over 25 years: $345,556.90
First payment: $1,913.29 interest, $785.07 principal
If the same 5% were compounded monthly, as a US calculator would assume, the payment would be $2,712.21. That is $13.85 a month too high. The semi-annual rule is why US mortgage calculators give slightly wrong answers for Canadian mortgages.
Example 2: frequency and amortization.
30-year amortization on the same mortgage: monthly payment $2,476.06. This is lower, but you pay interest for five extra years. Note that 30-year amortization on an insured mortgage is only available to eligible buyers; check your lender's current rules.
Accelerated bi-weekly on the 25-year mortgage: $2,698.36 ÷ 2 = $1,349.18 every two weeks. The mortgage is paid off in about 559 payments (about 21.5 years), with total interest of about $289,478, roughly $56,000 less than monthly payments.
Minimum down payment check: on a $700,000 home the minimum is 5% × $500,000 + 10% × $200,000 = $45,000.
Understanding your results
Payment per period is principal and interest only, unless you added property tax or condo fees.
Insurance premium is shown separately so you can see how much of the mortgage is insurance. Some provinces charge provincial sales tax on the premium. That tax is paid at closing and can't be added to the mortgage. The calculator flags it for Ontario, Quebec and Saskatchewan (VERIFY current list with each province before launch).
Effective annual rate: 5% compounded semi-annually equals 5.0625% a year.
Renewal: the payment shown assumes the same rate for the whole amortization. In practice your rate resets at each renewal, usually every 1–5 years.
Country notes
Stress test: federally regulated lenders must check you can afford an uninsured mortgage at the greater of 5.25% or your contract rate plus 2 points. This calculator shows the payment at your rate; your lender may approve a smaller loan.
Variable-rate mortgages may compound monthly. Check your mortgage contract.
Land transfer tax is a separate closing cost. Use the land transfer tax calculator.
For US loans, use the US mortgage calculator; for UK loans, the UK mortgage calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing up term and amortization. A 5-year term on a 25-year amortization means you'll renew, possibly at a different rate.
Entering an annual rate without semi-annual compounding. Canadian fixed-rate mortgages compound semi-annually by law; the calculator handles this.
Ignoring the stress test. You must qualify at a higher rate than you'll pay.
Forgetting prepayment privileges. Most closed mortgages allow lump sums of 10% to 20% a year without penalty; check yours.
Budgeting without land transfer tax and CMHC. Both can add thousands at closing.
Frequently asked questions
Why is a Canadian mortgage payment different from a US one at the same rate?
Canadian fixed-rate mortgages compound twice a year, so the monthly rate is a little lower than the quoted rate ÷ 12. On a $463,950 mortgage at 5% over 25 years, the difference is about $14 a month.
Do I need mortgage insurance?
If your down payment is under 20% of the purchase price, your mortgage must be insured against default. The premium depends on your loan-to-value and is usually added to the mortgage balance.
What is the minimum down payment in Canada?
5% on the first $500,000, and 10% on any portion from $500,000 up to $1.5 million. Homes priced at $1.5 million or more need 20%.
What's the difference between term and amortization?
The term is the length of your current contract and rate, for example 5 years. The amortization is the total time to pay off the mortgage, for example 25 years. You will usually renew several times within one amortization.
Is accelerated bi-weekly worth it?
It adds the equivalent of one extra monthly payment each year. That shortens a 25-year amortization by about three and a half years and cuts total interest, but it costs more each year. Plain bi-weekly payments, without acceleration, barely change the payoff date.
Is the CMHC premium included in the payment?
Yes, when insurance applies. The calculator adds the premium to the mortgage and calculates the payment on the larger amount.
Does this include the stress test?
No. It shows the payment at your contract rate. Your lender checks whether you qualify at the minimum qualifying rate.

Title tag
Cap Rate Calculator: Property Value From NOI | FigSumo (54 chars)
Meta description
Find a property's capitalization rate from net operating income and price, or the value implied by an NOI and a target cap rate. (128 chars)
Country
global
Status
rename (301)
Body words
1,003 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Cap Rate Calculator
The capitalization rate (cap rate) links a rental property's net operating income to its value. Investors use it to compare properties quickly and to estimate what a property is worth at the yields typical for its market. This calculator takes the annual net operating income and a cap rate and returns the implied property value and the monthly NOI.
How to use this calculator
1. Net operating income (NOI): the property's annual income after operating expenses but before mortgage payments and income tax. See below for how to work it out.
2. Cap rate: the yield you want to value the property at, usually taken from recent sales of similar properties in the same area.
Results: estimated property value and monthly NOI.
The formula
Cap rate = NOI ÷ Property value
Property value = NOI ÷ Cap rate
NOI = Effective gross income − Operating expenses
Effective gross income: rent and other income (parking, laundry) minus an allowance for vacancy and bad debt.
Operating expenses: property tax, insurance, maintenance and repairs, property management, utilities paid by the owner, HOA or service charges, and reserves for replacements.
Not included in NOI: mortgage principal and interest, depreciation, income tax, and major capital improvements.
To find the cap rate of a property listed for sale, divide its NOI by the asking price. The calculator works in the other direction; for the reverse you can do the division by hand.
Worked examples
Example 1: valuing a property at a 6% cap rate
NOI $48,000 a year
Value = 48,000 ÷ 0.06 = $800,000.00
Monthly NOI = $4,000.00
Example 2: building NOI for a duplex and finding its cap rate
Gross scheduled rent: $36,000.00 a year
Less 5% vacancy: effective gross income $34,200.00
Operating expenses: property tax $6,400, insurance $3,200, repairs and maintenance $2,600, reserves $1,800 = $14,000.00
NOI = $20,200.00
Asking price $350,000 → cap rate = 5.77%
What the same NOI is worth at other market cap rates:
At 5.5%: $367,272.73
At 6.5%: $310,769.23
Small changes in the cap rate move the value a lot. Raising NOI matters too: an extra $1,200 a year of NOI adds about $20,000.00 of value at a 6% cap rate.
Understanding your results
Higher cap rate = lower price relative to income. It usually signals higher perceived risk, weaker growth prospects or a less desirable location.
Lower cap rate = higher price relative to income. Common for prime locations and stable tenants.
Cap rate ignores financing. Two buyers paying the same price have the same cap rate whether they pay cash or borrow 80%. For your return on the cash you put in, use cash-on-cash return in the rental property calculator or the ROI calculator.
Cap rate is a snapshot. It uses one year's NOI and doesn't account for rent growth, a future sale or major repairs. For multi-year analysis, use the IRR calculator.
Getting NOI right
Sellers' figures often leave out vacancy, management (even if you'll self-manage, price your time) and reserves for roofs, boilers, appliances and parking surfaces. Use actual tax bills and insurance quotes. Check whether the listed NOI is "pro forma" (projected) or actual trailing 12-month income. An inflated NOI produces an inflated value.
Cap rates in context
Market cap rates vary by property type (apartments, offices, retail, industrial), location and interest-rate conditions. When interest rates rise, buyers generally demand higher cap rates, so values fall if NOI doesn't rise. Compare the cap rate with your mortgage rate: if the cap rate is below the rate on your loan, borrowing reduces your cash return (negative leverage).
Country notes
United States: property tax is often the largest operating expense; use the actual local rate (see the property tax calculator). Commercial lenders use NOI to set the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR).
Canada: budget for municipal property tax and, in some cities, vacancy taxes on empty homes. Rental income is taxable; capital cost allowance is a tax item and stays out of NOI.
United Kingdom: investors often talk about "yield" (gross yield = annual rent ÷ price; net yield ≈ cap rate). Include service charges, ground rent, letting agent fees and licensing costs in expenses. Mortgage interest relief for individual landlords is restricted to a basic-rate tax credit, which affects after-tax returns but not NOI.
Tips and common mistakes
Including the mortgage payment in expenses. NOI is before debt service.
Using gross rent instead of NOI. That's gross yield, which overstates returns.
Comparing cap rates across different markets or property types. They aren't like-for-like.
Ignoring capital expenditure. A property that needs a new roof has a lower true yield.
Quick check
Before relying on a cap rate, recompute NOI from the rent roll and the expense statements yourself rather than using the seller's figure.
Frequently asked questions
What is a good cap rate?
It depends on the market and risk. A "good" cap rate is one that reflects the property's risk and beats your cost of capital; compare with recent sales nearby.
How do I calculate cap rate?
Divide annual NOI by the purchase price or current value.
Does cap rate include mortgage payments?
No. It's an unleveraged measure.
Why do cap rates change with interest rates?
Investors compare property yields with bond yields and borrowing costs. Higher rates usually push cap rates up.
What is the difference between cap rate and ROI?
Cap rate measures income relative to price. ROI measures your total gain relative to the money you invested, including financing and appreciation.
Is a higher cap rate always better?
Not necessarily. It means more income per dollar paid, but often comes with more risk.

Cash Back vs Low APR Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/cash-back-vs-low-apr-calculator
Title tag
Cash Back vs Low APR Calculator for Car Deals | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Compare a dealer cash rebate against a low-rate financing offer. See which deal costs less over the loan term and by how much. (126 chars)
Country
global
Status
rename (301)
Body words
1,081 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Cash Back vs Low APR Calculator
Car makers often offer a choice: take a cash rebate off the price, or skip the rebate and get a low promotional interest rate. This calculator compares the total you would pay under each option over the same loan term and tells you which is cheaper and by how much.
How to use this calculator
1. Vehicle price: the negotiated price you will finance, before the rebate.
2. Cash rebate: the cash-back amount offered instead of the special rate. The calculator subtracts it from the amount financed.
3. Standard loan APR (no rebate): the rate you would get if you take the rebate, for example from your bank, credit union or the dealer's standard financing. Get a pre-approval so this figure is real.
4. Promotional APR (with rebate forfeited): the special rate offered if you give up the rebate, e.g. 0% or 1.9%.
5. Loan term (years): the same term is used for both options so the comparison is fair. Check that the promotional rate is available for the term you enter; low-rate deals are often limited to shorter terms.
Results: total cost of each option, the better option (lower total) and the savings.
The formula
Both options use the standard loan payment:
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Option A (rebate):  P = Price − Rebate, at the standard APR
Option B (low APR): P = Price, at the promotional APR
Total cost = PMT × n
r: APR ÷ 12; n: years × 12
The option with the lower total cost wins; savings = the difference between the two totals.
The comparison assumes no down payment, no trade-in and no sales tax, and that you keep the loan to the end.
Worked examples
Example 1: $35,000 car, $2,000 rebate or 1.9%, standard rate 6.9%, 5 years
Rebate: finance $33,000 at 6.9% → $651.88 a month, total $39,113.02
Low APR: finance $35,000 at 1.9% → $611.94 a month, total $36,716.50
Take the low APR; it saves $2,396.52
Example 2: $28,000 car, $3,500 rebate or 2.9%, standard rate 5.5%, 5 years
Rebate: finance $24,500 at 5.5% → $467.98 a month, total $28,078.71
Low APR: finance $28,000 at 2.9% → $501.88 a month, total $30,112.80
Better option: the cash rebate, saving $2,034.09
Break-even: the promotional rate would have to be below about 0.11% to beat the rebate here
The bigger the rebate and the lower the standard rate you can get, the more likely the rebate wins.
Understanding your results
Total cost is the sum of all monthly payments. It does not include any down payment, tax or fees, which are the same under both options in most deals.
Savings is the difference in total payments. The monthly payment also differs, so check the cheaper option fits your budget.
Paying cash? If you aren't financing at all, the rebate is pure savings and always wins.
Things the simple comparison misses
Sales tax on the rebate. In many US states, sales tax is charged on the price before a manufacturer rebate, so the rebate doesn't reduce the tax bill [VERIFY your state's rule]. Since both options then pay the same tax, the comparison above still holds.
Paying off early. If you expect to sell or pay off the car early, the low rate's advantage shrinks, because the interest saving builds up over the term while the rebate is immediate.
Shorter promotional terms. If the low APR only applies to 36 months, compare on 36 months. At 36 months, Example 1 costs $36,627.70 with the rebate and $36,034.67 with the 1.9% rate.
Credit approval. Promotional rates usually need top-tier credit. If you don't qualify, the rebate may be your only real option.
Negotiation. Agree the price first; ask about incentives afterwards.
Getting a real standard rate
The comparison is only as good as the standard APR you enter. Before visiting the dealer, apply for a pre-approval with a bank or credit union; it gives you a rate based on your actual credit file, usually valid for a few weeks. With that in hand, you can enter a real figure here, and you can ask the dealer to beat it. If you skip this step and guess a rate that is too high, the low-APR option will look better than it really is.
Country notes
United States: the Truth in Lending Act requires the APR and finance charge to be disclosed before you sign. The FTC warns buyers to watch for add-ons bundled into dealer financing.
Canada: manufacturer incentives work the same way; GST/HST and PST apply to the purchase price. Provincial consumer protection offices regulate dealer disclosure.
United Kingdom: "0% APR" or "cashback" offers are common with PCP and hire-purchase agreements. Compare the total amount payable shown on the finance quote.
Tips and common mistakes
Use a real standard rate. Get a loan quote from a bank or credit union before visiting the dealer.
Match the term. Comparing a 72-month rebate loan with a 36-month promotional loan is not like-for-like.
Don't count the rebate twice. It is already subtracted from the amount financed.
Check for extras. Some promotional deals require buying add-ons or using dealer financing with fees.
Frequently asked questions
Is 0% financing always better than a rebate?
No. It depends on the rebate size, your standard rate and the term. Large rebates combined with a decent standard rate often beat 0%.
What if I put money down?
Subtract the down payment from the vehicle price before entering it. The comparison remains valid as long as the down payment is the same under both options.
Does the calculator include sales tax?
No. Tax is usually the same under both options, so it does not change which one is cheaper.
Why is my monthly payment lower with the low APR even though I borrow more?
A large rate difference can outweigh the extra principal. Compare totals as well as payments.
Can I take both the rebate and the low rate?
Sometimes manufacturers allow it on certain models. If so, take both.
What is the break-even rate?
The promotional APR at which both options cost the same. Below it, the low APR wins.

CD Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/cd-calculator
Title tag
CD Calculator: Certificate of Deposit Interest | FigSumo (56 chars)
Meta description
Calculate the interest and maturity value of a certificate of deposit from deposit, APY or rate, term and compounding. Includes optional tax estimate. (150 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,056 (minimum 1,000)
H1: CD Calculator
A certificate of deposit (CD) pays a fixed rate for a fixed term. This calculator shows what your deposit will be worth at maturity and how much interest it earns, using the annual percentage yield (APY) the bank quotes. Enter the deposit, the APY and the term in months.
How to use this calculator
1. Initial deposit: the amount you put in when you open the CD.
2. Annual APY: the annual percentage yield on the bank's rate sheet. APY already includes the effect of compounding, so you don't need to know how often the bank compounds.
3. Term (months): the CD's length, e.g. 6, 12, 18, 24 or 60 months.
Results: maturity value and interest earned.
The formula
Because APY is the effective annual rate, growth for any term is:
Maturity value = P × (1 + APY)^(m ÷ 12)
Interest earned = Maturity value − P
P: initial deposit
APY: annual percentage yield as a decimal (4.25% = 0.0425)
m: term in months
This assumes interest stays in the CD until maturity. If you have the nominal rate (APR) instead, convert first: APY = (1 + APR ÷ k)^k − 1, where k is the number of compounding periods per year.
Worked examples
Example 1: $10,000 in a 12-month CD at 4.25% APY
Maturity value = 10,000 × 1.0425 = $10,425.00
Interest earned = $425.00
For a 12-month term, APY gives the interest directly: 4.25% of $10,000.
Example 2: $25,000 in a 30-month CD at 4.00% APY
Maturity value = 25,000 × 1.04^(30 ÷ 12) = 25,000 × 1.04^2.5 = $27,575.50
Interest earned = $2,575.50
A bank compounding monthly would need a nominal rate of 3.928% to produce a 4.00% APY
Understanding your results
Maturity value is what you'd receive at the end if you leave the money untouched and the bank compounds as the APY assumes.
Interest earned is before tax. CD interest is taxable as income in the US, Canada and the UK unless held in a tax-advantaged account.
Real return: if inflation is 3%, a 4.25% APY is a real return of about 1.21%. Use the inflation calculator to see buying power.
Interest paid out? Some CDs pay interest monthly to your checking account instead of compounding. Then the total interest is slightly lower than shown.
Early withdrawal penalties
Most CDs charge a penalty for withdrawing before maturity, often expressed as a number of months' interest. For example, a penalty of six months' interest on a $25,000 CD at about 4% would be roughly $500.00. Penalties can exceed the interest earned if you withdraw very early, cutting into your deposit. Read the account terms before you open the CD.
Ways to use CDs
CD ladder: split money across CDs that mature at different times (e.g. 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 years). Each year one matures, giving access to cash and a chance to reinvest at current rates.
Matching a goal: pick a term that ends when you need the money, such as a house deposit next year.
Rate lock: when rates are expected to fall, a longer CD locks in today's rate. When rates may rise, shorter terms keep flexibility.
CD or high-yield savings account?
A savings account lets you withdraw at any time, but its rate can change whenever the bank decides. A CD fixes the rate but locks the money away. If the CD's APY is only slightly above a good savings rate, the flexibility of the savings account may be worth more. If the gap is large and you are sure you won't need the money, the CD's guaranteed rate wins. You can model the savings account side with the savings calculator.
Country notes
United States: CDs at FDIC-insured banks are covered up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category; credit union share certificates are covered by the NCUA on the same basis. Interest is reported on Form 1099-INT.
Canada: the equivalent product is a GIC (guaranteed investment certificate). Eligible deposits at CDIC member institutions are covered up to $100,000 per category. GICs can be held in a TFSA or RRSP to shelter the interest.
United Kingdom: the equivalent is a fixed-rate bond or fixed-term savings account. Banks quote an AER, which works like APY. The FSCS protects up to £120,000 per person per authorised bank from 1 December 2025 (previously £85,000) [VERIFY]. Interest within the Personal Savings Allowance (£1,000 basic rate, £500 higher rate) is tax-free, or use a cash ISA.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing APY and APR. Enter the APY. If the bank only shows a rate and compounding frequency, convert first.
Ignoring penalties. Only lock away money you won't need before maturity.
Watching automatic renewal. Many CDs roll over into a new term at the bank's current rate unless you act during the grace period.
Exceeding insurance limits. Spread large sums across banks or ownership categories.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between APY and interest rate?
The interest rate (APR) is the nominal yearly rate. APY includes compounding, showing what you actually earn in a year. For comparing CDs, use APY.
How often do CDs compound?
It varies by bank: daily, monthly or quarterly. Because APY already reflects compounding, the calculator gives the right answer whichever the bank uses.
Is CD interest taxable?
Generally yes, as income in the year it is credited, even if you don't withdraw it, unless the CD is inside a tax-advantaged account.
Can I lose money in a CD?
Not from rate changes: the rate is fixed. You can lose some principal if an early withdrawal penalty exceeds the interest earned, and inflation can erode buying power.
What happens at maturity?
You can withdraw, move the money or let it renew. Banks give a short grace period, often around 7 to 10 days, to decide.
Are brokered CDs different?
Brokered CDs are bought through a brokerage and can be sold before maturity on a secondary market, where their price can be above or below what you paid.

Closing Cost Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/us/closing-cost-calculator
Title tag
Mortgage Closing Cost Calculator | FigSumo (42 chars)
Meta description
Estimate closing costs for a US home purchase by line item, from lender fees to title and prepaid items, and the cash needed to close. (134 chars)
Country
US
Status
new · tax year 2026
Body words
1,020 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Closing Cost Calculator
Closing costs are the fees and prepaid items you pay when a home purchase or refinance completes, on top of the down payment. They include lender charges, title and settlement fees, government recording fees and transfer taxes, and the first deposits into your escrow account. This calculator adds up the items you enter and shows your total closing costs and the cash you'll need to bring to closing.
How to use this calculator
Enter amounts from your Loan Estimate (which lenders must give you within three business days of applying) or quotes from title companies. Leave anything that doesn't apply at zero.
1. Loan amount and interest rate: used for points, origination and prepaid interest.
2. Lender charges: origination fee, discount points, application or underwriting fee.
3. Third-party services: appraisal, credit report, flood certification, survey, pest or home inspection.
4. Title and settlement: lender's title insurance, owner's title insurance (optional), settlement or escrow fee.
5. Government fees: recording fees and any state or local transfer taxes.
6. Prepaids: interest from closing to month end, the first year of homeowners insurance.
7. Initial escrow deposit: a few months of property tax and insurance.
8. Credits: seller concessions, lender credits and your earnest money deposit.
Results: total closing costs, closing costs as a percentage of the loan, and cash to close.
How it works
Closing costs = Lender charges + Third-party fees + Title/settlement + Government fees + Prepaids + Escrow deposits
Cash to close = Down payment + Closing costs − Seller and lender credits − Earnest money
Prepaid interest = Loan × Rate ÷ 365 × Days until the first of next month
There's no single national figure for closing costs; they depend on the state, the lender and the price. That's why the calculator uses your own itemised inputs rather than a percentage.
Worked example
$400,000 purchase, $80,000 down, $320,000 loan at 6.5%, closing 12 days before month end:
Item
Amount
Origination fee (1% of loan)
$3,200.00
Appraisal
$650.00
Credit report
$50.00
Lender's title insurance
$1,400.00
Owner's title insurance
$1,100.00
Settlement/escrow fee
$900.00
Recording fees
$250.00
State/local transfer tax
$0.00
Subtotal of fees: $7,550.00
Prepaid interest (12 days): $683.84
First-year homeowners insurance: $1,800.00
Escrow deposit (3 months' property tax on $4,800 a year, 2 months' insurance): $1,500.00
Total closing costs: $11,533.84 (3.60% of the loan)
With a $3,000 seller credit and $5,000 earnest money already paid, cash to close = $83,533.84.
Should you pay discount points?
One point (1% of the loan, $3,200.00) might lower the rate from 6.5% to 6.25% [the actual trade-off is lender-specific]. That saves $52.32 a month, so you'd break even after about 61 months. Points make sense only if you'll keep the loan longer than that.
Understanding your results
Prepaids and escrow aren't really fees. They're your own tax, insurance and interest paid in advance, but you still need the cash at closing.
Compare Loan Estimates. Section A (origination charges) is controlled by the lender; sections B and C are third-party services, some of which you can shop for.
Closing Disclosure: you must receive it at least three business days before closing. Compare it with the Loan Estimate; certain fees can't increase at all, and others only within a 10% tolerance.
Wire fraud warning: confirm wiring instructions by phone with your title company using a number you already know.
Ways to reduce closing costs
Shop lenders and title services.
Ask for seller concessions (subject to loan program limits).
Accept a lender credit in exchange for a slightly higher rate.
Check state or local first-time buyer assistance programs.
Close near the end of the month to reduce prepaid interest (it doesn't change total interest, only when you pay it).
State differences
Transfer taxes, recording fees and title insurance rates vary widely by state and county. Some states have no transfer tax; others charge it on both buyer and seller, or split it by custom. In some states attorneys handle closings, adding a legal fee. Check your county recorder and state revenue department.
Tips and common mistakes
Budgeting only for the down payment.
Leaving out escrow deposits, which can be several thousand dollars.
Assuming the seller pays everything because of a concession; check the cap.
Skipping owner's title insurance without understanding what it covers.
Reading your Loan Estimate
Lenders must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days of your application. Section A lists origination charges, B the services you can't shop for, and C the services you can shop for, such as title and settlement. Compare section A and the total in section J across lenders on the same day, since rates change daily. Three business days before closing you'll receive the Closing Disclosure; compare it line by line with the estimate and ask about any increase.
Frequently asked questions
How much are closing costs?
They vary by location, lender and price. Your Loan Estimate gives the best figure.
Who pays closing costs?
The buyer pays most, but sellers can contribute through concessions, and sellers pay their own costs (such as agent commissions).
Can closing costs be rolled into the loan?
On a purchase, usually not, although lender credits can cover some. On a refinance, they often can.
What is cash to close?
The total you need at closing: down payment plus closing costs, minus credits and deposits already paid.
Are closing costs tax-deductible?
Most aren't for a home you live in. Points and prepaid mortgage interest may be deductible if you itemize, and property tax paid at closing may count toward the SALT deduction.
What's the difference between a Loan Estimate and a Closing Disclosure?
The Loan Estimate comes early with estimated costs; the Closing Disclosure shows the final terms before closing.

Title tag
CMHC Mortgage Insurance Calculator | FigSumo (44 chars)
Meta description
Calculate the mortgage default insurance premium for a Canadian home from price and down payment, using the CMHC loan-to-value premium table. (141 chars)

H1: CMHC Insurance Calculator
In Canada, a mortgage with a down payment below 20% must carry mortgage default insurance. Lenders buy it from CMHC or a private insurer (Sagen, Canada Guaranty) and pass the premium on to you, usually by adding it to the mortgage. This calculator works out your minimum down payment, loan-to-value ratio, the premium and the insured mortgage amount, plus any provincial sales tax due on the premium.
How to use this calculator
1. Purchase price: the price of the home.
2. Down payment: in dollars or as a percentage.
3. Down payment source: traditional (your savings, RRSP Home Buyers' Plan, FHSA, a gift from family) or non-traditional (for example, borrowed funds). Non-traditional sources carry a higher premium at the highest loan-to-value band.
4. Province: some provinces charge sales tax on the premium.
5. Amortization: 25 years, or 30 years where eligible.
Results: minimum down payment, loan-to-value (LTV), premium rate, premium amount, total insured mortgage and PST payable at closing.
How it works
Minimum down payment (federal rules):
5% of the first $500,000
10% of the portion from $500,000 up to $1.5 million
Homes of $1.5 million or more need 20% and can't be insured
Premium = loan amount × rate from the CMHC table, based on LTV (loan ÷ price):
Loan-to-value
Premium on total loan
Up to 65%
0.60%
65.01% to 75%
1.70%
75.01% to 80%
2.40%
80.01% to 85%
2.80%
85.01% to 90%
3.10%
90.01% to 95%
4.00%
90.01% to 95%, non-traditional down payment
4.50%
Mortgages with less than 20% down must be insured; insurance at lower LTVs (portfolio or low-ratio insurance) is arranged by lenders and not usually paid by you, but the lower rows are shown for completeness.
Insured mortgage = Loan + Premium
Worked examples
Example 1: $500,000 home with 10% down
Loan = 500,000 − 50,000 = $450,000; LTV = 90%
Premium = 450,000 × 3.10% = $13,950.00
Insured mortgage = $463,950.00
In Ontario, PST at 8% on the premium = $1,116.00, payable at closing [VERIFY rate].
Spread over a 25-year mortgage at 4.5%, the premium adds roughly $77.21 a month to the payment.
Example 2: $800,000 home at the minimum down payment
Minimum down = 5% × 500,000 + 10% × 300,000 = $55,000.00 (6.875% of the price)
Loan $745,000.00; LTV 93.125% → 4.00%
Premium = $29,800.00; insured mortgage $774,800.00
With 15% down instead, the loan is $680,000.00 at 2.80%, a premium of $19,040.00. That's $10,760.00 less in premium, on top of the smaller loan.
Example 3: $1,000,000 home at the minimum down payment
Minimum down = 5% × 500,000 + 10% × 500,000 = $75,000.00 (7.5%)
Loan $925,000.00; LTV 92.5% → 4.00%
Premium = $37,000.00; insured mortgage $962,000.00
In Ontario, PST at 8% on the premium = $2,960.00, paid at closing [VERIFY rate]
Example 4: a few dollars across an LTV band
On a $600,000 home:
$59,000 down (9.83%): loan $541,000, LTV 90.17% → 4.00%, premium $21,640.00
$60,000 down (10%): loan $540,000, LTV 90.00% → 3.10%, premium $16,740.00
An extra $1,000 of down payment saves $4,900.00 of premium. Check where you sit against the band edges before finalising your down payment.
Understanding your results
The premium is a one-time charge, usually added to the mortgage, so you pay interest on it.
PST isn't added to the mortgage. Where it applies, you pay it in cash at closing.
It protects the lender, not you. If you default, the insurer pays the lender.
Insured mortgages often get lower rates than uninsured ones because the lender's risk is lower.
Stress test: insured borrowers must qualify at the higher of the contract rate plus 2 percentage points or 5.25%. See the mortgage affordability calculator.
Eligibility rules to know
Purchase price under $1.5 million.
Owner-occupied (1 to 4 units; small rental properties have separate rules).
Maximum amortization 25 years, or 30 years for first-time buyers and buyers of new builds [VERIFY current eligibility].
Gross debt service (GDS) and total debt service (TDS) ratio limits apply.
Tips and common mistakes
Using 5% for a home over $500,000. The 10% tier applies above $500,000.
Forgetting the PST in Ontario, Quebec or Saskatchewan.
Assuming 20% down is always best. It avoids the premium, but keeping cash for closing costs, land transfer tax and an emergency fund matters too.
Crossing an LTV band by a few dollars. A slightly bigger down payment can drop you into a lower premium rate.
Notes for US and UK readers
US: the closest equivalent is private mortgage insurance (PMI) on conventional loans with less than 20% down. It's usually a monthly charge rather than a one-time premium, and it can be cancelled once the loan reaches 80% of the original value, and ends automatically at 78%. FHA loans charge an upfront premium plus an annual one. See the PMI calculator.
UK: borrowers don't normally buy mortgage default insurance. Instead, lenders charge higher interest rates at higher loan-to-value ratios, and 95% mortgages are priced well above 75% ones. A government-backed mortgage guarantee scheme has supported 95% lending since 2021 [VERIFY current status].
Canadian buyers can't avoid the premium with less than 20% down, so comparing the premium with the extra time needed to save 20% is the key decision.
Frequently asked questions
When is CMHC insurance required?
When your down payment is less than 20% of the purchase price.
How much is CMHC insurance?
Between 2.80% and 4.00% of the loan for most buyers with less than 20% down (4.50% at 90.01–95% LTV with a non-traditional down payment).
Can I add the premium to my mortgage?
Yes, and most buyers do. Provincial sales tax on the premium can't be added.
Is CMHC insurance refundable?
Generally no, although some insurers offer partial refunds or portability if you move and port the mortgage.
What's the minimum down payment in Canada?
5% up to $500,000, 10% on the portion from $500,000 to $1.5 million, and 20% for $1.5 million or more.
Do private insurers charge the same?
Sagen and Canada Guaranty generally price close to CMHC, but check with your lender.

Title tag
College Cost Calculator: Future Tuition & Savings | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description
Project future college costs with tuition inflation and work out the monthly saving needed to reach the target by the start date. (129 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
1,091 (minimum 1,000)
H1: College Cost Calculator
This calculator projects what a college or university education will cost by the time a student enrolls. Enter today's annual cost, the years until enrollment, an education inflation rate and the number of years of study. It returns the estimated cost of the first year at enrollment and the total cost of the whole program.
How to use this calculator
1. Annual cost today: the full yearly cost of attendance at the kind of school you have in mind: tuition and fees, plus housing, food, books and transport if you want the full picture. College websites publish a "cost of attendance"; in the US, the College Navigator database lists them.
2. Years until enrollment: for a newborn, about 18; for a high-school sophomore, about 3.
3. Education inflation: how fast you expect costs to rise per year. Historic tuition increases have often outpaced general inflation, but the gap has varied a lot by decade and country [VERIFY a current long-run figure from the source you rely on, e.g. College Board "Trends in College Pricing"].
4. Years of college: usually 4 for a US bachelor's degree, 3 or 4 in the UK, 4 in Canada.
Results: estimated total college cost and first year cost (at enrollment).
The formula
Each year of study is inflated from today to the year it is paid:
Cost in study year k = C × (1 + g)^(Y + k),  k = 0, 1, …, N − 1
Total cost = Σ cost in each study year
C: annual cost today
g: education inflation as a decimal
Y: years until enrollment
N: years of college
The first year is C × (1 + g)^Y. Later years keep rising because inflation continues while the student is enrolled.
Worked examples
Example 1: $30,000 a year today, enrollment in 10 years, 5% inflation, 4 years
Year 1: 30,000 × 1.05^10 = $48,866.84
Year 2: $51,310.18
Year 3: $53,875.69
Year 4: $56,569.47
Total: $210,622.18
At today's prices four years would cost $120,000. Inflation adds about three quarters of that again over the 14 years.
Example 2: $12,000 a year today, 5 years away, 4% inflation, 4 years
First year: $14,599.83
Total: $61,997.67 (compared with $48,000.00 at today's prices)
To have the entire total saved by enrollment, earning 5% a year compounded monthly, you would need to put aside about $911.65 a month for five years. That is a cautious target: in practice the later years are paid while the remaining savings keep earning.
Understanding your results
First year cost is the bill for the year the student starts, in future dollars.
Total cost is the sum of all years in future dollars. It is not adjusted for financial aid, scholarships, grants or tax credits, which can reduce the net price substantially.
Sensitivity: inflation compounds, so small changes in the rate move the total a lot over long horizons. Try two or three rates.
Sticker price vs net price: many students pay less than the published cost of attendance. In the US, every college must offer a net price calculator on its website.
Ways to pay
Savings plans: in the US, 529 plans grow tax-free when used for qualified education expenses. In Canada, an RESP attracts the Canada Education Savings Grant of 20% on the first $2,500 contributed per year per child (up to $500 a year, $7,200 lifetime). In the UK, a Junior ISA allows £9,000 a year for a child [VERIFY current JISA limit].
Financial aid and scholarships: apply early. US students file the FAFSA; Canadian students apply through their province's student aid program; UK students apply to Student Finance.
Student loans: borrowing fills the gap, but compare repayment costs with the student loan calculator.
Work and cash flow: part-time work and paying some costs from income during study reduce what must be saved up front.
Country notes
United States: published costs vary widely between in-state public, out-of-state public and private colleges. The College Scorecard and College Navigator show costs, net prices and outcomes.
Canada: tuition is set by provinces and institutions; Statistics Canada publishes average tuition by province each year. The RESP grant rules are set out by Employment and Social Development Canada.
United Kingdom: in England, tuition fees for home students are capped by the government (£9,535 a year for 2025/26 [VERIFY 2026/27 cap]), and most students take a tuition fee loan, repaid through the tax system after graduation. Living costs are covered partly by maintenance loans. Scotland does not charge eligible Scottish students tuition fees.
Tips and common mistakes
Using tuition only. Housing and food can cost as much as tuition; include them for a realistic budget.
Ignoring aid. Use school net price calculators to estimate what you'd really pay.
Setting inflation at zero. Even modest rises compound over 10 to 18 years.
Waiting to start saving. The earlier contributions begin, the more growth does the work.
Frequently asked questions
What inflation rate should I use for college costs?
Look at recent published increases for the type of school you're considering, and run the calculator at a low and a high rate. There is no single correct figure.
Does the total include financial aid?
No. It is the full projected cost before grants, scholarships or loans.
Why does each year cost more than the last?
Prices keep rising while the student is enrolled, so year four is inflated for three more years than year one.
How much should I save each month?
Divide the total among your sources (savings, aid, loans, income). For the savings share, the savings calculator can find the monthly deposit to reach a target.
Should I include room and board?
Yes, if you expect to pay it. Living costs are a large part of the total, especially for students who live away from home.
Can I use this for graduate school?
Yes. Enter the annual cost, the years until the program starts and its length.
