Commission Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/commission-calculator
Title tag
Commission Calculator: Flat, Tiered & Percentage | FigSumo (58 chars)
Meta description
Work out sales commission from sale price and rate, including tiered structures. Also solves for the rate or the sale price needed. (131 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,001 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Commission Calculator
This commission calculator works out the commission on a sale at a flat percentage rate, and what is left of the sale amount after the commission is paid. It is useful for salespeople checking their pay, for home sellers estimating an agent's fee, and for businesses budgeting the cost of a sales team.
How to use this calculator
1. Sale amount: the value of the sale the commission is based on. For a home sale, the sale price; for a sales role, the revenue the plan counts (check whether it is before or after discounts and tax).
2. Commission rate: the percentage paid, as written in the commission plan or listing agreement.
Results: commission earned and net to seller (before other fees), which is the sale amount minus the commission.
The formula
Commission = Sale amount × Rate ÷ 100
Net to seller = Sale amount − Commission
To find the rate when you know the commission: Rate = Commission ÷ Sale amount × 100.
Worked examples
Example 1: $450,000 home sale at 3%
Commission = 450,000 × 0.03 = $13,500.00
Net to seller = $436,500.00, before other closing costs, taxes and mortgage payoff
Example 2: a tiered sales plan (done by hand)
Many sales plans pay a higher rate as sales grow. Suppose the plan pays 5% on the first $10,000 of monthly sales, 7% on $10,000–$25,000 and 10% above $25,000, and you sell $32,000:
First $10,000 × 5% = $500.00
Next $15,000 × 7% = $1,050.00
Last $7,000 × 10% = $700.00
Total commission = $2,250.00, an effective rate of 7.03%
The calculator handles one flat rate at a time. For tiers, run each band separately and add the results, as above.
Understanding your results
Commission earned is gross pay from that sale, before income tax and payroll deductions.
Net to seller is what remains for the seller from the sale price after commission. In real estate, other selling costs (transfer taxes, legal fees, repairs, mortgage payoff) come out as well.
Effective rate: on tiered or capped plans, divide total commission by total sales to compare plans fairly.
Common commission structures
Straight commission: pay is only commission. Income swings with sales.
Base salary plus commission: a fixed salary plus a smaller rate. For example, a $3,000 monthly base with 4% on $85,000 of sales pays $3,400.00 commission, for $6,400.00 in total.
Tiered (graduated): higher rates on higher bands of sales, as in Example 2.
Draw against commission: an advance on future commissions that is repaid from them.
Gross margin commission: paid on profit rather than revenue, so discounts reduce pay.
Residual commission: ongoing payments for as long as a customer keeps paying, common in insurance and subscriptions.
Real estate commissions
In a typical US home sale, the total commission is shared between the listing brokerage and the buyer's brokerage, and each brokerage then pays its agent a share. For example, on a $600,000 sale with a 5% total commission ($30,000.00), each side's brokerage might receive $15,000.00, and an agent on a 70% split would get $10,500.00 before expenses. The seller's net would be $570,000.00 before other costs. Commission rates are negotiable. Since August 2024, following the National Association of Realtors settlement, buyers' agent compensation is agreed separately in writing and is no longer offered through MLS listings [VERIFY wording against NAR/DOJ guidance].
Commission as a business cost
For a business, commission is a variable cost of each sale. A 10% commission on a product sold with a 30% gross margin takes a third of the profit on that sale. Before setting rates, check the margin on what is being sold with the margin calculator, and the number of sales needed to cover fixed costs with the break-even calculator. Paying commission on gross margin instead of revenue keeps sales staff from discounting away the profit.
Country notes
United States: commission is taxed as supplemental wages for employees. Employers may withhold federal income tax on supplemental wages at a flat 22% (37% above $1 million) [VERIFY in IRS Publication 15]. Independent contractors receive Form 1099-NEC and pay self-employment tax.
Canada: commissions are employment income subject to CPP, EI and income tax deductions. Commissioned employees can sometimes deduct certain expenses using Form T2200.
United Kingdom: commission is taxed through PAYE like salary, with Income Tax and National Insurance. Estate agents typically charge sellers a percentage plus VAT; the buyer usually pays no agent fee.
Tips and common mistakes
Check the commission base. Is it calculated on the price before discounts, after discounts, or on margin?
Watch for clawbacks. Commission may be reversed if a customer cancels or doesn't pay.
Add VAT or GST/HST where it applies to agent fees.
Compare total pay, not just the rate. A lower rate with a higher base can pay more.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate commission?
Multiply the sale amount by the commission rate as a decimal. A 6% commission on $20,000 is $1,200.
How do I find my commission rate?
Divide the commission by the sale amount and multiply by 100.
Does the calculator handle tiered rates?
Not automatically. Split the sale into bands, calculate each at its rate, and add them up.
Is commission taxed differently from salary?
It is taxable income in the same way, but US employers may withhold tax on it at a flat supplemental rate, so your paycheck withholding can look different.
Are real estate commission rates fixed?
No. They are negotiable between the seller (or buyer) and the brokerage.
What does "net to seller" include?
Only the sale amount minus the commission entered. Other costs of selling are not deducted.

Title tag
Compound Interest Calculator with Monthly Contributions | FigSumo (65 chars)
Meta description
See how money grows with compound interest: choose the compounding frequency, add regular deposits and compare the results with a year-by-year table and chart. (159 chars)
Country

1,041 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Compound Interest Calculator
Compound interest is interest earned on interest. Each period, the interest is added to the balance, and the next period's interest is calculated on that larger amount. The effect is small at first and grows over time. This calculator shows the growth year by year and separates your own deposits from the interest. You can also compare compounding frequencies.
How to use this calculator
1. Initial deposit: the amount you start with.
2. Annual interest rate: the nominal rate. If your bank quotes an APY or AER, use the rate converter to change it.
3. Compounding frequency: annually, quarterly, monthly, daily or continuously.
4. Regular contribution (optional): the amount, how often, and whether it is paid at the start or end of each period.
5. Time: years, and optionally months.
The formula
Lump sum:
A = P × (1 + r/m)^(m × t)
With equal contributions at the end of each compounding period:
A = P × (1 + i)^N + C × ((1 + i)^N − 1) / i
A: final balance
P: initial deposit
r: nominal annual rate (5% → 0.05)
m: compounding periods per year
t: years
i: rate per period = r/m
N: total periods = m × t
C: contribution per period
If contributions are made at the start of each period, multiply the contribution term by (1 + i).
Effective annual rate (EAR / APY / AER):
EAR = (1 + r/m)^m − 1          continuous: EAR = e^r − 1
When contributions are made at a different frequency from compounding, the calculator converts the rate to an equivalent rate per contribution period.
Worked examples
Example 1: lump sum plus monthly deposits. $10,000 initial, 5% compounded monthly, $250 added at the end of each month, for 15 years.
i = 0.05 / 12 = 0.0041667; N = 180
Lump sum part: 10,000 × 1.0041667^180 = $21,137.04
Deposits part: 250 × (1.0041667^180 − 1) / 0.0041667 = $66,822.24
Final balance: $87,959.28
Your money in: 10,000 + 250 × 180 = $55,000
Interest earned: $32,959.28
Example 2: does compounding frequency matter? $10,000 at 5% for 15 years, no deposits:
Compounding

Annually

$21,168.91
Moving from annual to monthly compounding adds $347.76. Moving from monthly to daily adds only $31.87. The rate and the time matter far more than the frequency. 5% compounded monthly is an effective annual rate of 5.116%.

Compounding works against you on debt
The same maths applies to money you owe. Unpaid credit card interest is added to the balance and then charged interest itself. See the credit card payoff calculator for how fixed payments break that cycle.

Understanding your results
Final balance: what you would have if the rate stays constant and every deposit is made on time.
Total contributions vs total interest: the chart separates them, so you can see when interest starts to outweigh deposits.
Year-by-year table: start balance, deposits, interest and end balance for each year. You can download it as CSV.
Real terms (optional): enter an inflation rate to see the result in today's money.
Taxes are not deducted. Interest in a taxable account may be taxed each year, which reduces growth. Tax-advantaged accounts work differently by country.
Country notes
US: banks must disclose an Annual Percentage Yield (APY) on deposit accounts. It is the same idea as the EAR above.
UK: savings accounts quote an AER (Annual Equivalent Rate), also the same concept.
Canada: GICs and savings accounts usually quote an annual rate with a stated compounding frequency. Enter both.
Tax-free growth options: Roth IRA (US), TFSA (Canada), ISA (UK).
Tips and common mistakes
Confusing the nominal rate with APY or AER. Enter the nominal rate with its compounding frequency, or convert first.
Assuming the rate stays fixed. Savings and investment returns change; run a lower-rate scenario.
Ignoring tax on interest. In a taxable account, growth is slower than the calculator shows.
Starting late. Example 3 shows that time matters more than the amount saved.
Forgetting inflation. Use the real-terms option to see purchasing power.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
Simple interest is paid only on the original amount. Compound interest is also paid on interest already earned. Over 15 years at 5%, $10,000 earns $7,500 of simple interest, compared with $11,137.04 compounded monthly.
How often is interest compounded?
It depends on the account. Many savings accounts compound daily or monthly, and some bonds compound semi-annually. The account terms will say.
What is the Rule of 72?
It's a quick estimate: 72 ÷ rate gives roughly the years needed to double your money. At 6%, it suggests 12 years; the exact answer with annual compounding is 11.9 years.
Can I use this for investments like index funds?
You can, but investment returns are not fixed. A steady rate in the calculator is a simplification. Try several rates to see a range, or use the investment calculator.
Does making deposits at the start of the month help?
Yes, a little. Each deposit earns one extra period of interest. Over long periods, the difference adds up.
What's continuous compounding?
It is the mathematical limit as compounding becomes infinitely frequent, A = P × e^(rt). It gives a slightly higher result than daily compounding, mainly of theoretical interest.

H1: CPP Contribution Calculator
Almost every worker in Canada outside Quebec contributes to the Canada Pension Plan (CPP) through payroll deductions or, if self-employed, on their tax return. This calculator works out your 2026 CPP contributions, including the second additional contribution (CPP2) on earnings above the first ceiling, and shows what your employer pays on top. It covers contributions only, not the pension you'll receive.
How to use this calculator
1. Annual employment or self-employment income: pensionable earnings for 2026, before deductions.
2. Employee or self-employed: self-employed people pay both the employee and employer shares.
3. Months covered (optional): if you turned 18, started receiving a CPP pension or became disabled during the year, the exemption and maximums are pro-rated.
Results: CPP contribution (base plus first additional), CPP2 contribution, total, employer contribution and, for the self-employed, the deductible portion.

The formula
CPP  = 5.95% × (min(Earnings, 74,600) − 3,500)
CPP2 = 4% × (min(Earnings, 85,000) − 74,600), if earnings exceed 74,600
Employers match both amounts. Self-employed people pay double.
Worked examples
Example 1: $60,000 salary
CPP = 5.95% × (60,000 − 3,500) = $3,361.75
CPP2 = $0 (earnings below the YMPE)
Of the CPP, the base portion (4.95%) is $2,796.75, which earns a non-refundable federal tax credit at 14% (about $391.55). The first additional portion (1%), $565.00, is a deduction from income.
Example 2: $80,000 salary
CPP = $4,230.45 (the maximum)
CPP2 = 4% × (80,000 − 74,600) = $216.00
Total employee contributions $4,446.45; the employer pays the same again.
Example 3: $100,000 salary
CPP $4,230.45 + CPP2 $416.00 = $4,646.45, the maximum employee total of $4,646.45.
Example 4: self-employed, $80,000 net business income
CPP = $8,460.90; CPP2 = $432.00; total $8,892.90
Half ($4,446.45) relates to the "employer" share, which is deductible from income; the rest is treated like employee contributions (credit and deduction as above).
Example 5: $30,000 part-time salary
CPP = 5.95% × (30,000 − 3,500) = $1,576.75
CPP2 = $0
Employer pays another $1,576.75
Example 6: turning 18 partway through the year
If you turn 18 in June, contributions apply only for the months after your birthday (July to December, 6 months). The basic exemption is pro-rated to 3,500 × 6 ÷ 12 = $1,750. On $20,000 earned in those months: 5.95% × (20,000 − 1,750) = $1,085.88 [VERIFY pro-rating method against CRA payroll guidance]. Enter 6 in "months covered" to see this.

Understanding your results
Contributions stop once you hit the maximums. Later paycheques in the year will have no CPP deducted.
Two jobs: each employer deducts CPP separately, so you may over-contribute. The excess employee contribution is refunded when you file your tax return; employer contributions aren't refunded.
Contributions are linked to your future pension. The enhancement (first and second additional contributions) is gradually raising the CPP retirement pension for people who contribute after 2019.
Take-home pay: CPP, EI and income tax all come off your pay; see the Canada take-home pay calculator.
Who contributes
Workers aged 18 to 70 with earnings above $3,500 outside Quebec.
You stop contributing at 70, or earlier if you're 65 to 70, receiving a CPP retirement pension and file an election (form CPT30 for employees) to stop.
Quebec workers contribute to the Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), administered by Retraite Québec with its own rates. This calculator doesn't cover the QPP.
What CPP pays
The CPP retirement pension can start from age 60 (reduced by 0.6% a month before 65) to 70 (increased by 0.7% a month after 65). The amount depends on how much and for how long you contributed. Service Canada's My Service Canada Account shows your contribution history and estimate. Compare the US system on the Social Security calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Applying CPP to all income. Only earnings between $3,500 and the ceilings count; investment income doesn't.
Forgetting CPP2 on earnings above $74,600.
Self-employed underestimates. You pay both shares, which can be a large bill at tax time.
Not claiming an overpayment when you've had more than one employer.
Notes for US and UK readers
US: the equivalent is Social Security tax, 6.2% each for employee and employer on wages up to $184,500 in 2026, plus 1.45% Medicare with no cap.
UK: employees pay Class 1 National Insurance at 8% on earnings between £12,570 and £50,270 a year and 2% above, with employers paying 15% above a lower threshold [VERIFY 2026/27 rates].
Unlike CPP, neither has a basic exemption that comes off every worker's earnings in the same way, so comparisons at a given salary need care.
Frequently asked questions
What is the maximum CPP contribution for 2026?
$4,230.45 for employees, plus up to $416.00 in CPP2: $4,646.45 in total. Self-employed: $9,292.90.
What is CPP2?
The second additional CPP contribution: 4% on earnings between $74,600 and $85,000 in 2026.
Do I get CPP contributions back?
Only if you over-contributed (for example, with two employers). Otherwise they fund your future CPP benefits.
Are CPP contributions tax-deductible?
The enhanced portions are deducted from income; the base portion earns a non-refundable tax credit.
Do I pay CPP on self-employment income?
Yes, both shares, through your income tax return (Schedule 8).
Does Quebec use CPP?
No. Quebec has the QPP.

Credit Card Minimum Payment Calculator | FigSumo (48 chars)
Meta description
See how long a card balance takes to clear on minimum payments, how much interest you pay, and what a fixed payment would save. (127 chars)
Country
global

1,239 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Credit Card Calculator
This calculator shows how long it takes to clear a credit card balance if you only make the minimum payment each month, and how much interest that costs. Enter the balance, the card's APR and how your issuer sets the minimum payment. The answer is usually a surprise: minimum payments are designed to keep the account in good standing, not to pay the debt off quickly.
How to use this calculator
1. Balance: the amount you owe today, from your latest statement or app.
2. APR: the purchase APR on the statement. If part of the balance is on a different rate (cash advance, promotional rate), use a weighted average or run each part separately.
3. Minimum payment (% of balance): the percentage of the balance your issuer requires each month. The terms and conditions or the statement's "minimum payment" section explain the formula.
4. Minimum payment floor: the lowest minimum the issuer will accept, such as $25 or $35, used when the percentage gives a smaller figure.
Results: months to pay off (min payments), total interest paid and total amount paid. No new purchases are assumed.
The formula
The calculator simulates the card month by month:
Interest this month = Balance × APR ÷ 12
Payment = max(Floor, Balance × Min %)   (never more than balance + interest)
New balance = Balance + Interest − Payment
It repeats until the balance is cleared or 600 months (50 years) have passed. Because the payment is a percentage of a shrinking balance, the payment shrinks too, which is why minimum-only payoff takes so long. When the percentage gets small, the floor takes over and finishes the debt.
Card issuers charge interest on the average daily balance, at a daily periodic rate (APR ÷ 365 or 360). The monthly approximation used here is close for a balance that isn't changing during the month.
Worked examples
Example 1: $5,000 at 21.99%, minimum 3% of balance, $35 floor
First month: interest = 5,000 × 0.2199 ÷ 12 = $91.62; minimum = max($35, 3% × 5,000) = $150.00
Months to pay off: 176 (about 14.7 years)
Total interest: $6,669.10; total paid $11,669.10
Example 2: the same card with a fixed $200 a month
Paying a steady $200 instead of the falling minimum clears the balance in 34 months with $1,748.69 of interest, a saving of $4,920.41. (Use the credit card payoff calculator to test fixed payments and payoff dates.)
When the minimum barely covers interest
With a 2% minimum and a $25 floor at 21.99%, the payment is only slightly larger than the interest for years. After the 50-year limit, $1,828.68 would still be owed, after $34,695.17 of interest. If your card's minimum works like this, paying only the minimum is not a realistic plan.
Understanding your results
Months to pay off assumes you never use the card again and the APR doesn't change.
Total interest paid is the cost of carrying the balance. Compare it with the original balance.
Total amount paid is everything you pay over the period.
If the result is 600 months, the debt is not cleared within 50 years with these settings (see the note above).
How issuers set minimum payments
Common formulas:
a fixed percentage of the balance (as modelled here), often 2–3%;
interest and fees for the month plus 1% of the balance;
a fixed floor such as $25–$35, or the whole balance if it is below the floor.
The second formula pays off much faster than a plain 2% because the 1% always reduces principal. Check your cardholder agreement to see which applies.
Ways to pay off faster
Pay a fixed amount, not the falling minimum. Keeping the payment at the first month's minimum cuts years off.
Pay more than once a month. Interest is charged on the daily balance, so earlier payments save interest.
Move the balance to a lower rate. A balance transfer card or a debt consolidation loan can help if the fees are low and you stop adding new debt.
Prioritize the highest APR if you have several cards (the avalanche method), or the smallest balance for motivation (the snowball method). The debt payoff calculator helps compare.
Ask the issuer for a lower rate. It costs nothing to ask, especially with a good payment record.
Country notes
United States: the CARD Act requires statements to show how long minimum-only payment would take and the cost, and what payment would clear the balance in 3 years. Most issuers offer a grace period on purchases if you pay the full statement balance by the due date.
Canada: the minimum payment for credit cards issued by federally regulated institutions must include interest and fees plus at least 1% of the balance [VERIFY current FCAC rule]. Quebec sets a higher minimum by law, rising to 5% of the balance [VERIFY phase-in schedule with the Office de la protection du consommateur].
United Kingdom: the minimum must cover at least interest, fees and 1% of the balance. Under FCA persistent debt rules, if you have paid more in interest and charges than principal over 18 months, your provider must contact you, and after 36 months offer a way to clear the balance faster. Card APRs are usually quoted as a representative APR.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the balance transfer rate as the APR. Use the rate that applies after any promotion ends.
Forgetting new spending. Every new purchase adds to the time and cost.
Ignoring fees. Late fees and over-limit fees make payoff slower.
Assuming the minimum is safe. It keeps you in good standing but is the most expensive way to repay.
Frequently asked questions
Why does paying the minimum take so long?
Because most of a small payment goes to interest, and on percentage-based minimums the payment falls as the balance falls, so principal shrinks very slowly.
How is credit card interest calculated?
Issuers apply a daily rate (APR ÷ 365 or 360) to the balance each day and add it up for the billing cycle. At 21.99%, the daily rate is about 0.0602%; on an average daily balance of $2,400 over 30 days, that is about $43.38 of interest.
Does this include new purchases?
No. It assumes the card is not used while you repay.
What does a 600-month result mean?
That the balance is not cleared within 50 years at these settings. Increase the payment percentage or floor, or use a fixed payment instead.
Will paying the minimum hurt my credit score?
Paying on time helps your payment history, but a high balance relative to your limit (utilization) can weigh on scores. Paying the balance down improves utilization.
Is a balance transfer worth it?
It can be, if the transfer fee is low, the promotional period is long enough, and you don't add new debt. Compare the fee with the interest you would save.

Title tag
Credit Card Payoff Calculator: Avalanche vs Snowball | FigSumo (62 chars)
Meta description
See how long credit card debt takes to pay off and the interest cost, compare fixed and minimum payments, and plan several cards with avalanche or snowball. (156 chars)
Country
global (US default)
Status
rename (301)
Body words
1,074 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Credit Card Payoff Calculator
Credit card interest is charged on whatever balance is left each month, so the payment you choose decides both how long the debt lasts and how much it costs. This calculator shows the payoff date and the total interest for a fixed monthly payment. It compares that with paying only the minimum, and for several cards it shows which order of repayment saves the most.
How to use this calculator
1. Single card: enter the balance, the APR and either the monthly payment you can afford or the number of months you want to be debt-free in.
2. Several cards: add each card's balance, APR and minimum payment. Then enter your total monthly budget for all cards.
3. Strategy for several cards: avalanche (highest APR first), snowball (smallest balance first) or a custom order.
4. Stop adding new purchases to the card while you use the plan, or include them as a monthly charge.
The formula
Most cards calculate interest daily on the average daily balance. A close monthly approximation is:
Interest_month = Balance × APR ÷ 12
New balance    = Balance + Interest_month − Payment
Repeat until the balance reaches zero. Total interest is the sum of every month's interest.
With a fixed payment P, the number of months has a closed form:
n = −ln(1 − B × r / P) / ln(1 + r),   r = APR ÷ 12
This only works if P is more than the first month's interest, B × r. If it isn't, the debt never shrinks.
Minimum payments are set by your card agreement. A common structure is "1% of the balance plus that month's interest, or $25 if higher". You can edit this in the calculator.
Worked examples
Example 1: one card, two payment levels. Balance $6,000, APR 22.99%, no new spending. First month's interest is 6,000 × 0.2299 ÷ 12 = $114.95.

Understanding your results
Payoff date and total interest: assumes the APR doesn't change and you add no new charges.
Monthly table: interest, payment, and the balance on each card.
Interest vs principal chart: shows how much of your money is going to interest at each stage.
Promotional rates: if a card has a 0% balance-transfer period, enter it with its end date. The calculator switches to the standard APR afterwards. Balance-transfer fees are entered separately.
Country notes
United States: card statements must show how long it would take to repay the balance making only minimum payments, and the monthly payment needed to repay it in 36 months. Compare those figures with this plan.
Canada: minimum payments and interest-free grace periods are set by the issuer within federal rules. Check your statement.
UK: card providers must take action if you are in persistent debt (paying more in interest and charges than principal over 18 months). Free debt advice is available from MoneyHelper.
Tips and common mistakes
Paying only the minimum. Example 1 shows how this stretches the debt over decades.
Closing paid-off cards immediately. It can raise your credit utilisation; consider keeping old cards open with no balance.
Missing the end of a 0% promotion. Any remaining balance then accrues interest at the standard rate.
Using the card while paying it off. New purchases can cancel out your extra payments.
Ignoring the highest rate. The avalanche method saves the most interest.
Frequently asked questions
Is avalanche or snowball better?
Avalanche always costs the same or less interest, because it targets the highest rate first. Snowball can help motivation by clearing small balances quickly. The calculator shows the cost difference for your cards.
Why does paying only the minimum take so long?
Because the minimum falls as the balance falls, and much of it goes to interest. In Example 1, the first minimum payment of $174.95 includes $114.95 of interest.
Should I consolidate or do a balance transfer?
A lower rate can reduce the cost if the fees and the rate after any promotion still beat your current APR, and if you don't add new debt. Use the debt consolidation calculator to compare.
Does the calculator use daily interest?
It uses a monthly approximation (APR ÷ 12). Daily-balance interest gives very similar totals for steady payments. Your statement is the exact figure.
What payment do I need to be debt-free in two years?
Choose "target months", enter 24, and the calculator returns the required payment. For the $6,000 card at 22.99%, it is about $314.21 a month.
Will paying off cards help my credit score?
Lower balances relative to your limits are generally viewed favourably by credit scoring models, but scoring formulas are proprietary and depend on many factors.

Currency Converter with Dated Exchange Rates | FigSumo (54 chars)
Meta description
Convert between USD, CAD, GBP, EUR and other currencies using a published reference rate, with the rate date and source shown on every result. (142 chars)

H1: Currency Converter
This converter changes an amount from one currency to another using exchange rates you enter. It works through the US dollar: you give the value of each currency per 1 USD, and it calculates the cross rate between them. That makes it handy for checking a bank's or card provider's rate against a published reference rate, budgeting a trip, or converting a price quoted abroad.
How to use this converter
1. Amount: the sum you want to convert, in the "from" currency.
2. From currency (units per 1 USD): how many units of your starting currency equal one US dollar. For US dollars, enter 1.
3. To currency (units per 1 USD): how many units of the target currency equal one US dollar.
Results: converted amount in the target currency and the amount in USD (estimate).
Where to get the rates: central banks publish daily reference rates, including the Federal Reserve (H.10 release), the Bank of Canada and the European Central Bank. Rates change throughout the day, so note the date of the rate you use. The tool does not fetch live rates.
The formula
Amount in USD = Amount ÷ From rate
Converted amount = Amount in USD × To rate
Cross rate (to per 1 from) = To rate ÷ From rate
Both rates are quoted against the dollar, so dividing one by the other gives the exchange rate between the two currencies directly.
Worked examples
The rates below are illustrations, not current market rates.
Example 1: CAD to GBP through the dollar
Suppose 1 USD = 1.38 CAD and 1 USD = 0.75 GBP. Convert C$500:
Amount in USD = 500 ÷ 1.38 = $362.32
Converted = $362.32 × 0.75 = £271.74
Cross rate: 0.75 ÷ 1.38 = 0.5435 GBP per CAD
Example 2: how much a card's exchange margin costs
You spend US$1,000 on a trip. At a mid-market rate of 1.38 CAD per USD, that is C$1,380.00. A provider whose rate is 2.5% worse than mid-market gives you only C$1,345.50 of value for the same Canadian dollars, a hidden cost of C$34.50. Enter the provider's rate and the reference rate to see the gap for your own amounts.
Converting the other way
To go from USD to another currency, enter 1 as the "from" rate. To find how many dollars one unit of a currency buys, divide 1 by its rate: at 1.38 CAD per USD, one Canadian dollar is 0.7246 USD.
Understanding your results
Converted amount uses exactly the rates you entered. If you entered mid-market rates, your bank or exchange bureau will usually give you less.
Amount in USD is an intermediate step; it is useful if you also want the dollar value.
Rates move. A conversion is only valid for the moment of the rate you used.
Mid-market, buy and sell rates
The mid-market rate is halfway between the prices at which banks buy and sell a currency. Consumers rarely get it. Providers make money through:
a margin (spread) built into the rate, often the largest cost;
fees, fixed or percentage-based;
dynamic currency conversion, where a shop or ATM abroad offers to charge you in your home currency. Its rate is usually worse; choosing the local currency is normally cheaper.
To compare offers, convert the same amount at each provider's rate after fees and see which gives the most foreign currency.
Budgeting a trip or purchase abroad
For travel, convert your daily budget at a cautious rate, about 3% worse than the reference rate, so card margins and ATM fees don't push you over. For a large purchase or a transfer (a house deposit, tuition, a car), small rate differences matter: 1% of $50,000 is $500. Get quotes from two or three providers on the same day, convert the same amount with each provider's rate here, and subtract their fees before choosing.
Country notes
United States: the Federal Reserve publishes noon buying rates in the H.10 release (weekly) for many currencies. Remittance transfers abroad must disclose the exchange rate and fees under the CFPB's Remittance Rule.
Canada: the Bank of Canada publishes daily average exchange rates, which the CRA accepts for converting foreign income on tax returns.
United Kingdom: the Bank of England publishes daily spot rates, and HMRC publishes monthly exchange rates for customs and VAT purposes.
Tips and common mistakes
Rate the wrong way round. Rates here are units per 1 USD. If a site shows "1 CAD = 0.72 USD", convert it: 1 ÷ 0.72 = 1.389 CAD per USD.
Mixing a buy rate with a sell rate. Use the same type of rate for both currencies.
Ignoring fees. Add fixed fees in the original currency before converting.
Old rates. Note the date. A rate from last month can be several percent off.
Frequently asked questions
Does this converter use live rates?
No. You enter the rates, so you control which reference you compare against. Central bank websites publish daily rates.
Why convert through US dollars?
Most rates are quoted against the dollar, so it is the easiest common reference. The cross rate between any two currencies follows from their dollar rates.
What is the mid-market rate?
The midpoint between the buy and sell prices on the wholesale market. It is the fairest benchmark for comparing what a provider charges.
Why did my bank give me a different amount?
Banks add a margin to the rate and may charge fees. The converter shows the result at the rate you entered, without fees.
How do I convert a price into my currency?
Enter the foreign price as the amount, its currency's per-USD rate as the "from" rate, and your currency's per-USD rate as the "to" rate.
Which rate should I use for tax purposes?
Use the rate your tax authority specifies: in the US, the IRS accepts yearly average or spot rates; in Canada, the Bank of Canada rate; in the UK, HMRC's published rates where they apply.

Debt Consolidation Calculator: Is One Loan Cheaper? | FigSumo (61 chars)
Meta description
Compare your current debts with a single consolidation loan, including fees. See the change in monthly payment, total interest and payoff time. (143 chars)

H1: Debt Consolidation Calculator
Debt consolidation replaces several debts with one new loan, ideally at a lower interest rate. This calculator compares your current path (keep paying what you pay now until the debts are gone) with taking a consolidation loan for a set term. It shows the new monthly payment, how long your current plan would take, the interest under each option and the estimated saving.
How to use this calculator
1. Total existing debt: the sum of the balances you want to consolidate, such as credit cards, store cards and personal loans.
2. Current weighted APR: the average rate across those debts, weighted by balance (see the example below for how to work it out).
3. Current total monthly payment: what you pay across all of them each month now.
4. Consolidation loan APR: the rate offered on the new loan. Use the APR, so fees are included where possible.
5. New loan term (years): the repayment period of the consolidation loan.
Results: new monthly payment, old payoff time, interest on the current path, interest with consolidation and interest savings (estimate).
The formula
Current path: the calculator steps through each month, charging interest at the weighted APR and subtracting your current payment until the balance reaches zero.
Interest = Balance × (Weighted APR ÷ 12);  Balance = Balance + Interest − Payment
Consolidation loan: a standard fixed payment,
PMT = D × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n),   interest = PMT × n − D
D: total debt; r: new APR ÷ 12; n: term in months
Savings = current-path interest − consolidation interest
Weighted APR = Σ(balance × APR) ÷ Σ balance.
Worked examples
Example 1: $15,000 at 18%, paying $450 a month, vs a 9.5% 5-year loan
Current path: 47 months, interest $5,950.81
Consolidation: $315.03 a month for 60 months, interest $3,901.68
Estimated saving: $2,049.14, and a lower monthly payment
Note the trade-off: the current path finishes sooner, but costs more interest. If you kept paying $450 a month on the new loan, you would clear it even faster and save more.
Example 2: three debts into one loan at 10.99% over 4 years
Debt
Balance
APR
Payment
Card A
$6,000

$180

Total debt $15,000.00; total payment $450.00
Weighted APR = (6,000 × 24.99 + 3,500 × 19.99 + 5,500 × 11.5) ÷ 15,000 = 18.88%
Current path: 48 months, interest $6,424.79
New loan: $387.61 a month, interest $3,605.28
Saving: $2,819.51
Understanding your results
New monthly payment is principal and interest on the consolidation loan.
Old payoff time is how long your current payment would take, assuming no new spending and the weighted APR staying constant.
Interest savings compares total interest only. It is an estimate: individual debts with different rates pay down in a different order in real life, and the weighted APR is an approximation.
When consolidation costs more
A longer term. The same $15,000 at 9.5% over 7 years cuts the payment to $245.16 but costs $5,593.42 of interest, more than the 5-year loan.
Fees. An origination fee of 5% added to the loan raises the payment to $330.78 and interest to $4,846.76 over 5 years. Add any fee to "Total existing debt" if it is financed, or compare APRs.
Running the cards back up. If the cleared cards fill up again, you end up with the loan and new card debt.
Secured consolidation. Using a home equity loan or remortgage can get a low rate, but it turns unsecured debt into debt secured on your home.
Country notes
United States: consolidation is usually a personal loan or a 0% balance transfer card. Non-profit credit counseling agencies offer debt management plans that can lower card rates without a new loan. The CFPB and FTC warn about debt settlement firms charging upfront fees.
Canada: banks and credit unions offer consolidation loans and lines of credit. A consumer proposal through a Licensed Insolvency Trustee is a formal alternative for serious debt.
United Kingdom: consolidation loans are regulated by the FCA, and lenders must check affordability. Free advice from MoneyHelper, StepChange or Citizens Advice can help you choose between a loan, a debt management plan or other options.
Tips and common mistakes
Compare APR and total cost, not just the monthly payment.
Keep the term short enough to beat your current payoff time, if you can afford the payment.
Close or freeze the cleared cards if you are tempted to reuse them, keeping in mind that closing old accounts can affect credit scores.
Check early repayment terms on the old debts and the new loan.
Frequently asked questions
Does debt consolidation hurt your credit score?
Applying causes a hard credit check, which may lower a score slightly for a while. Over time, lower card balances and on-time payments can help.
How do I calculate a weighted APR?
Multiply each balance by its APR, add the results, and divide by the total balance.
Is a lower monthly payment a good sign?
Not on its own. A lower payment over a longer term can cost more in total. Look at the interest figures.
What credit score do I need for a consolidation loan?
Lenders set their own criteria. Better credit usually means a lower rate; prequalification tools can show likely rates without a hard check.
Should I use a balance transfer card instead?
If the balance can be cleared within the 0% period and the transfer fee is lower than the interest saved, it can be cheaper. After the promotion, the rate jumps.
Can I consolidate student loans with this?
You can model the numbers, but government student loans have their own consolidation programs and protections that private loans do not.

Debt Payoff Calculator: Time and Interest to Debt-Free | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Find how long it takes to repay a debt at a fixed monthly payment, or the payment needed to be debt-free by a target date. (122 chars)
Country
global

1,021 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Debt Payoff Calculator
This calculator tells you how many months it will take to clear a debt with a fixed monthly payment, and how much interest you will pay along the way. It works for credit cards, personal loans, overdrafts, medical bills or any balance that charges interest. Change the payment to see how much time and money a larger payment saves.
How to use this calculator
1. Debt balance: what you owe today. Use the payoff figure from your lender if it differs from the statement balance.
2. APR: the annual interest rate on the debt, from your statement or loan agreement.
3. Monthly payment: the fixed amount you will pay every month. It must be more than one month's interest, or the debt will never shrink.
Results: months to payoff and total interest. The calculator assumes no new borrowing on the debt.
The formula
The calculator steps through each month:
Interest = Balance × APR ÷ 12
Balance = Balance + Interest − Payment
It counts months until the balance reaches zero (the last payment is smaller). There's also a direct formula for the number of payments:
n = −ln(1 − B × r ÷ PMT) ÷ ln(1 + r)
B: balance; r: APR ÷ 12; PMT: monthly payment
If PMT ≤ B × r, the logarithm is undefined: the payment never covers the interest.
Worked examples
Example 1: $8,000 at 12% with $250 a month
First month's interest: 8,000 × 0.01 = $80, so $170 reduces the balance
Months to payoff: 39
Total interest: $1,689.92
Raising the payment to $350 clears it in 27 months with $1,128.36 of interest, a saving of $561.56.
To be debt-free in 24 months instead, you would need to pay about $376.59 a month (the standard loan payment formula).
Example 2: $3,200 on a card at 24.99% with $120 a month
First month's interest: $66.64
Months to payoff: 40; total interest: $1,518.67
A high APR means a large share of each early payment goes to interest. This is why high-rate debts are usually the ones to clear first.
Understanding your results
Months to payoff assumes the rate stays the same and you make every payment on time.
Total interest is the extra you pay on top of the balance. Compare it across payment amounts to see the value of paying more.
"Payment must exceed monthly interest" means your payment doesn't even cover interest. Increase it, or look at a lower rate.
Paying off several debts: avalanche vs snowball
The calculator handles one debt at a time. With several, keep making the minimum on all of them and put every spare dollar towards one target:
Avalanche: target the highest APR first. This minimizes total interest.
Snowball: target the smallest balance first. You clear accounts sooner, which many people find motivating.
When the target is paid off, roll its whole payment into the next one. To plan this here, run each debt in turn: work out how long the first takes, then add its payment to the next debt from that month on.
Other ways to cut the cost
Consolidate high-rate debts into a single lower-rate loan; compare totals with the debt consolidation calculator.
Balance transfer to a 0% card, if the fee and promotional period make sense and you stop using the old card.
Negotiate. Lenders may lower rates or agree a payment plan, especially if you are struggling.
Find the money. The budget calculator shows where extra payments could come from.
Country notes
United States: non-profit credit counseling agencies (look for NFCC membership) can set up debt management plans. Debt settlement companies may charge high fees; the FTC warns about upfront-fee scams.
Canada: non-profit credit counselling is available, and formal options include a consumer proposal or bankruptcy through a Licensed Insolvency Trustee, regulated by the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy.
United Kingdom: free debt advice is available through MoneyHelper, StepChange, National Debtline and Citizens Advice. Formal options include debt management plans, IVAs and, in England and Wales, Debt Relief Orders, with the Breathing Space scheme pausing most enforcement for 60 days.
Tips and common mistakes
Stop adding to the debt. New charges undo the plan.
Automate the payment so it happens every month.
Keep a small emergency fund, or the next surprise bill goes on the card.
Check for prepayment penalties on loans before paying extra.
Don't ignore the smallest debts with fees. A debt that incurs a monthly fee can cost more than its APR suggests.
Frequently asked questions
How do I find out how long it will take to pay off my debt?
Enter the balance, APR and the amount you will pay each month. The calculator gives the number of months and total interest.
What if my payment is less than the interest?
The debt will grow. Increase the payment, ask the lender for a lower rate or seek free debt advice.
Is it better to pay off debt or save?
Paying off a high-interest debt is often a guaranteed "return" equal to its APR. Many people still keep a small emergency fund first so they don't need to borrow again.
Should I use the avalanche or snowball method?
Avalanche saves the most interest; snowball can be easier to stick with. The best method is the one you will follow.
Does this work for a mortgage or car loan?
Yes, for the time and interest of a fixed payment. For a full schedule, use the loan calculator.
Can I see a payment plan to finish by a date?
Not directly yet. Example 1 shows the formula; the loan calculator can find the payment for a given term.

Title tag
Debt-to-Income (DTI) Ratio Calculator | FigSumo (47 chars)
Meta description
Calculate front-end and back-end debt-to-income ratios from gross income and monthly debts, as lenders do when reviewing a mortgage or loan. (140 chars)
Country
global
Status
rename (301)
Body words
1,049 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Debt-to-Income Ratio Calculator
Your debt-to-income ratio (DTI) is the share of your gross monthly income that goes to debt payments. Lenders use it to judge whether you can take on a new loan, especially a mortgage. This calculator gives two versions: the front-end ratio (housing costs only) and the back-end ratio (housing plus all other debts).
How to use this calculator
1. Monthly gross income: income before tax and deductions. For a salary, divide the annual figure by 12. Include regular, documentable income such as bonuses, self-employment profit or benefits if a lender would count them. With a co-borrower, add both incomes.
2. Monthly housing payment: rent, or the mortgage payment including property tax, homeowners insurance, mortgage insurance and HOA dues if you're testing a mortgage application. Your Loan Estimate shows the full monthly figure.
3. Other monthly debt payments: minimum payments on credit cards, car loans, student loans, personal loans, child support and other recurring debts that appear on a credit report or court order. Don't include utilities, groceries, insurance premiums or phone bills.
Results: front-end DTI (housing) and back-end DTI (all debts), as percentages.
The formula
Front-end DTI = Housing payment ÷ Gross monthly income × 100
Back-end DTI  = (Housing payment + Other debt payments) ÷ Gross monthly income × 100
The CFPB defines DTI as all monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, which is the back-end ratio here.
Worked examples
Example 1: income $8,000, housing $1,800, other debts $600
Front-end = 1,800 ÷ 8,000 = 22.5%
Back-end = (1,800 + 600) ÷ 8,000 = 30.0%
Example 2: $72,000 salary, planned mortgage $1,650, car $420, student loan $250, card minimum $95
Gross monthly income = 72,000 ÷ 12 = $6,000.00
Other debts = $765.00
Front-end = 27.5%; back-end = 40.2%
At a 36% back-end ceiling (a commonly used rule of thumb, not a legal limit), total debts could be up to $2,160.00, leaving −$255.00 of headroom
Paying off the car loan before applying would bring the back-end ratio down to 33.2%
Understanding your results
Lower is better. A lower DTI means more of your income is free after debt payments, which lenders read as lower risk.
There is no single cut-off. As the CFPB notes, different loan products and lenders have different DTI limits. Rules of thumb you'll see include 28% front-end and 36% back-end for conventional loans; government-backed loans and automated underwriting can accept higher ratios when other factors are strong [VERIFY current FHA/Fannie Mae limits before citing figures].
DTI is only one factor. Credit history, down payment, savings (reserves) and employment stability also matter.
It ignores living costs. A DTI that a lender accepts can still be tight for your budget. Check the result in the budget calculator.
How to lower your DTI
Pay down or pay off a debt with a high monthly payment, such as a car loan.
Avoid new credit before applying for a mortgage.
Look at a cheaper home or larger down payment, which lowers the housing payment.
Add a co-borrower's income, if they will share responsibility for the loan.
Refinance or consolidate to lower monthly payments, keeping in mind that a longer term can cost more interest.
What lenders count as income and debt
Lenders count income they can verify and expect to continue: salary on pay stubs and W-2s or T4s, two-year averages of bonuses, overtime and self-employment profit (after business expenses), pensions, and some benefits. One-off payments and cash income without records usually don't count. On the debt side, they take the payments from your credit report plus the proposed housing payment. A card you pay off in full each month can still count at its minimum payment if a balance is reported. Before applying, pull your credit reports so you know exactly what a lender will see.
Country notes
United States: DTI is central to mortgage underwriting. Qualified Mortgage rules, FHA, VA and the guidelines of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac each treat DTI differently. VA loans also use a "residual income" test.
Canada: lenders use the Gross Debt Service (GDS) ratio (housing costs including property tax, heating and half of condo fees, divided by gross income) and the Total Debt Service (TDS) ratio (GDS plus other debts). For insured mortgages the commonly cited limits are 39% GDS and 44% TDS [VERIFY with CMHC]. Payments are tested at the higher of the contract rate plus 2% or 5.25% under the OSFI stress test. See the Canadian mortgage affordability calculator.
United Kingdom: lenders focus on affordability assessments under FCA rules and loan-to-income limits (the Bank of England limits how many mortgages lenders can make at 4.5 times income or more). DTI-style ratios appear in lender calculations but are rarely quoted to borrowers.
Tips and common mistakes
Using net instead of gross income. DTI uses gross (pre-tax) income.
Leaving out the full housing cost. Include property tax, insurance and HOA dues, not just principal and interest.
Counting the full card balance. Use the minimum monthly payment shown on the statement.
Forgetting co-signed loans. Lenders usually count them as your debt.
Frequently asked questions
What is a good debt-to-income ratio?
Lower is better. Many lenders are comfortable with a back-end ratio in the 30s or below, but limits vary by lender and loan type.
Is DTI based on gross or net income?
Gross income, before taxes and deductions.
Do utilities and insurance count as debt?
No. Only debt payments and housing costs count. Homeowners insurance is included as part of the housing payment for a mortgage.
What is the difference between front-end and back-end DTI?
Front-end includes only housing costs. Back-end includes housing plus all other monthly debt payments.
Does DTI affect my credit score?
No. Credit scores don't use income. But lenders look at DTI alongside your score.
How do I calculate DTI with irregular income?
Lenders usually average two years of documented income for self-employment or variable pay. Use a cautious monthly average.

Depreciation Calculator: Straight-Line & Declining | FigSumo (60 chars)

H1: Depreciation Calculator
Depreciation spreads the cost of an asset (a vehicle, machine, computer or building) over the years you use it. This calculator uses the straight-line method: the same amount is written off each year until the asset reaches its salvage value. Enter the cost, the salvage value and the useful life to get the annual and monthly depreciation.
How to use this calculator
1. Asset cost: what you paid to acquire the asset and get it ready for use, including delivery and installation.
2. Salvage value: what you expect it to be worth at the end of its useful life (resale or scrap value). Enter 0 if you expect nothing.
3. Useful life (years): how long you expect to use the asset. Accounting policies or tax rules often set typical lives by asset class.
Results: straight-line annual depreciation, monthly depreciation, and book value after full life (which equals the salvage value).
The formula
Annual depreciation = (Cost − Salvage value) ÷ Useful life
Monthly depreciation = Annual depreciation ÷ 12
Book value after t years = Cost − t × Annual depreciation
Cost − Salvage is the depreciable amount.
Book value is the asset's carrying value in the accounts, not its market value.
Worked examples
Example 1: $50,000 machine, $5,000 salvage, 7 years
Depreciable amount = 50,000 − 5,000 = $45,000
Annual depreciation = 45,000 ÷ 7 = $6,428.57
Monthly = $535.71
Book value after 3 years = $30,714.29; after 7 years = $5,000.00
Example 2: comparing methods on a $12,000 asset (done by hand)
Cost $12,000, salvage $2,000, life 5 years.
Straight-line: $2,000.00 every year.
Double-declining balance (rate = 2 ÷ 5 = 40% of the opening book value, stopping at salvage):

Sum-of-the-years' digits: the digits 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15, so year 1 is 5/15 of $10,000 = $3,333.33, falling to 1/15 = $666.67 in year 5.
All three write off the same $10,000 in total; they differ only in timing. Accelerated methods put more expense in the early years, which matches assets like vehicles and computers that lose value fastest when new.
Part-year example
If the Example 1 machine is put into service on 1 April, it is used for 9 months of the first financial year (to 31 December). A prorated first-year charge is $6,428.57 × 9 ÷ 12 = $4,821.43. Depreciation then continues at the full annual amount, and the remaining 3 months fall into an eighth year. The calculator gives the full-year figure, so prorate the first and last years yourself.
Understanding your results
Annual depreciation is the expense recorded each year. It is not a cash payment; the cash was spent when you bought the asset.
Monthly depreciation is useful for monthly management accounts.
Book value falls in a straight line to the salvage value. It can differ widely from what the asset would sell for.
Accounting depreciation vs tax depreciation
Businesses usually keep two sets of figures:
Financial statements use a method that reflects how the asset is used up (straight-line is the most common), under GAAP, IFRS or the relevant standards.
Tax returns follow the tax authority's rules, which can be quite different and often faster.
The calculator gives the accounting straight-line figure. For tax, use the rules for your country:
Country notes
United States: most business property placed in service after 1986 is depreciated for tax using MACRS, with recovery periods and conventions set out in IRS Publication 946. Section 179 expensing and bonus depreciation can allow much faster write-offs; check current limits and percentages for the tax year [VERIFY 2026 Section 179 limit and bonus depreciation rate].
Canada: the CRA uses capital cost allowance (CCA): assets are grouped into classes, each with a prescribed declining-balance rate, and a half-year rule usually applies in the year of purchase. Accelerated investment incentives have applied to some classes [VERIFY current status].
United Kingdom: depreciation in the accounts is not deductible for tax. Instead, businesses claim capital allowances, such as the Annual Investment Allowance (£1 million a year) and full expensing for companies on qualifying new plant and machinery [VERIFY against GOV.UK for 2026/27].
Tips and common mistakes
Using market value as salvage without thought. Salvage is your best estimate at the end of the useful life, not today's resale value.
Depreciating land. Land is generally not depreciated; separate it from the building's cost.
Mixing tax and book figures. Use the right method for the right purpose.
Forgetting part-year use. If you buy an asset mid-year, the first year's depreciation is often prorated by months.
Frequently asked questions
What is straight-line depreciation?
A method that spreads the depreciable amount (cost minus salvage) evenly over the asset's useful life.
How do I choose a useful life?
Base it on how long you realistically expect to use the asset. Accounting policies often set standard lives for each asset type; tax rules prescribe their own.
Can salvage value be zero?
Yes. Then the full cost is depreciated over the useful life.
Which depreciation method is best?
For financial reporting, the one that best reflects how the asset's benefits are used up. Straight-line is simplest; declining-balance fits assets that lose value quickly early on.
How do I depreciate a rental property?
In the US, residential rental buildings are depreciated over 27.5 years using straight-line under MACRS (land excluded). Canada and the UK use different rules. See the rental property calculator for returns.
Is depreciation a cash expense?
No. It allocates a past cash outlay over time, which is why it is added back in cash-flow calculations.
What is accumulated depreciation?
The total depreciation charged on an asset so far. Cost minus accumulated depreciation equals book value. After 3 years, the Example 1 machine has accumulated 3 × $6,428.57 of depreciation.

Title tag
Discount Calculator: Sale Price & Percent Off | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Find the sale price after a percentage or fixed discount, the amount saved, or the discount rate from original and sale prices. (127 chars)
Country

H1: Discount Calculator
This discount calculator gives the sale price and the amount you save when an item is reduced by a percentage. Enter the original price and the discount percent. It is quick for checking shelf tags, comparing deals, or working out a price for a sale you are running.
How to use this calculator
1. Original price: the regular price before the discount, without tax.
2. Discount: the percentage off, e.g. 25 for "25% off".
Results: sale price and you save (the discount in money).
The formula
You save   = Original price × Discount% ÷ 100
Sale price = Original price − You save  =  Original price × (1 − Discount% ÷ 100)
Worked examples
Example 1: $89.99 at 25% off
You save = 89.99 × 0.25 = $22.50
Sale price = 89.99 − 22.50 = $67.49
(The saving is 22.4975, which rounds to $22.50.)
Example 2: stacked discounts
A $120 jacket is 30% off, and you have a coupon for an extra 10% off the sale price.
After 30%: 120 × 0.70 = $84.00
After the extra 10%: 84 × 0.90 = $75.60
The combined discount is 37%, not 40%, because the second discount applies to the already-reduced price.
To do this in the calculator, run it twice: first with 30%, then enter the sale price as the new original price with 10%. If 8.25% sales tax applies at the register, the final cost is $81.84.
Example 3: "$15 off" or "20% off"?
On an $80 purchase:
$15 off: you pay $65.00
20% off: 80 × 0.80 = $64.00
The percentage wins here by $1.00. The break-even price is 15 ÷ 0.20 = $75: below $75, the fixed $15 is the better deal.
Example 4: a discount and then tax in Ontario
A $150 item at 20% off costs $120.00 before tax. Ontario's 13% HST is charged on the discounted price: 120 × 1.13 = $135.60.
Example 5: a UK sale price with VAT included
A £60 item (VAT included) is 25% off, so you pay £45.00. The VAT inside that price is 45 ÷ 6 = £7.50, because at the 20% standard rate VAT is one sixth of a VAT-inclusive price.

Understanding your results
Sale price is before sales tax or VAT, unless the original price already included tax (as UK and EU shelf prices do).
You save is the money discount. Big percentages on cheap items may save less than small percentages on expensive ones.
Other discount questions, solved by hand
Find the original price from a sale price: original = sale price ÷ (1 − discount). A $51 item marked "40% off" was originally $85.00.
Find the percent off from two prices: discount% = (original − sale) ÷ original × 100. $60 reduced by $15 is 25% off.
Buy one, get one free: you pay for one item and get two, an effective 50% discount per item, but only if you wanted two.
Buy one, get one half price: 25% off the pair.
Country notes
United States: shelf prices usually exclude sales tax, which is added at checkout on the discounted price. Manufacturer coupons can be taxed differently from store coupons in some states [VERIFY your state's rule].
Canada: prices are usually shown before GST/HST and PST, which are charged on the discounted price.
United Kingdom: displayed prices for consumers must include VAT. "Was/now" price claims must be genuine under the CMA's pricing guidance and consumer protection law; a "was" price should be one at which the item was actually sold for a meaningful period.
Tips and common mistakes
Adding stacked discounts together. 20% + 20% is 36% off, not 40%.
Comparing percent with amount off. "$10 off" beats "15% off" only for prices under about $66.67.
Forgetting shipping. A bigger discount can be cancelled out by delivery charges.
Trusting inflated "was" prices. Check the price history if you can.
Discounting tax-inclusive prices. In the UK, the discount applies to the VAT-inclusive price, and the VAT is reduced proportionally.
If you're the one offering the discount
A discount cuts profit by more than the percentage suggests. Suppose an item sells for $100 and costs you $60, leaving $40 of gross profit:
At 20% off, the price is $80 and the profit $20, half what it was.
To earn the same $40 total profit, you'd need to sell 2 items instead of 1.
At 10% off, profit is $30, so you'd need 1.33 times the sales volume to break even.
The rule: required sales multiple = old margin ÷ (old margin − discount), with both as percentages of the original price. With a 40% margin and a 20% discount, 40 ÷ 20 = 2. Check this before running a sale, and count any extra costs such as card fees and shipping.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate a discount?
Multiply the price by the discount percentage and divide by 100. Subtract that from the price to get the sale price.
How do I calculate 20% off?
Multiply the price by 0.80. For $45, that is $36.
Are two 25% discounts the same as 50% off?
No. Two 25% discounts give 43.75% off (0.75 × 0.75 = 0.5625 of the price).
How do I work out the original price?
Divide the sale price by (1 − discount as a decimal). For 30% off, divide by 0.70.
Is sales tax charged before or after the discount?
For store discounts, usually after, on the reduced price. Rules for manufacturer coupons and rebates vary.
What is the difference between a discount and a markdown?
A markdown is a permanent price reduction by the seller; a discount can be temporary or tied to a coupon or customer group. The maths is the same.

This discount calculator is for general information. Prices, tax treatment and retailer terms vary; check the final price at checkout.

Down Payment Calculator: How Much to Put Down | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Work out the down payment, loan amount and closing cash for a home price, and how much home a given down payment supports. (122 chars)
Country
global

1,028 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Down Payment Calculator
This calculator converts a down payment percentage into a dollar amount and shows the mortgage you would need for the rest of the price. Enter the home price and the percentage you plan to put down. Use it to set a savings target, check whether you will need mortgage insurance, or compare 5%, 10% and 20% down on the same home.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price: the purchase price you expect to pay, or a list price you are considering.
2. Down payment percent: the share of the price you will pay from your own funds, e.g. 5, 10 or 20.
Results: down payment amount and loan amount.
The formula
Down payment = Price × Down% ÷ 100
Loan amount  = Price − Down payment
Loan-to-value (LTV) = Loan amount ÷ Price × 100 = 100 − Down%
LTV matters because lenders price loans and require mortgage insurance based on it.
Worked examples
Example 1: $400,000 home, 20% down
Down payment = 400,000 × 0.20 = $80,000.00
Loan amount = $320,000.00; LTV = 80%
At 20% down, a conventional US mortgage normally needs no private mortgage insurance.
Saving $80,000.00 at $1,500 a month in an account earning 4% a year (compounded monthly) would take about 50 months (4.1 years). The savings calculator runs this for your own figures.
Example 2: $350,000 home at different percentages

$315,000.00

$280,000.00
Working backwards from the cash you have
If you have $60,000 and expect closing costs of about 3% of the price, and you want to put 10% down, the highest price you can cover is 60,000 ÷ (0.10 + 0.03) = $461,538.46 (down payment $46,153.85, closing costs $13,846.15). The calculator doesn't do this step yet, but the arithmetic is quick.
Understanding your results
Down payment amount is cash due at closing, on top of closing costs (which in the US often run a few percent of the price; see the closing cost calculator).
Loan amount is what you borrow before any financed fees. Use it in the mortgage calculator to get the monthly payment.
Bigger down payment: smaller loan, lower payment, less interest, and usually no mortgage insurance.
Smaller down payment: buy sooner and keep a cash cushion, but pay more interest and insurance.
Where the money can come from
Common sources are savings, proceeds from selling a current home, gifts from family, and some retirement or tax-advantaged accounts. Each comes with rules. Lenders want to see where large deposits came from, usually through two or more months of bank statements, so avoid moving money around just before you apply. Borrowed money (for example, a personal loan) generally can't be used as a down payment on a conventional mortgage, and it would raise your debt-to-income ratio anyway. Down payment assistance programs, run by some states, provinces and cities, can help first-time buyers with grants or deferred loans.
Country notes
United States
Conventional loans can allow as little as 3% down for some first-time buyers; FHA loans 3.5% with a qualifying credit score; VA and USDA loans can need nothing down for eligible borrowers [VERIFY current program minimums].
With less than 20% down on a conventional loan, lenders usually require private mortgage insurance (PMI). Under CFPB guidance, you can ask to cancel PMI once the balance reaches 80% of the original value, and it ends automatically at 78% (for most loans closed on or after 29 July 1999). Estimate it with the PMI calculator.
Canada
Minimum down payments are set by federal rules (FCAC):
up to $500,000: 5%;
$500,000 to under $1.5 million: 5% of the first $500,000 plus 10% of the rest;
$1.5 million or more: 20%.
For an $800,000 home, the minimum is C$55,000.00 (6.88% of the price). With less than 20% down, mortgage default insurance is required; see the CMHC insurance calculator. First-time buyers can use an FHSA or the RRSP Home Buyers' Plan towards the deposit.
United Kingdom
UK buyers call it a deposit. Mortgages are commonly offered from 5% or 10% deposit, with better rates at 25% and 40% (loan-to-value bands of 75% and 60%). The Lifetime ISA adds a 25% government bonus on up to £4,000 a year for first-time buyers, with a £450,000 property price cap [VERIFY cap]. Budget separately for Stamp Duty Land Tax in England and Northern Ireland (see the stamp duty calculator).
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting closing costs. The down payment isn't the only cash you need.
Emptying your savings. Keep an emergency fund after closing; new homes bring unexpected bills.
Ignoring gift rules. Lenders usually need a gift letter for money from family.
Choosing 20% at any cost. Waiting years to save 20% can cost more than mortgage insurance if prices rise; compare both paths.
Frequently asked questions
Do I need 20% down to buy a house?
No. Many loans accept less, but in the US you'll usually pay mortgage insurance below 20% on a conventional loan, and in Canada insurance is required below 20%.
What is the minimum down payment in Canada?
5% on the first $500,000, 10% on the portion from $500,000 to $1.5 million, and 20% at $1.5 million or more.
Does the down payment include closing costs?
No. Closing costs are separate and are paid at closing in addition to the down payment.
What is loan-to-value?
The loan amount as a percentage of the property's value. 20% down equals 80% LTV.
Can I use gift money?
Usually yes, with documentation. Rules depend on the lender and loan program.
Is a bigger down payment always better?
It lowers your payment and interest, but tying up all your cash can leave you exposed. Balance the down payment with an emergency fund.

Title tag
FHA Loan Calculator with Upfront & Annual MIP | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Estimate an FHA mortgage payment including upfront and annual mortgage insurance premium, property tax and homeowners insurance. (128 chars)
Country
US
Status

1,026 (minimum 1,000)
H1: FHA Loan Calculator
FHA loans are US mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration, popular with first-time buyers because they allow a small down payment and more flexible credit standards. This calculator estimates the monthly payment on an FHA loan, including the two kinds of FHA mortgage insurance: the upfront mortgage insurance premium (UFMIP), which is usually added to the loan, and the annual MIP, which is paid monthly.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price: the purchase price.
2. Down payment (%): FHA's minimum is 3.5% with a credit score of 580 or higher, and 10% with a score from 500 to 579 [VERIFY in HUD Handbook 4000.1].
3. Base interest rate: the note rate on your Loan Estimate.
4. Term (years): usually 30 or 15.
5. Upfront MIP (%): a percentage of the base loan; 1.75% for most forward purchase loans [VERIFY]. The calculator adds it to the loan balance, which is how most borrowers pay it.
6. Annual MIP (%): a yearly percentage of the loan, divided into monthly payments. For most 30-year loans with less than 5% down it is 0.55% [VERIFY HUD Mortgagee Letter 2023-05 table].
Results: base loan, loan with upfront MIP, principal and interest (P&I) payment, estimated monthly MIP and total monthly (estimate).
The formula
Base loan        = Price × (1 − Down% ÷ 100)
UFMIP            = Base loan × Upfront MIP%
Loan with UFMIP  = Base loan + UFMIP
P&I              = L × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n),  L = loan with UFMIP, r = rate ÷ 12, n = years × 12
Monthly MIP      ≈ Base loan × Annual MIP% ÷ 12
Total monthly    = P&I + Monthly MIP
HUD calculates annual MIP on the average outstanding balance for each year, so the real premium falls slightly each year. The calculator uses the base loan, which gives the first-year figure.
Worked examples
Example 1: $300,000 home, 3.5% down, 6.5%, 30 years
Down payment: $10,500.00; base loan $289,500.00
UFMIP at 1.75%: $5,066.25, financed → loan $294,566.25
P&I: $1,861.86
Annual MIP at 0.55%: $132.69 a month
Total: $1,994.55 a month, before property tax and insurance
Example 2: $250,000 home, 10% down, 6.0%, 15 years
Base loan $225,000.00; UFMIP $3,937.50; loan $228,937.50
P&I: $1,931.90
With 10% down on a 15-year loan, the annual MIP rate is much lower (0.15% in the 2023 table [VERIFY]): $28.12 a month
Total: $1,960.03 a month
Understanding your results
P&I is the loan payment. It is calculated on the loan including the financed UFMIP, so you pay interest on the premium too.
Monthly MIP is the FHA insurance premium. It protects the lender, not you.
Total monthly excludes property tax, homeowners insurance and any HOA dues. Add these for the full housing payment lenders use in debt-to-income checks.
How long you pay MIP
For FHA loans with case numbers assigned since June 2013, annual MIP lasts for the life of the loan if your original down payment was under 10%, and for 11 years if it was 10% or more [VERIFY in HUD Mortgagee Letter 2013-04 and later letters]. Many borrowers remove MIP by refinancing into a conventional loan once they have about 20% equity. Conventional PMI, by contrast, can be cancelled at 80% LTV and ends automatically at 78% (CFPB). Compare with the PMI calculator.
FHA requirements in brief
Loan limits vary by county and are updated every year; check HUD's FHA mortgage limits lookup.
Property standards: the home must be appraised by an FHA-approved appraiser and meet minimum property requirements.
Primary residence: FHA loans are for homes you live in.
Debt-to-income: FHA allows higher ratios than many conventional loans when other factors compensate [VERIFY current limits].
Seller concessions: sellers can contribute toward closing costs up to a limit.
FHA or conventional?
FHA often suits borrowers with lower credit scores or small down payments, because its rates and insurance don't rise as steeply with lower scores. Borrowers with strong credit and 5% or more down often pay less with a conventional loan, mainly because PMI can be cancelled. Run both: this calculator for FHA, and the mortgage calculator plus PMI for conventional.
Country notes
FHA loans are US-only. In Canada, the closest equivalent is mortgage default insurance from CMHC or private insurers, required when the down payment is under 20%; see the CMHC insurance calculator. In the UK, there's no government-insured mortgage of this kind; high-LTV lending is offered by lenders directly, and the government has run mortgage guarantee schemes at times.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting the UFMIP. It's added to the loan unless you pay it in cash.
Using the wrong MIP rate. It depends on LTV, term and loan amount.
Comparing payment only. FHA's lifetime MIP can make it costlier over the long run.
Ignoring county limits. In expensive areas, the price you want may exceed FHA limits.
Frequently asked questions
What is the minimum down payment for an FHA loan?
3.5% with a credit score of at least 580; 10% with scores from 500 to 579 [VERIFY].
What is UFMIP?
A one-time FHA insurance premium, usually 1.75% of the base loan, normally added to the loan balance.
Can I remove FHA MIP?
If you put down 10% or more, annual MIP ends after 11 years. Otherwise it usually lasts for the life of the loan, unless you refinance.
Is MIP the same as PMI?
Both protect the lender, but MIP is FHA's government-backed insurance with set rates and duration, while PMI applies to conventional loans and can be cancelled earlier.
Does the payment include property tax and insurance?
No. Add them separately for the full monthly cost.
Are FHA loans only for first-time buyers?
No. Any eligible borrower buying a primary residence can use one.

Title tag
FHSA Calculator: First Home Savings Account | FigSumo (53 chars)
Meta description
Project First Home Savings Account savings and tax deductions using the $8,000 annual and $40,000 lifetime limits. (114 chars)
Country
CA
Status
new · tax year 2026
Body words
1,029 (minimum 1,000)
H1: FHSA Calculator
The First Home Savings Account (FHSA) lets first-time buyers in Canada save up to $40,000 for a home with a tax deduction on the way in and tax-free withdrawals on the way out, combining the best features of an RRSP and a TFSA. This calculator projects your FHSA balance, checks contributions against your participation room, and estimates the tax refunds your deductions could generate.
How to use this calculator
1. Year you opened your first FHSA. Room starts accumulating only once you open an account.
2. Planned contribution each year.
3. Unused room carried forward from the previous year (up to $8,000).
4. Expected annual return on your investments in the account.
5. Marginal tax rate: your combined federal and provincial rate, to estimate refunds. The Canada income tax calculator shows it.
6. Years until you buy.
Results: projected balance, total contributions, investment growth, estimated tax refunds and a warning if a contribution would exceed your room.
How the limits work
Annual participation room: $8,000 in the year you open your first FHSA.
Carry-forward: unused room from a year can be carried forward, but only up to $8,000. So the most you can put in during a single year is $16,000.
Lifetime limit: $40,000 in contributions (and transfers from RRSPs) across all your FHSAs.
Investment income doesn't use room. Growth inside the account isn't counted.
Over-contributions are taxed at 1% a month on the highest excess amount until removed.
Time limit: the account must be used or closed by the end of the 15th year after you first open one, or the year you turn 71, whichever is earlier [VERIFY wording on CRA]. Unused funds can be transferred to an RRSP or RRIF without affecting RRSP room.
Eligibility: Canadian resident, at least 18 (19 in some provinces) and under 72, and a first-time home buyer (you didn't live in a home you or your spouse or common-law partner owned at any time in the current year or the previous four calendar years).
The formula
Contributions at the start of each year, growing at rate r:
Balance after year k = (Balance after year k−1 + Contribution) × (1 + r)
Tax refund ≈ Contributions deducted × Marginal tax rate
You don't have to deduct contributions in the year you make them; you can carry deductions forward to a year when your income and tax rate are higher.
Worked examples
Example 1: maximum contributions for five years
$8,000 at the start of each year for five years, earning 5%:
Balance = $46,415.30
Contributions $40,000; growth $6,415.30
At a 30% marginal rate, deductions are worth about $12,000.00 in refunds.
After the refunds, the $46,415.30 you can withdraw tax-free cost you $28,000 out of pocket.
A couple who are both first-time buyers can each open an FHSA, doubling this to $92,830.61.
Example 2: opening the account and catching up
Open an FHSA in 2026 and contribute nothing that year. In 2027 you can contribute $16,000 ($8,000 new room plus $8,000 carried forward), then $8,000 a year for three years. At 5%, the balance after five years is $45,929.10. Opening the account early, even with a small amount, starts the room clock.
Using the money
A qualifying withdrawal to buy a first home is tax-free and doesn't need to be repaid. You need a written agreement to buy or build a qualifying home in Canada before 1 October of the year after the withdrawal, and you must intend to live in it within a year of buying. You can combine an FHSA withdrawal with the RRSP Home Buyers' Plan (up to $60,000 [VERIFY]), but HBP withdrawals must be repaid over 15 years (about $4,000.00 a year on $60,000) while FHSA withdrawals don't.
Non-qualifying withdrawals are added to your taxable income.
