Tips and common mistakes
Waiting to open an account. Room only starts when you open one.
Carrying forward more than $8,000. Only $8,000 of unused room carries forward.
Contributing more than your room across multiple FHSAs.
Withdrawing before you have a written purchase agreement.
Holding cash for years. If your purchase is several years away, consider an investment mix that suits your timeline.
Checklist before you buy
Before withdrawing, confirm that you're a first-time home buyer, that you have a written agreement to buy or build a qualifying home in Canada before 1 October of the following year, and that you plan to live in it within a year. Fill in Form RC725 and give it to your FHSA issuer, so no tax is withheld from the withdrawal. If you also use the RRSP Home Buyers' Plan, keep a record of both withdrawals for your tax return.
Frequently asked questions
How much can I put in an FHSA?
$8,000 a year (up to $16,000 with carry-forward) and $40,000 in total.
Are FHSA contributions tax deductible?
Yes, and you can carry the deduction forward.
Is the FHSA withdrawal taxable?
Not if it's a qualifying withdrawal for a first home.
What happens if I don't buy a home?
You can transfer the balance to an RRSP or RRIF tax-free, without using RRSP room, or withdraw it as taxable income.
Can I have an FHSA and use the Home Buyers' Plan?
Yes, for the same home.
Does FHSA growth count toward the $40,000 limit?
No. Only contributions and RRSP transfers count.

Freelance Hourly Rate Calculator | FigSumo (42 chars)
Meta description
Work out the hourly or day rate you need to charge from your target income, business expenses, taxes, time off and billable hours. (130 chars)

H1: Freelance Rate Calculator
Freelancers and contractors often underprice because they divide the salary they want by 2,080 hours. But you pay your own taxes, benefits and business costs, and you can't bill every working hour. This calculator works backwards from the income you want to the hourly and day rate you need to charge.
How to use this calculator
1. Target income: the annual pay you want for yourself, as you'd think of a salary.
2. Benefits to replace: health insurance, retirement contributions, and the value of paid leave if not covered by time off below.
3. Business expenses: software, equipment, insurance, accountant, coworking, marketing, travel.
4. Tax allowance (%): the share of profit to set aside for income tax and self-employment tax or National Insurance. Use your own figure from a tax calculator.
5. Working weeks: 52 minus holidays, public holidays, sick days and training.
6. Hours per week and utilisation (%): the share of working hours you can actually bill. Admin, sales and gaps between projects mean 50% to 75% is common for many freelancers.
7. Hours per day for a day rate.
Results: revenue needed, billable hours, required hourly rate, day rate and an employee-salary comparison.
The formula
Pre-tax need = Target income + Benefits + Expenses
Revenue needed = Pre-tax need ÷ (1 − Tax allowance)
Billable hours = Working weeks × Hours per week × Utilisation
Hourly rate = Revenue needed ÷ Billable hours
Day rate = Hourly rate × Hours per day
The tax step is a simplification: it treats tax as a flat share of revenue. It's deliberately conservative; your actual tax depends on deductions and rates.
Worked examples
Example 1: a US freelancer
Target income $80,000; benefits $12,000; expenses $9,000 → pre-tax need $101,000.00
Tax allowance 25% → revenue needed $134,666.67
46 working weeks × 40 hours × 65% utilisation = 1,196 billable hours
Hourly rate = $112.60; day rate (8 hours) $900.78
Dividing $80,000 by 2,080 hours gives $38.46 an hour, less than half the rate this freelancer actually needs.
Example 2: a UK contractor
Target £50,000; pension £6,000; expenses £4,000 → £60,000.00
Tax and NI allowance 28% → revenue £83,333.33
44 weeks × 37.5 hours × 70% = 1,155 billable hours
Hourly rate £72.15; day rate (7.5 hours) £541.13
Example 3: a Canadian freelancer
Target $70,000; benefits $8,000; expenses $6,000 → $84,000.00
Tax allowance 30% → revenue $120,000.00
45 weeks × 35 hours × 60% = 945 billable hours
Hourly rate = $126.98; day rate (7 hours) $888.89

Every hour of admin, sales or downtime has to be paid for by billable hours, which is why the rate rises so quickly at low utilisation.
Pricing a project
At Example 1's rate (rounded up), a project you estimate at 30 hours should be priced at about $3,390.00, plus a contingency for scope creep.
Retainers
A retainer is a fixed monthly fee for a set number of hours or a defined service. At Example 1's rate, a 20-hour monthly retainer is 20 × $112.60 = $2,252.00. Some freelancers offer a small discount, for example 5% ($2,139.40), in exchange for guaranteed income, which raises utilisation and can justify the lower price. Agree what happens to unused hours (lost, carried forward or refunded) before you start.
Understanding your results
Utilisation is the biggest lever. Going from 65% to 75% billable cuts the hourly rate you need by more than 13%.
Expenses are deductible, so they reduce tax; the flat tax allowance may overstate tax slightly.
Market check: compare the result with what clients pay for similar work. If the market rate is lower, adjust hours, expenses or your target, or specialise.
Value pricing: for some work, pricing by outcome or by project rather than by hour can earn more.
Country notes
United States: self-employed people pay 15.3% self-employment tax on 92.35% of net profit (Social Security part capped at the wage base), plus income tax, usually through quarterly estimated payments. See the self-employment tax calculator.
Canada: self-employed people pay both shares of CPP (11.9% plus CPP2 at 8% on higher earnings in 2026), plus income tax. EI is optional for the self-employed.
United Kingdom: sole traders pay Income Tax and Class 4 National Insurance on profits; contractors working through a limited company need to consider IR35 rules, which can treat them as employees for tax.
Tips and common mistakes
Using 2,080 hours (40 × 52) as billable time.
Forgetting unpaid time: holidays, sick days, admin, sales.
Leaving out the employer-equivalent costs you now pay: pension, health cover, payroll taxes.
Never raising rates. Review them yearly.
Testing your rate
Check the result against the market. Look at rates on freelance platforms and industry surveys for your field and region. If your calculated rate is far above them, cut costs, raise your billable hours or specialise. If it's far below, you may be undercharging.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate my freelance hourly rate?
Add your target income, benefits and expenses, gross it up for tax, and divide by realistic billable hours.
What utilisation rate should I use?
Track your own time. Many freelancers bill between half and three-quarters of their working hours.
How do I set a day rate?
Multiply your hourly rate by the hours in a typical day you'd bill.
Should I charge more than my old salary per hour?
Usually much more, because you cover your own costs and unbillable time.
Does this include VAT or sales tax?
No. Add VAT or GST/HST on top if you're registered.
How much should I set aside for tax?
It depends on your country and income; use the relevant tax calculator for a better estimate than a flat percentage.

Title tag
Future Value Calculator: Lump Sum and Regular Payments | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Calculate the future value of a lump sum and a series of payments at a given rate, with payment timing and compounding options. (127 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,003 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Future Value Calculator
The future value of a sum of money is what it grows to after a number of years at a given interest rate, once compound interest has been added. Enter the amount you have today, the annual rate, the number of years and how often interest compounds. The calculator returns the future value.
How to use this calculator
1. Present value: the lump sum you start with, e.g. a deposit or an investment you make today.
2. Annual rate: the nominal yearly interest rate or expected return, as a percentage.
3. Years: how long the money grows.
4. Compounds per year: how often interest is added: 1 (annually), 2 (semi-annually), 4 (quarterly), 12 (monthly) or 365 (daily). Your account terms say which applies.
Result: future value.
The formula
FV = PV × (1 + r ÷ m)^(m × t)
FV: future value
PV: present value
r: annual rate as a decimal
m: compounding periods per year
t: years
The growth (interest earned) is FV − PV. If interest compounded continuously, the limit of this formula would be FV = PV × e^(r × t).
Worked examples
Example 1: $10,000 at 7% for 10 years, compounded monthly
FV = 10,000 × (1 + 0.07 ÷ 12)^(12 × 10) = $20,096.61
Growth: $10,096.61
How compounding frequency changes the same deposit:
Compounding
Future value
Annually (1)
$19,671.51
Quarterly (4)
$20,015.97
Monthly (12)
$20,096.61
Daily (365)
$20,136.18
Continuous
$20,137.53
More frequent compounding helps, but the gains shrink as frequency rises. The rate and the time matter far more.
Example 2: $25,000 at 4.5% for 18 years, compounded quarterly
FV = 25,000 × (1 + 0.045 ÷ 4)^(4 × 18) = $55,944.13
If inflation averages 2.5% a year over the same period, that sum is worth about $35,869.47 in today's money (divide by 1.025^18).
Understanding your results
Future value is in future dollars. It doesn't account for inflation, taxes or fees.
It assumes a constant rate. Savings rates change; investment returns vary year to year. For investments, treat the rate as an assumption and test a range.
Doubling time: the "rule of 72" estimates years to double as 72 ÷ rate. At 7%, that is about 10.3 years; the exact figure with annual compounding is ln 2 ÷ ln 1.07 = 10.24 years.
How long to reach a target
You can also rearrange the formula to find the time needed:
t = ln(FV ÷ PV) ÷ (m × ln(1 + r ÷ m))
Growing $10,000 to $25,000 at 7% compounded monthly takes ln(2.5) ÷ (12 × ln(1 + 0.07 ÷ 12)) = 13.1 years. At 5% it would take 18.4 years. This is a quick way to check whether a goal is realistic before committing to a plan.
Uses in everyday planning
Savings goals: how much a deposit you make today will be worth when a child starts school or when you plan to retire.
Comparing accounts: run two rates and compounding frequencies side by side to see the difference in money, not percentages.
Cost of waiting: money you invest 5 years later has 5 fewer years to compound; compare the two future values to see what delay costs.
Future value vs present value
Future value moves money forward in time; present value moves it back. They are the same equation rearranged: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r ÷ m)^(m × t). Use the present value calculator when you know the amount you need later and want to know what it's worth today.
Adding regular deposits
This calculator handles a single lump sum. If you also add money every month, the future value of those deposits is calculated with the annuity formula, FV = PMT × ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i, and added to the lump-sum result. The compound interest calculator and annuity calculator do this for you.
Country notes
United States: savings rates are quoted as APY, which already includes compounding. If you enter an APY, set compounds per year to 1 so you don't count compounding twice.
Canada: banks quote GIC and savings rates as annual rates with a stated compounding frequency; for registered accounts (TFSA, RRSP) growth isn't taxed each year.
United Kingdom: savings rates are quoted as AER, which works like APY. With an AER, use 1 compounding period per year.
Tips and common mistakes
Double-counting compounding. APY and AER already include compounding; enter them with 1 period per year.
Using percentages as decimals. Enter 7 for 7%.
Ignoring tax. Interest in a taxable account is taxed each year, which lowers the effective growth rate.
Forgetting inflation. A large future number can buy less than you expect.
Over-optimistic returns. For long horizons, small rate changes have large effects; test several rates.
Quick check
Rerun Example 1 with a 5% rate to see how sensitive the result is to the return you assume.
Frequently asked questions
What is future value?
The value of money at a future date after interest or investment growth is added.
How does compounding frequency affect future value?
More frequent compounding adds interest on interest sooner, so the future value is slightly higher at the same nominal rate.
What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
Simple interest is earned only on the original amount; compound interest is also earned on interest already added. See the simple interest calculator.
Can I calculate future value with monthly contributions?
Not in this tool yet. Use the compound interest calculator, or add the annuity formula result yourself.
What rate should I use for investments?
There's no guaranteed figure. Many people test a cautious and an optimistic rate and plan around the cautious one.
How do I find the rate needed to reach a target?
Rearrange: r = m × ((FV ÷ PV)^(1 ÷ (m × t)) − 1). For example, doubling in 10 years with annual compounding needs about 7.18%.

In Canada, sales tax on most goods and services is the federal Goods and Services Tax (GST) or, in five provinces, the Harmonized Sales Tax (HST), which combines GST and a provincial portion. Some provinces add their own provincial sales tax instead. This calculator adds the right taxes for your province to a pre-tax price, or works backwards from a total to the pre-tax amount.

2. Amount: the price.
3. Amount is: before tax or after tax.
Results: GST or HST, PST/QST where it applies, the total, or (reverse mode) the pre-tax amount and tax included.

The formulas

Worked examples

HST = 100 × 13% = $13.00; total $113.00
Example 2: $100 in Quebec
GST = $5.00; QST = 100 × 9.975% = $9.98
Total = $114.98
In British Columbia, the same purchase is $112.00 (5% GST + 7% PST).
Example 3: removing HST from a receipt
You paid $56.50 in Ontario.
Pre-tax price = 56.50 ÷ 1.13 = $50.00; HST included = $6.50
Example 4: Nova Scotia's rate cut
A $250 purchase in Nova Scotia now carries $35.00 of HST at 14%, compared with $37.50 at the previous 15% rate.

You paid $57.49 in Quebec.

The rate depends on where it's delivered: $1,260.00 in Alberta, $1,356.00 in Ontario and $1,380.00 in New Brunswick. That's a $120.00 difference for the same item.

For businesses
Registration: you must register for GST/HST once your worldwide taxable supplies exceed $30,000.00 over four consecutive calendar quarters (the small supplier threshold). You can register voluntarily below it.
Input tax credits: registrants recover the GST/HST they pay on business purchases. If you charge $455.00 of HST on $3,500 of sales and paid $260.00 on $2,000 of business purchases, you remit the difference: $195.00.
Zero-rated and exempt supplies: basic groceries, prescription drugs and medical devices are zero-rated (taxed at 0%, input tax credits allowed). Many health, educational and financial services and long-term residential rents are exempt (no tax, no input tax credits).
Place of supply rules decide which province's rate applies when selling across provinces.
Understanding your results
Rounding: businesses round tax to the cent, so a cent of difference is normal.
Rebates: some provinces rebate their portion of HST on items such as children's clothing, books or diapers (Ontario point-of-sale rebates, for example), so the tax at the till may be lower than the full rate.
Households: the GST/HST credit is a tax-free quarterly payment to lower-income households, based on your tax return.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the wrong province. Online purchases are taxed at the rate where they're delivered.
Taking 13% of a total to find the HST. Divide by 1.13 instead.
Forgetting PST in BC, Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Quebec.
Charging tax on zero-rated basic groceries.
Notes for US and UK readers
Canadian shelf prices usually exclude GST/HST and PST, like US prices exclude state sales tax, so the total at the till is higher than the sticker. That's the opposite of the UK, where VAT is included in displayed prices. Visitors to Canada generally can't reclaim GST/HST on goods they take home, as the federal visitor rebate programme ended in 2007, although some tour packages qualify for a rebate [VERIFY]. For US state sales tax, see the sales tax calculator; for UK VAT, the VAT calculator.
Quick check
Check the province of supply, not the seller's province.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between GST and HST?
GST is the 5% federal tax. HST combines GST with a provincial portion in Ontario, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island.
What is the sales tax in Ontario?
13% HST.
What is the sales tax in Quebec?
5% GST plus 9.975% QST, 14.975% in total.
How do I calculate GST backwards?
Divide the total by 1 plus the rate (1.05 for 5% GST), then subtract.
When do I need to register for GST/HST?
Once your taxable supplies exceed $30,000 over four consecutive calendar quarters.
Is there GST on groceries?
Basic groceries are zero-rated; snack foods, soft drinks and restaurant meals are taxable.

Title tag
HELOC Calculator: Draw-Period and Repayment Payments | FigSumo (62 chars)
Meta description
Estimate home equity line of credit payments during the interest-only draw period and the repayment period, plus available credit from equity. (142 chars)
Country

1,022 (minimum 1,000)
H1: HELOC Calculator
A home equity line of credit (HELOC) lets you borrow against your home's equity as you need it, up to a credit limit. Most HELOCs have two phases: a draw period (often 10 years) when you can borrow and usually pay interest only, and a repayment period (often 20 years) when you can no longer draw and must repay principal and interest. This calculator shows the payment in each phase, the jump between them, the total interest and how much credit remains available.
How to use this calculator
1. HELOC credit limit: the maximum the lender has approved. If you don't have one yet, estimate it from your equity (see below).
2. Amount drawn: how much you expect to borrow. It must not exceed the limit.
3. Interest rate: the current rate on the line. HELOC rates are usually variable: an index (in the US, typically the prime rate) plus a margin.
4. Draw period (years): from your HELOC agreement; 10 years is common.
5. Repayment period (years): commonly 15 or 20 years.
Results: interest-only monthly payment during the draw period, repayment-phase payment, the payment increase at the switch, total interest and available credit.
The formula
Draw period (interest only):
Payment = Balance × Rate ÷ 12
Repayment period (amortizing):
Payment = B × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
B: balance at the end of the draw period; r: rate ÷ 12; n: repayment years × 12
Available credit = Credit limit − Amount drawn
The calculator assumes the whole amount is drawn at the start, only interest is paid during the draw period, and the rate stays constant.
Worked examples
Example 1: $40,000 drawn on a $100,000 line at 8.75%, 10-year draw, 20-year repayment
Interest-only payment = 40,000 × 0.0875 ÷ 12 = $291.67 a month
Available credit: $60,000.00
Repayment payment over 240 months: $353.48 a month
Payment increase at the end of the draw period: $61.82
Total interest over 30 years: $79,836.23
That jump catches many borrowers by surprise. Paying some principal during the draw period reduces it.
Example 2: how big a line can I get, and what if rates rise?
Lenders cap the combined loan-to-value (CLTV): all loans secured on the home ÷ its value. With a home worth $500,000, a mortgage balance of $280,000 and an 85% CLTV cap, the maximum line is 500,000 × 0.85 − 280,000 = $145,000.00.
Drawing $60,000 at 9.75% costs $487.50 a month interest-only. If the prime rate rises two points, the rate becomes 11.75% and the payment rises to $587.50, an extra $100.00 a month.
Understanding your results
Interest-only payment is the minimum during the draw period on many HELOCs. It doesn't reduce what you owe.
Repayment-phase payment is what you'll pay once drawing ends, if the balance is unchanged and the rate is the same.
Total interest depends heavily on the rate path. Treat it as an illustration.
Available credit is unused limit you could still draw (subject to the lender's terms; lenders can freeze or reduce lines in some situations).
HELOC vs home equity loan vs cash-out refinance
HELOC: flexible draws, variable rate, interest-only option. Suits ongoing or uncertain costs (a renovation in stages).
Home equity loan: a lump sum at a fixed rate with fixed payments; see the home equity loan calculator.
Cash-out refinance: replaces your mortgage with a larger one. It can make sense when the new mortgage rate is similar to or lower than your current rate; see the refinance calculator.
Country notes
United States: interest on a HELOC is deductible only if the money is used to buy, build or substantially improve the home securing it, and the total qualifying mortgage debt is within limits (IRS Publication 936). Lenders must give the CFPB's "What you should know about home equity lines of credit" booklet.
Canada: HELOCs are often combined with a mortgage in a "readvanceable" product. Federally regulated lenders can lend up to 65% of the home's value on a HELOC, within an 80% total loan-to-value limit including the mortgage (OSFI B-20) [VERIFY current B-20 wording]. Interest is generally not tax-deductible unless the money is borrowed to earn investment or business income.
United Kingdom: HELOCs are uncommon. Homeowners usually take a further advance from their mortgage lender, remortgage, or take a second-charge mortgage, all regulated by the FCA.
Tips and common mistakes
Planning only for the interest-only payment. Budget for the repayment-phase payment.
Ignoring variable rates. Test the payment at a rate 2–3 points higher.
Using a HELOC for everyday spending. The loan is secured on your home; falling behind can lead to foreclosure.
Missing fees. Some HELOCs charge annual fees, early closure fees or minimum draw requirements.
Frequently asked questions
How is a HELOC payment calculated?
During the draw period, usually interest only: balance × rate ÷ 12. In the repayment period, as an amortizing loan over the remaining term.
How much can I borrow with a HELOC?
Typically up to a CLTV limit set by the lender, such as 80% to 90% of the home's value minus your mortgage balance, subject to credit and income checks.
Is HELOC interest tax-deductible?
In the US, only when the funds are used to buy, build or substantially improve the home, within IRS limits.
Can the rate change?
Most HELOCs have variable rates that move with an index such as the prime rate. Some lenders let you fix the rate on part of the balance.
What happens at the end of the draw period?
You can no longer borrow, and payments switch to principal plus interest, which can raise the payment sharply.
Can I pay off a HELOC early?
Usually yes, but check for early closure fees.

Home Equity Loan Calculator: Borrowing Limit & Payment | FigSumo (64 chars)

H1: Home Equity Loan Calculator
A home equity loan lets you borrow a lump sum against the equity in your home and repay it in fixed monthly installments, usually at a fixed rate. It is sometimes called a second mortgage. This calculator gives the monthly payment, the total of payments and the total interest for the amount, rate and term you enter, with an amortization chart. The section below shows how to work out how much a lender might let you borrow.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: the lump sum you plan to borrow. Check it against your equity limit first (Example 2).
2. Interest rate: the rate in the lender's offer. Use the APR to include fees.
3. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): common terms are 5 to 30 years.
Results: monthly payment, total of payments, total interest paid, the rate used and a chart of the balance over time.
The formula
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Total interest = PMT × n − P
P: loan amount
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: years × 12 + months
How much can you borrow? Lenders cap the combined loan-to-value (CLTV):
CLTV = (Mortgage balance + Home equity loan) ÷ Home value
Maximum loan = Home value × CLTV limit − Mortgage balance
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 over 5 years at 7.5%
PMT = $400.76
Total of payments $24,045.54; total interest $4,045.54
Example 2: maximum loan at 85% CLTV, then the payment
Home value $450,000; mortgage balance $260,000; lender's CLTV limit 85%.
Maximum loan = 450,000 × 0.85 − 260,000 = $122,500.00
At 8.25% over 15 years: $1,188.42 a month, total interest $91,415.95
Over 10 years: $1,502.49 a month, total interest $57,799.36
Borrowing only $50,000 instead would leave the CLTV at 68.9%, which can qualify for a better rate with some lenders.
Example 3: 10 or 20 years on $50,000 at 8%
10 years: $606.64 a month, total interest $22,796.56
20 years: $418.22 a month, total interest $50,372.81
The longer term lowers the payment by $188.42 a month but more than doubles the interest.

Understanding your results
Monthly payment is principal and interest on the second loan only. Your first mortgage payment continues as before.
Total interest assumes you keep the loan for the full term.
The chart shows the balance falling slowly at first, then faster, as more of each payment goes to principal.
Home equity loan, HELOC or cash-out refinance?
Home equity loan: one lump sum, fixed rate and payment. Suits a single known cost, such as a roof replacement.
HELOC: draw as needed, variable rate, often interest-only for years; compare with the HELOC calculator.
Cash-out refinance: one new, larger first mortgage. Worth considering when current mortgage rates are close to or below your existing rate; see the refinance calculator.
Costs to expect
Home equity loans can carry closing costs similar to a mortgage: an appraisal, origination fee, title search and recording fees. Some lenders waive them in exchange for a higher rate or an early-closure fee if you repay within a few years. In the US, the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure set these out. Put the fees into the APR calculator to compare offers fairly.
Country notes
United States: interest may be deductible only if the money is used to buy, build or substantially improve the home that secures the loan, within the overall mortgage debt limit (IRS Publication 936). Federal law gives a three-day right of rescission on most home equity loans on your primary residence.
Canada: fixed-sum second mortgages are less common than HELOCs; borrowers usually refinance or use a HELOC. Federally regulated lenders are limited to 80% loan-to-value on refinancing under OSFI B-20.
United Kingdom: the equivalent is a second-charge mortgage or a further advance from your existing lender. Both are regulated by the FCA, and lenders must check affordability.
Tips and common mistakes
Borrowing the maximum by default. A lower CLTV leaves a safety margin if home prices fall.
Comparing rates without fees. Use APR.
Using equity for short-lived spending. A 15-year loan for a holiday means paying for it long after it's over.
Forgetting the risk. The loan is secured on your home.
Questions to ask the lender
Ask whether the rate is fixed, what closing costs and appraisal fees apply, and whether there's a prepayment penalty or an early-closure fee. Ask how much the lender will let you borrow as a share of your home's value, since limits of 80% to 90% combined loan-to-value are common. Get the answer in writing and compare at least two lenders, using the APR as well as the rate.
Frequently asked questions
How much can I borrow with a home equity loan?
Typically up to 80%–90% CLTV, minus what you owe on your mortgage, subject to credit and income checks. Lenders set their own limits.
Are home equity loan rates fixed?
Usually, yes. That's the main difference from a HELOC.
Is home equity loan interest tax-deductible?
In the US, only if the money is used to buy, build or substantially improve the home securing the loan, within IRS limits.
How long does it take to get a home equity loan?
Often a few weeks, because the lender needs an appraisal and title work.
Can I pay it off early?
Usually, but check for prepayment or early closure fees.
What happens if I sell the house?
Both the first mortgage and the home equity loan are repaid from the sale proceeds.

How Much House Can I Afford? Affordability Calculator | FigSumo (63 chars)
Meta description
Estimate an affordable home price from your income, debts, down payment and rate using debt-to-income ratios, or work backwards from a monthly budget. (150 chars)
Country

Body words
1,037 (minimum 1,000)
H1: House Affordability Calculator
Lenders decide how much to lend mainly from your income, your other debts and the payment the new loan would need. This calculator recreates that logic. It finds the largest monthly housing payment that fits a chosen debt-to-income (DTI) limit, turns that payment into a loan amount, and adds your down payment to get a price. You can change the limits, and a budget mode starts from the payment you are comfortable with instead.
How to use this calculator
1. Gross annual income: household income before tax.
2. Monthly debt payments: car, student loan, credit card minimums, child support and similar. Leave out rent and utilities.
3. Down payment and interest rate / term.
4. Property tax, insurance and HOA: monthly estimates. These use up part of the budget before principal and interest.
5. DTI limits: the defaults are 28% (front-end, housing only) and 36% (back-end, all debts). This is a common rule of thumb, not a legal limit. Lenders and loan programs set their own limits, so change these to match your lender's.
The formula
Gross monthly income   G = annual income ÷ 12
Front-end cap          F = G × front-end limit
Back-end cap           K = G × back-end limit − other monthly debts
Housing budget         H = min(F, K)
P&I budget             M = H − property tax − insurance − HOA − PMI
Maximum loan           L = M × (1 − (1 + r)^−n) / r
Affordable price       = L + down payment
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: term × 12
When the down payment is under 20%, PMI is estimated and subtracted from the budget. Each extra dollar of PMI lowers the maximum loan, so the calculator solves for the price iteratively.
Worked examples
Example 1: income-based. Income $100,000; other debts $500/month; tax + insurance $400/month; 6.5% for 30 years; 20% down; limits 28/36.
G = $8,333.33
Front-end cap: 0.28 × 8,333.33 = $2,333.33
Back-end cap: 0.36 × 8,333.33 − 500 = $2,500.00
Housing budget = the lower of the two = $2,333.33 (front-end binds)
P&I budget: 2,333.33 − 400 = $1,933.33
Maximum loan at 6.5%, 360 months: $305,874.25
With a 20% down payment, the price = loan ÷ 0.8 = $382,342.81, so the down payment needed is about $76,469
Example 2: debts change the answer. Raise other debts to $1,000/month and keep everything else the same. The back-end cap falls to 3,000 − 1,000 = $2,000.00. That is now lower than the front-end cap, so the housing budget drops to $2,000. P&I = $1,600, and the maximum loan falls by about 17%. Paying off a $500-a-month car loan can matter as much as a pay rise.
How income changes the answer
Same assumptions as Example 1 (other debts $500/month, tax and insurance $400/month, 6.5% over 30 years, 20% down, 28/36):

Understanding your results
Affordable price: what the ratios allow, not a recommendation. Many people choose to borrow less to leave room for saving, childcare or repairs.
Which limit binds: the result says whether the front-end or back-end ratio limited you. If it is the back-end ratio, reducing other debt raises your budget.
Payment breakdown: principal and interest, tax, insurance, HOA and PMI, so you can check the total against your own monthly budget.
Budget mode: enter the monthly payment you want, and the calculator returns the price instead.
Country notes
United States: the CFPB says different loan products and lenders have different DTI limits. Loans that meet the federal Qualified Mortgage definition have their own underwriting rules. FHA and VA programs use their own ratios (VERIFY current program limits before adding presets).
Canada: lenders use gross debt service (GDS) and total debt service (TDS) ratios and must test you at a stress-test rate. Use the Canadian mortgage calculator to check payments. A Canada-specific affordability mode is planned; see GAP-ANALYSIS.
UK: lenders use an affordability assessment based on income and outgoings, with stress-tested rates. Treat this US-style DTI result as a rough guide only.
Tips and common mistakes
Borrowing the maximum you're approved for. Leave room for repairs, savings and changes in income.
Leaving out property tax, insurance and HOA fees. They can add hundreds a month to the payment.
Forgetting closing costs. Budget 2% to 5% of the price on top of the down payment in the US.
Counting on future pay rises. Base the budget on income you have now.
Draining your emergency fund for the down payment. Keep a cushion for the first months of ownership.
Frequently asked questions
What is the 28/36 rule?
It's a rule of thumb: keep housing costs to 28% of gross monthly income, and all debt payments to 36%. Lenders may allow higher ratios, and loan programs differ, so you can change both numbers.
Does this use gross or take-home income?
Gross, because that is what lenders use in DTI ratios. To check comfort against take-home pay, use the paycheck calculator, then budget mode.
Why does a higher interest rate reduce what I can afford?
More of the same monthly budget goes to interest, so the same payment supports a smaller loan. At 6.5%, every $100 of monthly P&I supports about $15,800 of loan over 30 years.
Are property taxes included?
Yes, when you enter them. They come out of the housing budget before the loan size is calculated, so higher-tax areas support a lower price for the same income.
Should I count my partner's income?
Only if they will be on the loan. Lenders count the income and debts of everyone applying.
Is this a pre-approval?
No. A lender's pre-approval checks your credit, income documents and assets. This is an estimate to help you plan before you apply.

HSA Calculator: Tax Savings and Growth (2026) | FigSumo (55 chars)

H1: HSA Calculator
A health savings account (HSA) is a tax-advantaged account for medical costs, available if you're covered by a high-deductible health plan (HDHP). It's the only account in the US tax code with a triple advantage: contributions are deductible (or pre-tax through payroll), growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. This calculator checks your 2026 contribution limit, estimates your tax savings and projects your balance.
How to use this calculator
1. Coverage type: self-only or family HDHP.
2. Age 55 or older: adds a $1,000 catch-up contribution.
3. Months of HDHP coverage in the year, if not the full year.
4. How you contribute: through payroll (also avoids FICA) or directly (deducted on your tax return).
5. Employer contribution: counts toward the limit.
6. Federal and state marginal tax rates.
7. Balance, expected growth, years and annual medical spending for the projection.
Results: your 2026 limit, room left after employer contributions, tax savings this year, and the projected balance.
2026 limits

For 2027 the limits rise to $4,500 (self-only) and $9,000 (family).
How it works
Limit = Annual limit (by coverage) + Catch-up (if 55+), pro-rated by months eligible
Your room = Limit − Employer contributions
Tax savings = Contribution × (Federal rate + State rate + FICA 7.65% if via payroll)
FICA savings apply only to payroll contributions through a cafeteria plan; direct contributions are deducted for income tax but not FICA. Employer contributions are also free of income tax and FICA.
Worked examples
Example 1: family coverage, maximum contribution through payroll
22% federal bracket, 5% state tax, contributions through payroll:
Tax savings = 8,750 × (22% + 5% + 7.65%) = $3,031.88
The $3,031.88 saved means the $8,750 deposit costs you about $5,718.12 of take-home pay.
Contributing directly instead saves $2,362.50 (no FICA saving).
If your employer puts in $1,000, you can contribute $7,750.00 yourself.
Example 2: self-only coverage at age 56
Limit = $4,400 + $1,000 = $5,400
Example 3: investing the HSA for retirement
Contributing $4,400 a year for 25 years and investing it at 6% gives about $241,403.85, from $110,000.00 of contributions, if you pay medical costs from other money and keep receipts. Qualified medical withdrawals stay tax-free at any time, including for expenses incurred years earlier (after the HSA was opened).
Example 4: direct contributions in a state with no income tax
Self-only coverage, 24% federal bracket, no state income tax, contributing from your bank account rather than payroll:
Tax savings = 4,400 × 24% = $1,056.00
Through payroll, the same contribution would also save 7.65% FICA, $336.60 more

Partial-year coverage
With family HDHP coverage for 7 months, the pro-rated limit is about $5,104.17, unless you use the last-month rule (coverage on 1 December lets you contribute the full amount, provided you stay eligible through the following year).
Using HSA money
Qualified expenses: deductibles, copays, prescriptions, dental, vision and many other medical costs (IRS Publication 502).
Non-qualified withdrawals are taxed as income plus a 20% penalty before 65; after 65 the penalty doesn't apply, so the HSA works like a traditional IRA for non-medical spending.
No use-it-or-lose-it: balances roll over every year and stay with you if you change jobs.
Medicare: once you enroll in Medicare, you can't contribute, but you can still spend the balance (including on Medicare premiums other than Medigap).
Understanding your results
Eligibility matters. You must be covered by an HDHP and have no disqualifying coverage (such as a general-purpose health FSA or Medicare), and you can't be claimed as someone else's dependent.
State tax: a few states don't follow federal HSA rules and tax contributions or earnings [VERIFY your state].
Compare with a 401(k). After capturing any 401(k) match, many people prioritise the HSA for its tax treatment; see the 401(k) calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Over-contributing when you and your employer both contribute. Excess contributions face a 6% excise tax each year until removed.
Leaving the balance in cash if you're saving long term.
Losing receipts. Keep records to justify tax-free withdrawals.
Contributing after enrolling in Medicare.
Notes for Canadian and UK readers
There's no direct equivalent of an HSA in either country, because most medical care is publicly funded. In Canada, some employers offer a health spending account, a benefit that reimburses medical and dental costs tax-free, and individuals can claim eligible medical expenses as a non-refundable tax credit. In the UK, NHS care is free at the point of use; private medical insurance provided by an employer is normally a taxable benefit in kind, and there's no tax-free personal medical savings account. People moving to the US from either country can open an HSA only once they're covered by a qualifying HDHP.
Frequently asked questions
What is the HSA limit for 2026?
$4,400 self-only and $8,750 family, plus $1,000 if you're 55 or older.
Do I need a high-deductible plan?
Yes, an HSA-eligible HDHP.
Can I invest my HSA?
Most providers let you invest once your balance passes a minimum.
What happens to my HSA if I leave my job?
It's yours to keep.
Can I use my HSA for my spouse's expenses?
Yes, for your spouse and tax dependants, even if they aren't on your plan.
What is the deadline for contributions?
The tax filing deadline for the year, usually April 15 of the following year.

Inflation Calculator: Future Cost and Buying Power | FigSumo (60 chars)
Meta description
See how a price or a sum of money changes over time at an inflation rate you choose. Phase 2: historical CPI data for the US, Canada and UK. (140 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
1,009 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Inflation Calculator
Inflation is the rise in prices over time, which means each dollar, pound or loonie buys a little less each year. This calculator shows the effect at a steady inflation rate in both directions: what something that costs a given amount today would cost in the future, and what a future amount is worth in today's money.
How to use this calculator
1. Amount today: a price, salary, savings balance or budget in today's money.
2. Years: how far ahead you want to look.
3. Inflation rate: the yearly rate you expect, as a percentage. Central banks in the US, Canada and the UK each aim for 2% inflation over time, which is a common starting assumption for long-range planning. For the recent past, use the official consumer price index (CPI) figures listed in the sources.
Results:
Future cost (same purchasing power): what you'd need in the future to buy what the amount buys today.
Today's dollars equivalent: what the same nominal amount, received in the future, is worth in today's money.
The formula
Future cost       = Amount × (1 + i)^n
Today's equivalent = Amount ÷ (1 + i)^n
i: inflation rate as a decimal
n: number of years
Inflation compounds: each year's rise applies to the already higher price level.
Worked examples
Example 1: $1,000 over 10 years at 3%
Future cost = 1,000 × 1.03^10 = $1,343.92
Today's equivalent of $1,000 received in 10 years = 1,000 ÷ 1.03^10 = $744.09
At 3% a year, prices roughly double in about 23.4 years (the rule of 72 gives 72 ÷ 3 = 24).
Example 2: a $65,000 salary over 20 years at 2.5%
To keep the same buying power, the salary would need to be $106,510.07 in 20 years.
A $65,000 salary that never rose would be worth only $39,667.61 in today's money by then.
Understanding your results
Future cost is useful for setting savings targets: retirement income, college, a house deposit.
Today's equivalent shows the real value of a fixed future amount, such as a fixed pension or a sum promised years from now.
Inflation is not constant. Actual rates swing, sometimes sharply. Try a few rates to see a range.
Personal inflation differs. Official CPI tracks an average basket. Your costs may rise faster or slower depending on what you spend on (rent, fuel, childcare, healthcare).
Inflation and your money
Real return: an investment earning 5% when inflation is 3% has a real return of (1.05 ÷ 1.03) − 1 = 1.94%.
Pay rises: a 2% raise when inflation is 4% is a real pay cut of −1.92%.
Cash savings: money in an account paying less than inflation loses buying power, even though the balance grows.
Debt: fixed-rate debt gets easier to repay in real terms when inflation is high, because your income tends to rise while the payment stays the same.
Working backwards: the average rate between two prices
If a basket cost $100 twelve years ago and costs $150 today, the average annual inflation rate is (150 ÷ 100)^(1 ÷ 12) − 1 = 3.44%. This calculator doesn't solve for the rate yet, but the formula works with any two prices and a number of years.
Country notes
United States: the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the Consumer Price Index (CPI-U) monthly, and its CPI Inflation Calculator converts prices between past years. The Federal Reserve's 2% target is defined using the PCE price index.
Canada: Statistics Canada publishes the CPI monthly, and the Bank of Canada's inflation-control target is the 2% midpoint of a 1–3% range. The Bank of Canada also offers a historical inflation calculator.
United Kingdom: the Office for National Statistics publishes CPI, CPIH and RPI. The Bank of England's target is 2% CPI inflation. Some pensions, student loan interest and rail fares have used RPI, which usually runs higher than CPI.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing nominal and real figures. Keep them separate: inflate costs and use nominal returns, or use real returns and today's costs.
Using a single recent year. A spike or dip isn't a good long-run assumption.
Forgetting taxes. Tax is charged on nominal gains, so high inflation can mean tax on gains that are not real.
Assuming wages keep pace. They often do over long periods, but not always in the short run.
Frequently asked questions
What inflation rate should I use?
For long-range planning, many people start with the central banks' 2% target and test 3% or more as a cautious case. For the past, use official CPI data.
How do I calculate what money from the past is worth today?
Multiply the old amount by (1 + rate)^years, using the average inflation rate for that period. Official CPI-based calculators (BLS, Bank of Canada, Bank of England) use actual index values.
What is the difference between CPI and core inflation?
Core measures leave out volatile items, typically food and energy, to show the underlying trend. Headline CPI includes everything.
Why does my own cost of living rise faster than official inflation?
Your spending pattern differs from the average basket. If rent or energy is a big share of your budget and those prices rise quickly, your personal inflation is higher.
Does the calculator use historical data?
Not yet. It applies the constant rate you enter. Historical CPI data for the US, Canada and the UK is planned.
How does inflation affect retirement planning?
It raises the income you'll need. The retirement calculator can show results in today's money.

Title tag
Interest Calculator: Simple and Compound Interest | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description
Calculate interest earned or owed with simple or compound interest, deposits or withdrawals, and tax. Compare compounding frequencies. (134 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,008 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Interest Calculator
This calculator works out the interest earned on savings, or owed on a sum, over a period of time, using either simple interest or compound interest with monthly compounding. Enter the principal, the annual rate and the time in years, then choose the interest type. The result shows the interest, the total amount and, for comparison, what the other method would give.
How to use this calculator
1. Principal: the starting amount, whether a deposit or a sum borrowed.
2. Annual rate: the yearly interest rate as a percentage.
3. Time (years): the period. Quarter-years are fine; enter 1.5 for 18 months.
4. Interest type: Simple (interest only on the principal) or Compound (monthly) (interest added to the balance every month and then earning interest itself).
Results: the interest, the total amount (principal plus interest), the principal, a comparison figure from the other method, and a breakdown chart.
The formulas
Simple interest
I = P × r × t
Compound interest, monthly
A = P × (1 + r ÷ 12)^(12 × t)
I = A − P
P: principal
r: annual rate as a decimal
t: time in years
A: total amount at the end
Simple interest grows in a straight line. Compound interest curves upward because each month's interest is calculated on a larger balance.
Worked examples
Example 1: $10,000 at 5% for 3 years
Compound (monthly): A = 10,000 × (1 + 0.05 ÷ 12)^36 = $11,614.72, so interest = $1,614.72
Simple: I = 10,000 × 0.05 × 3 = $1,500.00
Compounding adds $114.72 over three years.
Over 20 years the gap grows: simple interest gives $10,000.00, monthly compounding $17,126.40.
Example 2: $2,500 at 4.25% for 18 months (1.5 years)
Simple: 2,500 × 0.0425 × 1.5 = $159.38
Compound (monthly): $164.26
Understanding your results
Interest is before tax. In most taxable accounts, interest is taxed as income in the year it is credited.
Total amount is what the balance would be at the end (or what you'd owe, for a loan with no payments).
Compare other method shows how much compounding matters for your figures.
The rate is assumed fixed. Variable savings rates change; re-run with new rates as they move.
Simple or compound: which applies?
Simple interest is used for some short-term loans, many car loans in the US (as simple-interest amortizing loans), bonds' coupon payments, and some promissory notes.
Compound interest applies to most savings accounts, CDs and GICs, credit cards (daily compounding) and investments that reinvest income.
Monthly compounding is assumed here. Many savings accounts compound daily and pay monthly, which gives a very similar result. If you have an APY or AER, use the compound interest calculator with annual compounding so the rate isn't compounded twice.
How banks actually credit interest
Most savings accounts calculate interest every day on the closing balance and credit it monthly. The daily rate is the annual rate divided by 365 (some institutions use 360). For $10,000 at 5%, one day's interest is 10,000 × 0.05 ÷ 365 = $1.37. Over a 30-day month that adds up to $41.10, very close to the monthly-compounding figure the calculator uses ($41.67 for the first month). The small difference comes from day counts, not a different method.
If you add or withdraw money during the period, interest changes from that day. The calculator assumes the balance only changes through interest. For regular deposits, use the savings calculator.
Interest on borrowing
For a loan or card with no repayments, the total amount shows what the debt would grow to. Card balances usually compound daily at rates far above savings rates, so the growth is much faster. At 22% compounded monthly, $2,000 grows to $3,846.52 in 3 years if nothing is paid. Use the credit card calculator to see the effect of minimum payments.
Country notes
United States: banks must disclose APY under the Truth in Savings Act (Regulation DD). Interest of $10 or more from a bank is usually reported on Form 1099-INT.
Canada: interest income is fully taxable unless earned inside a TFSA, RRSP or similar registered plan.
United Kingdom: savings rates are quoted as AER. The Personal Savings Allowance lets basic-rate taxpayers earn £1,000 of interest tax-free a year (higher-rate £500, additional-rate £0), and cash ISAs are tax-free.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering months as years. Convert months to years (18 months = 1.5).
Comparing a simple rate with a compound one. Convert both to an effective annual rate first.
Forgetting tax. Interest is often taxable, which lowers your real return.
Ignoring inflation. A 4% interest rate with 3% inflation is about a 1% real return.
Quick check
Check whether the rate you're quoted is nominal or effective.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between simple and compound interest?
Simple interest is calculated only on the original principal. Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus interest already added, so it grows faster.
How often does interest compound in this calculator?
Monthly, when you choose the compound option.
Can I use this for a loan?
Yes, to see the interest that builds up if nothing is repaid. For loans with regular payments, use the loan calculator.
How do I calculate interest for part of a year?
Enter the time as a fraction of a year: 6 months is 0.5.
Is APY simple or compound?
APY is the effective annual rate including compounding. It lets you compare accounts that compound at different frequencies.
Does the result include tax?
No. Subtract tax at your marginal rate if the interest is taxable.
Why is my bank's figure slightly different?
Banks usually compound daily and use exact day counts, and some round each day's interest. The calculator's monthly method gives a close estimate.

Title tag
Interest Rate Calculator: Find the Rate on a Loan | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description
Work out the interest rate implied by a loan amount, monthly payment and term. Useful for checking a dealer or lender quote. (124 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
1,006 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Interest Rate Calculator
If you know how much you're borrowing, the monthly payment and the term, this calculator finds the interest rate the lender is charging. It is the quickest way to check a quote that gives only a payment, such as "just $465 a month for 60 months", and to compare it with other offers.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: the amount you will actually borrow (the amount financed).
2. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): the repayment period. For 5 years, enter 5 and 0; for 42 months, enter 3 and 6.
3. Monthly payment: the payment you have been quoted, excluding any insurance or add-ons billed separately.
Results: the interest rate, the total of monthly payments, the total interest paid and an amortization chart.
The formula
The rate is the value of r that makes the standard payment formula match your payment:
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Annual rate = r × 12
P: loan amount
n: number of monthly payments
r: monthly rate (unknown)
There is no algebraic way to isolate r, so the calculator searches numerically (bisection) until the payment from the formula equals your payment, then reports r × 12 to three decimals. If the payments add up to no more than the loan amount, there is no positive rate and the calculator says so.
Worked examples
Example 1: $32,000 over 3 years at $960 a month
36 payments of $960 = $34,560.00
Total interest = $2,560.00
Interest rate = 5.065%
Example 2: checking a car dealer's quote
A dealer quotes $465 a month for 60 months on $24,000 financed.
Implied rate: 6.091%
Total paid $27,900.00; interest $3,900.00
Check: a $24,000 loan at 6.091% over 60 months gives a payment of $465.00.
If a credit union offers the same loan at a payment of $445, that payment implies 4.277%; the $20 difference each month is worth $1,200 over the loan.
How payment and rate move together
For $24,000 over 60 months, each percentage point on the rate adds roughly $11 to the monthly payment:

Small-looking payment differences add up to large differences in interest over a five-year loan.
Understanding your results
Interest rate is the nominal annual rate (monthly rate × 12) that matches the payment. It is the right figure to compare with quotes that state a rate.
It is not the APR if fees are involved. If fees were added to the loan or deducted from what you receive, enter the amount you actually receive to see the APR-style rate. The APR calculator handles fees directly.
Total interest assumes you make every payment for the full term.
Rounding: quoted payments are rounded to the cent, so the implied rate can differ from the lender's stated rate in the third decimal place.
When the rate looks wrong
Very high rate: the payment may include optional products (warranties, insurance) rolled into it, or the loan amount may be smaller than you think.
Rate near zero or an error: the payments barely exceed the loan amount; check you entered the right term.
Different from the advertised rate: promotions often apply to shorter terms or top credit tiers only.
Country notes
United States: lenders must disclose the APR and finance charge under the Truth in Lending Act before you sign. Use this tool to check the numbers line up.
Canada: lenders must disclose the annual percentage rate and total cost of borrowing. Provincial consumer protection laws cover dealer financing.
United Kingdom: credit agreements must state the APR and total amount payable under the Consumer Credit Act. Car finance often uses PCP with a final balloon payment, which this calculator does not model.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the vehicle price instead of the amount financed. Subtract the down payment and trade-in.
Leaving out the months field. A 42-month loan entered as 3 years gives the wrong rate.
Comparing payments on different terms. Compare the rate and total cost.
Ignoring balloons. If the deal has a large final payment, this tool will understate the rate.
Quick check
Check that the term you enter matches the payment frequency.
Frequently asked questions
How do I find the interest rate on a loan?
Enter the loan amount, term and monthly payment. The calculator solves for the rate that matches.
Why is there no simple formula for the rate?
Because the rate appears in both the numerator and an exponent in the payment equation. It has to be found by trial and improvement, which the calculator does instantly.
Is the result an APR?
It is the nominal rate implied by the amount and payment. It equals the APR when there are no fees.
Can I use this for a mortgage?
Yes, for a fixed-rate loan with equal monthly payments. Exclude escrow amounts (tax and insurance) from the payment.
What if my loan has weekly or bi-weekly payments?
Convert to a monthly equivalent only for a rough check; for an exact answer you need a calculator that uses the actual payment frequency.
Does it work for savings?
No. For savings growth, use the compound interest calculator.
Can a lower payment hide a higher rate?
Yes. Stretching the term lowers the payment even at a higher rate. Always compare the rate (or APR) and the total interest, not the payment alone.
What rate is "good" for my loan?
It depends on the loan type, term, your credit and current market rates. Get two or three quotes for the same amount and term and compare the implied rates here.

Investment Calculator: Growth, Contributions & Returns | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Project investment growth from a starting amount, regular contributions and an expected return, or solve for the return, contribution or time you need. (151 chars)
Country

H1: Investment Calculator
This calculator projects what an investment could grow to if it earned a steady average return. You can also run it backwards to find the contribution, return or time needed for a target. Because real markets don't deliver a steady return, it shows a low, base and high scenario side by side, and lets you subtract fees and inflation, the two things that most often make projections look better than reality.
How to use this calculator
1. Solve for: end balance (default), monthly contribution, required return, starting amount or number of years.
2. Starting amount and regular contribution, with frequency and timing (start or end of each period).
3. Expected annual return: a long-run average before fees. Try a range of values rather than a single number.
4. Annual fees (optional): fund expense ratios plus any platform or advisory fee.
5. Inflation (optional): shows the result in today's money.
6. Years to invest.
The formula
Using a monthly rate i derived from the annual return net of fees:
FV = P × (1 + i)^n + C × ((1 + i)^n − 1) / i        (contributions at end of month)
FV_start = FV + C × ((1 + i)^n − 1)                 (contributions at start of month: each earns one extra month)
Real value = FV ÷ (1 + inflation)^years
P: starting amount
C: monthly contribution
i: (annual return − annual fee) ÷ 12, matching a nominal rate compounded monthly
n: months
Solve for return has no closed-form answer, so the calculator finds i numerically (bisection) until FV matches your target to the cent.
Worked examples
Example 1: 25 years of steady investing. $5,000 to start, $300 a month (end of month), 7% a year, no fees, 25 years.
i = 0.07 / 12; n = 300
End balance: $271,648.60
Contributions: 5,000 + 300 × 300 = $95,000
Investment growth: $176,648.60, nearly twice what you put in
With contributions at the start of each month: $273,066.22

Two percentage points either way changes the result by roughly $75,000 to $112,000. That is why a single projection should never be treated as a forecast.
Example 2: fees and inflation.
Fees: with a 1% annual fee, the 7% gross return becomes 6% net, and the end balance falls to $230,223.04. The fee costs $41,425.56 over 25 years.
Inflation: at 2.5% a year, the $271,648.60 is worth about $146,524.70 in today's money.
Lump sum or regular investing?
Example 1 invests $95,000 in total over 25 years and ends with $271,648.60. If the whole $95,000 had been invested on day one at the same steady 7%, it would grow to $543,914.73, because every dollar has longer to compound. Most people invest from income as it arrives, so this isn't a like-for-like choice. With real (volatile) returns, investing gradually also changes the risk you take, and a constant-rate calculator can't capture that.
Example 3: solving for the monthly contribution. To reach $500,000 in 30 years at 6%, starting from $10,000, you'd need about $437.80 a month.
Example 4: solving for the required return. Turning $50,000 into $100,000 in 10 years with no contributions needs an annual return of 2^(1/10) − 1 = 7.18% (annual compounding). If that's above what your mix of investments can reasonably earn, add contributions or extend the time frame.

Understanding your results
End balance: nominal value at the end, assuming every contribution is made and the return is the same every year.
Contributions vs growth: the chart shows when growth starts to outpace your contributions. In Example 1, cumulative growth overtakes total contributions in year 17.
Real value: use this when comparing with today's prices or goals.
Sequence of returns: real portfolios rise and fall. Two investors with the same average return can end with different balances, depending on when the good and bad years arrived. This calculator does not simulate volatility.
Taxes: not deducted. Using tax-advantaged accounts can change the after-tax result substantially.
Country notes
US: see the 401(k) and Roth IRA calculators for 2026 contribution limits and tax treatment.
Canada: see the RRSP and TFSA calculators.
UK: see the ISA calculator. Stocks and shares ISAs shelter growth and dividends from UK tax.
Tips and common mistakes
Using one optimistic return. Run a range, such as 4%, 6% and 8%.
Ignoring fees. Example 2 shows how a 1% fee reduces the end balance.
Comparing nominal and real figures. Turn on inflation when the goal is in today's money.
Stopping contributions in a downturn. Regular investing buys more units when prices are low.
Forgetting tax-advantaged accounts. They can change the after-tax result more than a small difference in return.
Frequently asked questions
What return should I assume?
There is no guaranteed figure. Historical averages depend heavily on the asset mix, the period and the country, and past returns don't predict future ones. Use a range (the scenario band) and consider a conservative base case.
Why do fees matter so much?
They are taken every year from the whole balance, so they compound against you. In Example 1, a 1% fee reduces the end balance by about 15%.
Should contributions be at the start or end of the month?
Use whichever matches when you invest. Contributions at the start earn one extra month of growth each time, which slightly increases the result.
What does "solve for return" tell me?
It shows the average annual return needed to reach a goal with your contributions and time frame. If the required return is very high, you may need to contribute more, invest for longer or adjust the goal.
Does this account for dividends?
Yes, if your expected return is a total return, meaning dividends are reinvested. If you use a price-only return, the projection will understate growth for income-paying investments.
Is this investment advice?
No. It's a mathematical projection. Investments can lose value. For personal recommendations, consult a licensed adviser.

Title tag
Traditional IRA Calculator: Tax-Deferred Growth | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Compare a traditional IRA with a taxable account. Uses 2026 IRA limits ($7,500, $1,100 catch-up) and your tax rates now and in retirement. (138 chars)
Country
US
Status
rename (301) · tax year 2026
Body words
1,014 (minimum 1,000)
H1: IRA Calculator
This calculator projects the balance of a traditional IRA at retirement and estimates what it's worth after income tax on withdrawal. Enter your current balance, how much you'll add each year, the years until you withdraw, an expected return and the tax rate you expect in retirement. For 2026, the IRA contribution limit is $7,500, plus a $1,100 catch-up if you're 50 or older (IRS, IR-2025-111).
How to use this calculator
1. Current balance: the value of your traditional IRA today, from your latest statement.
2. Annual contribution: what you'll put in each year. The 2026 limit is $7,500 ($8,600 at 50+), and you can't contribute more than your taxable compensation for the year. The limit is shared across all your traditional and Roth IRAs.
3. Years until withdrawal: how long until you start taking money out.
4. Expected return: the yearly growth you assume after fund fees.
5. Tax rate at withdrawal: your expected average tax rate on IRA withdrawals in retirement (federal plus state).
Results: pre-tax balance and after-tax balance (estimate).
The formula
Pre-tax balance = B × (1 + g)^n + C × ((1 + g)^n − 1) ÷ g
After-tax balance = Pre-tax balance × (1 − Tax rate)
B: current balance; C: annual contribution; g: expected return; n: years
Growth compounds annually, and contributions are added at the end of each year.
Traditional IRA withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income (except any after-tax basis from nondeductible contributions), so applying your expected tax rate to the whole balance gives a rough spendable value.
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 balance, $7,500 a year for 20 years at 7%, 22% tax in retirement
Pre-tax balance = $384,859.88
After 22% tax: $300,190.71 (tax of $84,669.17)
Your own money in: $170,000.00
If the contributions are deductible and you're in the 22% bracket today, each $7,500 contribution also cuts this year's tax by about $1,650.00.
Example 2: starting at 50 with the catch-up
$0 today, $8,600 a year for 15 years at 6.5%, 12% expected tax rate:
Pre-tax balance: $207,966.66
After tax: $183,010.66
The value of starting early
Two savers each contribute $7,500 a year at 7%. One starts 30 years before retirement, the other 20 years before. The early starter ends with $708,455.90 pre-tax; the later starter with $307,466.19. The extra 10 years of contributions ($75,000) produce $400,989.71 more, because the early money has longer to compound.
Understanding your results
Pre-tax balance is the account value before any withdrawals.
After-tax balance is a simple estimate. In practice you withdraw over many years, and each year's withdrawals are taxed at that year's rates.
Returns vary. Use a cautious return and test a range.
Required minimum distributions (RMDs) start at age 73 for most people (75 for those born in 1960 or later [VERIFY]); see the RMD calculator.
Traditional or Roth?
Traditional IRA: contributions may be tax-deductible now; withdrawals are taxed later. Better if you expect a lower tax rate in retirement.
Roth IRA: no deduction now; qualified withdrawals are tax-free. Better if you expect a higher or similar rate later. Income limits apply to direct Roth contributions (2026 phase-out: $153,000–$168,000 single, $242,000–$252,000 married filing jointly). Compare with the Roth IRA calculator.
If your tax rate is the same now and later, a deductible traditional IRA and a Roth IRA give the same after-tax result for the same pre-tax contribution.
Deduction rules
You can always contribute to a traditional IRA if you have earned income, but the deduction phases out at certain incomes if you (or your spouse) are covered by a workplace retirement plan. The 2026 phase-out ranges are published in IRS Notice 2025-67 [VERIFY ranges before quoting]. If you can't deduct, contributions are "nondeductible" and you must track the basis on Form 8606.
Early withdrawals
Withdrawals before age 59½ are generally subject to a 10% additional tax on top of income tax, unless an exception applies (for example, first-time home purchase up to $10,000, qualified higher-education costs, or certain medical expenses). See IRS Publication 590-B.
Country notes
The IRA is US-only. In Canada, the closest equivalent is the RRSP (deductible now, taxed on withdrawal); see the RRSP calculator. In the UK, a personal pension (SIPP) works similarly, with tax relief on contributions and 25% usually tax-free at withdrawal; see the workplace pension calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Contributing over the limit. Excess contributions face a 6% excise tax each year until corrected.
Missing the deadline. You can contribute for 2026 until the tax filing deadline in April 2027.
Ignoring fees. Lower the expected return by fund costs.
Forgetting state tax in the withdrawal tax rate.
Frequently asked questions
What is the IRA contribution limit for 2026?
$7,500, or $8,600 if you're 50 or older by the end of the year, across all your traditional and Roth IRAs combined.
Are traditional IRA contributions tax-deductible?
Often, yes. If you or your spouse have a workplace plan, the deduction phases out above certain incomes.
When do I have to start withdrawing?
Required minimum distributions generally begin at 73 under current law.
How is the IRA taxed when I withdraw?
Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income, except for any nondeductible contributions (basis).
Does the calculator compound monthly?
No. It compounds annually and adds contributions at the end of each year.
Can I have an IRA and a 401(k)?
Yes. Workplace plan coverage can limit the traditional IRA deduction but not the right to contribute.
Can I contribute to an IRA if I don't work?
You need taxable compensation, but a spouse filing jointly can make a spousal IRA contribution based on the working spouse's compensation.

IRR Calculator

https://figsumo.com/irr-calculator
Title tag
IRR Calculator: Internal Rate of Return | FigSumo (49 chars)
Meta description
Find the internal rate of return for a series of cash flows, plus NPV at a chosen discount rate. Handles irregular amounts. (123 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,007 (minimum 1,000)
H1: IRR Calculator
The internal rate of return (IRR) is the yearly rate of return that a series of cash flows earns. Technically, it is the discount rate at which the net present value (NPV) of all the flows equals zero. Enter the cash flows in order, starting with the initial investment as a negative number, and the calculator finds the IRR. It also shows the undiscounted total of the flows.
How to use this calculator
1. Cash flows (comma-separated, t=0 first): type each period's net cash flow, in order, separated by commas.
The first value is time 0, usually the investment, entered as a negative number (money going out).
Each later value is the net cash at the end of period 1, 2, 3 and so on. Use negative numbers for further outlays.
Periods must be evenly spaced. If you enter yearly flows, the IRR is yearly.
Example input: -100000, 25000, 30000, 35000, 40000, 45000.
Results: internal rate of return (IRR) and NPV at 0% discount, which is simply the sum of all the flows.
The formula
IRR is the rate r that solves:
NPV = CF0 + CF1 ÷ (1 + r) + CF2 ÷ (1 + r)^2 + … + CFn ÷ (1 + r)^n = 0
CF0 … CFn: the cash flows at times 0 to n
r: the internal rate of return per period
There's no direct formula for r when there are more than two flows, so the calculator uses Newton's method: it starts at 10% and improves the guess using the slope of the NPV curve until the change is negligible. It reports the IRR to three decimal places.
Worked examples
Example 1: a project costing $100,000
Flows: −100,000, then 25,000, 30,000, 35,000, 40,000 and 45,000 over five years.
IRR = 19.71%
Sum of flows (NPV at 0%): $75,000.00
At an 8% discount rate, NPV = $36,679.88 (positive, so the project beats 8%)
At 20%, NPV = −$704.09 (negative, because 20% is above the IRR)
Example 2: a rental property bought for cash
Buy for $250,000; receive $18,000 a year of net rent for five years; sell at the end of year 5 for $300,000 (net of selling costs).
Flows: −250,000, 18,000, 18,000, 18,000, 18,000, 318,000
IRR = 10.45%
NPV at a 6% required return: $50,000.00
A check: single in, single out
−50,000 now and +80,000 in five years gives an IRR of 9.86%, which equals (80,000 ÷ 50,000)^(1/5) − 1 = 9.86%, the compound annual growth rate.
Monthly flows
A small business owner invests $12,000 and expects $1,100 a month for 12 months. Entering −12000 followed by twelve 1100s gives a monthly IRR of 1.498%. Annualized, that is (1 + monthly IRR)^12 − 1 = 19.53%. Always annualize before comparing with yearly rates.
Understanding your results
IRR above your required return (hurdle rate or cost of capital) means the investment adds value at that rate; below it, it doesn't.
NPV at 0% is the plain profit before considering the time value of money.
IRR is a percentage, not a size. A small project can have a higher IRR than a large one but create less total value. Compare NPVs at your required rate when choosing between projects.
Timing matters. Money received earlier raises the IRR.
Limits of IRR
Multiple answers: if the flows change sign more than once (e.g. −, +, −), there can be more than one IRR, or none. Treat results from such flows with caution and look at NPV instead.
Reinvestment assumption: IRR implicitly assumes interim cash flows can be reinvested at the IRR itself. The modified IRR (MIRR) uses a more realistic reinvestment rate.
Uneven dates: for flows on irregular dates, you need XIRR, which uses actual day counts. This tool assumes equal periods.
Size and duration: IRR alone can favor short, small projects over larger, longer ones that create more wealth.
IRR vs ROI vs CAGR
ROI is total gain ÷ cost, ignoring timing; see the ROI calculator.
CAGR is IRR for the special case of one outlay and one final value.
IRR handles any pattern of flows, including several deposits and withdrawals; it is the money-weighted return.
Country notes
The maths is universal. In practice, US and Canadian private equity and real estate funds report net IRR to investors; UK and other investment platforms often show money-weighted returns, which are IRRs. For tax, the cash flows you enter should be after tax if you want an after-tax IRR.
Tips and common mistakes
Wrong sign on the investment. The initial outlay must be negative.
Missing zero years. If nothing happens in a year, enter 0 so the timing stays right.
Mixing monthly and yearly flows. Keep one period length; a monthly IRR can be annualized as (1 + r)^12 − 1.
Including financing twice. Use either unlevered flows (project only) or levered flows (after loan payments), not a mix.
Quick check
Enter the initial investment as negative.
Frequently asked questions
What is a good IRR?
One that is higher than your required return for the risk. What counts as good depends on the investment type and your alternatives.
How is IRR different from ROI?
ROI ignores when money arrives. IRR accounts for timing, so it's a better measure for multi-year investments.
Why does the calculator say the IRR can't be computed?
The flows may not change sign (for example, all positive), or the method didn't converge. Check the signs and order.
Can I use monthly cash flows?
Yes. The result is a monthly IRR. Annualize it with (1 + monthly IRR)^12 − 1.
What is NPV?
Net present value: the sum of all flows discounted to today at a chosen rate. A positive NPV means the investment beats that rate.
Is IRR the same as yield to maturity?
For a bond, yes in principle: YTM is the IRR of buying the bond and holding it to maturity.

Payback Period Calculator

2. CFA Institute: "Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS)" money-weighted returns (accessed 14 Oct 2026). https://www.gipsstandards.org/

ISA Calculator (2026/27)
