Title tag
ISA Calculator 2026/27: Allowance, LISA Bonus & Growth | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Plan your £20,000 ISA allowance for 2026/27, add the Lifetime ISA 25% bonus and project tax-free growth for cash or stocks and shares ISAs. (139 chars)
Country
UK
Status
new · tax year 2026/27 (6 April 2026 – 5 April 2027); cash ISA change from 6 April 2027 noted
Body words
1,114 (minimum 1,000)
H1: ISA Calculator (2026/27)
An Individual Savings Account (ISA) shelters interest, dividends and capital gains from UK tax. In 2026/27 you can put in up to £20,000 across all your ISAs. A Lifetime ISA (LISA) adds a 25% government bonus on up to £4,000 of that. This calculator tracks how your allowance is split, adds any LISA bonus, and projects tax-free growth for cash or investments.
How to use this calculator
1. Your age: used for the LISA checks and the cash ISA change coming in 2027.
2. Planned contributions for 2026/27 by ISA type: cash, stocks and shares, Lifetime and innovative finance. The calculator warns you if the total goes over £20,000.
3. Contribution pattern: a lump sum or monthly.
4. Expected rate: an AER for cash, or an assumed average return for investments (try a range).
5. Years to project, and whether to repeat the same contribution each year.
The formula
Allowance check (2026/27):
cash + stocks & shares + LISA + innovative finance ≤ £20,000
LISA ≤ £4,000 (counts inside the £20,000)
LISA bonus = 25% × LISA contributions (max £1,000 a year)
Growth (annual contributions at year-end):
FV = B × (1 + r)^n + C × ((1 + r)^n − 1) / r
For monthly saving, the calculator uses the monthly equivalent rate.
LISA withdrawal charge: if you withdraw for any reason other than buying your first home, reaching 60 or terminal illness, a 25% charge applies to the amount withdrawn.
Worked examples
Example 1: using the full allowance for 10 years. £20,000 a year, 5% a year, 10 years, starting from £0:
FV = 20,000 × (1.05^10 − 1) / 0.05 = £251,557.85
Contributions: £200,000
Tax-free growth: £51,557.85
A smaller plan: £5,000 a year at 4% for 10 years gives £60,030.54. Of that, £10,030.54 is interest that would otherwise count towards your Personal Savings Allowance.
Example 2: the Lifetime ISA bonus, and the cost of the withdrawal charge.
Pay in £4,000 → bonus £1,000 → £5,000 in the account (before growth)
If you withdraw that £5,000 for a non-qualifying reason, the 25% charge is £1,250, so you get back £3,750. That is £250 less than you paid in. The charge removes the bonus and takes 6.25% of your own money.
Example 3: a cash ISA versus the Personal Savings Allowance. A higher-rate taxpayer with £30,000 at 4.5% earns £1,350 of interest a year. Outside an ISA, £500 is covered by the Personal Savings Allowance and £850 is taxed at 40%, costing £340.00 a year. In a cash ISA, the tax is nil. A basic-rate taxpayer earning the same interest would pay 20% on £350 (£70.00).
Example 4: a stocks and shares ISA over 20 years. £300 a month at an assumed 6% average annual return (compounded monthly) grows to about £138,612.27, from £72,000 of contributions. All growth and dividends are tax-free, and nothing needs to go on a tax return.
Understanding your results
Allowance used / remaining: across all ISA types for the current tax year. Unused allowance doesn't carry forward after 5 April.
Projected value: with the LISA bonus included where applicable. Investment values can fall as well as rise.
Tax saved: for comparison, the calculator can estimate the tax you'd pay on the same interest or dividends outside an ISA. It uses your band and the Personal Savings and Dividend Allowances.
Country notes
LISA rules: you must be 18 or over but under 40 to open one, and you can pay in until you turn 50. For a first home, the property must cost £450,000 or less, and you must buy it at least 12 months after your first payment in.
Cash ISA change: from 6 April 2027, the annual cash ISA limit for people under 65 falls to £12,000, within the £20,000 overall limit. For those 65 or older, cash ISA saving stays within the full £20,000. The calculator will apply this from the 2027/28 tax year.
Comparable accounts: Canada's TFSA and the US Roth IRA.
Notes for US and Canadian readers
The nearest equivalents are the Roth IRA in the US, which also gives tax-free growth but has income limits and withdrawal rules (see the Roth IRA calculator), and the TFSA in Canada, whose unused room carries forward, unlike the ISA allowance (see the TFSA calculator). UK residents who move abroad can keep an ISA but can't add new money while non-resident, and the other country may tax the income.
Tips and common mistakes
Paying more than £20,000 into ISAs in one tax year. The excess isn't tax-free and must be removed.
Withdrawing from a Lifetime ISA early. The 25% charge takes back more than the bonus.
Moving money between ISAs by withdrawing it. Use an ISA transfer so it keeps its tax-free status.
Leaving the allowance unused. It doesn't carry forward after 5 April.
Frequently asked questions
What is the ISA allowance for 2026/27?
£20,000 in total across cash, stocks and shares, innovative finance and Lifetime ISAs. Up to £4,000 of it can go into a Lifetime ISA.
Can I pay into more than one ISA in a year?
Yes. GOV.UK says you can save up to £20,000 in one account or split it across several accounts, as long as the total stays within the limit. The exception is the Lifetime ISA: you can pay into only one in a tax year. If your ISA is "flexible", money you take out and put back in the same tax year doesn't use up extra allowance.
How does the Lifetime ISA bonus work?
The government adds 25% of what you pay in, up to £1,000 a year on £4,000 of contributions, until you turn 50.
What happens if I take money out of a Lifetime ISA early?
Unless it's for a qualifying first-home purchase, after age 60 or due to terminal illness, a 25% withdrawal charge applies. As Example 2 shows, you can get back less than you paid in.
Do I pay tax on ISA interest or gains?
No UK Income Tax or Capital Gains Tax is due on interest, dividends or gains inside an ISA, and you don't need to declare them.
Is the cash ISA limit changing?
Yes. From 6 April 2027, people under 65 will be able to put at most £12,000 a year into cash ISAs, within the £20,000 overall limit.

H1: Land Transfer Tax Calculator
Land transfer tax is a provincial (and in some cities, municipal) tax paid by the buyer when property changes hands. It's due on closing and can't be added to your mortgage, so it's one of the largest cash costs of buying a home in Canada. This calculator estimates provincial and municipal land transfer tax for your purchase, including first-time buyer rebates.
How to use this calculator
1. Province: each province sets its own tax and calls it something different (land transfer tax in Ontario, property transfer tax in British Columbia, the "welcome tax" in Quebec).
2. City: select Toronto (or Montreal) where a municipal tax applies on top.
3. Purchase price: the value of the consideration, usually the sale price.
4. First-time buyer: for provincial and municipal rebates or exemptions where eligible.
Results: provincial tax, municipal tax, rebates, and total due at closing.
How it works
Land transfer tax is marginal: each slice of the price is taxed at its own rate, and the slices are added together. Ontario's rates (for transfers on or after 1 January 2017) are:
Portion of price
Rate
Up to $55,000
0.5%
$55,000 to $250,000
1.0%
$250,000 to $400,000
1.5%
$400,000 to $2,000,000
2.0%
Over $2,000,000 (land with one or two single-family homes)
2.5%
Worked examples
Example 1: $400,000 in Ontario (outside Toronto)
0.5% × 55,000 = $275.00
1.0% × 195,000 = $1,950.00
1.5% × 150,000 = $2,250.00
Total = $4,475.00
Example 2: $600,000 in Ontario
The first $400,000 costs $4,475.00, plus 2% × 200,000 = $4,000.00
Provincial tax = $8,475.00 (1.41% of the price)
In Toronto, the municipal land transfer tax uses matching rates at this price [VERIFY], so the total roughly doubles to $16,950.00. A first-time buyer eligible for the full Ontario refund (up to $4,000 [VERIFY]) and Toronto rebate (up to $4,475 [VERIFY]) would pay about $8,475.00.
Example 3: a $2.5 million detached home in Ontario
Provincial tax = $48,975.00, including 2.5% on the portion over $2 million.
Example 4: $900,000 in British Columbia
1% × 200,000 = $2,000.00
2% × 700,000 = $14,000.00
Property transfer tax = $16,000.00, compared with $14,475.00 provincial tax in Ontario
Example 5: an Ontario first-time buyer at $400,000
The Ontario first-time buyer refund covers up to $4,000 of provincial tax [VERIFY current maximum]. On Example 1's $4,475.00, the buyer would pay about $475.00. At $600,000, the refund still covers only $4,000 of the $8,475.00 bill.

Other provinces
British Columbia: property transfer tax of 1% on the first $200,000, 2% to $2 million and 3% above, plus a further 2% on residential value over $3 million [VERIFY]. On a $900,000 home that's $16,000.00 before any exemption. First-time buyers and buyers of new homes may qualify for full or partial exemptions under price limits [VERIFY current thresholds].
Quebec: the duties on transfers of immovables ("welcome tax") use brackets that are indexed each year, with higher municipal rates in Montreal and some other cities [VERIFY].
Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, PEI, Newfoundland and Labrador: each charges a provincial or municipal deed transfer tax with its own rates [VERIFY].
Alberta and Saskatchewan: no land transfer tax; buyers pay land titles registration fees based on value, which are much smaller.
Understanding your results
Payable at closing, typically through your lawyer or notary.
Not added to the mortgage. Budget for it in cash alongside the down payment, legal fees, inspection and moving costs.
Rebates may be paid at closing or claimed afterwards, depending on the province and how your lawyer registers the transfer.
CMHC premium isn't included. See the CMHC insurance calculator.
First-time buyer rules (summary)
Eligibility usually requires that you've never owned a home anywhere, that you're a Canadian citizen or permanent resident, and that you'll occupy the home within a set period (Ontario requires occupation within nine months) [VERIFY]. If a spouse has owned a home while being your spouse, the refund may be reduced or unavailable.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting the municipal tax in Toronto. It can double the bill.
Assuming rebates cover everything. On pricier homes, the rebate covers only part of the tax.
Leaving it out of the cash budget. Lenders won't lend it to you.
Using last year's rates. Rebates and thresholds are adjusted from time to time.
Notes for US and UK readers
US: many states and some counties and cities charge a real estate transfer tax or deed stamps, usually a small percentage of the price. Depending on local custom, the seller often pays it, unlike Canada, where the buyer pays. See the closing cost calculator.
UK: the equivalent is Stamp Duty Land Tax in England and Northern Ireland, LBTT in Scotland and LTT in Wales, also paid by the buyer. See the Stamp Duty calculator.
Frequently asked questions
Who pays land transfer tax?
The buyer.
How is land transfer tax calculated in Ontario?
Marginally: 0.5%, 1%, 1.5%, 2% and 2.5% on successive portions of the price.
Do I pay land transfer tax in Alberta?
No. Alberta charges land titles registration fees instead.
Can I add land transfer tax to my mortgage?
No. It's due in cash at closing.
How much is the first-time buyer rebate?
Up to $4,000 in Ontario and up to $4,475 in Toronto [VERIFY]; other provinces differ.
Is land transfer tax deductible?
Not for a principal residence. For a rental or business property, it's generally added to the property's cost base.

The first-time buyer column is never more than £600 lower, because relief only widens the nil-rate band by £30,000 at 2%. The ADS column shows why the supplement dominates the cost of second homes and buy-to-let purchases in Scotland.
Additional Dwelling Supplement: key points
It applies if, at the end of the day of the purchase, you own two or more dwellings and you're not replacing your main residence.
If you buy a new main home before selling your old one, you pay ADS but can claim a repayment if you sell the previous main home within 36 months [VERIFY current period].
It applies to companies buying residential property in most cases.
Properties worth under £40,000 are ignored when counting dwellings.
Paying LBTT
Your solicitor normally submits the LBTT return and pays the tax to Revenue Scotland within 30 days of the effective date (usually the date of entry). A return is required for most residential purchases of £40,000 or more, even when no tax is due.
Understanding your results
Cash cost: LBTT is paid upfront, usually from your own funds. Some lenders allow you to borrow more to cover it, but it then accrues interest.
Effective rate shows tax as a share of the price.
Leases and non-residential property use different tables.
Tips and common mistakes
Using English SDLT rates for a Scottish property. Scotland has its own bands.
Claiming first-time buyer relief jointly when one buyer has owned a home before. All buyers must qualify.
Forgetting ADS when keeping your old home.
Missing the ADS refund deadline after selling your former main residence.
How LBTT differs from SDLT and LTT
Lower starting point: Scotland's nil-rate band (£145,000) is above England's £125,000 but well below Wales's £225,000.
First-time buyers: relief is small in Scotland (worth up to £600), larger in England (no SDLT up to £300,000 on homes up to £500,000) and absent in Wales.
Second homes: Scotland adds an 8% supplement on the whole price; England adds 5 points to every band; Wales uses a separate higher-rates table.
Use the Stamp Duty calculator and the LTT calculator to compare.
What to have ready
Before you run the numbers, gather the agreed price, whether you're a first-time buyer, and whether you'll own any other home worldwide on the date of completion. Owning another home usually triggers the Additional Dwelling Supplement (ADS), payable on the whole price. If you're replacing your main home and sell the old one within the allowed period, you may be able to reclaim the ADS from Revenue Scotland, so keep completion dates and receipts. Your solicitor submits the LBTT return and pays the tax, normally within 30 days of the effective date. [VERIFY]
Frequently asked questions
How much LBTT will I pay on a £250,000 house?
£2,100 (2% on the £105,000 above £145,000), or £1,500 as a first-time buyer.
What is the first-time buyer relief in Scotland?
The nil-rate band rises from £145,000 to £175,000, saving up to £600.
What is the ADS rate?
8% of the total price from 5 December 2024.
Who pays LBTT?
The buyer.
Can ADS be refunded?
Yes, if you sell your previous main residence within the allowed period after buying the new one.
Does LBTT apply to the whole of the UK?
No. England and Northern Ireland have SDLT; Wales has Land Transaction Tax (see the LTT calculator).

Title tag
Lease Calculator: Payment, Rate or Residual | FigSumo (53 chars)
Meta description
Solve a general lease for the payment, implied rate or residual value. Works for equipment and vehicle leases with any term. (124 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,007 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Lease Calculator
This lease calculator estimates the regular monthly payment on a lease of a vehicle, machine, IT equipment or other asset. You enter the asset's value at the start, its expected residual (buyout) value at the end, the financing rate and the term. The payment covers the value the asset loses while you use it, plus a finance charge on the money tied up in it.
How to use this calculator
1. Asset value: the price the lease is based on (the capitalized cost), after any discount or upfront payment that reduces it.
2. Residual / buyout: the value the lessor expects the asset to have at the end of the term, or the agreed buyout price.
3. Financing rate (APR): the annual interest rate built into the lease. For car leases quoted as a money factor, multiply by 2,400 to get an approximate APR.
4. Lease term (months): the length of the lease.
Results: estimated monthly lease payment and total lease payments.
The formula
Depreciation charge = (Asset value − Residual) ÷ Term
Finance charge      = (APR ÷ 12) × (Asset value + Residual) ÷ 2
Payment             = Depreciation charge + Finance charge
The depreciation charge spreads the lost value evenly over the term.
The finance charge applies the monthly rate to the average amount tied up in the asset, (start value + end value) ÷ 2.
This is the same as the car-lease "money factor" method, because APR ÷ 2,400 × (value + residual) = (APR ÷ 12) × (value + residual) ÷ 2. A 6% APR is a money factor of 0.0025.
Payments are treated as monthly, with no tax added.
Worked examples
Example 1: $40,000 asset, $15,000 residual, 6% APR, 48 months
Depreciation = (40,000 − 15,000) ÷ 48 = $520.83
Finance = 0.005 × (40,000 + 15,000) ÷ 2 = $137.50
Payment = $658.33 a month
Total lease payments = $31,600.00, plus the $15,000 buyout if you choose to keep the asset
Example 2: $120,000 of equipment, 10% residual, 7.5%, 60 months
Residual = $12,000
Depreciation = 108,000 ÷ 60 = $1,800.00; finance = $412.50
Payment = $2,212.50; total $132,750.00
Equipment lessors often price with an exact annuity formula instead of the average-balance shortcut. With payments at the end of each month, the exact payment would be $2,239.10; with payments in advance (at the start of each month, which is common), $2,225.19. The shortcut is a good first estimate but can differ from a lessor's quote by a few percent on long terms.
Understanding your results
Monthly payment excludes sales tax, VAT, insurance, maintenance and fees.
Total lease payments is the cost of using the asset for the term. Add the buyout (residual) if you plan to keep it; compare that total with buying outright or financing with a loan.
Higher residual = lower payment, but a higher buyout price if you keep the asset.
Lease or buy?
Leasing keeps cash free, can match costs to the asset's useful life, and may include maintenance. Buying (with cash or a loan) usually costs less over the asset's full life if you keep it a long time. To compare:
1. Add up total lease payments plus any end-of-lease costs.
2. Compare with the loan payments on the same asset (use the loan calculator) minus its expected resale value at the end of the same period.
3. Consider tax treatment, which differs by country and lease type.
Types of leases
Operating lease (or true lease): the lessor keeps the risks of ownership; you return the asset at the end.
Finance (capital) lease: most of the risks and rewards pass to you; it works much like a loan.
Lease with a $1 buyout or bargain purchase option: effectively a purchase financed over time.
Under current accounting standards (ASC 842 in the US, IFRS 16 internationally), most leases longer than 12 months appear on the lessee's balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
Country notes
United States: for tax, a true lease is usually deductible as a rental expense, while a lease that is in substance a purchase is treated like a financed asset (depreciation plus interest). The IRS looks at the substance of the agreement, not its name.
Canada: lease payments on business assets are generally deductible; for passenger vehicles the CRA caps deductible lease costs [VERIFY 2026 monthly limit].
United Kingdom: business contract hire and finance leases have different VAT and tax treatment. VAT is usually charged on each rental; businesses can often reclaim it, with restrictions on cars.
Tips and common mistakes
Using list price as the asset value. Negotiate the price first; the lease is built on it.
Ignoring end-of-term charges. Return conditions, excess use and wear can add costs.
Comparing rate-free quotes. Ask for the implied interest rate or money factor.
Forgetting tax. Add sales tax or VAT to the payment where it applies.
Frequently asked questions
How is a lease payment calculated?
Depreciation over the term plus a finance charge on the average amount of value tied up in the asset.
What is a residual value?
The asset's expected value (or agreed buyout price) at the end of the lease.
What is the difference between APR and money factor?
They express the same thing in different forms: APR ≈ money factor × 2,400.
Can I use this for a car lease?
Yes. For car-specific inputs like down payment and a direct money factor, the auto lease calculator is more convenient.
Are lease payments paid in advance?
Many leases require the first payment at signing (in advance). That slightly lowers each payment compared with payments in arrears at the same rate.
Is leasing cheaper than buying?
Not usually over the full life of an asset, but it can be better for cash flow, flexibility or assets that become obsolete quickly.

Life Insurance Needs Calculator (DIME Method) | FigSumo (55 chars)

Estimate how much life insurance cover you may need from debts, income replacement, mortgage and education costs. Not a quote or advice. (136 chars)

H1: Life Insurance Needs Calculator
How much life insurance do you need? The answer depends on what your family would have to pay for without your income: daily living costs for a number of years, the mortgage and other debts, children's education and final expenses, minus what you already have. This calculator uses that needs-based approach to estimate a coverage amount. It doesn't quote premiums or recommend a product.
How to use this calculator
1. Income to replace (per year): often less than your full salary, because your own living costs and taxes would stop. Many people use 70% to 80% of take-home or gross pay.
2. Years of support: until your youngest child is independent, or your partner reaches retirement.
3. Real rate of return (optional): if you want the present value of the income stream (the lump sum that, invested, would pay it out).
4. Mortgage balance and other debts: car loans, student loans, credit cards.
5. Final expenses: funeral and estate costs.
6. Education fund: future college or university costs you want covered.
7. Existing life insurance (including group cover through work) and savings and investments available to your family.
Results: total needs, resources available and additional coverage needed.
The formula
Needs = Income replacement + Mortgage + Debts + Final expenses + Education
Coverage needed = Needs − Existing life insurance − Savings and investments
Income replacement can be calculated two ways:
Simple: annual amount × years.
Present value: annual amount × (1 − (1 + r)^−n) ÷ r × (1 + r), with payments at the start of each year and r a real (after-inflation) return. This is the lump sum that would fund the payments.
Worked example
Earner on $70,000 a year, partner and two children; replace 80% ($56,000.00 a year) for 15 years.
Income replacement, simple method: $840,000.00
Present value at a 2% real return: $733,949.93
Mortgage: $240,000; other debts: $15,000; final expenses: $12,000; education fund: $80,000
Total needs: $1,080,949.93
Existing group life cover $100,000 and savings $60,000: $160,000.00
Additional coverage needed: $920,949.93
A common shortcut, 10 times salary, would suggest $700,000.00. The needs-based figure is more tailored because it accounts for the mortgage, education goals and existing assets.
Example 2: a stay-at-home parent
No salary, but replacing childcare and household help would cost about $15,000 a year until the youngest child is 12, in 10 years:
Present value at 2% real: 15,000 × (1 − 1.02⁻¹⁰) ÷ 0.02 × 1.02 = $137,433.55
Final expenses $12,000
Coverage needed ≈ $149,433.55, less any existing cover
Example 3: a single earner with a mortgage and no dependants
If nobody relies on your income, needs may be just the debts others would inherit responsibility for (often none, if loans are only in your name) and final expenses. Many single people without dependants need little or no individual cover, beyond any free group cover through work.

The longer the period, the more the present value method reduces the lump sum, because the money is invested and drawn down over time.
Understanding your results
Term vs permanent: for income replacement over a fixed period, many families look at term life insurance, which covers a set number of years. Permanent (whole or universal) life insurance lasts for life and builds cash value at a higher cost. Which suits you depends on your goals.
Stay-at-home parents: include the cost of childcare and household work, even without a salary.
Social Security survivor benefits may replace part of the income for children under 18 and a surviving spouse caring for them; you can treat an estimate as a resource. See the Social Security calculator.
Group cover through work often ends when you leave the job; don't rely on it entirely.
Review the figure after major life events: marriage, a new child, a home purchase or a pay rise.
Tax notes
Life insurance death benefits are generally not subject to federal income tax for the beneficiary. Proceeds can be included in the insured's estate for estate tax purposes if the insured owned the policy, which matters only for large estates (the 2026 basic exclusion is $15 million); see the estate tax calculator.
Canada and the UK
The same needs-based method works elsewhere. In Canada, life insurance proceeds are generally tax-free to beneficiaries, and the CPP pays a death benefit and survivor's pension. In the UK, policies written in trust usually keep proceeds outside the estate for Inheritance Tax; employer "death in service" cover is common.
Tips and common mistakes
Using gross salary for 30 years without considering that needs fall as children grow.
Forgetting debts or counting the mortgage twice (once in income and once as a lump sum).
Ignoring inflation in long time frames; use a real return.
Insuring only the main earner.
Overlooking existing assets, which reduce the need.
Frequently asked questions
How much life insurance do I need?
Enough to cover your family's needs (income replacement, debts, education and final costs) minus the resources they'd already have.
Is 10 times my salary enough?
It's a rough rule of thumb. A needs-based calculation is more accurate for your situation.
Should I include my mortgage?
Yes, if you want your family to be able to pay it off.
Are life insurance payouts taxable?
Generally not for federal income tax, though interest on delayed payouts is taxable.
Do I need life insurance if I'm single without dependants?
Possibly not, beyond final expenses or debts someone else would have to pay.
How often should I review my coverage?
After major life changes and every few years.

Title tag
Loan Calculator: Monthly Payment, Interest & Schedule | FigSumo (63 chars)
Meta description
Find the monthly payment, total interest and payoff schedule for any fixed-rate loan, and see how term, rate and fees change the true cost. (139 chars)
Country
global (currency follows locale: USD/CAD/GBP)
Status
keep
Body words
1,098 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Loan Calculator
Use this calculator for personal loans, car loans, student loans and any other fixed-rate loan that you repay in equal instalments. Enter the amount, rate and term to get the regular payment and the total interest. It works backwards too: give it a payment you can afford, and it finds the loan amount or the time needed to pay it off.
How to use this calculator
1. Choose what to solve for: payment, loan amount, term or interest rate.
2. Loan amount: the amount you borrow, before any fee.
3. Interest rate: the nominal annual rate in your loan agreement.
4. Term: years and/or months.
5. Upfront fee (optional): an origination or arrangement fee. If it is deducted from the money you receive, the calculator shows the resulting APR as well as the payment.
6. Payment frequency: monthly by default; bi-weekly and weekly are also available.
The currency follows your country setting. The maths is the same in every country.
The formula
For a loan repaid in equal instalments (an amortizing loan):
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
PMT: payment per period
P: principal (amount borrowed)
r: interest rate per period = annual rate ÷ payments per year
n: total number of payments
Total interest = PMT × n − P.
To solve for the term:
n = −ln(1 − P × r / PMT) / ln(1 + r)
This only works when PMT is larger than the first period's interest, P × r. Otherwise the loan never shrinks.
To solve for the rate or the APR, there is no closed-form answer. The calculator searches numerically for the rate that makes the payments' present value equal to the amount you actually received.
Worked examples
Example 1: personal loan. $15,000 at 9% for 4 years, monthly.
r = 0.09 / 12 = 0.0075; n = 48
PMT = 15,000 × 0.0075 / (1 − 1.0075^−48) = $373.28 a month
Total paid: $17,917.23 · total interest: $2,917.23
First payment: $112.50 interest (15,000 × 0.0075) and $260.78 principal
Shortening the term to 3 years (36 payments) raises the payment to $477.00 and lowers total interest to $2,171.86, a saving of $745.37.
Example 2: an upfront fee changes the real rate. The same loan, with a 3% origination fee ($450) taken out of the loan proceeds. You receive $14,550 but still repay $373.28 a month for 48 months on $15,000. Solving for the rate that links $14,550 to those payments gives an APR of about 10.61%, compared with the 9% headline rate. This is why comparing APRs is fairer than comparing headline rates.
Other loan structures
Not every loan is repaid in equal instalments. Two other common structures:
Deferred-payment (lump-sum) loan: nothing is paid until maturity, when principal and all accrued interest are due together: FV = P × (1 + r)^n. For example, $10,000 at 6% compounded monthly for 5 years means $13,488.50 is due at the end.
Zero-coupon bond (borrower's view): you receive less than face value today and repay the face value at maturity. The amount received is PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^n. A $10,000 face value due in 10 years at 5% compounded annually raises $6,139.13 today.
Both are available as modes in the calculator (DEV-TASKS T-412). Compounding frequency can be set separately from payment frequency.
Understanding your results
Payment is the fixed instalment. The last payment can differ by a few cents because of rounding.
Total interest is the cost of borrowing. Two loans with the same payment can have very different total costs if their terms differ.
Amortization schedule: shows each payment split into interest and principal, and the remaining balance. Interest falls over time because it is charged on a shrinking balance.
APR (when a fee is entered): an estimate of the yearly cost including the fee. Lenders calculate the legally disclosed APR under their own country's rules, so use their figure for official comparisons.
Country notes
United States: lenders must disclose the APR and finance charge under the Truth in Lending Act. Federal student loans and mortgages have dedicated calculators on FigSumo.
Canada: federally regulated lenders must tell you the loan amount, the interest rate, the term, the payment and any fees. The FCAC also notes that lenders may not charge more than 35% a year, counting all interest, fees and costs. Mortgages are different: they use semi-annual compounding, so use the Canadian mortgage calculator.
UK: consumer credit offers quote a representative APR. Not every borrower gets that rate, so enter the rate you are actually offered.
Tips and common mistakes
Comparing loans by rate alone. Fees change the true cost; compare APRs.
Choosing the longest term for the lowest payment. It costs the most interest.
Mixing monthly and annual rates. Enter the annual rate; the calculator divides by 12.
Forgetting prepayment penalties. Check them before planning to pay early.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between interest rate and APR?
The interest rate is what's charged on the balance. The APR adds certain fees and expresses the total as a yearly rate, so you can compare loans with different fee structures.
Does paying extra reduce my interest?
Yes, for a standard amortizing loan, because extra money reduces the principal that interest is charged on. Check your agreement for prepayment penalties first. Use the amortization calculator to model extra payments.
Why is a longer term cheaper per month but more expensive overall?
Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, and a longer term keeps the balance higher for longer. In Example 1, four years costs $745.37 more interest than three.
Can I use this for an interest-only or balloon loan?
No. This page models fully amortizing loans, where the balance reaches zero with the last regular payment. Interest-only and balloon structures leave part of the principal to be repaid at the end. Ask your lender for their schedule.
How is a daily-interest loan different?
Some loans charge interest daily on the balance. The total is very close to the monthly result if you pay on time, but paying early or late changes the interest slightly.
What payment frequency should I choose?
Use whatever your lender's schedule is. Bi-weekly payments on a loan that charges interest by period will reduce total interest slightly compared with monthly.

H1: Loan Comparison Calculator
When you have more than one loan offer, the lowest monthly payment isn't always the cheapest loan. Rates, terms and fees all change the total cost. This calculator puts up to three loans side by side and shows each one's monthly payment, total interest, fees, total cost and APR, so you can see which is cheapest overall and which is easiest on your monthly budget.
How to use this calculator

2. Interest rate (annual)
3. Term in months or years
4. Upfront fees: origination, arrangement or processing fees. Choose whether the fee is deducted from the money you receive, paid upfront, or added to the loan.

How it works

Understanding your results
Compare like with like. If terms differ, the shorter loan usually has a higher payment and lower total cost.
Fees matter more on short loans and small amounts. A $750 fee on a two-year loan adds more to the APR than on a five-year loan.
Prepayment: if you plan to pay early, a loan with a large upfront fee loses its advantage; check prepayment penalties too.
Variable rates: the comparison assumes the rate stays fixed. For variable loans, run a higher-rate scenario.
What to check in each offer
APR and finance charge (US Truth in Lending disclosures; the UK and Canada also require APR in credit advertising and agreements).
Whether the rate is fixed or variable.
Origination, late and prepayment fees.
Any optional add-ons (insurance, protection products) included in the payment.
Whether the offer is a firm approval or a pre-qualification estimate.
Tips and common mistakes
Choosing on monthly payment alone.
Ignoring how fees are paid. A fee deducted from proceeds means you receive less.
Comparing a 5-year loan with a 7-year loan by total interest alone without considering affordability.
Forgetting the credit impact. Rate shopping within a short window is usually treated as a single inquiry for mortgages and auto loans [VERIFY scoring model rules].
Notes for US, Canada and UK borrowers
US: the Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the APR, finance charge, amount financed and total of payments in a standard box, which makes offers easy to compare side by side.
Canada: federally regulated lenders must give a cost of borrowing disclosure showing the APR and total cost, and you can usually prepay a closed personal loan, though check for fees.
UK: lenders must show a representative APR in adverts, and at least 51% of successful applicants must get that rate or better. Your personal rate can be higher, so compare the rate you're actually offered. You also have 14 days to withdraw from most credit agreements.
Frequently asked questions
How do I compare two loans?
Look at the total cost (payments plus fees) for the same amount, and the APR. Then check the payment fits your budget.
Is a lower interest rate always better?
Not if it comes with large fees or a longer term. Compare total cost and APR.
What is the difference between APR and interest rate?
The interest rate is the cost of borrowing the principal; APR also includes most fees, expressed as an annual rate.
Should I pay points to get a lower rate?
Only if you'll keep the loan past the breakeven month.
Can I compare loans with different terms?
Yes, but remember a longer term usually costs more overall even if the payment is lower.
Does the calculator include prepayment penalties?
No. Add them to fees if you expect to pay off early.

H1: LTT Calculator (Wales)

LTT = £61,750.00
When higher rates apply
You'll own two or more residential properties worth £40,000 or more at the end of the day of purchase, and the new one doesn't replace your main residence.
Companies and most other non-individual buyers pay higher rates on residential property.
If you buy a new main home before selling your old one, you pay higher rates but can claim a refund if you sell the previous home within the allowed period [VERIFY current period with the WRA].
Property owned anywhere in the world counts.

Your solicitor or conveyancer submits the LTT return and pays the tax to the Welsh Revenue Authority, normally within 30 days of completion. A return is needed for most residential purchases of £40,000 or more.

The calculator covers standard residential purchases. Some situations need different treatment and usually a conveyancer's advice:
Multiple dwellings bought in one transaction, which may be taxed differently.

Shared ownership and other schemes where you buy a share of the property.
Transfers between spouses or on divorce, which are often exempt.
Gifts where no money changes hands, unless the transfer includes taking on a mortgage.

From 5% up to 17% across six bands, since 11 December 2024.

The Welsh Revenue Authority.

Usually within 30 days of completion, through your solicitor.

Yes, with separate non-residential rates.

Title tag
Profit Margin Calculator: Margin vs Markup | FigSumo (52 chars)
Meta description
Find gross margin, markup, profit, cost or price from any two values. Explains the difference between margin and markup with examples. (134 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,010 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Margin Calculator
Gross margin is the share of each sale left after paying for the goods or services sold. This calculator takes revenue and cost of goods sold (COGS) and returns gross profit and gross margin. Business owners use it to check pricing, compare products, and see how discounts or cost increases affect profit.
How to use this calculator
1. Revenue: sales for the item, product line or period, excluding sales tax or VAT collected for the government.
2. Cost of goods sold: the direct cost of what you sold, such as purchase price or materials, direct labor, inbound shipping and packaging. Overheads like rent and marketing are not part of COGS.
Results: gross profit and gross margin.
The formula
Gross profit = Revenue − COGS
Gross margin = Gross profit ÷ Revenue × 100
Margin is always measured against the selling price (revenue). That is the key difference from markup, which is measured against cost:
Markup = Gross profit ÷ COGS × 100
To set a price that gives a target margin:
Price = Cost ÷ (1 − Target margin)
Worked examples
Example 1: revenue $250,000, COGS $150,000
Gross profit = 250,000 − 150,000 = $100,000.00
Gross margin = 100,000 ÷ 250,000 = 40.00%
The same profit expressed as markup = 100,000 ÷ 150,000 = 66.67%
Example 2: pricing a product for a 35% margin
A product costs $18.
Price = 18 ÷ (1 − 0.35) = $27.69
Gross profit per unit: $9.69; markup: 53.85%
A common mistake is to add 35% to cost instead: 18 × 1.35 = $24.30, which gives a margin of only 25.93%.
Example 3: blended margin across products
A shop sells two products in a month:
Product
Revenue
COGS
Margin
A
$30,000
$21,000
30.00%
B
$10,000
$4,000
60.00%
Total
$40,000
$25,000
37.50%
The blended margin is total gross profit ÷ total revenue, not the average of the two percentages (which would be 45%). Product A dominates because it brings in more revenue. Enter the totals in the calculator to get the blended figure.
Understanding your results
Gross profit is the money available to pay overheads (rent, salaries, marketing) and leave a profit.
Gross margin lets you compare products and businesses of different sizes. Higher is better, but "good" margins vary widely by industry: grocery retail runs on thin margins while software can be very high.
Gross margin is not net profit. Operating expenses, interest and tax come out after it.
Margin and discounting
Discounts hit margin hard. Selling a $100 item that costs $60 gives a 40% margin. A 10% discount to $90 drops the margin to 33.33%, and gross profit falls from $40 to $30 per unit, so you would need 33.3% more unit sales to make the same gross profit. Before running a sale, check the volume you'd need with the break-even calculator.
Margin vs markup at a glance
Margin
Equivalent markup
20%
25%
25%
33.33%
33.33%
50%
40%
66.67%
50%
100%
Formula: markup = margin ÷ (1 − margin); margin = markup ÷ (1 + markup). The markup calculator works from the cost side.
Ways to improve gross margin
Raise prices where customers value the product; even small rises flow straight to gross profit.
Cut direct costs by negotiating supplier prices, ordering in larger quantities or reducing waste and returns.
Change the mix: promote higher-margin products and bundles.
Control discounting: set a floor price below which staff can't discount.
Charge for extras such as delivery, installation or rush orders instead of absorbing them.
Track margin monthly by product. A slow drift down often signals rising supplier costs that haven't been passed on.
Country notes
United States and Canada: exclude sales tax, GST/HST and PST from revenue; they belong to the government, not the business.
United Kingdom: for VAT-registered businesses, calculate margin on prices excluding VAT. Use the VAT calculator to strip VAT out of a gross price first. (The VAT "margin scheme" for second-hand goods is a different, tax-specific concept.)
Tips and common mistakes
Confusing margin and markup. A 50% markup is a 33.33% margin.
Leaving costs out of COGS. Forgetting shipping, payment fees or packaging overstates margin.
Including sales tax in revenue. It inflates both revenue and margin.
Looking only at percentage. A lower-margin product that sells in volume can produce more gross profit.
Margin or markup for pricing? Either works if you use it consistently. Retailers often think in margin because it relates directly to sales revenue; many trades and manufacturers use markup on cost. Convert between them with the table above.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between margin and markup?
Margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price; markup is profit as a percentage of the cost. The same sale has a lower margin than markup.
How do I calculate gross margin?
Subtract COGS from revenue, divide by revenue, and multiply by 100.
How do I price for a specific margin?
Divide the cost by (1 − target margin as a decimal). For a 40% margin on a $30 cost: 30 ÷ 0.60 = $50.
What is a good gross margin?
It depends on the industry and business model. Compare with businesses like yours and with your own history.
Can margin be negative?
Yes, if COGS exceeds revenue, meaning each sale loses money before overheads.
Does gross margin include overheads?
No. Operating margin and net margin include overheads and other costs.
How do I calculate margin from a price that includes VAT or GST?
Remove the tax first. For UK VAT at 20%, divide the gross price by 1.2; for Ontario HST at 13%, divide by 1.13. Then calculate margin on the net price.
What is contribution margin?
Price minus all variable costs per unit (COGS plus variable selling costs such as commissions and payment fees). It is the figure used in break-even analysis.

Title tag
Markup Calculator: Price From Cost and Markup | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Calculate selling price from cost and markup percentage, or markup from cost and price, with the matching gross margin. (119 chars)
Country

679 (minimum 600)
H1: Markup Calculator
Markup is how much you add to the cost of a product to set its selling price, expressed as a percentage of cost. Retailers, wholesalers, contractors and makers use it to price consistently. This calculator works out the selling price from cost and markup, the markup from cost and price, or the cost from price and markup, and shows the gross profit and gross margin for each.
How to use this calculator
Enter any two of the three values:
1. Cost: what the item costs you (purchase price, or materials and labour).
2. Markup (%): the percentage you add to cost.
3. Selling price: the price before sales tax or VAT.
Results: the missing value, plus gross profit (price − cost) and gross margin (profit as a percentage of price).
The formulas
Selling price = Cost × (1 + Markup)
Markup = (Price − Cost) ÷ Cost
Cost = Price ÷ (1 + Markup)
Gross profit = Price − Cost
Margin = (Price − Cost) ÷ Price
Converting between the two:
Margin = Markup ÷ (1 + Markup)
Markup = Margin ÷ (1 − Margin)
Worked examples
Example 1: pricing from cost
Cost $40; markup 50%.
Price = 40 × 1.5 = $60.00
Profit $20.00; margin 20 ÷ 60 = 33.33%
Example 2: finding the markup
Cost $40; you sell at $55.
Markup = 15 ÷ 40 = 37.50%
Margin = 15 ÷ 55 = 27.27%
Example 3: working back to the maximum cost
You want to sell at $80 with a 60% markup.
Maximum cost = 80 ÷ 1.6 = $50.00
Example 4: markup on a margin target
A 40% margin needs a markup of 0.4 ÷ 0.6 = 66.67%. A 25% markup gives a margin of only 2000.00%.
Markup vs margin at common levels
Markup
Margin
10%
9.09%
20%
16.67%
25%
20.00%
33.33%
25.00%
50%
33.33%
100%
50.00%
A 100% markup (doubling the cost, often called "keystone" pricing in retail) is a 50% margin. A $3.20 item at a 150% markup sells for $8.00.
Chained markups
A wholesaler buys at $18.50 and adds 20% ($22.20); a retailer adds 25% to that. The shelf price is $27.75. Markups multiply rather than add: 20% then 25% is 50% overall, not 45%.
Understanding your results
Markup is on cost; margin is on price. The same profit gives a bigger markup percentage than margin percentage. Mixing them up is the most common pricing mistake. See the margin calculator.
Gross profit isn't net profit. Rent, wages, marketing and other overheads still need covering; the break-even calculator shows how many units you need to sell.
Price before tax. Add US sales tax at checkout, or include VAT/GST in UK and Canadian consumer prices; see the VAT calculator.
Discounts cut margin faster than you might expect: a 20% discount on a 50% markup leaves a 20% markup (16.67% margin).
Choosing a markup
Markups vary hugely by industry: groceries operate on thin margins, while jewellery and restaurant drinks carry high markups. Consider:
What competitors charge
Your overheads per unit
Volume: high-volume items can carry lower markups
Perceived value and brand
Payment processing and returns costs
Tips and common mistakes
Calculating margin as markup (or the reverse).
Leaving costs out: shipping in, packaging, card fees.
Adding markups instead of multiplying them when there are several stages.
Ignoring tax in consumer-facing prices where it must be included.
Frequently asked questions
What is the formula for markup?
Markup = (Price − Cost) ÷ Cost × 100.
What's the difference between markup and margin?
Markup is profit as a percentage of cost; margin is profit as a percentage of the selling price.
What markup gives a 50% margin?
100%.
How do I add a 30% markup?
Multiply the cost by 1.3.
Is a 50% markup the same as a 50% margin?
No. A 50% markup is a 33.33% margin.
Should markup include overheads?
Your markup needs to be high enough that total gross profit covers overheads and leaves a profit.

Title tag
Marriage Penalty Calculator: Joint vs Single Tax (2026) | FigSumo (65 chars)
Meta description
Compare two people's 2026 federal income tax filing single with filing jointly to see whether marriage creates a tax penalty or bonus. (134 chars)
Country
US
Status
rename (301) · tax year 2026

1,007 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Marriage Tax Calculator
Getting married changes how you file your federal income tax return, and that can raise or lower the total tax the two of you pay. This calculator compares the tax two partners would owe filing as single people with the tax they'd owe filing jointly as a married couple, using the 2026 federal brackets. The difference is the "marriage bonus" (you pay less) or "marriage penalty" (you pay more).
How to use this calculator
1. Partner 1 taxable income: income after deductions (standard or itemized) for the year. On a past return, this is the "taxable income" line of Form 1040.
2. Partner 2 taxable income: the same for the other partner.
Results: tax if both file single, tax if married filing jointly, and the marriage bonus / penalty (joint tax minus the combined single tax; a negative number is a bonus).
Because the inputs are taxable income, the standard deduction is not applied by the tool. For 2026 the standard deduction is $16,100 single and $32,200 married filing jointly (exactly double), so subtracting each person's deduction before entering incomes gives a like-for-like comparison.
The formula
Tax(single) = T_single(Income1) + T_single(Income2)
Tax(joint)  = T_joint(Income1 + Income2)
Bonus (−) or penalty (+) = Tax(joint) − Tax(single)
T applies the 2026 tax brackets (IRS IR-2025-103):
Rate

Married filing jointly
10%
up to $12,400
up to $24,800
12%

to $100,800
22%

above
Joint brackets are exactly twice the single brackets up to the 32% band, so for most couples the bracket effect is zero. Differences appear when incomes are very unequal (a bonus) or when combined income reaches the 35% and 37% bands (a possible penalty).
Worked examples
Example 1: $90,000 and $60,000
Single: $14,512.00 + $7,912.00 = $22,424.00
Joint on $150,000: $22,424.00
Bonus/penalty: $0.00. Both incomes sit within brackets that double exactly.
Example 2: one earner with $150,000, the other with none
Single (the earner alone): $28,598.00
Joint: $22,424.00
Marriage bonus: $6,174.00. The joint brackets let the higher earner use the wider bands.
Example 3: high incomes, $500,000 and $400,000
Single total: $252,538.50
Joint on $900,000: $255,164.50
Marriage penalty: $2,626.00. The joint 35% band ends at $768,700, well below twice the single threshold of $640,600.
Understanding your results
A bonus usually appears when one partner earns much more than the other.
A penalty from brackets alone only arises at high combined incomes. Below that, real-world penalties usually come from other rules (next section).
This is a bracket comparison. It doesn't include credits, other taxes or state tax.
Other sources of marriage penalties and bonuses
These aren't in the calculator but often matter more than brackets:
Earned Income Tax Credit: income limits for married couples are not double the single limits, so two low-to-moderate earners can lose some or all of the credit.
State and local tax (SALT) deduction cap: the cap is the same for single and joint filers [VERIFY 2026 amount and phase-down under the 2025 law], which can penalize two itemizing homeowners.
Net Investment Income Tax and Additional Medicare Tax: thresholds are $200,000 single and $250,000 joint, not double (IRS Topic 559 and Topic 560).
Head of household: an unmarried parent may file as head of household, which has better brackets than single. Marrying gives up that status.
Child Tax Credit: $2,200 per child for 2026; phase-out thresholds are $200,000 single and $400,000 joint [VERIFY], so it is usually neutral.
State taxes: some states' brackets for couples are not double those for singles.
Filing separately
Married couples can also file separately (MFS). For 2026, MFS brackets match single up to $256,225, then the 35% band ends at $384,350. MFS rarely lowers total tax and blocks several credits, but it can help in specific cases such as income-driven student loan repayment or separating liability.
Country notes
The US is unusual in taxing married couples jointly. Canada taxes each person individually; spouses can share some credits and split eligible pension income. The UK also taxes individuals; the Marriage Allowance lets a non-taxpayer transfer £1,260 of personal allowance to a basic-rate spouse. Use the Canada and UK income tax calculators for those systems.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering gross salary. Use taxable income, after deductions.
Forgetting the year. Your filing status for the whole year depends on whether you're married on 31 December.
Ignoring withholding. After marrying, update your Form W-4 so your paychecks withhold the right amount; see the W-4 withholding calculator.
Quick check
Compare both spouses' state taxes too.
Frequently asked questions
Is there a marriage penalty in 2026?
From brackets alone, only at high combined incomes (around the 35% and 37% bands). Other rules, such as the EITC and some thresholds, can create penalties at lower incomes.
Why do most couples see $0?
Because 2026 joint brackets are exactly double the single brackets up to the 32% band, and the joint standard deduction is double the single one.
Do I have to file jointly when married?
No. You can file jointly or separately. Joint filing usually costs less.
When does marriage count for tax?
If you're married on the last day of the year, you're treated as married for the whole year.
Does this include state taxes?
No. State rules vary; some have their own marriage penalties.
What about Social Security and Medicare taxes?
Payroll taxes are calculated per worker and are unaffected by marriage, except the Additional Medicare Tax threshold.

Mortgage Amortization Calculator

Title tag
Mortgage Amortization Schedule Calculator | FigSumo (51 chars)
Meta description
Print a month-by-month mortgage amortization schedule and see how extra payments change your payoff date and total interest. (124 chars)
Country

H1: Mortgage Amortization Calculator
A mortgage amortization schedule shows how each monthly payment is split between interest and principal, and how your loan balance falls over the life of the mortgage. Enter the loan amount, rate and term to see the payment, the total interest and a chart of the balance, cumulative interest and cumulative payments. This page explains how to read the schedule and what it tells you about equity, refinancing and extra payments.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: the mortgage principal, i.e. the price minus your down payment, plus any financed fees. It is on your Loan Estimate or mortgage statement.
2. Interest rate: the note rate (not the APR).
3. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): usually 30 or 15 years.
Results: monthly payment (principal and interest), total of payments, total interest paid, and an amortization chart, with the first payments listed in a table.
The formula
PMT = L × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Interest(k)  = Balance(k−1) × r
Principal(k) = PMT − Interest(k)
Balance(k)   = Balance(k−1) − Principal(k)
L: loan amount; r: annual rate ÷ 12; n: months
Each month's interest is rounded to the cent, and the last payment is adjusted to clear the balance exactly.
Worked example: $400,000 at 6.5% for 30 years
Payment: $2,528.27 a month
Total of 360 payments: $910,179.81; total interest: $510,179.81
Payment 1: $2,166.67 interest and $361.60 principal
Yearly summary

Milestones:

The balance falls below half the original loan in month 257 (21.4 years in).
Shorter term: the same $400,000 over 15 years at 6.0% costs $3,375.43 a month but only $207,576.56 in total interest.
Understanding your results
Front-loaded interest. Early payments are mostly interest because interest is charged on a large balance. That is not a penalty; it's how amortization works.
Equity build-up. Equity grows with each principal payment and with any rise in the home's value. Slow early principal is why selling within a few years often returns little equity once selling costs are paid.
Total interest assumes you keep the loan to the end. Most people move or refinance sooner.
Payment excludes escrow. Property tax, insurance and mortgage insurance are paid on top; they don't change the amortization.
Using the schedule
PMI removal (US): on a conventional loan, PMI ends automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original home value. If the $400,000 loan above was on a $500,000 home, that happens at month 26. You can ask to cancel at 80%. See the PMI calculator.
Refinancing: the schedule shows your balance at any point, which you need to compare a refinance; see the refinance calculator.
Extra payments: each extra dollar of principal skips future interest. The mortgage payoff calculator shows the time and interest saved.
Tax records (US): interest paid each year is reported on Form 1098 if you itemize.
Country notes
United States: most mortgages are fixed for 15 or 30 years, so a single schedule covers the whole loan.
Canada: mortgages are amortized over up to 25 years (30 for some insured first-time buyers and new builds [VERIFY current rules]), but the rate is usually fixed for a 5-year term and then renewed. Interest on fixed-rate mortgages is compounded semi-annually by law, so the monthly rate is slightly lower than rate ÷ 12. Use the Canadian mortgage calculator.
United Kingdom: "repayment" mortgages amortize like this, usually over 25 to 35 years, with fixed rates for 2 to 5 years before reverting. Interest-only mortgages don't amortize. See the UK mortgage calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the APR as the rate. The schedule uses the note rate; APR includes fees.
Forgetting financed fees. If fees are added to the loan, include them in the amount.
Reading year 1 as typical. Interest falls and principal rises every year.
Comparing loans by payment only. A longer term cuts the payment but adds a lot of interest.
Quick check
In the first year of the $400,000 example, interest is well over three-quarters of each payment. Rerun it with a 15-year term to see how much faster equity builds.
Frequently asked questions
Why is most of my early mortgage payment interest?
Interest is charged on the outstanding balance, which is largest at the start. As the balance falls, more of each payment goes to principal.
How much of my loan will I have paid off after 5 years?
For the example above, the balance after 5 years is $374,444.08, so about $25,000 of principal has been repaid. Run your own loan to see your figure.
Does an extra payment change the schedule?
Yes. It reduces the balance immediately, so every later payment has more principal and less interest, and the loan ends sooner.
Is a 15-year mortgage better than a 30-year one?
It costs much less interest and usually has a lower rate, but a higher payment. The 30-year offers flexibility; you can still pay extra.
Why does my lender's schedule differ by a few cents?
Lenders round slightly differently and may use exact day counts for the first payment.
What is negative amortization?
When payments don't cover the interest, so the balance grows. Standard fixed-rate mortgages don't do this.
What is the difference between this and the general amortization calculator?
The maths is identical. This page focuses on mortgages: equity, PMI milestones, refinancing and country rules. For car loans and personal loans, use the amortization calculator.

Title tag
Mortgage Calculator with PMI, Taxes, Insurance & HOA | FigSumo (62 chars)
Meta description
Estimate your full monthly mortgage payment: principal, interest, property tax, homeowners insurance, PMI and HOA, with an amortization schedule. (145 chars)
Country
US (default); see /ca/mortgage-calculator and /uk/mortgage-calculator
Status

Body words
1,435 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Mortgage Calculator
The monthly payment on a home loan is more than principal and interest. Enter a price, a down payment and a rate, and this calculator adds property tax, homeowners insurance, private mortgage insurance (PMI) and HOA dues. It then shows the full monthly cost, the interest over the life of the loan, and the month your PMI can come off.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price and down payment. Type the down payment in dollars or as a percent. The loan amount is the price minus the down payment.
2. Interest rate and term. Use the note rate from your Loan Estimate (not the APR) and the term in years: 30, 20, 15 or a custom length.
3. Property tax. Enter the yearly bill, or a percent of the price if you don't know it yet. Your county assessor or the listing usually has last year's figure.
4. Homeowners insurance. Enter the annual premium from a quote.
5. PMI. If you put down less than 20% on a conventional loan, the calculator turns PMI on automatically and starts it at 0.5% of the loan per year. This is a placeholder: real PMI rates depend on your credit score, loan-to-value and insurer, so replace it with your quote.
6. HOA and extra payments (optional). Add monthly HOA dues, and any extra monthly, yearly or one-time principal payments.
The result updates as you type. You can copy a link that reproduces your exact inputs.
The formula
The principal-and-interest (P&I) part of a fixed-rate mortgage uses the standard amortizing-loan formula:
M = P × r × (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n − 1)
M: monthly principal and interest payment
P: loan amount (price − down payment)
r: monthly interest rate = annual rate ÷ 12 (6.5% → 0.065 ÷ 12 = 0.0054167)
n: number of monthly payments = years × 12
Each month, the interest due is the current balance × r. The rest of M reduces the balance. On top of P&I, the calculator adds:
Monthly total = M + (annual property tax ÷ 12) + (annual insurance ÷ 12) + (PMI rate × loan ÷ 12) + HOA
PMI is dropped from the total in the month the scheduled balance reaches 78% of the original home value. That is the point where federal law generally requires automatic termination for conventional loans on a principal residence.
Worked examples
Example 1: 20% down, no PMI. Home price $400,000, down payment $80,000 (20%), loan $320,000, 6.5% for 30 years, property tax 1.1% of price ($4,400/yr), insurance $1,800/yr.
r = 0.065 / 12 = 0.00541667; n = 360
P&I: M = $2,022.62
Property tax: 4,400 ÷ 12 = $366.67
Insurance: 1,800 ÷ 12 = $150.00
Monthly total: $2,539.28
Total interest over 30 years: $2,022.62 × 360 − $320,000 = $408,142.36 (the calculator rounds the final payment, so the exact figure can differ by a few cents)
In the first payment, $1,733.33 goes to interest (320,000 × 0.00541667) and only $289.28 to principal.
Example 2: 10% down, with PMI. Same home, $40,000 down, loan $360,000, PMI 0.5% per year (illustrative).
P&I: $2,275.44
PMI: 360,000 × 0.005 ÷ 12 = $150.00
Tax and insurance as before: $516.67
Monthly total: $2,942.11
The scheduled balance falls to $320,000 (80% of the $400,000 original value) after payment 95 (just under 8 years). From then you can ask your servicer to cancel PMI. It reaches $312,000 (78%) after payment 109, when PMI should end automatically if you are current on payments.
Understanding your results
Monthly payment is what leaves your account each month, provided your lender collects tax and insurance through escrow. Escrow amounts change when tax bills or premiums change; the P&I part of a fixed-rate loan does not.
Total interest shows how much the term costs you. In Example 1, a 15-year term at the same rate would raise P&I to $2,787.54 a month but cut total interest to $181,757.84, less than half of the 30-year figure. If a lender quotes a lower rate for the shorter term, the gap grows further.
Rate sensitivity: on the same $320,000 loan, 6.0% gives $1,918.56 and 7.0% gives $2,128.97. Half a point moves the payment by roughly $100 a month.
Amortization schedule: early payments are mostly interest. Extra principal payments made early save the most.
Ways to pay the loan off sooner
Extra monthly principal: even a small fixed amount, made from the first year, shortens the loan noticeably. Use the extra-payment fields to see the new payoff month.
Bi-weekly payments: paying half the monthly amount every two weeks gives 26 half-payments a year, which equals 13 monthly payments. Check first that your servicer applies each half-payment straight away, not just once a month, and that it doesn't charge a fee for the service.
Lump sums: a bonus or tax refund applied to principal lowers every later interest charge.
Shorter term at refinance: see the refinance calculator.
Before paying extra, check your note for any prepayment penalty, and consider whether higher-interest debt or an emergency fund should come first. The calculator shows the interest saved. It can't tell you whether that is the best use of the money.
Country notes
United States (this page): these figures are estimates. Your Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure are the official numbers. FHA and VA loans have their own mortgage insurance or funding fee rules, which this page does not model; see the FHA and VA calculators.
Canada: fixed-rate mortgages are quoted with semi-annual compounding, and down payments under 20% require mortgage default insurance. Use the Canadian mortgage calculator.
UK: repayment vs interest-only, fixed-rate periods and stamp duty work differently. Use the UK mortgage calculator and the stamp duty calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Leaving out taxes, insurance and PMI. Add them to see the full monthly housing cost.
Comparing rates without points and fees. Use the APR or a loan comparison.
Assuming an adjustable rate stays low. Run a scenario at a higher rate after the fixed period.
Stretching to the maximum loan. A lower payment leaves room for repairs and savings.
Forgetting to shop around. Quotes from several lenders on the same day often differ.
Frequently asked questions
Does the monthly payment include property tax and insurance?
Only if you enter them. Many lenders collect them monthly through an escrow account, so including them gives a more realistic monthly cost. The P&I figure on its own is what the loan formula produces.
When can I stop paying PMI?
For most conventional loans on a principal residence that closed on or after 29 July 1999, you can ask your servicer in writing to cancel PMI once the balance is scheduled to reach 80% of the home's original value. It must end automatically at 78%, provided you are current on payments. There are other conditions, such as a good payment history and no second liens. FHA and VA loans follow different rules.
Why is my lender's payment different from this one?
Lenders may round differently, start interest on a different date, or include escrow amounts based on actual tax bills. They may also add a cushion to escrow. Use your Loan Estimate as the reference.
Is a 15-year mortgage better than a 30-year?
It costs far less interest, but the monthly payment is higher. In Example 1, the 15-year P&I is $764.92 a month more. Which suits you depends on your budget and other goals; this calculator only shows the trade-off.
How much do extra payments save?
It depends on the size and timing. Enter an extra monthly amount and compare total interest with and without it. On the amortization calculator, an extra $200 a month on a $250,000, 6%, 30-year loan saves about $86,233 in interest and pays the loan off 93 months early.
What is the difference between interest rate and APR?
The interest rate determines your payment. The APR also folds in certain fees, such as points and origination charges, so you can compare offers. Enter the interest rate in this calculator.
Does this include closing costs?
No. Closing costs (lender fees, title, appraisal, prepaid items) are listed on your Loan Estimate and are paid at closing. They don't change the monthly payment unless they are financed into the loan.

Mortgage Payoff Calculator: Pay Off Your Mortgage Early | FigSumo (65 chars)
Meta description
See how extra monthly, yearly or lump-sum payments shorten your mortgage and how much interest you save, or the payment needed to finish by a date. (147 chars)

1,006 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Mortgage Payoff Calculator
Paying a little extra on your mortgage each month can take years off the loan and save a large amount of interest. This calculator compares your standard payment with the same payment plus an extra amount, and shows how many months the loan will now take and roughly how much interest you save.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price: the purchase price of the home.
2. Down payment: the percentage you paid (or will pay) up front. The calculator subtracts it to get the loan amount.
3. Interest rate: the annual rate on the mortgage.
4. Loan term (years): the original term, usually 30 or 15.
5. Extra monthly payment: the amount you will add to every monthly payment, applied to principal.
Results: standard monthly payment, payment with the extra amount, payoff time in months and years, and interest saved (estimate).
If you already have a mortgage, enter a price and down payment that give your original loan amount, and the original rate and term. (A mode that starts from your current balance is planned.)
The formula
The standard payment comes from the amortization formula:
PMT = L × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
L: loan amount = price × (1 − down%)
r: annual rate ÷ 12; n: term × 12
With extra payments, the calculator steps month by month:
Interest = Balance × r
Principal = (PMT + Extra) − Interest
Balance = Balance − Principal
until the balance reaches zero. Interest saved = interest on the standard schedule − interest with extra payments.
Worked examples
Example 1: $350,000 home, 20% down, 6.75%, 30 years, +$200 a month
Loan: $280,000.00
Standard payment: $1,816.07; with the extra $200: $2,016.07
Payoff time: 271 months (22.6 years) instead of 360, about 7.4 years sooner
Interest saved: about $107,581.50 (standard-schedule interest is $373,790.68)
Example 2: $300,000 loan at 6.25%, comparing extra amounts
Standard payment $1,847.15.
Extra per month
Payoff
Interest saved
$100
313 months (26.1 years)
$57,088.13
$500
211 months (17.6 years)
$169,901.87
One extra payment a year (the effect of paying half the payment every two weeks, 26 half-payments a year) is roughly the same as adding $153.93 a month. That clears this loan in about 293 months and saves about $80,269.55.
Understanding your results
Payoff time is how long the loan lasts with the extra payment, assuming you make it every month from the start.
Interest saved is an estimate. Real savings depend on when you start paying extra and whether your lender applies the money to principal straight away.
Your monthly obligation doesn't change. The extra is voluntary; you can usually stop if money gets tight.
Early years matter most. Extra principal paid early avoids interest for the rest of the loan.
Is paying off early right for you?
Paying extra gives a guaranteed return equal to your mortgage rate. Before doing it, many people check that they:
have an emergency fund of a few months' spending;
have no higher-rate debt, such as credit cards, which should usually be paid first;
are getting any employer match on retirement savings, which is a higher return.
If your mortgage rate is low and you could earn more elsewhere, investing instead may come out ahead, though with risk. There's no single right answer; compare the options with your own numbers.
Country notes
United States: most mortgages can be prepaid without penalty; the CFPB notes that some loans have prepayment penalties, which must be disclosed. Tell your servicer the extra amount is for principal. Paying down a conventional loan to 78% of the original value also ends PMI automatically (CFPB).
Canada: closed mortgages limit prepayments, typically 10% to 20% of the original principal a year plus payment increases, depending on the lender; going over can trigger a penalty of three months' interest or an interest-rate differential. Check your mortgage contract.
United Kingdom: many fixed-rate mortgages allow overpayments of up to 10% of the balance a year without an early repayment charge. Overpaying above the allowance during a fixed period can cost an ERC of several percent. Variable-rate deals often have no limit.
Tips and common mistakes
Not marking payments as principal. Some servicers hold extra money as a prepayment of the next instalment unless told otherwise.
Paying a "biweekly service" fee. You can get the same effect free by adding one-twelfth of a payment each month.
Draining savings. Money paid into the house is hard to get back without borrowing.
Ignoring prepayment limits in Canada and the UK.
Quick check
Check your statement for your exact remaining balance.
Frequently asked questions
How much interest can I save by paying extra?
It depends on your balance, rate and time left. On a 30-year loan, even $100–$200 a month often saves tens of thousands of dollars.
Is it better to pay a lump sum or extra every month?
Money paid earlier saves more interest. A lump sum today saves more than the same amount spread over the year.
Does paying extra lower my monthly payment?
Usually not; it shortens the term. Some lenders will recast (re-amortize) the loan after a large lump sum, which lowers the payment.
Should I pay off my mortgage or invest?
Compare your mortgage rate with the after-tax return you expect from investing, and consider risk and liquidity.
Do biweekly payments really help?
Yes, because 26 half-payments equal 13 full payments a year. Adding one-twelfth of a payment each month does the same.
Will paying extra hurt my credit?
No. Paying off a mortgage early may slightly change your credit mix, but it doesn't harm your payment history.

Mutual Fund Calculator

Title tag
Mutual Fund Calculator: Returns After Fees | FigSumo (52 chars)
Meta description
Project a mutual fund investment after expense ratio and sales charges. See how fees reduce the ending balance over time. (121 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
1,015 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Mutual Fund Calculator
This calculator projects the value of a mutual fund (or ETF) investment, with a starting amount and regular monthly additions, and shows how much the fund's annual expenses cost you over time. Enter the initial investment, the monthly amount, the number of years, the gross return you expect and the fund's expense ratio.
How to use this calculator
1. Initial investment: the lump sum you invest at the start.
2. Monthly investment: the amount you add each month, for example by automatic investment.
3. Years: how long you'll keep investing.
4. Gross annual return: the return you assume before fund costs. Use a cautious long-run figure; returns are never guaranteed.
5. Expense ratio: the fund's ongoing annual charge as a percentage, from its prospectus or fact sheet (called the management expense ratio, MER, in Canada and the ongoing charges figure, OCF, in the UK).
Results: future value after expenses, future value before expenses and cost of expenses (estimate).
The formula
Net return = Gross return − Expense ratio
FV = P × (1 + i)^n + M × ((1 + i)^n − 1) ÷ i
P: initial investment; M: monthly investment
i: monthly rate = net annual return ÷ 12; n: years × 12
Monthly contributions are added at the end of each month, and growth compounds monthly.
The "before expenses" figure uses the gross return. The difference between the two is the estimated cost of fees, including the growth those fees would have earned.
Worked examples
Example 1: $5,000 plus $200 a month for 15 years, 8% gross, 0.5% expenses
Money invested: $41,000.00
Before expenses (8%): $85,742.25
After expenses (7.5%): $81,569.71
Cost of expenses: $4,172.54
Example 2: why expense ratios matter over 30 years
$25,000 to start, $500 a month, 7% gross return, 30 years:
Expense ratio
Value after 30 years
0.03% (typical broad index fund)
$807,491.90
0.50%
$727,883.99
1.00%
$652,821.90
The gap between 0.03% and 1.00% is $154,670.00. Fees compound just like returns.
Understanding your results
After expenses is the more realistic projection, but still before tax and before any sales loads or advisory fees.
Cost of expenses shows the long-run price of the fund's ongoing charge.
Returns vary. A real fund's yearly returns swing up and down; this projection assumes a smooth average. See the average return calculator for why averages can mislead.
Other fund costs
Sales loads: some funds charge a front-end load on purchases. A 5.75% load on $10,000 means only $9,425.00 is invested. At 6.5% for 10 years, that grows to $18,022.33, versus $19,121.84 without the load.
12b-1 fees (US) are part of the expense ratio; trailing commissions (Canada) are part of the MER.
Platform and advisory fees are charged separately by many brokers and advisers. Add them to the expense ratio for a full picture.
Trading costs inside the fund are not in the expense ratio but still reduce returns.
Choosing between funds with this calculator
Run the calculator once for each fund you are considering, keeping the gross return the same and changing only the expense ratio. The difference in the after-expenses value is the price of choosing the more expensive fund. Then ask whether that fund offers something worth the cost, such as a strategy you can't get cheaply elsewhere. Broad index funds and ETFs tracking the same market are close substitutes, so their costs are the main difference between them. For actively managed funds, compare the fee with the fund's long-run record after costs against a suitable index, keeping in mind that past outperformance often doesn't last.
Country notes
United States: fund costs appear in the prospectus fee table. The SEC's Mutual Fund Cost Calculator (via FINRA's Fund Analyzer) lets you compare funds. Funds pay out taxable distributions in taxable accounts; holding them in a 401(k) or IRA defers tax.
Canada: the fund facts document lists the MER and any trailing commission. Since 2022, funds can't charge deferred sales charges (DSC) on new purchases. Hold funds in a TFSA or RRSP to shelter growth.
United Kingdom: the key information document shows the ongoing charges figure; platforms add their own fees. A stocks and shares ISA (£20,000 a year allowance) or a pension shelters growth from tax.
Tips and common mistakes
Using recent returns as the assumption. A fund's best five years are not a forecast.
Ignoring all-in costs. Add platform or advice fees to the expense ratio.
Comparing funds on past returns alone. Costs are one of the few things you know in advance.
Stopping contributions in downturns. Regular investing buys more units when prices are low (dollar-cost averaging).
Frequently asked questions
What is an expense ratio?
The percentage of a fund's assets taken each year to pay for management and running costs. It is deducted inside the fund, so you don't see a separate bill.
How much does a 1% fee cost over time?
More than it sounds: it compounds. Example 2 shows tens of thousands of dollars on a modest plan over 30 years.
What return should I assume?
There's no reliable figure. Many people test several rates, such as 4%, 6% and 8%, and plan around the lower ones.
Is a mutual fund different from an ETF?
Both pool money into a portfolio. ETFs trade on an exchange during the day and often have lower costs; mutual funds trade once a day at the closing price.
Does the calculator include taxes?
No. Taxes on distributions and gains depend on the account type and your country.
Why is the "before expenses" figure higher?
Because it assumes the fund's costs were zero. The difference is what the expense ratio costs you.
