Title tag
Payback Period Calculator (Simple & Discounted) | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Find how long an investment takes to recover its cost from expected cash flows, with simple and discounted payback periods. (123 chars)
Country
global

1,003 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Payback Period Calculator
The payback period is how long it takes for an investment's cash returns to repay what it cost. This calculator gives the simple payback period when the investment produces the same cash flow each year. Enter the upfront cost and the expected annual cash inflow (or saving) to get the answer in years and months.
It is a quick screening test for projects such as new equipment, energy-saving upgrades, solar panels or a small business purchase.
How to use this calculator
1. Initial investment: the total upfront cost, including purchase, installation and setup.
2. Annual cash flow: the net cash the investment brings in (or saves) each year, after its own running costs. For an energy upgrade, it is the yearly saving on bills.
Results: simple payback period in years and months (approx.).
The formula
Payback period (years) = Initial investment ÷ Annual cash flow
Months = Years × 12
This assumes the same cash flow every year and ignores the time value of money.
Worked examples
Example 1: $50,000 machine saving $12,000 a year
Payback = 50,000 ÷ 12,000 = 4.17 years, about 50 months
Example 2: uneven cash flows (by hand)
A $40,000 project returns $8,000, $12,000, $15,000, $15,000 and $10,000 in years 1 to 5.
Year
Cumulative cash flow
1
$8,000.00
2
$20,000.00
3
$35,000.00
4
$50,000.00
After year 3, $35,000 has been recovered; the remaining $5,000 comes from year 4's $15,000, a third of the way through. Payback ≈ 3.33 years.
Discounted payback
Money received later is worth less. Discounting Example 1's $12,000 a year at 8% (each year's flow divided by 1.08^year), the cumulative discounted cash reaches $50,000 after about 5.28 years, longer than the simple 4.17 years.
Understanding your results
Shorter payback = faster recovery of your money and less exposure to things going wrong.
Payback ignores everything after the payback point. Two projects with the same payback can have very different total returns. Check the total with the ROI calculator or the IRR calculator.
It ignores the time value of money unless you use the discounted version.
Many businesses set a maximum payback (for example 3 years for equipment) as a rough risk filter, alongside other measures.
Uses and examples
Energy upgrades: an $18,000 solar installation that saves $1,400 a year on electricity pays back in about 12.9 years, before any tax credits or rebates. Check government incentives first, because they shorten payback considerably. Estimate your current electricity use with the electricity calculator.
Equipment: compare the payback of buying versus leasing.
Business purchases: how long the profits take to repay the price.
Marketing: customer acquisition cost ÷ monthly margin per customer gives months to recover acquisition spending.
Payback vs other measures
Measure
What it tells you
Weakness
Payback period
How fast you get your money back
Ignores later cash and timing
ROI
Total gain relative to cost
Ignores timing
NPV
Value added at a chosen discount rate
Needs a discount rate
IRR
Annual rate of return
Can mislead with odd cash flows
Payback for a home energy upgrade, step by step
1. Get the installed price, then subtract any grant, rebate or tax credit you will definitely receive.
2. Estimate the yearly saving from past bills: for example, kilowatt-hours saved × your price per kWh, or the drop in gas use × your gas price.
3. Subtract any new running costs, such as servicing.
4. Divide the net cost by the net yearly saving.
5. Compare the answer with the equipment's expected life. If payback is close to the end of its life, the upgrade may never pay off financially, although comfort or emissions may still justify it.
Energy prices change, so test a higher and a lower price to see how sensitive the payback is.
Country notes
The maths is universal; incentives differ:
United States: federal tax credits for some home energy improvements have changed under the 2025 tax law [VERIFY current status of residential clean energy credits on irs.gov].
Canada: federal and provincial programs have offered grants or loans for home energy retrofits [VERIFY current programs on natural-resources.canada.ca].
United Kingdom: grants such as the Boiler Upgrade Scheme can reduce the upfront cost of heat pumps [VERIFY current grant amount on GOV.UK].
Include any grant or credit as a reduction in the initial investment.
Tips and common mistakes
Using revenue instead of net cash flow. Subtract running costs.
Forgetting maintenance and replacement costs that occur during the payback period.
Ignoring incentives and tax effects, which change both the cost and the cash flows.
Treating payback as the only test. Use it with ROI or NPV.
Frequently asked questions
What is a good payback period?
It depends on the type of investment and your risk tolerance. Shorter is safer; many businesses look for payback well within the asset's useful life.
How do I calculate payback with uneven cash flows?
Add the yearly flows until the total reaches the investment, then work out the fraction of the final year needed, as in Example 2.
What is discounted payback?
Payback calculated with each year's cash flow discounted to present value. It is always longer than simple payback.
Does payback account for profit after it is reached?
No. That is its main weakness.
Can the payback period be infinite?
If the annual cash flow is zero or negative, the investment never pays back.
Should I include tax?
For a realistic figure, use after-tax cash flows and include any tax credits.
How is payback different from break-even?
Break-even finds the sales volume at which revenue covers costs in a period. Payback finds the time it takes for cumulative cash to repay an upfront investment. See the break-even calculator.

Payment Calculator: Solve for Payment or Term | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Find the payment for a loan amount and term, or the term needed for a payment you can afford. Fixed-rate loans of any length. (125 chars)

H1: Payment Calculator
This payment calculator answers the two questions people most often ask about a loan: "what will my payment be?" and "if I pay a fixed amount each month, how long until it's paid off?" Enter the loan amount, interest rate and term to get the monthly payment, or enter the amount you can afford each month to find how many payments it will take.
How to use this calculator
Fixed term (find the payment)
1. Loan amount: the principal you will borrow or currently owe.
2. Interest rate: the annual rate on the loan.
3. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): the repayment period.
Fixed payment (find the time)
1. Loan amount and interest rate as above.
2. Monthly payment: the amount you'll pay each month.
Results: monthly payment (or number of payments), total of payments, total interest paid, and an amortization chart.
The formulas
Payment for a fixed term
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Number of payments for a fixed payment
n = −ln(1 − P × r ÷ PMT) ÷ ln(1 + r)
P: loan amount
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: number of monthly payments
PMT: monthly payment
The term formula only works if PMT is more than one month's interest (P × r). If it isn't, the balance never falls. When n isn't a whole number, the last payment is smaller than the others.
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 at 7.5% over 5 years
PMT = $400.76
Total of 60 payments: $24,045.54; total interest: $4,045.54
How the term changes the same loan:
Term
Payment
Total interest
36 months
$622.12
$2,396.48
48 months
$483.58
$3,211.75
60 months
$400.76
$4,045.54
72 months
$345.80
$4,897.76
Example 2: paying a fixed $500 a month on $20,000 at 7.5%
n = −ln(1 − 20,000 × 0.00625 ÷ 500) ÷ ln(1.00625) = 46.17
So 47 payments, the last one smaller; total interest $3,086.63
At $400 a month: 61 payments, interest $4,055.39
Example 3: a card balance of $12,000 at 18% with $250 a month
First month's interest: $180.00, so $70 reduces the balance
86 payments; total interest $9,375.29
Understanding your results
Monthly payment covers principal and interest. Taxes, insurance and fees are extra.
Total interest is the full cost of borrowing if you keep to the schedule.
A shorter term means a higher payment but much less interest.
The chart shows how the balance falls slowly at first, then faster.
Monthly vs bi-weekly payments
Some lenders allow payments every two weeks. On the $20,000 loan at 7.5%, a 5-year schedule of 130 bi-weekly payments costs $184.71 each, with total interest of $4,012.32, slightly less than monthly because the balance falls a little sooner. A different idea is to pay half the monthly payment ($200.38) every two weeks: that adds up to 13 monthly payments a year and pays the loan off months early. Check that your lender applies bi-weekly payments as they arrive rather than holding them until the monthly due date.
Choosing a payment
A comfortable payment leaves room in your budget for savings and surprises. Lenders look at your debt-to-income ratio; you should also check the full monthly budget with the budget calculator. If the payment for the term you want is too high, the options are a longer term (more interest), a smaller loan, or a lower rate.
Country notes
United States: for consumer loans, the Truth in Lending disclosure shows the payment schedule, APR and finance charge.
Canada: lenders must disclose the cost of borrowing. Canadian mortgages compound semi-annually, so for a mortgage use the Canadian mortgage calculator.
United Kingdom: credit agreements show the APR and total amount payable. You have a legal right to repay a regulated personal loan early; the lender may charge compensation of up to 1% of the amount repaid early, or 0.5% if less than a year of the agreement remains [VERIFY on FCA guidance].
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing up rate and APR. Use the interest rate for the payment; compare offers by APR.
Choosing the longest term by default. It keeps payments low but costs the most.
Paying just above the interest. On high-rate debt, small payments take years; test larger amounts.
Forgetting fees rolled into the loan amount.
Quick check
Check that the term is entered in years or months as the form expects.
Frequently asked questions
How is a monthly loan payment calculated?
With the amortization formula PMT = P × r ÷ (1 − (1 + r)^−n), using the monthly rate and number of payments.
How long will it take to pay off my loan with a fixed payment?
Use the fixed-payment mode, or the formula n = −ln(1 − P × r ÷ PMT) ÷ ln(1 + r).
Why does a small payment increase save so much?
Every extra dollar goes to principal, which stops interest being charged on it for the rest of the loan.
Does the payment include insurance or taxes?
No. It is principal and interest only.
Can I use this for a mortgage?
Yes, for principal and interest on a fixed-rate loan. The mortgage calculator adds taxes and insurance.
What if the payment doesn't cover the interest?
The loan will never be repaid at that payment. Increase the payment or look for a lower rate.
What happens if I miss a payment?
Interest keeps building on the unpaid balance, and late fees and credit-report damage can follow. If you can't pay, contact the lender before the due date to ask about options.
Is a fixed or variable rate better for planning payments?
A fixed rate gives the same payment for the whole term, which makes budgeting easy. A variable rate can start lower but the payment can rise; test higher rates if you choose one.

Defined Benefit Pension Calculator | FigSumo (44 chars)
Meta description
Estimate an annual defined-benefit pension from years of service, final average salary and the plan's accrual rate (for example 1.5% or 2% a year). (147 chars)
Country

1,013 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Pension Calculator (Defined Benefit)
This calculator estimates the yearly and monthly income from a defined benefit (DB) pension: the kind of workplace pension that pays a set income based on your salary and years of service, rather than on investment returns. Enter your years of service, your final average salary and the plan's benefit factor (accrual rate) to get the estimated annual and monthly pension.
How to use this calculator
1. Years of service: the credited years (or years and months as a decimal) in the plan. Your annual pension statement shows your credited service.
2. Final average salary: the pensionable pay the plan uses, often an average of your highest or final 3 to 5 years. Check the plan's definition; some plans exclude overtime or bonuses.
3. Benefit factor (% per year): the percentage of salary earned for each year of service, from the plan booklet. For example 2% per year, or 1/60 (1.667%) or 1/80 (1.25%) in many UK schemes.
Results: estimated annual pension and estimated monthly pension, before tax.
The formula
Annual pension = Benefit factor × Final average salary × Years of service
Monthly pension = Annual pension ÷ 12
For example, 2% × 25 years = 50% of final average salary.
Worked examples
Example 1: 25 years, $85,000 final average salary, 2% factor
Annual pension = 0.02 × 85,000 × 25 = $42,500.00
Monthly pension = $3,541.67
Example 2: a 1/60th scheme with 30 years and £62,000 pensionable pay
Annual pension = 30 ÷ 60 × 62,000 = £31,000.00, or £2,583.33 a month. The calculator shows a $ sign, but the arithmetic is the same in pounds.
Enter the factor as 1.6667 to reproduce this in the calculator.
Retiring early
Many plans cut the pension for each year you retire before normal retirement age. If Example 1's plan reduced benefits by 5% a year and you retired 3 years early, the pension would fall to $36,125.00 a year ($3,010.42 a month). Reductions differ widely; check your plan's early retirement table.
Understanding your results
The figure is before tax. DB pensions are taxed as income in the US, Canada and the UK.
Inflation: if the pension isn't indexed, its buying power falls. After 15 years of 2.5% inflation, $42,500.00 buys what $29,344.79 buys today. Many public plans index pensions; many private plans don't, or cap increases.
Normal retirement age matters. The formula gives the unreduced pension at the plan's normal age.
Survivor options: choosing a joint-and-survivor pension usually reduces your own payment.
Lump sum or monthly pension?
Some plans offer a one-time lump sum instead of the monthly pension. One way to compare: the present value of the pension. Paid for 25 years and discounted at 5%, Example 1's $42,500.00 a year is worth about $598,992.64 today. A lump-sum offer well below that is poor value at that discount rate; one above it may be attractive, especially if you're in poor health or want control. Living longer than expected favors the monthly pension, which is a form of longevity insurance. The annuity payout calculator shows what a lump sum could pay if you drew it down yourself.
Country notes
United States: private DB plans are covered by ERISA, and the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation (PBGC) insures benefits up to legal limits if a plan fails. Federal employees under FERS earn 1% per year (1.1% if retiring at 62 or later with 20 years); for example, 1.1% × $95,000 × 30 years = $31,350.00 [VERIFY with OPM]. Social Security is separate; see the Social Security calculator.
Canada: many public-sector plans use about 2% per year, often integrated with CPP (a lower rate on earnings up to the YMPE). CPP and OAS are paid on top; see the CPP calculator. Plans are regulated federally or provincially.
United Kingdom: DB schemes (final salary or career average, CARE) commonly use accrual rates such as 1/60 or 1/80. The Pension Protection Fund protects members of eligible schemes if the employer becomes insolvent. Most workers today are in defined contribution schemes instead; see the workplace pension calculator. The State Pension is separate.
Defined benefit vs defined contribution
DB: the employer promises an income; investment risk sits with the plan.
DC (401(k), RRSP group plans, UK workplace pensions): your pot depends on contributions and returns; you carry the risk. Use the retirement calculator for DC savings.
Tips and common mistakes
Using current salary instead of final average salary. Plans average over a set period.
Ignoring integration with government pensions. Some plans reduce benefits to account for Social Security or CPP.
Forgetting early retirement reductions. They can be large.
Assuming indexation. Check whether and how the pension rises each year.
Frequently asked questions
How is a defined benefit pension calculated?
Usually as accrual rate × pensionable salary × years of service, with adjustments for early retirement and survivor options.
What is a typical accrual rate?
It varies; 1% to 2% per year is common in North America, and 1/60 to 1/80 in UK schemes.
Is my pension taxed?
Yes, as income in most cases. Some UK schemes allow a tax-free lump sum by exchanging part of the pension.
Should I take the lump sum?
It depends on the offer, your health, other income and how comfortable you are managing investments. Compare it with the present value of the pension and get advice.
What happens to my pension if my employer goes bust?
In the US, the PBGC insures private DB benefits up to limits; in the UK, the Pension Protection Fund covers eligible schemes; in Canada, protection varies by province (Ontario has the PBGF).
Does the calculator include inflation increases?
No. It gives the starting pension. Increases depend on the plan's rules.

H1: Personal Loan Calculator
A personal loan is a fixed sum, usually unsecured, that you repay in equal monthly installments over a set term. People use them to consolidate card debt, pay for home improvements, cover medical bills or make a large purchase. This calculator gives the monthly payment, the total you'll repay and the total interest, with a chart of how the balance falls.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: how much you want to borrow. If the lender deducts an origination fee from the funds, see the fee section below.
2. Interest rate: the annual rate from your offer or prequalification. Personal loan rates depend heavily on credit score and income.
3. Loan term (years) and Loan term (months): most personal loans run 1 to 7 years.
Results: monthly payment, total of payments, total interest paid, the rate, and an amortization chart.
The formula
PMT = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
Total interest = PMT × n − P
P: loan amount
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: years × 12 + months
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 at 7.5% over 5 years
PMT = $400.76
Total of payments $24,045.54; interest $4,045.54
Example 2: $10,000 at 12.99% over 3 years with a 5% origination fee
PMT = $336.89; interest $2,128.09
The 5% fee ($500) is deducted, so you receive $9,500.00 but repay $10,000 plus interest. The real cost, as an APR, is about 16.62%.
To receive a full $10,000 after the fee, you'd need to borrow about $10,526.32 (10,000 ÷ 0.95), which raises the payment to $354.62.
Why people use personal loans to clear cards
Paying $336.89 a month against a $10,000 card balance at 24.99% would take 47 months and cost $5,736.69 in interest, versus $2,128.09 on the 3-year loan. The saving only holds if the cards aren't run up again.
Example 3: consolidating three cards
Balances of $3,000 at 22.99%, $4,500 at 19.99% and $2,500 at 26.99% total $10,000 at a weighted average rate of 22.64%. A 3-year personal loan at 11% would cost $327.39 a month and $1,785.94 in total interest. Paying the same $327.39 a month across the cards at 22.64% would take longer and cost more, so the loan helps, provided the cards aren't run up again.
Example 4: paying off early
On Example 1's $20,000 loan, the balance after 24 payments is about $12,883.56. Paying it off then saves the remaining interest of about $1,543.76 (the 36 remaining payments of $400.76 total $14,427.32), assuming no prepayment fee.

Understanding your results
Monthly payment is fixed for the term (for fixed-rate loans, the most common type).
Total interest is the cost of borrowing if you make every payment on schedule.
Fees aren't included unless you add them to the amount. Compare offers by APR with the APR calculator.
Early payoff: many personal loans can be paid off early with no penalty, which cuts the interest.
What affects your rate
Credit score and history: the biggest factor. Better credit means lower rates.
Debt-to-income ratio: lenders check whether the new payment is affordable; see the debt-to-income calculator.
Term: longer terms often carry slightly higher rates.
Secured vs unsecured: loans backed by savings or a vehicle can be cheaper.
Lender type: banks, credit unions and online lenders price differently. Prequalification with a soft credit check lets you compare without affecting your score.
Country notes
United States: federal credit unions can't charge more than an 18% APR on most loans under NCUA rules [VERIFY current cap]. Lenders must disclose the APR and finance charge (Truth in Lending). The CFPB warns about advance-fee loan scams: legitimate lenders don't ask for fees before approving a loan.
Canada: the federal criminal interest rate cap fell to 35% APR on 1 January 2025 [VERIFY]. Provinces regulate payday and high-cost lenders.
United Kingdom: personal loans are regulated under the Consumer Credit Act and FCA rules. Lenders advertise a "representative APR" that at least 51% of approved applicants receive; your rate may be higher. You have a 14-day right to withdraw from a credit agreement.
Tips and common mistakes
Comparing rates without fees. Use APR.
Borrowing more than you need because you're approved for it.
Choosing the longest term for the lowest payment. It costs the most interest.
Applying to many lenders at once with hard checks; use prequalification first.
Ignoring the reason for borrowing. For consolidation, have a plan to avoid new debt.
Quick check
Ask each lender whether an origination fee is deducted from the amount you receive.
Frequently asked questions
How is a personal loan payment calculated?
With the standard amortization formula using the monthly rate and the number of payments.
What is an origination fee?
A one-time fee, often a percentage of the loan, usually deducted from the money you receive. It raises the APR above the interest rate.
Is a personal loan better than a credit card?
For a planned expense or consolidation, a personal loan usually has a lower rate and a fixed payoff date. Cards can be cheaper if you can repay within a 0% promotional period.
Can I pay off a personal loan early?
Often yes, without penalty, but check the agreement for prepayment fees.
Does a personal loan affect my credit score?
Applying causes a hard inquiry; on-time payments build positive history; missed payments hurt it.
What term should I choose?
The shortest term with a payment you can comfortably afford.

PMI Calculator

PMI Calculator: Cost and Removal Date | FigSumo (47 chars)

Estimate private mortgage insurance cost and the month PMI can be cancelled at 80% or ends automatically at 78% of original value. (130 chars)

H1: PMI Calculator
Private mortgage insurance (PMI) is usually required on a conventional mortgage when your down payment is less than 20% of the home's value. It protects the lender if you default, and you pay for it, typically as a monthly charge added to your mortgage payment. This calculator estimates your monthly PMI, your total payment, and when PMI can be cancelled under federal rules.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price: the purchase price or appraised value, whichever is lower (the "original value").
2. Down payment: in dollars or as a percentage.
3. Interest rate and loan term.
4. Annual PMI rate (%): from your Loan Estimate. There's no official rate; it depends on credit score, down payment, loan type and insurer. Rates commonly fall somewhere between about 0.3% and 1.5% of the loan a year [VERIFY with your lender].
Results: loan amount, loan-to-value (LTV), monthly PMI, principal and interest, total monthly payment, the month PMI can be requested off (80% LTV) and automatically ends (78% LTV), and total PMI paid.
How it works
Loan = Price − Down payment
LTV = Loan ÷ Original value
Monthly PMI = Loan × Annual PMI rate ÷ 12
Cancellation (Homeowners Protection Act, for most loans closed on or after 29 July 1999):
You can ask your servicer to cancel PMI when the balance is scheduled to reach 80% of the original value, or earlier if extra payments get you there.
PMI ends automatically when the balance is scheduled to reach 78% of the original value, if you're current on payments.
It also ends at the midpoint of the loan term (for example, after 15 years of a 30-year loan) if it hasn't already.
The calculator uses the original amortization schedule to find these dates.
Worked examples
Example 1: $400,000 home, 10% down
Loan $360,000 at 6.5% for 30 years; PMI 0.5% a year.
Monthly PMI = 360,000 × 0.005 ÷ 12 = $150.00 ($1,800.00 a year)
Principal and interest: $2,275.44; total $2,425.44 before taxes and insurance
Balance reaches 80% of $400,000 ($320,000) at payment 95 (about 7.9 years); you can request cancellation then.
Balance reaches 78% ($312,000) at payment 109 (about 9.1 years), when PMI ends automatically.
Total PMI paid to automatic termination: $16,350.00 ($14,250.00 if you request removal at 80%).
With $300 a month extra, the balance reaches $320,000 at payment 56 (about 4.7 years), saving roughly $5,850.00 of PMI on top of the interest savings.
Example 2: 5% down
A $400,000 home with $20,000 down needs a $380,000 loan. If the PMI rate is 0.8% because of the higher LTV, PMI is $253.33 a month.
Example 3: when does PMI end?
Example 1's $360,000 loan on a $400,000 home, at 6.5% over 30 years, with no extra payments:
You can ask to cancel PMI when the balance reaches 80% of the original value, $320,000: after about 95 months (7.9 years)
PMI ends automatically at 78%, $312,000: after about 109 months (9.1 years)
At $150 a month, that's roughly $14,250 of PMI before you can request cancellation. Extra principal payments, or a new appraisal showing the home has risen in value, can bring the date forward; lenders set their own rules for value-based cancellation.
Understanding your results
PMI rate drivers: a higher credit score and bigger down payment lower the rate.
Monthly PMI is constant under the most common borrower-paid monthly plan, based on the original loan.
Other PMI types: single-premium (paid upfront), split-premium, and lender-paid PMI (built into a higher interest rate, which doesn't cancel).
Rising home values: some servicers allow cancellation based on a new appraisal showing enough equity, usually after a minimum period [VERIFY servicer and investor rules].
PMI vs other mortgage insurance
FHA loans have an upfront and annual mortgage insurance premium (MIP), and for most loans with less than 10% down MIP lasts for the life of the loan; see the FHA loan calculator.
VA loans have no monthly mortgage insurance but a one-time funding fee; see the VA loan calculator.
USDA loans charge a guarantee fee.
Is PMI worth it?
PMI lets you buy sooner with less cash. Compare the PMI cost with the cost of waiting to save 20% (rent paid and possible price changes). On Example 1, PMI totals $16,350.00 over about 9.1 years. Some buyers use a second mortgage ("piggyback" 80-10-10) to avoid PMI, at the cost of a higher-rate second loan.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting to request cancellation at 80%. Automatic termination comes later, at 78%.
Assuming PMI is tax-deductible. The mortgage insurance premium deduction expired after 2021 [VERIFY whether restored for 2026].
Confusing PMI with homeowners insurance. PMI protects the lender; homeowners insurance protects your home.
Using the current value for automatic termination; the rules use the original value.
Quick check
Ask your servicer for the original value it uses for cancellation.
Frequently asked questions
When is PMI required?
On most conventional loans with less than 20% down.
How much does PMI cost?
It depends on your loan and credit; your Loan Estimate shows the exact amount.
When does PMI go away?
You can request removal at 80% LTV based on the original value; it ends automatically at 78% or at the loan's midpoint.
Can I remove PMI early?
Yes, by paying down the balance to 80% of the original value, or in some cases with a new appraisal.
Does refinancing remove PMI?
If the new loan is 80% or less of the current value, a new conventional loan won't need PMI.
Is FHA mortgage insurance the same as PMI?
No. FHA MIP has different rules and often can't be cancelled.

Present Value Calculator: Lump Sum and Annuity | FigSumo (56 chars)
Meta description
Discount a future amount or a stream of payments to today's value at a chosen rate. Shows the present value formula with your numbers. (134 chars)

H1: Present Value Calculator
Present value (PV) tells you what a future sum is worth in today's money, given a rate of return you could earn in the meantime (the discount rate). It's the reverse of future value. Enter the future amount, the discount rate and the number of years to see the present value.
How to use this calculator
1. Future value: the amount you'll receive (or need) in the future.
2. Discount rate: the annual rate used to bring the amount back to today. Use the return you could reasonably earn on money of similar risk, or your borrowing rate if you'd otherwise borrow.
3. Years: how far in the future the amount is.
Result: present value. The tool discounts monthly: it divides the annual rate by 12 and discounts over years × 12 months.
The formula
PV = FV ÷ (1 + r ÷ 12)^(12 × t)
FV: future value
r: annual discount rate as a decimal
t: years
With annual discounting the formula is PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)^t, which gives a slightly higher PV. At a 0% rate, PV equals FV.
Worked examples
Example 1: $100,000 in 10 years at 6%
PV = 100,000 ÷ (1 + 0.06 ÷ 12)^120 = $54,963.27
With annual discounting: $55,839.48
How the discount rate changes the answer:
Discount rate
Present value of $100,000 in 10 years
3%
$74,109.56
6%
$54,963.27
9%
$40,793.73
The higher the rate, or the longer the wait, the less a future sum is worth today.
Example 2: how much to set aside today
You'll need $25,000 for a car in 5 years and can earn 4% (compounded monthly).
PV = 25,000 ÷ (1 + 0.04 ÷ 12)^60 = $20,475.08
That's the lump sum to invest now.
Example 3: lump sum or annual payments?
A prize offers $1,000,000 now or $60,000 a year for 20 years, paid at the end of each year. At a 5% discount rate, the payments are worth 60,000 × (1 − 1.05⁻²⁰) ÷ 0.05 = $747,732.62 today, so the lump sum is worth more, before tax. At a 2% rate, the payments would be worth $981,086.00, and the choice flips. The answer depends entirely on the return you can realistically earn.
Example 4: a future cost in today's money
Expecting a $50,000 expense in 20 years and assuming 3% inflation a year, the amount in today's purchasing power is 50,000 ÷ 1.03²⁰ = $27,683.79 (annual compounding). Here the "discount rate" is inflation, not an investment return.

Present value of a series of payments
For regular equal payments, use the annuity formula:
PV = PMT × (1 − (1 + i)^−n) ÷ i
$1,000 a month for 10 years at 5% (i = 0.05 ÷ 12, n = 120) has a present value of $94,281.35.
A prize paid as $50,000 a year for 20 years at a 5% discount rate is worth $623,110.52 today if paid at the end of each year, or $654,266.04 if the first payment comes immediately. Compare that with any lump-sum alternative.
The current tool handles single amounts; add up the PV of separate amounts, or use the formula above for a level series.
Understanding your results
Present value is the amount that, invested today at the discount rate, would grow to the future value.
The discount rate is a judgment. It should reflect what you'd give up (opportunity cost) and the risk that the future money doesn't arrive.
Inflation: discounting at a nominal rate gives a nominal PV. To think in purchasing power, use the inflation calculator or a real discount rate.
Where present value is used
Comparing a lump sum with payments: pensions, lottery prizes, legal settlements and structured payouts.
Valuing investments: bonds (see the bond calculator), rental property and businesses are valued by discounting future cash flows.
Net present value (NPV): subtract the cost of an investment from the PV of its returns. Positive NPV means it beats your discount rate; see the IRR calculator.
Savings targets: how much to put aside now for a future cost.
Country notes
The maths is the same everywhere. Discount rates used in official contexts differ: the US Office of Management and Budget publishes discount rates for federal project analysis (Circular A-4/A-94), and HM Treasury's Green Book sets a 3.5% social time preference rate for UK public projects. For personal decisions, use your own opportunity cost.
Tips and common mistakes
Mismatched compounding. This tool discounts monthly; textbooks often use annual. State which you're using.
Using an unrealistically high rate makes future money look worthless; too low overstates it.
Ignoring risk. A promised payment that may not arrive deserves a higher discount rate.
Forgetting taxes on the future amount.
Quick check
Match the discount rate's period to the cash-flow period.
Frequently asked questions
What is present value?
The value today of money you'll receive in the future, after discounting at a chosen rate.
What discount rate should I use?
The return you could earn on an alternative with similar risk. For safe amounts, a high-quality savings or government bond rate; for risky ones, higher.
Why is present value less than future value?
Because money today can earn a return. To end up with the future amount, you need less than that amount now.
How do I find the present value of monthly payments?
Use PV = PMT × (1 − (1 + i)^−n) ÷ i with the monthly rate and number of payments.
Does the calculator compound annually or monthly?
Monthly. For annual discounting, use FV ÷ (1 + r)^t.
What is the difference between PV and NPV?
PV is the value of future cash; NPV subtracts what you pay today.

Property Tax Calculator | FigSumo (33 chars)
Meta description
Estimate annual US property tax from assessed value and your local tax rate or mill levy, minus any homestead or other exemptions you enter. (140 chars)

H1: Property Tax Calculator
Property tax is the main source of funding for US local governments, schools and services. Your bill depends on your home's assessed value, any exemptions you qualify for and the combined tax rate set by your county, city, school district and special districts. This calculator estimates your annual and monthly property tax from those inputs and shows your effective tax rate.
How to use this calculator
1. Market value: the home's value, or the assessor's market value from your notice.
2. Assessment ratio (%): the share of market value that's taxed. Some states assess at 100%; others use a fraction (and some use different ratios for homes and businesses).
3. Exemptions ($): homestead, senior, veteran or disability exemptions that reduce taxable value.
4. Tax rate: either as a percentage or in mills (dollars per $1,000 of taxable value). Your tax bill or county website shows it.
Results: assessed value, taxable value, annual property tax, monthly amount (useful for escrow) and effective tax rate (tax ÷ market value).
The formulas
Assessed value = Market value × Assessment ratio
Taxable value = Assessed value − Exemptions
Annual tax = Taxable value × Rate          (rate as a decimal)
Annual tax = Taxable value × Mills ÷ 1,000 (rate in mills)
Effective rate = Annual tax ÷ Market value
Worked examples
Example 1: a 1.2% rate on a $350,000 home
Assessed at 100%: $350,000
Annual tax = $4,200.00 ($350.00 a month in escrow)
With a $50,000 homestead exemption, taxable value is $300,000 and tax is $3,600.00
Example 2: mills and a partial assessment ratio
Market value $300,000; assessment ratio 40%; rate 70 mills.
Assessed value = $120,000.00
Tax = 120,000 × 70 ÷ 1,000 = $8,400.00
Effective rate = 2.80%
A 70-mill rate sounds high, but on a 40% assessment the effective rate is lower. Always compare effective rates, not nominal ones.
Example 3: a large homestead exemption
Market value $400,000, assessed at 100%, a $100,000 homestead exemption and a 2.0% rate:
Taxable value = $300,000
Annual tax = $6,000.00 ($500.00 a month); effective rate 1.50%
Without the exemption, the bill would be $8,000.00, so it's worth checking you've applied.

Effective rates vary several-fold between states and even between neighbouring towns, so a home's tax bill can change the true cost of buying it as much as a change in mortgage rate.
How property tax changes
Reassessment: if your home is reassessed 8% higher at the same rate, the Example 1 bill rises by about $336.00.
Assessment caps: many states limit annual increases in assessed value for homesteads (for example, a 3% cap would keep the Example 1 taxable value from rising more than 3%, a bill of $4,326.00). Caps often reset when a home is sold, so a buyer may pay much more than the seller did.
Rates are set each year by local budgets.
Appealing your assessment
If the assessed value seems too high, compare it with recent sales of similar homes and check the property record for errors (square footage, bedrooms, lot size). Appeals have strict deadlines, often 30 to 60 days after the assessment notice [VERIFY your county].
Understanding your results
Escrow: most mortgage lenders collect 1/12 of the annual tax with each payment and pay the bill for you; the mortgage calculator can include it.
Federal deduction: if you itemize, property tax counts toward the state and local tax (SALT) deduction, which is capped [VERIFY 2026 SALT cap and phase-out]. At a 24% marginal rate, deducting $4,200 would be worth up to $1,008.00.
Buying a home: budget for the tax at the new assessed value, not the seller's bill.
Rentals: property tax is an operating expense in NOI; see the rental property calculator.
Canada and the UK
Canada: municipalities levy property tax as assessed value × a mill rate (municipal plus education), with assessments by provincial agencies such as MPAC in Ontario and BC Assessment. Some provinces offer homeowner grants or deferral programs.
UK: homes pay Council Tax based on valuation bands (in England, still based on 1991 values), not a percentage of current value. Commercial property pays business rates.
Worked comparisons for Canada and the UK
Canada: a home assessed at $600,000 in a municipality with a combined residential rate of 0.75% pays about $4,500 a year (illustrative rate; use your city's published rate).
UK: Council Tax doesn't depend on a percentage. In England, the average Band D bill for 2025/26 was about £2,280 [VERIFY], and bands A to H are charged as fixed fractions of Band D, from 6/9 to 18/9. Single occupants get a 25% discount.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the purchase price with the old rate without checking the assessment ratio.
Forgetting special assessments and district levies listed separately on the bill.
Missing exemptions. Homestead exemptions often require an application.
Comparing nominal mill rates across states. Use effective rates.
Frequently asked questions
How is property tax calculated?
Taxable value (assessed value minus exemptions) times the tax rate.
What is a mill?
One-tenth of a cent: $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable value.
What is a homestead exemption?
A reduction in taxable value (or a cap on increases) for your primary residence, available in many states.
Can I deduct property tax?
Yes, if you itemize, within the SALT cap.
Why did my property tax go up?
Your assessed value rose, local rates increased, an exemption expired, or a cap reset after a sale.
When is property tax paid?
It varies: annually, semi-annually or quarterly, often through your mortgage escrow.

Refinance Calculator

Title tag
Mortgage Refinance Calculator: Break-Even & Savings | FigSumo (61 chars)
Meta description
Compare your current mortgage with a refinance offer: the new payment, the break-even point on closing costs and the lifetime interest, including cash-out. (155 chars)
Country
US default (works for any fixed-rate loan)
Status
keep
Body words
1,040 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Refinance Calculator
Refinancing replaces your current loan with a new one, usually to get a lower rate, change the term or take out cash. A lower payment isn't the whole story. Closing costs take time to earn back, and a longer new term can raise the total you pay even at a lower rate. This calculator puts the current loan and the new offer side by side, so you can see the monthly saving, the break-even month and the lifetime cost.
How to use this calculator
1. Current loan: remaining balance (from your latest statement), interest rate and remaining term.
2. New loan: offered rate, new term, and the closing costs from the lender's Loan Estimate.
3. Points (optional): discount points you pay to buy down the rate. One point is 1% of the new loan amount.
4. Cash-out (optional): extra cash you take, added to the new loan.
5. Pay costs upfront or roll them in: rolling costs into the loan increases the new balance.
The formula
Both payments use the standard formula:
PMT = B × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
B: balance (current) or new loan amount (balance + cash-out + any financed costs)
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: remaining months (current) or new term in months
Then:
Monthly saving       = Current PMT − New PMT
Break-even (months)  = Upfront costs ÷ Monthly saving
Lifetime difference  = (Current PMT × remaining months) − (New PMT × new months + upfront costs)
The break-even figure assumes you stay in the home and keep the new loan at least that long. If the monthly saving is zero or negative, there is no break-even point.
Worked examples
Example 1: lower rate, reset to 30 years. Current: $300,000 balance at 7%, 27 years (324 months) left. New: $300,000 at 6% for 30 years, $6,000 closing costs paid upfront.
Current payment: $2,063.44
New payment: $1,798.65
Monthly saving: $264.79
Break-even: 6,000 ÷ 264.79 = 22.66 months, so in the 23rd month
Remaining interest: current loan $368,556.11; new loan $347,514.57
The new loan saves $21,041.54 in interest, or $15,041.54 after the $6,000 of costs. You also make payments for three more years.
Example 2: lower rate, shorter term. The same refinance on a 25-year term:
New payment: $1,932.90, still $130.54 less than today
Total interest: $279,871.26, which is $88,684.85 less than keeping the current loan
Paid off two years earlier than the current loan
Here the trade-off is a smaller monthly saving (so a slower break-even, about 46 months on the same $6,000) for a much bigger lifetime saving.
Understanding your results
Monthly saving: the change in principal and interest. Escrow for tax and insurance is usually unchanged.
Break-even month: when the cumulative savings first exceed the upfront costs. If you might sell or refinance again before then, the refinance probably costs more than it saves.
Lifetime cost comparison: includes the closing costs, so you can see whether the lower rate really wins over the whole period.
Cash-out: a larger new balance raises the payment and the interest. The calculator shows that cost separately so you can judge the cash on its own terms.
Refinancing other kinds of debt
The same break-even logic works for any loan:
Auto loans: a lower rate can cut the payment, but stretching the term may increase total interest.
Student loans: in the US, refinancing federal loans with a private lender ends federal benefits such as income-driven repayment options. Weigh that before comparing rates.
Credit cards: a personal loan or balance transfer at a lower rate can reduce interest; include transfer fees as upfront costs.
Enter the remaining balance, rate and months of the existing debt as the "current loan" to compare.
Country notes
United States: your Loan Estimate lists the closing costs; compare offers using the same page. Points can be worth it if you'll keep the loan past the point break-even.
Canada: breaking a mortgage term early can cost a prepayment penalty, often three months' interest or an interest rate differential. Ask your lender, and enter the penalty as an upfront cost.
UK: remortgaging during a fixed deal may trigger an early repayment charge. Add it, plus any arrangement and legal fees, as upfront costs.
Tips and common mistakes
Looking only at the monthly saving. Check the break-even point against how long you'll stay.
Restarting the clock. A new 30-year loan on a mortgage with 22 years left can cost more interest overall.
Ignoring closing costs. Rolling them into the loan raises the balance and interest.
Forgetting prepayment penalties on the existing loan.
Refinancing federal student loans casually. You give up federal protections.
Frequently asked questions
How much lower does my rate need to be to refinance?
There's no fixed rule. What matters is how quickly the monthly saving pays back the costs, compared with how long you expect to keep the loan. The calculator's break-even figure answers that for your numbers.
Why could a lower rate cost me more overall?
If you restart a long term, you pay interest for more months. Always compare lifetime cost, not just the monthly payment.
Should I roll closing costs into the loan?
It avoids paying cash now, but you pay interest on those costs for the life of the loan. The calculator shows both versions.
What are discount points?
They are an upfront fee, 1% of the loan per point, paid for a lower rate. Divide the cost of the points by the monthly saving they create to get their own break-even point.
Does refinancing affect my credit?
Applying usually involves a credit check. The new loan replaces the old one on your credit report. Rate-shopping within a short window is treated differently by scoring models; ask the lender.
What about cash-out refinancing?
It increases your loan balance and the interest you pay, and it reduces your home equity. Compare its cost with other ways of borrowing before you choose it.

Rent Affordability Calculator: How Much Rent? | FigSumo (55 chars)

H1: Rent Affordability Calculator
How much rent can you afford? This calculator applies a percentage-of-income rule to your monthly income and returns a rent budget. The common starting point is 30% of gross income, but the right share depends on your other costs, debts and savings goals, so the page also explains the tests landlords use and how to check the result against a full budget.
How to use this calculator
1. Monthly income: your gross (before-tax) monthly income. Include every regular source you can document: salary, self-employment, benefits. For a household, combine incomes if everyone will be on the lease.
2. Percent of income for rent: the share you want to spend. The default is 30%.
Result: suggested monthly rent.
The formula
Rent budget = Monthly income × Percent ÷ 100
Worked examples
Example 1: the 30% rule
Gross monthly income $6,000.00 (about $72,000.00 a year)
Rent budget = 6,000 × 0.30 = $1,800.00
Example 2: comparing percentages
For $4,500 gross a month:
25%: $1,125.00
30%: $1,350.00
35%: $1,575.00
Example 3: the 50/30/20 check on take-home pay
If the same household's take-home pay is $4,580 a month, the 50/30/20 approach allows $2,290.00 for all needs (rent, utilities, groceries, transport, minimum debt payments), $1,374.00 for wants and $916.00 for savings and extra debt repayment. Rent has to fit inside the needs share alongside everything else.
Example 4: a UK renter on £45,000
30% of gross monthly income: 3,750 × 0.30 = £1,125.00
Letting-agent rule of 30 times the monthly rent: 45,000 ÷ 30 = £1,500.00
The agent's test allows a higher rent than the 30% guide, but passing referencing doesn't make a rent comfortable. Use the lower figure as your budget.
Example 5: flatmates in Canada
Two people earning $3,900 and $3,900 a month combined ($7,800) and both on the lease: 30% is $2,340.00. If one earns more, split the rent in proportion to income or equally, but agree it in writing.
Example 6: utilities paid separately
If the 30% budget is $1,800 and electricity, internet and renter's insurance come to about $200 a month, the most you should offer the landlord is $1,600.00.

Understanding your results
The result is a ceiling, not a target. Living below it frees money for savings and emergencies.
Add utilities and renter's insurance. If they're not included in rent, they reduce what you can pay the landlord.
High-cost cities. In many large cities, renters spend well over 30%. The US Department of Housing and Urban Development calls households paying more than 30% of income on housing "cost-burdened" and over 50% "severely cost-burdened".
Use net income for a stricter test. 30% of take-home pay is noticeably less than 30% of gross. The take-home pay calculator gives your net figure.
What landlords look for
Income multiple: many US landlords want annual gross income of about 40 times the monthly rent. On $72,000.00 a year that's a maximum rent of $1,800.00; a $2,100 apartment needs $84,000.00 a year.
UK: letting agents commonly require annual income of around 30 times the monthly rent (£63,000.00 for £2,100 a month), and may ask for a guarantor otherwise.
Credit and references: credit history, rental history and employment checks are standard. Debt payments matter too; see the debt-to-income calculator.
Country notes
United States: HUD's 30% benchmark is used for affordability programs. Security deposit limits and rent control vary by state and city.
Canada: CMHC treats housing costing less than 30% of before-tax household income as affordable. On $5,200 a month, 32% would be $1,664.00. Several provinces (including Ontario and British Columbia) set annual limits on rent increases for existing tenancies [VERIFY 2026 guideline amounts].
United Kingdom: in England, the Tenant Fees Act caps tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent for annual rent below £50,000, and deposits must be protected in a government-approved scheme. Rents are typically quoted per calendar month (pcm).
Plan for rent increases
A lease renewal at 3% a year takes a $1,800 rent to $1,854.00 after one year and $2,086.69 after five. If your income doesn't keep pace, the share of income going on rent creeps up. In Ontario and British Columbia, rent increases for most existing tenancies are capped by a provincial guideline each year; in most US states and in England there's no general cap, though notice rules apply [VERIFY current local rules].
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting move-in costs: deposit, first month, moving and furniture.
Using income you can't document. Landlords usually need proof.
Ignoring commuting costs. A cheaper flat further out may cost more overall.
Not leaving room for savings. An emergency fund protects you from falling behind on rent.
Frequently asked questions
What is the 30% rule for rent?
Spend no more than 30% of gross monthly income on rent. It's a guideline from US housing policy, not a law.
Should I use gross or net income?
Landlords use gross. For your own budget, check the rent against take-home pay too.
How much income do I need for a $2,000 apartment?
At 30% of gross, about $6,667 a month ($80,000 a year). Under the 40× rule, $80,000 a year.
Does rent include utilities?
Sometimes. Check the listing and add any utilities you'll pay separately.
What if rent is more than 30% of my income?
Many people pay more, especially in big cities. Cut other costs, consider roommates, or look at the budget calculator to see what fits.
Is renting or buying cheaper?
It depends on prices, rates and how long you'll stay. Try the rent vs buy calculator.

Title tag
Rent vs Buy Calculator: Total Cost Comparison | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Compare the total cost of renting and buying over the years you plan to stay, including equity, appreciation, investment returns and fees. (138 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,044 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Rent vs Buy Calculator
Is it cheaper to rent or to buy where you live? The answer depends on home prices, mortgage rates, how fast rents rise and, above all, how long you plan to stay. This calculator compares the total cost of renting with the net cost of buying over a period you choose, after counting the equity you'd own at the end.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price: the price of the home you'd buy.
2. Down payment (%): the share you'd pay upfront.
3. Mortgage rate: the annual interest rate.
4. Mortgage term (years): the length of the loan, usually 30 in the US, or the amortization period in Canada and the UK (often 25).
5. Comparison period (years): how long you expect to stay.
6. Monthly rent: the rent for a comparable home.
7. Rent increase per year (%): expected annual rent growth.
8. Home maintenance (% of value per year): repairs and upkeep; 1% is a common rule of thumb.
Results: total rent cost, net buy cost (after equity), the difference and a note saying which costs less.
How it works
Renting: the tool adds up 12 months of rent each year, raising the rent by your increase rate at the end of each year.
Buying: it adds the down payment, every monthly mortgage payment over the comparison period and annual maintenance (percentage × home price). It then subtracts the equity you'd hold at the end: home price minus the remaining loan balance.
Net buy cost = Down payment + Mortgage payments + Maintenance − (Home price − Remaining balance)
Difference = Net buy cost − Total rent
A negative difference means buying cost less over the period.
What the model leaves out: property tax, home insurance, closing and selling costs, home price growth, and the return you could earn by investing the down payment instead. The examples show how to add them.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default scenario over 7 years
$400,000 home, 20% down, 6.5% over 30 years; rent $2,200 rising 3% a year; maintenance 1%.
Monthly mortgage payment: $2,022.62
Total paid out for buying (down payment, payments, maintenance of $28,000.00): $277,899.88
Remaining balance after 7 years: $289,331.98, so equity = $110,668.02
Net buy cost: $167,231.87
Total rent: $202,289.00
Difference: −$35,057.13, so buying looks cheaper by this measure.
Example 2: adding the costs the tool leaves out
Using the same scenario:
Closing costs of 3% plus selling costs of 6% add $36,000.00, raising the buy cost to $203,231.87 (difference $942.87: now renting is cheaper).
Home price growth of 3% a year would lift the value to $491,949.55, a gain of $91,949.55 that reduces the buy cost.
Investing the $80,000 down payment at 5% instead would have earned about $32,568.03; that forgone return adds to the cost of buying.
Net of all three: buy cost $143,850.36 against rent $202,289.00, a difference of −$58,438.65.
Over a short stay the transaction costs dominate. Over 3 years, the net buy cost is $73,349.41 before transaction costs ($109,349.41 with them) against $81,599.76 of rent.
Understanding your results
Time horizon matters most. Buying has large upfront and exit costs; the longer you stay, the more they're spread out and the more equity you build.
Early payments are mostly interest. In year one of a 30-year loan, most of each payment is interest; see the amortization calculator.
Renting has flexibility value that doesn't appear in the numbers: you can move without selling, and the landlord pays for major repairs.
The comparison is only fair if the renter invests the difference. If renting is cheaper each month but the savings get spent, the buyer may still end up wealthier.
Country notes
United States: mortgage interest and property tax are deductible only if you itemize, which fewer households do since the standard deduction ($32,200 for married couples filing jointly in 2026) rose. Gains on a main home up to $250,000 ($500,000 for couples) are excluded from tax if you meet the ownership and use tests. Use the closing cost calculator for upfront costs.
Canada: buyers pay land transfer tax (plus a municipal tax in Toronto), and CMHC insurance if the down payment is under 20%. Gains on a principal residence are generally tax-free. First-time buyers can save in an FHSA.
United Kingdom: Stamp Duty Land Tax (England and Northern Ireland), LBTT (Scotland) or LTT (Wales) can be a large upfront cost, with relief for first-time buyers in some cases. Leasehold flats add ground rent and service charges. Mortgages are usually fixed for 2 to 5 years, so the rate will change during a long comparison.
Tips and common mistakes
Comparing rent with the mortgage payment alone. Owners also pay maintenance, tax, insurance and transaction costs.
Using the comparison period as the mortgage term. A 7-year stay doesn't mean a 7-year loan.
Assuming prices always rise. Try a 0% or negative growth scenario.
Ignoring the down payment's opportunity cost.
Frequently asked questions
How long do I need to stay for buying to make sense?
Often 5 years or more, but it depends on prices, rates and transaction costs. Run the calculator with several comparison periods.
Is rent money wasted?
No. Rent buys housing and flexibility, just as mortgage interest, tax and maintenance do for owners. Only the principal repayment builds equity.
What maintenance percentage should I use?
1% of the home's value a year is a common starting point; older homes may need more.
Does the calculator include home appreciation?
Not yet. Example 2 shows how to account for it by hand.
Why does the net buy cost subtract equity?
Because at the end of the period you'd own that share of the home, which you could sell.
Should I include the price-to-rent ratio?
It's a useful screen: home price ÷ annual rent. Here 400,000 ÷ $26,400.00 ≈ 15. Higher ratios generally favour renting.

Title tag
Rental Property Calculator: Cash Flow and ROI | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Estimate monthly cash flow, cap rate and return on a rental property from rent, vacancy, mortgage and operating expenses. (121 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,006 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Rental Property Calculator
Before buying a rental, you need to know whether the rent will cover the mortgage and running costs, and by how much. This calculator takes the monthly rent and the main monthly costs and returns the monthly cash flow, the annual net operating income (NOI) and the operating expense ratio.
How to use this calculator
1. Monthly rent: the rent you expect to collect. Check comparable listings rather than relying on the seller's figure.
2. Mortgage payment: monthly principal and interest. Use the mortgage calculator to estimate it.
3. Taxes and insurance (monthly): property tax plus landlord insurance, divided by 12.
4. Other monthly costs: maintenance, management, HOA or service charges, utilities you pay, and a vacancy allowance.
Results: monthly cash flow, net operating income (annual) and expense ratio.
The formulas
Cash flow (monthly) = Rent − (Mortgage + Taxes and insurance + Other costs)
NOI (annual) = (Rent − Taxes and insurance − Other costs) × 12
Expense ratio = (Taxes and insurance + Other costs) ÷ Rent
NOI excludes the mortgage, so it measures the property's performance regardless of financing. Cash flow includes the mortgage, so it's what lands in your account each month.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default figures
Rent $2,200; mortgage $1,400; taxes and insurance $350; other costs $200.
Cash flow = 2,200 − 1,950 = $250.00 a month ($3,000.00 a year)
NOI = (2,200 − 350 − 200) × 12 = $19,800.00
Expense ratio = 550 ÷ 2,200 = 25%
If the property cost $300,000 and you put in $70,000 cash (down payment and closing costs):
Cap rate = $19,800.00 ÷ 300,000 = 6.60%
Cash-on-cash return = $3,000.00 ÷ 70,000 = 4.29%
Example 2: adding vacancy and maintenance
Allow 5% vacancy (rent effectively $2,090.00) and 8% of rent for maintenance on top of the $200 (other costs $376.00):
Cash flow = −$36.00 a month (−$432.00 a year)
NOI = $16,368.00
A deal that looked positive becomes negative once realistic allowances are included. Enter the vacancy and maintenance allowances in "Other monthly costs" to see this in the tool.
Example 3: a UK higher-rate landlord
Rent £1,200 a month, mortgage interest £500 a month (interest-only), other costs £200 a month:
Pre-tax cash flow = (1,200 − 500 − 200) × 12 = £6,000 a year
Taxable rental profit (interest not deductible) = 14,400 − 2,400 = £12,000
Tax at 40% = £4,800, less a 20% credit on £6,000 of interest (£1,200) = £3,600
After-tax cash flow = £2,400
If interest were fully deductible, as it was before 2017, the tax would be £2,400. The restriction turns a 40%-taxpayer's £6,000 profit into £2,400 after tax, which is why many UK landlords now buy through limited companies [VERIFY whether that suits your situation with an adviser].
Example 4: quick screening rules
The 1% rule: some US investors look for monthly rent of at least 1% of the price. Example 1's $2,200 on a $300,000 property is 0.73%, below that guide.
Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR): NOI ÷ annual mortgage payments = 19,800 ÷ 16,800 = 1.18. Lenders that size loans on rental income often look for at least about 1.2 [VERIFY lender requirements].
Rules of thumb only screen deals; the full cash flow calculation decides.
Understanding your results
Positive cash flow means the rent covers all costs including the mortgage. Negative means you'll top up each month, betting on appreciation or loan paydown.
NOI is what lenders and buyers use to value a property; see the cap rate calculator.
Expense ratio: operating costs as a share of rent (mortgage excluded). Many investors budget roughly 35% to 50% for long-term residential rentals once vacancy, repairs, capital reserves and management are counted [VERIFY ranges for your market]. A very low ratio usually means something has been left out.
Cash flow isn't total return. Mortgage principal repayment and any price growth add to wealth; tax, transaction costs and major repairs subtract.
Costs people forget
Vacancy between tenants and letting fees
Repairs and capital items (roof, boiler/furnace, appliances)
Property management, often 8% to 12% of rent
Licensing, safety certificates and inspections
Legal costs and eviction risk
Country notes
United States: rental income and expenses go on Schedule E. Residential rental buildings are depreciated over 27.5 years, which reduces taxable income (but not cash flow). Some cities require rental registration.
Canada: report rental income on form T776. Capital cost allowance (CCA) is optional and can be recaptured on sale. Some cities, including Vancouver and Toronto, charge vacant-home taxes.
United Kingdom: individual landlords can't deduct mortgage interest from rental profits; they get a tax credit at 20% of finance costs instead. Buy-to-let lenders test rent against the mortgage at a stressed rate; see the buy-to-let mortgage calculator. Deposits must be protected and landlords need gas safety certificates and EPCs.
Tips and common mistakes
Assuming 100% occupancy. Budget for vacancy.
Using an interest-only payment when the loan is repayment, or the other way round.
Leaving out insurance increases and property tax reassessment after purchase.
Counting tax depreciation as cash. It's an accounting deduction.
Frequently asked questions
What is a good cash flow for a rental?
There's no universal number; many investors want a positive cash flow after realistic vacancy and repairs, with a cushion for surprises.
What's the difference between NOI and cash flow?
NOI is before mortgage payments; cash flow is after.
What is the 1% rule?
A rough screen that monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price. It ignores taxes, insurance and rates, so use it only as a first filter.
What is cash-on-cash return?
Annual cash flow divided by the cash you invested.
Should I include my own labor?
Yes. If you self-manage, price your time as a management fee to compare properties fairly.
How is rental income taxed?
Net rental profit is taxable income in the US, Canada and the UK, with rules that differ by country.

Title tag
Retirement Calculator: How Much Will I Have Saved? | FigSumo (60 chars)
Meta description
Estimate retirement savings at your chosen age, their value in today's money and how long withdrawals could last, with adjustable return and inflation. (151 chars)
Country
global (country notes for Social Security, CPP/OAS, State Pension)
Status
keep
Body words
1,079 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Retirement Calculator
Retirement planning comes down to three questions. How much will I have when I stop working? What will that be worth in today's money? And how long will it last once I start taking money out? This calculator answers all three from your current savings, monthly contributions, an assumed return and inflation. Government pensions are entered as separate monthly income, so the gap between what they pay and what you need is clear.
How to use this calculator
1. Current age and retirement age.
2. Current retirement savings across all accounts.
3. Monthly contribution, including any employer contribution. Add an annual increase if you expect it to rise with your pay.
4. Expected return before retirement and after retirement. People often assume a lower return once retired, if they plan to hold more conservative investments.
5. Inflation, used to show results in today's money.
6. Retirement income: your planned monthly spending and any expected government or workplace pension.
The formula
Accumulation (monthly compounding, contributions at the end of each month):
B_ret = S × (1 + i)^n + C × ((1 + i)^n − 1) / i
Real value = B_ret ÷ (1 + π)^years
S: current savings
C: monthly contribution
i: annual return ÷ 12
n: months until retirement
π: annual inflation
Drawdown: each month the balance earns the post-retirement rate, then the withdrawal W is taken out:
B_(k+1) = B_k × (1 + j) − W
The calculator counts the months until the balance reaches zero. For a fixed number of years Y, the sustainable withdrawal is:
W = B_ret × j / (1 − (1 + j)^−(12Y))
Worked examples
Example 1: age 38, retiring at 65. $80,000 saved, $800 a month, 6% a year, 2.5% inflation, 27 years to go (324 months).
Growth of existing savings: 80,000 × 1.005^324 = $402,618.75
Growth of contributions: 800 × (1.005^324 − 1) / 0.005 = $645,237.50
Balance at 65: $1,047,856.25
Total contributed: 80,000 + 800 × 324 = $339,200
In today's money: $537,969.11 (÷ 1.025^27)
Example 2: how long will it last? Starting with the $1,047,856.25 above, withdrawing $5,000 a month and earning 4% a year in retirement:
The money lasts about 30 years (361 monthly withdrawals) before it runs out.
Those withdrawals are fixed in nominal dollars, so their buying power falls with inflation. If you want spending to rise with prices, enter the inflation-adjusted option, and the balance runs down sooner.
A rule of thumb many people check against: a first-year withdrawal of 4% of savings. Here that is 4% × $537,969.11 (in today's money) ≈ $21,519 a year. The rule comes from historical studies of US markets and is not a guarantee.
Rules of thumb (and their limits)
Commonly quoted planning shortcuts. None is official guidance:
Replace a share of pre-retirement income: some planners aim for 70–80% of final income. Your real need depends on housing, health and travel plans.
Save a fixed share of pay: for example 10–15% including employer contributions. Starting later usually means saving more.
4% initial withdrawal: discussed in Example 2.
The calculator lets you replace each shortcut with your own numbers, which is more reliable than any rule.
Understanding your results
Balance at retirement (nominal and real): the real figure is the one to compare with today's spending.
Contributions vs growth: in Example 1, growth makes up about two-thirds of the final balance. That share depends heavily on how long the money is invested.
Gap analysis: planned spending minus pension income gives the monthly amount your savings need to cover. The calculator shows whether your projected balance can fund it to your chosen age.
Limitations: a constant return, no taxes, and no allowance for changing spending or health costs. Run several scenarios.
Country notes
United States: Social Security retirement benefits can start at 62, with reductions. Full retirement age is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, and delaying past that up to 70 increases the benefit. Your personal estimate is available from your my Social Security account. Tax-advantaged accounts: 401(k), IRA/Roth IRA.
Canada: the standard age to start a CPP retirement pension is 65. You can start it as early as 60, with payments reduced by 0.6% a month, or as late as 70, with an increase of 0.7% a month. Old Age Security is paid separately. Enter your estimates from your My Service Canada Account. Savings options: RRSP, TFSA.
UK: the State Pension age is set by date of birth and is rising. Check your forecast on GOV.UK. Workplace pensions and ISAs supplement it.
Tips and common mistakes
Using an optimistic return. Test lower returns and longer lifespans.
Forgetting inflation. A target in today's money needs more in future dollars or pounds.
Ignoring state pensions and Social Security. They reduce the savings you need.
Underestimating healthcare and long-term care costs in later life.
Not revisiting the plan. Recheck every year or after a big change.
Frequently asked questions
How much do I need to retire?
It depends on the income you want, the government pensions you'll receive, when you retire and how long you live. Start with your expected annual spending in retirement, take off pension income, and use the drawdown tab to see what balance would fund the rest.
What return should I assume?
Use a long-term average appropriate to your investment mix, net of fees. Then test a lower figure as well. Small changes compound over decades. In Example 1, 1 percentage point either way makes a six-figure difference.
Why show "today's money"?
Because $1 million in 27 years will buy much less than $1 million today. At 2.5% inflation it has the buying power of about $538,000 today.
Should I include my employer's contributions?
Yes. Add them to the monthly contribution, or use the 401(k) calculator to model the match in detail.
Is the 4% rule safe?
It's a historical guideline, not a promise. Some people use more flexible strategies that adjust withdrawals after bad years. A licensed financial planner can help you choose.
Does this include taxes on withdrawals?
No. Withdrawals from traditional 401(k)s, IRAs, RRSPs and most pensions are generally taxable income. Roth IRA, TFSA and ISA withdrawals are generally tax-free if the rules are met.

H1: RMD Calculator
Once you reach a certain age, the IRS requires you to take a minimum amount out of most tax-deferred retirement accounts each year: a required minimum distribution (RMD). This calculator works out the RMD for a traditional IRA (and similar accounts) from your age and the account balance on December 31 of the previous year, using the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table.
How to use this calculator
1. Your age: your age on your birthday in the distribution year (not today's age if your birthday hasn't arrived).
2. Prior Dec. 31 account balance: the account's fair market value at the end of last year. Your custodian reports it on Form 5498 or the year-end statement.
Results: distribution period (the IRS life-expectancy factor) and the required minimum distribution for the year.
The formula
RMD = Prior December 31 balance ÷ Distribution period
The distribution period comes from Table III (Uniform Lifetime Table) in IRS Publication 590-B, which applies to most account owners. It shrinks each year as you age, so the share of the account you must withdraw rises. Selected factors [VERIFY each against Pub 590-B Appendix B before publishing]:

(Using the age-85 factor by mistake would give $51,250.00, far more than required.)

When RMDs start
Under the SECURE 2.0 Act:
Age 73 if you were born from 1951 to 1959.
Age 75 if you were born in 1960 or later.
Your first RMD can be delayed until April 1 of the year after you reach RMD age, but then you must also take the second RMD by December 31 of that year, which can push you into a higher bracket. Later RMDs are due by December 31 each year.
Which accounts have RMDs
Traditional, SEP and SIMPLE IRAs: yes. You can total the RMDs for all your IRAs and take the amount from any one or more of them.
401(k), 403(b) and 457(b) plans: yes, calculated separately for each plan (403(b)s can be aggregated with each other). If you still work for the employer and don't own 5% or more, you can usually delay that plan's RMD until you retire.
Roth IRAs: no RMDs for the original owner. Since 2024, designated Roth accounts in workplace plans also have no lifetime RMDs.
Inherited accounts follow different rules, including the 10-year rule for many non-spouse beneficiaries.
Understanding your results
The RMD is a minimum. You can withdraw more, but extra withdrawals don't count toward next year's RMD.
It is taxable as ordinary income (except any after-tax basis). Plan your withholding; custodians can withhold federal tax from the distribution. The income tax calculator helps estimate the tax.
Missing an RMD triggers an excise tax of 25% of the shortfall, reduced to 10% if corrected within the correction window (SECURE 2.0).
Ways to manage RMDs
Qualified charitable distributions (QCDs): from age 70½, you can give directly from an IRA to charity (up to an annual limit, indexed [VERIFY 2026 QCD limit]). QCDs count toward the RMD and aren't taxable income.
Roth conversions before RMD age reduce future RMDs, at the cost of tax on the conversion now.
Timing: taking the RMD early in the year is simple; late in the year leaves more time invested. Either is allowed.
Country notes
RMDs are a US rule. Canada has a similar requirement for RRIFs, with prescribed minimum withdrawal percentages starting the year after the RRIF is opened; RRSPs must be converted by the end of the year you turn 71. The UK has no compulsory withdrawals from pensions; you can leave a pension invested for as long as you like, although from April 2027 unused pension funds are due to fall within the estate for Inheritance Tax [VERIFY].
Tips and common mistakes
Using the wrong balance. It's the prior December 31 value, not today's.
Forgetting accounts. Each workplace plan has its own RMD.
Delaying the first RMD without planning for two taxable distributions in one year.
Ignoring the spouse exception. A much younger spouse beneficiary means a lower RMD.
Frequently asked questions
At what age do I have to take RMDs?
73 if born 1951–1959; 75 if born in 1960 or later.
How is the RMD calculated?
Prior year-end balance divided by your factor from the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table.
Do Roth IRAs have RMDs?
Not for the original owner.
What is the penalty for missing an RMD?
An excise tax of 25% of the amount not taken, which can drop to 10% if corrected promptly.
Can I take more than the RMD?
Yes. The RMD is only the minimum.
Can I take my IRA RMD from one account?
Yes, for IRAs: calculate each IRA's RMD, add them up and withdraw the total from any of your IRAs. Workplace plans are different.

Title tag
ROI Calculator: Return on Investment & Annualized ROI | FigSumo (63 chars)
Meta description
Calculate return on investment from amount invested and returned, plus annualized ROI when you enter the holding period. (120 chars)
Country
global
