1,007 (minimum 1,000)
H1: ROI Calculator
Return on investment (ROI) measures how much you gained or lost relative to what you put in. It's the quickest way to compare the results of different investments, business projects or purchases. Enter the net gain and the cost to get the ROI as a percentage and the final value.
How to use this calculator
1. Amount gained (net profit): what you made after costs. Enter a negative number for a loss. Include income received (dividends, rent) and subtract fees, commissions and taxes you want to account for.
2. Cost of investment: the total you invested, including purchase fees.
Results: ROI (%) and final value (cost plus gain).
The formula
ROI = Net gain ÷ Cost × 100
Net gain = Final value + Income received − Cost
ROI doesn't consider time. A 15% return over one year and over ten years show the same ROI, which is why you should also look at the annualized figure:
Annualized ROI = (1 + ROI)^(1 ÷ years) − 1
Worked examples
Example 1: the default figures
Gain $15,000 on a $100,000 investment
ROI = 15,000 ÷ 100,000 = 15%; final value $115,000.00
If that took 3 years, the annualized return is 4.77% a year.
Example 2: comparing two investments
A: invest $10,000, gain $4,000 over 2 years → ROI 40%, annualized 18.32%
B: invest $20,000, gain $9,000 over 5 years → ROI 45%, annualized 7.71%
B has the higher ROI, but A earned more per year. For investments of different lengths, compare annualized figures.
Example 3: counting fees and a loss
Sell for $12,000 a holding bought for $10,000, with $150 in purchase fees and $90 in sale fees.
Net gain = 12,000 − 10,000 − 150 − 90 = $1,760.00; cost including purchase fees $10,150
ROI = 17.34%
A loss works the same way: losing $2,500 on $10,000 is an ROI of −25%. To get back to $10,000 from $7,500 you then need a gain of 33.33%, more than the percentage lost.
Example 4: a rental property bought with cash
Purchase $250,000 plus $10,000 of closing costs: cost $260,000
Net rent after expenses: $14,400 a year for 5 years = $72,000
Sold for $300,000, less $18,000 in selling costs = $282,000
Net gain = 282,000 + 72,000 − 260,000 = $94,000
ROI = 36.15%, annualized about 6.37% a year
The annualized figure here treats the gain as if it all arrived at the end. Because the rent came in every year, the true annual return is a little higher; the IRR calculator handles that timing.
Example 5: an advertising campaign
You spend $2,000 on ads that bring $9,000 of sales at a 40% gross margin:
Gross profit from those sales: $3,600
ROI = (3,600 − 2,000) ÷ 2,000 = 80%
Return on ad spend (ROAS) = 9,000 ÷ 2,000 = 4.5×
ROAS uses revenue, so it always looks better than ROI. A ROAS of 2.5× at a 40% margin is break-even: 2.5 × 0.40 = 1.
Real ROI after inflation
The 15% ROI over 3 years in Example 1, with 3% inflation a year, is a real return of 1.15 ÷ 1.03³ − 1 = 5.24% over the period.
Understanding your results
ROI is a ratio, so it works for anything with a cost and a gain: shares, property, a marketing campaign or new equipment.
It ignores timing of cash flows. If money goes in or comes out at different times, use the IRR calculator or the average return calculator.
It ignores risk. A higher ROI from a riskier bet isn't automatically better.
Inflation: a 15% ROI over 3 years with 3% annual inflation is a smaller real gain; see the inflation calculator.
ROI in business decisions
For a project, net gain is the extra profit it generates (revenue minus extra costs). A $5,000 marketing campaign that brings in $8,000 of extra gross profit has an ROI of 60%. Make sure "gain" is profit, not revenue, and include staff time. For how long it takes to recover the outlay, see the payback period calculator.
Country notes
ROI is calculated the same way everywhere, but after-tax ROI depends on the country:
United States: gains on assets held over a year qualify for long-term capital gains rates; see the capital gains tax calculator.
Canada: half of a capital gain is taxable for most individuals [VERIFY]; gains inside a TFSA are tax-free.
United Kingdom: Capital Gains Tax applies above the annual exempt amount (£3,000 for 2026/27 [VERIFY]); ISAs shelter gains.
ROI and related measures
Measure
What it tells you
Accounts for time?
ROI
Total gain as a share of cost
No
Annualized ROI / CAGR
Average yearly growth rate
Yes
IRR
Rate that sets the value of all cash flows to zero
Yes, including timing
Return on equity (ROE)
Profit relative to the owner's own money, after debt
Depends on the period used
When someone quotes a return, ask which of these it is and over what period.
Tips and common mistakes
Using revenue as gain. Subtract the costs.
Leaving out fees and taxes. They can turn a small gain into a loss.
Comparing ROIs over different periods without annualizing.
Forgetting income. Dividends, interest and rent count toward the gain.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate ROI?
Divide the net gain by the cost and multiply by 100.
What is a good ROI?
It depends on the risk and time involved. Compare it with alternatives of similar risk, such as an index fund or a savings rate.
Can ROI be negative?
Yes. A negative ROI means you lost money.
What's the difference between ROI and annualized return?
ROI is the total return over the whole period; annualized return spreads it into an equivalent yearly rate.
Does ROI include taxes?
Only if you subtract them from the gain. Doing so gives after-tax ROI.
What's the difference between ROI and IRR?
ROI ignores timing; IRR accounts for when each cash flow happens.

Title tag
Roth IRA Calculator 2026: Contribution Limits & Growth | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Project tax-free Roth IRA growth and check how much you can contribute in 2026 based on your income, filing status and age. (123 chars)

US

rename (301) · tax year 2026 (contributions for 2026 may be made until the 2027 filing deadline)

1,012 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Roth IRA Calculator (2026)
A Roth IRA is funded with money you've already paid tax on. In return, qualified withdrawals, including all the growth, are tax-free. This calculator does two jobs. It checks how much you're allowed to contribute for 2026, because the limit shrinks at higher incomes. Then it projects how the account could grow and how much of the final balance would be tax-free growth.
How to use this calculator
1. Filing status and modified adjusted gross income (MAGI). These determine whether your limit is reduced.
2. Age: at 50 or older, a catch-up amount is added.
3. Taxable compensation: you can't contribute more than you earned from work. A spouse with little or no income may be able to use the other spouse's compensation when filing jointly.
4. Current Roth balance, yearly contribution, expected return and years for the growth projection.
5. Optional comparison: enter a tax rate to compare with investing the same amount in a taxable account.
The formula
2026 contribution limit: $7,500, plus $1,100 if you're 50 or older ($8,600). The limit is shared across all your traditional and Roth IRAs.
Income phase-out (2026 MAGI):
Filing status
Full contribution below
No contribution at or above
Single / head of household
$153,000
$168,000
Married filing jointly
$242,000
$252,000
Married filing separately (lived with spouse)
$0
$10,000
Inside the range, the IRS worksheet in Publication 590-A reduces the limit in proportion:
Reduced limit = Limit − Limit × (MAGI − lower threshold) ÷ (range width)
The result is rounded up to the next $10. If it is above $0 but below $200, you can contribute $200.
Growth (annual contributions at year-end):
FV = B × (1 + r)^n + C × ((1 + r)^n − 1) / r
B: current balance
C: yearly contribution
r: annual return
n: years
Worked examples
Example 1: maximum contributions for 25 years. $7,500 a year, 7% average annual return, starting from $0.
FV = 7,500 × (1.07^25 − 1) / 0.07 = $474,367.78
Contributions: 25 × 7,500 = $187,500
Tax-free growth: $286,867.78, provided withdrawals are qualified
The contribution limit has been raised over time for inflation. Keeping it flat at $7,500 makes this estimate conservative on that point.
Example 2: partial contribution in the phase-out. Single filer under 50, MAGI $160,000.
Into the range by: 160,000 − 153,000 = $7,000 of a $15,000 range
Reduction: 7,500 × 7,000 ÷ 15,000 = $3,500
Maximum Roth contribution: $4,000 (already a multiple of $10)
At MAGI $168,000 or more, the direct Roth contribution limit is $0.
Understanding your results
Allowed contribution: your 2026 limit after the age, compensation and income tests.
Projected balance: split into contributions (which you can generally withdraw at any time without tax or penalty) and earnings (tax-free only for qualified distributions).
Comparison with a taxable account: shows the effect of paying no tax on growth, using your tax rate. It's a simplification; real taxable accounts depend on the mix of dividends, capital gains and holding periods.
Converting a traditional IRA to a Roth
A conversion moves money from a traditional IRA into a Roth IRA. The pre-tax amount you convert is added to your taxable income for that year. Converting $10,000 at a 22% marginal rate adds about $2,200 of federal tax. There are no income limits on conversions. Each conversion has its own five-year period for the 10% additional tax if the converted amount is withdrawn before age 59½. The calculator models contributions only; Publication 590-B explains conversions in full.
Country notes
US only. Similar tax-free accounts: Canada's TFSA and the UK's ISA, with different limits and rules.
Timing: contributions for 2026 can be made until the tax-filing deadline in 2027 (not including extensions).
Tips and common mistakes
Contributing above the income limit. Excess contributions face a 6% excise tax each year until fixed.
Confusing the five-year rules. There's one for earnings and another for each conversion.
Missing the deadline. Contributions for a tax year can be made until the filing deadline the following April.
Leaving contributions in cash. Money must be invested inside the account to grow.
Assuming Roth is always better. If your tax rate in retirement will be lower, a traditional account may win.
Frequently asked questions
What is the Roth IRA limit for 2026?
$7,500, or $8,600 if you're 50 or older by the end of the year. It's a combined limit for all your traditional and Roth IRAs, and it can't exceed your taxable compensation.
What are the 2026 income limits?
For single and head-of-household filers, the phase-out range is $153,000–$168,000 of MAGI. For married filing jointly, it is $242,000–$252,000.
When are Roth withdrawals tax-free?
Earnings are tax-free in a qualified distribution, which generally means the account has been open for at least five tax years and you are 59½ or older (or meet another qualifying condition, such as disability). Your own contributions can be withdrawn at any time without tax or penalty.
Can I contribute to a Roth IRA and a 401(k)?
Yes. The IRA limit is separate from the 401(k) deferral limit. Your income still has to be within the Roth IRA limits.
What if I contribute too much?
Excess contributions are subject to a 6% excise tax for each year they stay in the account. You can avoid it by withdrawing the excess, and any earnings on it, by your return's due date (including extensions).
Is a Roth better than a traditional IRA?
A Roth tends to suit you better if you expect a similar or higher tax rate in retirement. A traditional IRA tends to suit you better if you expect a lower rate. Deductibility of traditional IRA contributions also depends on income and workplace plan coverage.

RRSP Calculator 2026: Tax Refund, Limit & Growth | FigSumo (58 chars)

Estimate your RRSP tax refund, check your deduction limit against the 2026 maximum of $33,810 and project tax-deferred growth to retirement. (140 chars)

H1: RRSP Calculator (2026)
A Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) gives you a tax deduction when you contribute, and the investments grow tax-deferred until you withdraw them. This calculator estimates the refund a contribution could create for your province and income, checks the 2026 contribution limit, and projects the account's growth. It also helps you compare it with a TFSA.
How to use this calculator
1. Province and taxable income before the contribution. The calculator works out the tax saved across your brackets.
2. Contribution amount for the 2026 tax year.
3. Deduction limit (optional): enter the figure from your latest notice of assessment, or let the helper estimate it from last year's earned income and any pension adjustment.
4. Growth inputs: current RRSP balance, yearly contribution, expected return and years to retirement.
5. Optionally reinvest the refund to see how much that adds over time.
The formula
Deduction limit for 2026 (simplified CRA method):
Limit = unused room carried forward
      + min(18% × 2025 earned income, $33,810)
      − 2025 pension adjustment (PA)
      (+ PAR − net PSPA where applicable)
Refund estimate:
Tax saved = Tax(taxable income) − Tax(taxable income − contribution)
This uses the federal and provincial 2026 brackets. If the contribution moves you down a bracket, the saving is spread across more than one rate.
Growth:
FV = B × (1 + r)^n + C × ((1 + r)^n − 1) / r
Worked examples
Example 1: refund on a $10,000 contribution. An Ontario employee with $75,000 salary (taxable income $74,273 after enhanced CPP and CPP2) contributes $10,000.
Taxable income falls to $64,273. That is still above the federal $58,523 and Ontario $53,891 thresholds, so the whole $10,000 is deducted at 20.5% federal + 9.15% Ontario = 29.65%
Estimated tax saving: $2,965
Ontario surtax and the Health Premium are unchanged at this income, so they don't add to the saving
The 2026 limit check: 18% × $75,000 of 2025 earned income = $13,500, below the $33,810 cap, so this person has $13,500 of new room before any pension adjustment.
Example 2: long-term growth. $10,000 a year for 25 years at 6% a year, from $0:
FV = 10,000 × (1.06^25 − 1) / 0.06 = $548,645.12
Contributions: $250,000
Growth: $298,645.12, tax-deferred until withdrawal
Withdrawals are taxable income. The benefit is largest if your tax rate in retirement is lower than when you contributed.
Example 3: the Home Buyers' Plan. First-time buyers can withdraw up to $60,000 from their RRSPs tax-free to buy a qualifying home. The withdrawal must be repaid over 15 years, so a $60,000 withdrawal needs repayments of $4,000 a year once repayment starts; any amount not repaid in a year is added to your taxable income. Withdrawals made from 2022 to 2025 have a longer grace period before repayment begins [VERIFY start year for your withdrawal].
Example 4: deadline and room. Contributions made in the first 60 days of 2027 can be deducted on your 2026 return. New room each year is 18% of the previous year's earned income up to the annual maximum ($33,810 for 2026 [VERIFY]), less any pension adjustment; your Notice of Assessment shows the exact figure.
Understanding your results
Tax saving: an estimate of the reduction in income tax for 2026. The refund you actually receive depends on what was withheld from your pay.
Room after contribution: your remaining deduction limit. Over-contributions of more than $2,000 above your limit are taxed at 1% a month.
Projected balance: in nominal dollars, before tax on withdrawal.
RRSP vs TFSA: with the same pre-tax money, the two give equal after-tax results when your tax rate is the same at contribution and withdrawal. The RRSP wins if your rate falls in retirement; the TFSA wins if it rises.
Country notes
Deadline: contributions made in the first 60 days of 2027 can be deducted on your 2026 return. The CRA publishes the exact dates each year.
Age: you can contribute to your own RRSP until 31 December of the year you turn 71, when it must be converted (usually to a RRIF or an annuity).
Quebec: the deduction applies, but provincial tax savings are calculated under Quebec's system (not yet supported).
Home Buyers' Plan (HBP): first-time buyers who meet the conditions can withdraw up to $60,000 from their RRSPs to buy or build a qualifying home, and repay it over a 15-year period.
For the US equivalent, see the 401(k) calculator; for the UK, the ISA calculator and workplace pensions.
Tips and common mistakes
Contributing above your room. Over-contributions beyond the $2,000 buffer are taxed at 1% a month.
Withdrawing early. Withdrawals are taxed and the room is lost (except under the Home Buyers' Plan and Lifelong Learning Plan).
Forgetting to invest the refund. Spending it reduces the plan's advantage.
Choosing an RRSP over a TFSA on a low income. If your tax rate will be higher in retirement, a TFSA may be better.
Frequently asked questions
What is the RRSP limit for 2026?
The dollar maximum for 2026 is $33,810. Your personal limit is 18% of your 2025 earned income, up to that maximum, minus any pension adjustment, plus unused room from earlier years. It is shown on your notice of assessment.
How much will my RRSP refund be?
About your marginal tax rate times your contribution, assuming the whole amount falls in one bracket. In Example 1, it is 29.65% of $10,000, or $2,965. If the contribution crosses a bracket, the calculator splits it across the rates.
What happens if I over-contribute?
You can be up to $2,000 over your limit without penalty. Beyond that, the excess is taxed at 1% per month until it's removed or absorbed by new room.
When is the RRSP deadline for the 2026 tax year?
Contributions made from 3 March 2026 (the day after the 2025-year deadline of 2 March 2026) to the 60th day of 2027 count for the 2026 return. Check the CRA’s published dates.
Should I use an RRSP or a TFSA?
It depends mostly on your tax rate now compared with later, and on whether you'll need the money before retirement. The comparison tab shows both outcomes for your numbers. See also the TFSA calculator.
Is the refund free money?
It's tax deferred, not tax avoided. You will pay tax when you withdraw. Investing the refund makes the RRSP's advantage much larger.

H1: Salary Calculator
This salary calculator converts pay between hourly, weekly, monthly and annual figures. Enter what you're paid and how often, plus your weekly hours, and it shows the equivalent gross pay for each period. It's useful for comparing a job offer quoted as a salary with one quoted by the hour, or for budgeting from a monthly figure.
How to use this calculator
1. Pay amount: the figure you're paid, before tax.
2. Pay is per: Hour, Week, Month or Year.
3. Hours per week: your contracted or usual weekly hours. This is used to convert to and from hourly pay.
Results: estimated annual salary, monthly (gross), weekly (gross) and hourly (gross).
The formulas
The tool first converts your pay to an annual figure, then divides it back out:
Hourly → Annual = Rate × Hours per week × 52
Weekly → Annual = Weekly pay × 52
Monthly → Annual = Monthly pay × 12
Monthly = Annual ÷ 12
Weekly  = Annual ÷ 52
Hourly  = Annual ÷ (52 × Hours per week)
It assumes 52 paid weeks a year, so paid holidays count as working weeks. That's the standard way employers quote salaries.
Worked examples
Example 1: $30 an hour, 40 hours a week
Annual = 30 × 40 × 52 = $62,400.00
Monthly: $5,200.00; weekly: $1,200.00
If you're paid every two weeks (26 pay periods): $2,400.00 per paycheck; twice a month (24 pay periods): $2,600.00 per paycheck.
Example 2: a $75,000 salary
Hourly at 40 hours a week: $36.06
Monthly: $6,250.00; bi-weekly: $2,884.62
Adjusting for unpaid time. If you take 10 days off unpaid plus 11 public holidays (8 hours each), you'd work 1,912 hours a year. That makes your effective rate $39.23 an hour. This matters when you compare a salaried job with contract work that pays only for hours worked; see the freelance rate calculator.
Example 3: overtime
At $25 an hour for 40 hours, plus 5 hours of overtime at time-and-a-half in 48 weeks of the year, gross annual pay is $61,000.00. Enter overtime separately because the tool's hourly conversion assumes a single rate.
Example 4: a UK salary of £35,000 at 37.5 hours
Hourly: 35,000 ÷ (52 × 37.5) = £17.95
Monthly: £2,916.67; weekly: £673.08
Example 5: $24 an hour in Canada at 37.5 hours
Annual: 24 × 37.5 × 52 = $46,800.00
Monthly: $3,900.00; bi-weekly: $1,800.00

Understanding your results
All figures are gross. Tax, social insurance and pension contributions come out before you're paid. For take-home pay, use the US paycheck calculator, the Canada take-home pay calculator or the UK take-home pay calculator.
Months aren't equal. "Monthly" is annual ÷ 12. Someone paid weekly gets 52 paychecks a year, so some months have five paydays.
Bi-weekly isn't twice monthly. 26 bi-weekly payments is more than 24 semi-monthly payments; each check is smaller.
Part-time hours: 25 hours a week at $22 an hour is $28,600.00 a year.
Country notes
United States: the Fair Labor Standards Act requires overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate for non-exempt employees after 40 hours in a workweek. The federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour, but many states and cities set higher rates.
Canada: overtime rules and minimum wages are set by provinces, with federal rules for federally regulated workplaces. The federal minimum wage is indexed each April [VERIFY current rate]. Ontario's standard overtime threshold is 44 hours a week.
United Kingdom: the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over is £12.71 an hour from April 2026, or £24,784.50 a year at 37.5 hours a week. A full-time week is often quoted as 37.5 hours: £32,000 a year is £16.41 an hour, or £615.38 a week. Full-time workers are entitled to 5.6 weeks of paid holiday (28 days, which can include bank holidays).
Tips and common mistakes
Using 40 hours when your contract says 37.5 (or the reverse).
Comparing gross salary to net pay. Compare like with like.
Forgetting benefits. Health insurance, pension matches and paid leave add to the value of a salaried offer.
Using 4 weeks a month. A month is about 4.33 weeks on average (52 ÷ 12).
Comparing job offers
When comparing offers, convert both to the same period and add the value of benefits: employer retirement contributions, health cover, paid leave and bonuses. A $70,000 salary with a 5% retirement match is worth about $3,500 a year more than the same salary without one. Also compare commuting costs and expected hours, because a higher salary with longer hours can mean a lower hourly rate.
Frequently asked questions
How do I convert hourly pay to a salary?
Multiply the hourly rate by weekly hours and by 52.
How much is $20 an hour per year?
At 40 hours a week, $41,600 a year before tax.
How many working hours are in a year?
2,080 at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks; fewer if you subtract unpaid time off.
Is the result before or after tax?
Before tax (gross).
Why does my monthly pay differ from the calculator?
Your employer may pay bi-weekly or weekly, or deduct taxes and benefits. The calculator shows gross annual ÷ 12.
How do I compare a contract rate with a salary?
Convert the salary to an hourly rate using the hours you'd actually work, then add the value of benefits and paid leave.

H1: Salary Sacrifice Calculator
Salary sacrifice (also called salary exchange) is an agreement to give up part of your salary in return for a non-cash benefit from your employer, most often a pension contribution. Because your taxable pay falls, you pay less Income Tax and National Insurance, and your employer saves employer NI too. This calculator shows the effect on your take-home pay and how much each pound into your pension really costs you in 2026/27.
How to use this calculator
1. Annual salary: before the sacrifice.
2. Amount to sacrifice: in pounds or as a percentage of salary.
3. Scottish taxpayer: Scottish Income Tax bands differ.
4. Student loan plan: sacrifice reduces the pay used for student loan repayments.
5. Employer NI passed on: the share of the employer's 15% NI saving it adds to your pension (0% if it keeps the saving).
Results: take-home pay before and after, Income Tax saved, employee NI saved, student loan reduction, employer NI saved, total pension contribution and the net cost to you.
How it works
New salary = Salary − Sacrifice
Net cost = Sacrifice − Income Tax saved − NI saved − Student loan saved
Savings are at your marginal rates for 2026/27 (England, Wales and Northern Ireland):

Worked examples
Example 1: £50,000 salary, 5% (£2,500) into a pension
Income Tax saved: 20% × 2,500 = £500.00
NI saved: 8% × 2,500 = £200.00
Net cost to you: £1,800.00 for £2,500 in your pension
Employer NI saved: £375.00. If the employer passes it all on, your pension gets £2,875.00.
Compare a relief-at-source personal pension: you pay £2,000.00 and HMRC adds basic-rate relief to make £2,500.00, but there's no NI saving. Salary sacrifice is £200 cheaper here.
With a Plan 2 student loan, your repayments also fall by £225.00, bringing the net cost down to £1,575.00.
Example 2: bringing a £60,000 salary down to the higher-rate threshold
Sacrifice £9,730.00 to reduce pay to £50,270:
Tax saved at 40%: £3,892.00; NI saved at 2%: £194.60
Net cost: £5,643.40, so each £1 into the pension costs 58p.
Example 3: £110,000 salary, sacrificing £10,000
Pay drops to £100,000, restoring £5,000 of Personal Allowance.
Income Tax saved: 40% × 10,000 + 40% × 5,000 = £6,000.00
NI saved: £200
Net cost: £3,800.00 for £10,000 in the pension

Income Tax saved: 20% × 900 = £180.00
NI saved: 8% × 900 = £72.00
Net cost to you: £648.00
Employer NI saved: 15% × 900 = £135.00; if passed on, the pension receives £1,035.00
That's £1,035 in the pension for £648 of take-home pay, a 60% uplift before any investment growth.

Scottish taxpayers
Scotland has more Income Tax bands, including a 21% intermediate rate, a 42% higher rate, a 45% advanced rate and a 48% top rate [VERIFY 2026/27 Scottish bands]. National Insurance is the same UK-wide, so a Scottish higher-rate taxpayer saves 42% + 2% = 44% on each pound sacrificed. Tick the Scottish taxpayer box to use these rates.
Other salary sacrifice benefits
Electric car schemes: low benefit-in-kind rates make EV leases through salary sacrifice popular. A £400-a-month lease sacrificed by a higher-rate taxpayer saves about £2,016.00 a year in tax and NI before the benefit-in-kind charge.
Cycle to work, childcare (for schemes that started before October 2018) and extra holiday can also be sacrificed.
Things to check
Minimum wage: the sacrifice can't reduce your cash pay below the National Minimum or Living Wage (£12.71 an hour from April 2026 for workers aged 21+).
Mortgages and credit: lenders see your lower salary, which may reduce how much you can borrow.
Statutory pay: maternity, paternity and sick pay can be based on the lower salary.
Life cover and pay-linked benefits: check whether they use the pre-sacrifice salary.
Annual allowance: total pension contributions over £60,000 a year (tapered for high incomes) can trigger a tax charge.
Future changes: the government announced a £2,000-a-year cap on NI-free salary sacrifice into pensions from April 2029 [VERIFY]. Income Tax relief isn't affected by that announcement.
Understanding your results
Take-home falls by less than the sacrifice, because tax and NI also fall.
Higher earners gain most from the tax relief; basic-rate taxpayers gain most from the NI saving relative to relief at source.
Child Benefit: sacrifice reduces adjusted net income, which can reduce or remove the High Income Child Benefit Charge.
Tips and common mistakes
Sacrificing below the minimum wage. Cash pay can't fall below the National Living Wage.
Forgetting the effect on mortgage applications. Lenders may use your lower salary.
Assuming the employer passes on its NI saving. Ask; many don't.
Ignoring the annual allowance if you're a high earner making large contributions.
Frequently asked questions
Is salary sacrifice worth it?
For pension contributions, it's usually the cheapest way to save because you save NI as well as Income Tax.
Does salary sacrifice affect my State Pension?
Not as long as your earnings stay above the Lower Earnings Limit, so you still get NI credits.
Can I change my salary sacrifice amount?
Usually at set times (often once a year) or after a life event, depending on your employer's scheme.
Does salary sacrifice reduce student loan repayments?
Yes, because repayments are based on your reduced pay.
Do Scottish taxpayers save more?
The relief depends on Scottish bands: 21% for intermediate, 42% for higher and 45% for advanced rates.
Will my employer pass on its NI saving?
Some do, some don't. Ask HR.

Sales Tax Calculator: Add or Remove Tax | FigSumo (49 chars)

Add sales tax to a price or work back from a tax-inclusive total. Enter your combined state and local rate for the exact amount. (128 chars)

H1: Sales Tax Calculator
In the United States, sales tax is added at the register on top of the shelf price, and the rate depends on where you buy: the state rate plus any county, city or special-district rates. This calculator adds sales tax to a pre-tax price and shows the tax and the total you'll pay.
How to use this calculator
1. Price before tax: the listed price of the item or the total of your purchase.
2. Sales tax rate (%): the combined rate for the place of sale. Your receipt, the state revenue department's rate lookup, or the retailer's checkout page will show it.
Results: sales tax and total price.
The formula
Sales tax = Price × Rate ÷ 100
Total = Price + Sales tax
To work backwards from a total that already includes tax:
Pre-tax price = Total ÷ (1 + Rate ÷ 100)
Tax included = Total − Pre-tax price
To find the rate from a receipt: Rate = Tax ÷ Pre-tax price × 100.
Worked examples
Example 1: $99.99 at 8.25%
Tax = 99.99 × 0.0825 = $8.25
Total = $108.24
Example 2: working back from a receipt total
You paid $54.12 including 7.25% tax.
Pre-tax price = 54.12 ÷ 1.0725 = $50.46
Tax included = $3.66
Example 3: combining state and local rates
A 6% state rate plus 2.25% local rates gives a combined rate of 8.25%. On a $1,250 purchase, that's $103.12 in tax and $1,353.12 in total.
Example 4: finding the rate
If a $40.00 purchase shows $3.30 tax, the rate is 8.25%.
Example 5: the same $1,500 laptop in different places
Oregon (no sales tax): $1,500.00
At California's 7.25% statewide base rate: $1,608.75
At a 10.25% combined rate found in some California cities: $1,653.75
The $153.75 spread is why the delivery address matters for online orders.

Understanding your results
Discounts come off before tax in most cases: a $100 item marked down to $80 at 8.25% costs $86.60 including $6.60 tax. Manufacturer coupons can be treated differently from store coupons in some states.
Rounding: retailers round the tax to the nearest cent, usually per transaction; occasional one-cent differences from the calculator are normal.
What's taxable varies. Many states exempt or reduce tax on groceries and prescription drugs; clothing is exempt in some states; services are taxed in some states and not others.
How US sales tax works
No national sales tax. Sales tax is set by states and local governments.
Five states have no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon. Alaska allows local sales taxes.
Highest state rate: California's statewide base rate is 7.25%, and local add-ons push combined rates higher in many areas. Combined state and local rates in some localities exceed 10% [VERIFY current highest combined rates].
Use tax: if you buy from an out-of-state seller that doesn't collect tax, you may owe use tax at your home state's rate. Since the 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair Supreme Court decision, states can require large online sellers to collect tax even without a physical presence.
Vehicles: many states tax a car on the price after the trade-in value is deducted. At 6%, tax on a $30,000 car is $1,800.00 on the full price or $1,320.00 after an $8,000 trade-in, depending on the state rule. See the auto loan calculator.
Federal deduction: if you itemize, you can deduct state and local general sales taxes instead of state income tax, within the SALT cap [VERIFY 2026 SALT cap and phase-out]. The IRS has a sales tax deduction calculator.
Canada and the UK
Canada and the UK use value-added style taxes. In Canada, GST (5%) or HST (combined federal–provincial) applies, with provincial sales tax charged separately in British Columbia, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Quebec; see the GST/HST calculator. In the UK, prices shown to consumers include VAT, normally 20%; see the VAT calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using only the state rate. Add local rates for the actual delivery or purchase address.
Applying tax to the wrong amount. Shipping and handling are taxable in some states and not others.
Dividing by the rate to reverse. To remove tax, divide by (1 + rate), not multiply by (1 − rate).
Assuming online purchases are tax-free. Most large retailers now collect tax.
Keeping records
If you itemize deductions, you can deduct either state income tax or state and local sales tax, not both. Residents of states with no income tax often choose sales tax. You can use the IRS optional sales tax tables or your actual receipts, plus the tax on big purchases such as a car. Keep receipts for large items, since the calculator's figures help you check what you paid. [VERIFY]
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate sales tax?
Multiply the price by the rate (as a decimal), then add it to the price.
How do I remove sales tax from a total?
Divide the total by 1 plus the rate. At 8%, divide by 1.08.
Which states have no sales tax?
Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire and Oregon have no statewide sales tax.
Is sales tax charged on shipping?
It depends on the state and whether shipping is separately stated.
Can I deduct sales tax on my federal return?
Yes, if you itemize and choose sales tax instead of state income tax, subject to the SALT limit.
Why is my rate different from my neighbour's?
Local rates vary by city, county and special district, so addresses near each other can have different combined rates.

Savings Calculator: Reach a Savings Goal Faster | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Plan a savings goal: see how long it takes at your deposit level or the monthly amount you need, with interest, annual deposit increases and tax on interest. (157 chars)

H1: Savings Calculator
Whether you are saving for an emergency fund, a deposit on a home or a car, it helps to know two things: how long the goal will take at the rate you can save, and how much you'd need to put away to reach it by a certain date. This calculator answers both, and includes interest, yearly increases to your deposits and tax on interest.
How to use this calculator
1. Choose a mode: How much will I have?, How long will it take? or How much do I need to save each month?
2. Starting balance: what you have saved already.
3. Regular deposit: an amount and frequency. You can add an annual increase, for example 3% a year as your pay rises.
4. Interest rate: your account's APY/AER. The calculator compounds monthly at the equivalent rate.
5. Goal and/or time frame, depending on the mode.
6. Tax on interest (optional): if your account is taxable, enter your marginal rate on interest. Leave it at 0% for tax-free accounts.
The formula
The balance after n months, with monthly deposits D, is:
B_n = B_0 × (1 + i)^n + D × ((1 + i)^n − 1) / i
B_0: starting balance
i: monthly rate. For a quoted APY/AER: i = (1 + APY)^(1/12) − 1. For a nominal rate compounded monthly: i = rate ÷ 12
n: number of months
Required deposit to reach goal G in n months:
D = (G − B_0 × (1 + i)^n) × i / ((1 + i)^n − 1)
Time to goal: the calculator steps month by month until the balance reaches G. This handles deposit increases and tax correctly.
If tax on interest is entered, each month's interest is multiplied by (1 − tax rate) before it is added.
Worked examples
Example 1: how long to save $25,000? Starting balance $5,000, $400 deposited each month, 4% nominal annual rate compounded monthly (i = 0.003333), no tax.
After 44 months the balance is $24,710.69. After 45 months it is $25,193.06, so the goal is reached in 3 years 9 months.
Your deposits: 5,000 + 45 × 400 = $23,000. Interest earned: $2,193.06.
Example 2: what deposit reaches $25,000 in 3 years? Same start and rate, n = 36.
5,000 × 1.003333^36 = $5,636.36 of the goal comes from the starting balance plus its interest
D = (25,000 − 5,636.36) × 0.003333 / (1.003333^36 − 1) = $507.15 a month
Total deposits: $18,257.40 + $5,000 = $23,257.40, so interest covers the remaining $1,742.60
Saving $107.15 more each month brings the goal forward by 9 months.
Example 3: building an emergency fund. Monthly essential spending of $3,500 suggests an emergency fund of three to six months, $10,500 to $21,000. Saving $500 a month from zero at a 4% APY reaches $10,500 in 21 months, with a balance of $10,850.98.
Example 4: the effect of tax on interest. $20,000 earning 4.5% in a taxable account, with interest taxed at 24%, earns $900.00 a year before tax and $684.00 after, an after-tax rate of 3.42%. In a tax-free account the full $900.00 stays.

Understanding your results
Final balance or time to goal: assumes the rate stays the same. Savings rates change, so recheck every few months.
Interest earned: shown before and after tax if you entered a tax rate.
Real value: with an inflation rate entered, the calculator shows what the goal is worth in today's money. A goal three years away may need to be larger than today's price.
Chart: deposits and interest are stacked, so you can see how much each contributes.
Country notes
United States: interest in a regular savings account is generally taxable as ordinary income. FDIC insurance covers at least $250,000 per depositor at each FDIC-insured bank (ownership categories apply).
Canada: interest outside registered accounts is fully taxable. A TFSA shelters it. CDIC covers eligible deposits up to $100,000 per insured category at each member institution.
UK: the Personal Savings Allowance lets basic-rate taxpayers earn £1,000 of interest tax-free (£500 for higher-rate). Cash ISAs are tax-free. FSCS protects eligible deposits up to £120,000 per person per authorised firm, from 1 December 2025.
Tips and common mistakes
Leaving savings in a low-rate account. Compare high-yield and easy-access rates regularly.
Confusing APY or AER with a nominal rate. Enter the rate type the calculator asks for.
Ignoring inflation. A balance that grows slower than prices loses buying power.
Saving for everything in one pot. Separate goals make progress easier to track.
Frequently asked questions
How much should I keep in an emergency fund?
There's no single right number. It depends on your income stability, dependants and fixed costs. Many people base it on several months of essential spending. Use the calculator to plan whatever target you choose.
Is APY the same as the interest rate?
Not quite. The APY (US) or AER (UK) includes the effect of compounding over a year. If your account quotes APY/AER, choose that option, and the calculator converts it to the correct monthly rate.
Should I include deposit increases?
If you expect to raise your savings as your income rises, yes. Even a small yearly increase noticeably shortens long goals.
What if my rate changes?
Run the calculator again with the new rate from the current balance. For fixed-term deposits (CDs, GICs, fixed-rate bonds), the rate is locked for the term.
Does tax really make a difference?
On larger balances, yes. At a 22% tax rate, 4% interest becomes about 3.12% after tax. Tax-free accounts avoid this.
Can I reach my goal faster by investing instead?
Investments may earn more over long periods but can lose value, so they are generally less suitable for short-term goals. That's a personal decision; this calculator assumes a savings account with a steady rate.

H1: Self-Employment Tax Calculator
If you work for yourself in the United States, you pay Social Security and Medicare tax through self-employment (SE) tax, covering both the employee and employer shares that would normally be split with an employer. This calculator estimates your 2026 SE tax from your net profit, including the Social Security wage base cap and the Additional Medicare Tax, and shows the half you can deduct.
How to use this calculator
1. Net self-employment profit: income minus business expenses, from Schedule C (or your share of partnership earnings from Schedule K-1).
2. W-2 wages (optional): if you also have a job, wages subject to Social Security tax reduce the room left under the wage base.
3. Filing status: for the Additional Medicare Tax threshold.
Results: net earnings from self-employment, Social Security portion, Medicare portion, total SE tax, deductible half and Additional Medicare Tax (if any).
The formula (2026)
Net earnings (NE) = Net profit × 92.35%
Social Security part = 12.4% × min(NE, 184,500 − W-2 wages)
Medicare part = 2.9% × NE
SE tax = Social Security part + Medicare part
Deduction = SE tax ÷ 2
92.35% (100% − 7.65%) mirrors the fact that employees don't pay FICA on the employer's share.
$184,500 is the 2026 Social Security wage base.
Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% applies to combined wages and SE income above $200,000 (single, head of household), $250,000 (married filing jointly) or $125,000 (married filing separately). It's reported on Form 8959 and isn't part of the deductible half.
No SE tax is due if net earnings are under $400.
Worked examples
Example 1: $80,000 net profit
NE = 80,000 × 0.9235 = $73,880.00
SE tax = 15.3% × $73,880.00 = $11,303.64 (14.13% of profit)
Deductible half: $5,651.82, which reduces your adjusted gross income for income tax
An employee earning $80,000 would see only $6,120.00 withheld for FICA; the employer pays the other half, and SE tax combines both.
Example 2: $250,000 net profit, single
NE = $230,875.00
Social Security: 12.4% × 184,500 = $22,878.00 (capped)
Medicare: 2.9% × $230,875.00 = $6,695.38
SE tax = $29,573.38
Additional Medicare Tax: 0.9% × (NE − 200,000) = $277.88
Example 3: a job plus a side business
W-2 wages $150,000 and SE profit $60,000:
NE = $55,410.00; room under the wage base = 184,500 − 150,000 = $34,500
Social Security: 12.4% × 34,500 = $4,278.00
Medicare: 2.9% × $55,410.00 = $1,606.89
SE tax = $5,884.89
Example 4: a $30,000 side business, no other job
NE = 30,000 × 0.9235 = $27,705.00
SE tax = 15.3% × $27,705.00 = $4,238.86
Deductible half: $2,119.43
Example 5: below the $400 threshold
Net profit of $420 gives net earnings of 420 × 0.9235 = $387.87, which is under $400, so no SE tax is due. You may still need to report the income for income tax.

Paying SE tax
Estimated taxes: you generally need to make quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) covering both income tax and SE tax if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. If your SE tax is $11,304 and your income tax is $8,000, quarterly payments of about $4,825.91 would cover the year.
Due dates: usually April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.
Safe harbor: paying 100% of last year's tax (110% if your AGI was over $150,000) in timely installments generally avoids an underpayment penalty.
Understanding your results
SE tax is in addition to income tax. Your total tax is SE tax plus federal (and state) income tax on profit after deductions. See the income tax calculator.
Retirement contributions (SEP IRA, solo 401(k)) reduce income tax but not SE tax.
The qualified business income deduction can reduce income tax on pass-through profit; it doesn't reduce SE tax.
S corporations: owners who take a salary pay FICA through payroll and receive remaining profit as distributions not subject to SE tax, but the salary must be reasonable.
Tips and common mistakes
Applying 15.3% to the whole profit. Use 92.35% of profit first.
Forgetting the wage base when you also have W-2 wages.
Skipping estimated payments, which can lead to penalties.
Not tracking expenses. Every legitimate deductible expense lowers both income tax and SE tax.
Notes for Canada and UK readers
Self-employed people in other countries face a similar "both halves" rule:
Canada: self-employed workers pay both the employee and employer CPP contributions, 11.9% on earnings between $3,500 and $74,600 in 2026, plus 8% CPP2 above that up to $85,000. See the CPP calculator.
UK: self-employed people pay Class 4 National Insurance on profits, at a main rate of 6% between £12,570 and £50,270 and 2% above [VERIFY 2026/27 rates]. Class 2 contributions are no longer compulsory but can be paid voluntarily to protect State Pension entitlement.
US citizens living abroad may still owe SE tax unless a totalization agreement assigns their coverage to the other country; the US has such agreements with both Canada and the UK.
Frequently asked questions
What is the self-employment tax rate for 2026?
15.3%: 12.4% Social Security (up to the $184,500 wage base) and 2.9% Medicare.
Do I pay SE tax on all my profit?
On 92.35% of it, with the Social Security part capped at the wage base.
Is SE tax deductible?
Half of it is deductible when figuring adjusted gross income.
When do I have to pay SE tax?
If net earnings are $400 or more. You'll typically pay through quarterly estimated taxes.
Does SE tax count toward Social Security benefits?
Yes. It earns credits and counts toward your benefit, like FICA on wages.
Do side gigs count?
Yes. Freelance and gig income is self-employment income.

H1: Simple Interest Calculator
Simple interest is charged or earned only on the original principal, never on interest already added. It's used for many short-term loans, some auto loans, accrued interest on bonds, and certain savings products. This calculator gives the interest and the final amount from the principal, the annual rate and the time in years.
How to use this calculator
1. Principal: the amount borrowed or deposited.
2. Annual rate (%): the yearly interest rate.
3. Time (years): the length of time. Use decimals for part years (6 months = 0.5).
Results: simple interest and final amount (principal plus interest).
The formula
I = P × r × t
A = P + I = P × (1 + r × t)
P: principal
r: annual rate as a decimal (4.5% = 0.045)
t: time in years
Rearranged:
Rate: r = I ÷ (P × t)
Time: t = I ÷ (P × r)
Principal: P = I ÷ (r × t)
For days, use t = days ÷ 365 (some lenders use 360).
Worked examples
Example 1: $10,000 at 4.5% for 2 years
I = 10,000 × 0.045 × 2 = $900.00
A = $10,900.00
Example 2: a 90-day loan
$5,000 at 6% for 90 days, on a 365-day basis:
I = 5,000 × 0.06 × 90 ÷ 365 = $73.97
Example 3: finding the rate or the time
You paid $600 interest on $8,000 over 18 months. Rate = 600 ÷ (8,000 × 1.5) = 5.00%.
How long for $12,000 at 5% to earn $1,500? t = 1,500 ÷ (12,000 × 0.05) = 2.5 years.
Example 4: £2,000 at 7% for 9 months
t = 9 ÷ 12 = 0.75 years
I = 2,000 × 0.07 × 0.75 = £105.00
Example 5: does the day count matter?
$50,000 at 8% for 120 days:
365-day basis: 50,000 × 0.08 × 120 ÷ 365 = $1,315.07
360-day basis: 50,000 × 0.08 × 120 ÷ 360 = $1,333.33
The 360-day convention, common in US commercial lending, adds $18.26 here. Check the loan agreement.

Converting to a compound annual rate
$10,000 growing to $10,900 over 2 years is 4.5% simple, but only (10,900 ÷ 10,000)^(1/2) − 1 = 4.40% a year compounded. Use the compound figure to compare it with a savings account's AER or APY.
Simple vs compound interest
With compound interest, interest earns interest. On $10,000 at 4.5%:

After 2 years compound interest earns $920.25 against $900.00; after 10 years it's $5,529.69 against $4,500.00. The gap grows with time and rate. For savings, compounding works in your favour; see the compound interest calculator.
Where simple interest is used
Auto loans and some personal loans use simple interest computed daily on the outstanding balance. At 6.9% on a $25,000 balance, interest accrues at about $4.73 a day, so paying early in the cycle saves a little and paying late costs a little. Because the balance falls with each payment, the interest charged also falls.
Bond accrued interest: when you buy a bond between coupon dates, you pay the seller the interest accrued since the last coupon. For $1,000 of a 5% bond 73 days after a coupon, accrued interest is about $10.00 (actual/365 basis; conventions vary).
Short-term business credit and promissory notes.
Some certificates of deposit that pay interest out rather than reinvesting it.
Understanding your results
The final amount is principal plus interest for the full period, assuming no payments in between.
For loans with regular payments, total interest is less than P × r × t because the principal falls over time. Use the loan calculator for amortized loans.
Rates are annual. A monthly rate of 1% is 12% a year in simple terms.
Country notes
United States: the Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the APR and total finance charge, so you can compare simple-interest loans with others.
Canada: the Interest Act requires that when a rate is stated for a period shorter than a year, the equivalent annual rate must also be disclosed.
United Kingdom: consumer credit agreements must show the APR under the Consumer Credit Act. Some UK savings accounts pay a "gross" (AER) rate that already reflects compounding.
Short-term loans: a warning
Fees on payday loans are often quoted per $100 for two weeks, which looks like simple interest but is very expensive. The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's example is a $15 fee per $100 borrowed for two weeks, an APR of almost 400% (15% × 26 two-week periods = 390% before any compounding). Canada caps the cost of payday loans by regulation and the UK caps them at 0.8% a day, but both are still far costlier than mainstream credit [VERIFY current Canadian cap].
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing months and years. Convert months to years first (18 months = 1.5).
Using a percentage as a whole number. 4.5% is 0.045.
Assuming simple interest on a credit card. Cards compound daily or monthly.
Ignoring the day-count basis (360 vs 365) on short-term loans.
Quick check
Confirm whether your agreement uses a 360-day or a 365-day year.
Frequently asked questions
What is the simple interest formula?
I = P × r × t.
Is simple interest better than compound interest?
For borrowers, yes, at the same rate. For savers, compound interest pays more.
How do I calculate simple interest for months?
Divide the months by 12 to get years: I = P × r × (months ÷ 12).
Do car loans use simple interest?
Most US auto loans charge simple interest on the daily balance.
How do I calculate interest for days?
I = P × r × days ÷ 365 (or 360, depending on the lender).

Title tag
Social Security Claiming Age Calculator | FigSumo (49 chars)
Meta description
Compare Social Security benefits by claiming age using your full-retirement-age estimate from SSA, and find the break-even age between options. (143 chars)
Country
US
Status
rename (301) · tax year 2026
Body words
1,024 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Social Security Calculator
Your Social Security retirement benefit depends on your lifetime earnings and the age you start claiming. This calculator estimates the monthly benefit from your average indexed monthly earnings (AIME), using the Social Security Administration's benefit formula, and adjusts it for claiming before or after your full retirement age (FRA).
How to use this calculator
1. Average indexed monthly earnings (AIME): your highest 35 years of earnings, adjusted for wage growth, divided by 420 months. Your SSA statement at ssa.gov/myaccount shows your earnings record; the SSA's own calculators compute AIME for you.
2. Claim age: the age you plan to start benefits, from 62 to 70.
3. Full retirement age: 67 if you were born in 1960 or later; between 66 and 67 for earlier birth years.
Results: estimated monthly benefit, primary insurance amount (PIA) at full retirement age, and a note.
The formula
Step 1: primary insurance amount. For people turning 62 in 2026, the PIA is:
PIA = 90% of AIME up to $1,286
    + 32% of AIME from $1,286 to $7,749
    + 15% of AIME above $7,749
The two thresholds are the bend points, set for the year you turn 62. They rise each year with average wages. The formula replaces a larger share of income for lower earners.
Step 2: adjust for claiming age.
Early: benefits fall by 5/9 of 1% for each of the first 36 months before FRA, and 5/12 of 1% for each month beyond 36. Claiming at 62 with an FRA of 67 cuts the benefit by 30%.
Delayed: delayed retirement credits add 2/3 of 1% for each month after FRA (8% a year), up to age 70.
Worked examples
Example 1: AIME $5,500, claiming at 67
90% × 1,286 = $1,157.40
32% × (5,500 − 1,286) = $1,348.48
PIA = $2,505.88 a month at full retirement age, about 46% of AIME.
Claiming at other ages:
At 62: $1,754.12 (30% less)
At 65: $2,171.76
At 70: $3,107.29 (24% more)
Example 2: AIME $9,000
$1,157.40 + $2,068.16 + 15% × (9,000 − 7,749) = $187.65
PIA = $3,413.21, about 38% of AIME. Higher earners get a smaller replacement rate.
When does waiting pay off?
Comparing claiming at 62 and 70 for Example 1 and ignoring cost-of-living adjustments and investment returns, the larger checks from 70 make up for the eight years of missed payments at about age 80.4. If you expect to live past that, delaying pays more over your lifetime; health, other income and a spouse's benefits matter too.

Example 3: a spousal benefit
A spouse with little work history can receive up to 50% of the worker's full-retirement-age benefit, claimed at the spouse's own full retirement age. With the worker's $2,000, that's up to $1,000 a month. Claiming the spousal benefit early reduces it, but unlike the worker's own benefit, it doesn't grow after full retirement age.
Understanding your results
Today's dollars, roughly. The estimate doesn't include future cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs), which raise benefits each year after you become eligible.
The PIA is rounded down to the next lower dime by SSA; the tool shows the unrounded figure.
Not everyone qualifies. You need 40 credits (about 10 years of covered work) for a retirement benefit.
Spousal and survivor benefits aren't included. A spouse can receive up to 50% of your PIA at their full retirement age.
Taxes and work
Social Security tax: employees pay 6.2% on wages up to the wage base ($184,500 in 2026), matched by the employer; the self-employed pay both halves.
Earnings test: if you claim before FRA and keep working, benefits are temporarily withheld when earnings exceed an annual limit [VERIFY 2026 limits]. Withheld benefits are credited back at FRA.
Income tax on benefits: up to 85% of benefits can be taxable depending on your combined income. The base thresholds ($25,000 single, $32,000 married filing jointly) aren't indexed.
Country notes
This calculator covers the US program. Canada pays the CPP (see the CPP calculator) and Old Age Security; the UK pays the State Pension, based on National Insurance years rather than earnings. The US has totalization agreements with both countries so periods of work can count toward eligibility.
Tips and common mistakes
Using current salary as AIME. AIME averages 35 years, including any zero years.
Assuming FRA is 65. It's 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later.
Forgetting the spouse. For married couples, the higher earner delaying increases the survivor benefit.
Claiming early while working without checking the earnings test.
Frequently asked questions
How is my Social Security benefit calculated?
SSA indexes your earnings, averages the top 35 years into an AIME, applies the bend-point formula to get the PIA, and adjusts for your claiming age.
What is my full retirement age?
67 if born in 1960 or later.
How much less do I get at 62?
30% less than your PIA if your FRA is 67.
How much more do I get by waiting until 70?
8% a year after FRA, so 24% more at 70 with an FRA of 67.
Do benefits go up with inflation?
Yes, through annual COLAs.
Where can I get my official estimate?
From your my Social Security account at ssa.gov.

H1: Stamp Duty Calculator (England & Northern Ireland)
Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) is paid when you buy a home in England or Northern Ireland. It works like income tax: the price is split into bands, and each band is charged at its own rate. This calculator applies the current residential rates, first-time buyer relief, the higher rates for additional properties and the surcharge for non-UK residents. It shows the tax on each band and the total.
How to use this calculator
1. Purchase price (the "chargeable consideration").
2. Buyer type:
Standard: moving home, or buying your only property.
First-time buyer: you and anyone you are buying with have never owned a home anywhere in the world, and you'll live in it as your main home.
Additional property: after the purchase you'll own more than one residential property worth £40,000 or more, and you are not replacing your main residence.
3. Non-UK resident: tick this if the 2% surcharge applies to you.
4. The result shows SDLT due, the band table and the effective rate.
The formula
SDLT = Σ rate_band × (portion of price inside the band)
Standard residential rates (England & NI):
Portion of price
Rate
up to £125,000
0%
£125,001 – £250,000
2%
£250,001 – £925,000
5%
£925,001 – £1.5 million
10%
above £1.5 million
12%
First-time buyers (price £500,000 or less): 0% up to £300,000, then 5% from £300,001 to £500,000. Above £500,000, the relief does not apply and standard rates are charged on the whole price.
Additional properties: add 5 percentage points to every band (5%, 7%, 10%, 15%, 17%).
Non-UK residents: add a further 2 percentage points to every band. This can be combined with the additional property surcharge.
Worked examples
Example 1: £350,000 home.
Standard buyer: 0% × 125,000 + 2% × 125,000 + 5% × 100,000 = £0 + £2,500 + £5,000 = £7,500 (effective rate 2.14%)
First-time buyer: 0% × 300,000 + 5% × 50,000 = £2,500, a saving of £5,000
Additional property: 5% × 125,000 + 7% × 125,000 + 10% × 100,000 = £6,250 + £8,750 + £10,000 = £25,000
Example 2: other prices, standard buyer.
£295,000: 2% × 125,000 + 5% × 45,000 = £2,500 + £2,250 = £4,750. This matches the worked example published on GOV.UK.
£1,000,000: £0 + £2,500 + 5% × 675,000 (£33,750) + 10% × 75,000 (£7,500) = £43,750, an effective rate of 4.38%
Example 3: the £500,000 first-time buyer cliff.
At £500,000: 5% × £200,000 = £10,000
At £510,000: relief is lost, so standard rates apply to the whole price: £15,500
A £10,000 higher price costs £5,500 more in SDLT

Understanding your results
SDLT due is payable to HMRC within 14 days of completion. Your solicitor or conveyancer usually files the return and pays on your behalf.
Band table: shows exactly which part of the price is taxed at each rate.
Effective rate: total SDLT ÷ price. It's useful for comparing properties at different prices.
Relief not modelled: multiple dwellings, shared ownership elections, and properties with mixed residential and non-residential use. These need professional advice.
Country notes
Scotland: Land and Buildings Transaction Tax (LBTT), administered by Revenue Scotland, with its own bands and an additional dwelling supplement.
Wales: Land Transaction Tax (LTT), administered by the Welsh Revenue Authority.
Canada: most provinces charge a land transfer tax instead; see the land transfer tax calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using old thresholds. The nil-rate band fell from £250,000 to £125,000, and first-time buyer relief from £425,000 to £300,000, on 1 April 2025. Older articles and calculators may still show the previous figures.
Assuming first-time buyer relief applies above £500,000. It doesn't, and standard rates then apply to the whole price.
Forgetting overseas property when deciding whether the additional property rates apply.
Missing the refund window for the higher rates after selling your old home.
Using SDLT for Scotland or Wales, which have their own taxes.
Quick check
Confirm the completion date, because the rates that apply depend on it.
Frequently asked questions
Who counts as a first-time buyer?
Everyone buying must never have owned a freehold or leasehold interest in a residential property, in the UK or abroad, and must intend to live in the property as their main residence. The price must be £500,000 or less.
Do I pay stamp duty on a property under £125,000?
Not as a standard buyer or first-time buyer. If the additional property rates apply, 5% is due from the first pound (as long as the property is £40,000 or more).
Can I get the 5% surcharge back?
If you buy a new main home before selling your previous one, you may be able to claim a refund of the higher rates once the previous main home is sold, within the time limits set by HMRC. Check the conditions on GOV.UK.
Who pays the 2% non-resident surcharge?
In general, buyers who were not present in the UK for at least 183 days during the 12 months before the purchase. There are specific rules for joint buyers and companies.
When must stamp duty be paid?
You must file an SDLT return and pay within 14 days of completion. Penalties and interest can apply if you are late.
Does stamp duty apply to the whole price or only part?
Only the part of the price within each band is charged at that band's rate. First-time buyers buying above £500,000 are the exception: they lose the relief and pay standard rates on the whole price.

H1: Student Loan Calculator
Student loans are usually repaid in fixed monthly installments over a set term, like other amortizing loans. This calculator shows the monthly payment, total of payments and total interest for a student loan, so you can see what a balance will cost and how the term changes it. It works for US federal and private loans on a standard (level-payment) plan, Canadian student loans and private education loans elsewhere.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan amount: your current balance, or the total you expect to borrow. Include any unpaid interest that has been or will be capitalized (added to the principal).
2. Interest rate: your loan's annual rate. If you have several loans with different rates, run each separately or use a weighted average rate.
3. Loan term (years) and (months): 10 years is the US federal standard repayment term; private loans are often 5 to 20 years.
Results: monthly payment, total of payments, total interest paid and an amortization chart.
The calculator assumes a fixed rate and equal payments. It doesn't model income-driven repayment, forgiveness or deferment.
The formula
Payment = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
P: loan balance
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: number of monthly payments
Worked examples
Example 1: $20,000 at 7.5% over 5 years
Payment = $400.76
Total paid $24,045.54, of which interest $4,045.54
Example 2: $30,000 at 6.39% on a 10-year plan
Payment = $338.97; total interest $10,676.07
Stretching to 20 years: payment $221.73, total interest $23,216.01
Paying $100 a month extra on the 10-year schedule clears the loan in 86 months (about 7.2 years), cutting interest to $7,395.92, a saving of $3,280.15. Enter the higher payment as a shorter term to see this, or use the debt payoff calculator.
Example 3: $45,000 at 5.5% over 15 years
Payment = $367.69
Total interest $21,183.76
On a 10-year term instead: $488.37 a month and $13,604.19 of interest
Example 4: a weighted average rate
Loans of $10,000 at 4.5% and $20,000 at 6.5% have a weighted average rate of (10,000 × 4.5 + 20,000 × 6.5) ÷ 30,000 = 5.83%, not the simple average of 5.5%. Enter $30,000 at 5.83% for a close estimate of the combined payment.
Interest before repayment
Unsubsidized loans accrue interest while you're in school. $30,000 at 6.39% accrues about $5.25 a day; over four and a half years of study and grace, that's roughly $8,626.50 of simple interest. If it's capitalized, your repayment balance starts higher. Paying the interest as it accrues avoids this.

Country notes
United States: federal Direct Loan rates are fixed for the life of each loan and reset every July 1 for new loans, based on the 10-year Treasury auction. For 2025–26 the undergraduate rate was 6.39% [VERIFY 2026–27 rates on studentaid.gov]. Federal loans also charge an origination fee deducted from each disbursement. Repayment plan rules changed under 2025 legislation (including a new Repayment Assistance Plan) [VERIFY]; this page doesn't model income-driven plans. Up to $2,500 of student loan interest a year may be deductible, subject to income limits.
Canada: Canada Student Loans have no interest on the federal portion since April 2023. Repayment starts six months after you finish school, and the Repayment Assistance Plan can reduce or pause payments based on income. Provincial portions may still charge interest, which varies by province [VERIFY].
United Kingdom: UK student loans work differently: repayments are a percentage of income above a threshold, not a fixed installment, and remaining balances are written off after a set period. Use the UK student loan repayment calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting capitalized interest in the balance.
Averaging rates without weighting by balance.
Assuming a longer term is cheaper because the payment is lower.
Refinancing federal loans without weighing lost protections.
Missing autopay discounts. Many servicers and lenders cut the rate by 0.25 percentage points for autopay.
Before you borrow or refinance
List each loan's balance, rate and servicer before using the calculator, because a single blended rate can hide one expensive loan. Pay the highest-rate loan first when you have spare money. Federal US loans come with income-driven plans and forgiveness options that private loans don't, so think hard before refinancing them privately. Set up autopay if your servicer offers a rate reduction for it, and check your loan statements once a year.
Frequently asked questions
How is my student loan payment calculated?
Using the amortization formula with your balance, rate and term.
What is the standard repayment term?
10 years for most US federal loans.
Should I pay extra on my student loans?
Extra payments reduce interest and shorten the loan. Make sure they're applied to principal, ideally on the highest-rate loan.
Does this calculator include income-driven repayment?
No. It models fixed payments only.
Is student loan interest tax deductible?
In the US, up to $2,500 a year, phased out at higher incomes. In Canada, interest on government student loans can qualify for a non-refundable tax credit.
What happens if I can't afford my payment?
Contact your servicer. Federal and Canadian government loans have options to reduce or pause payments.

TFSA Calculator: Contribution Room & Growth (2026)

Title tag
TFSA Calculator 2026: Contribution Room & Growth | FigSumo (58 chars)
Meta description
Work out your TFSA contribution room for 2026 from the year you turned 18, including withdrawals, and project tax-free growth of your savings. (142 chars)

H1: TFSA Calculator: Contribution Room & Growth (2026)
A Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) lets Canadian residents aged 18 and older save or invest without paying tax on interest, dividends or capital gains, and withdrawals are tax-free too. The most common mistake is over-contributing, because room is personal and depends on your age, your residency and your past withdrawals. This calculator works out your 2026 room using the CRA rules, then projects how your TFSA could grow.
How to use this calculator
1. The year you turned 18 (or the year you became a Canadian resident, if later). Room starts accumulating from that year, but not before 2009.
2. Total contributions you have made in past years, and total withdrawals made before 2026.
3. Contributions and withdrawals so far in 2026.
4. Growth inputs: current TFSA balance, yearly contribution, expected return and years.
For the most accurate figure, compare the result with your CRA account. It is updated after financial institutions report each year's transactions.
The formula
Room in 2026 = Σ annual dollar limits for each year you were 18+ and resident (from 2009)
             − all contributions before 2026
             + all withdrawals before 2026
             − contributions already made in 2026
Withdrawals made in 2026 are added back on 1 January 2027, not straight away.
Annual TFSA dollar limits (CRA):
Years
Limit each year
2009–2012
$5,000
2013–2014
$5,500
2015
$10,000
2016–2018
$5,500
2019–2022
$6,000
2023
$6,500
2024–2026
$7,000
The sum from 2009 to 2026 is $109,000. The limit is indexed to inflation and rounded to the nearest $500.
Growth (annual contributions at year-end): FV = B × (1 + r)^n + C × ((1 + r)^n − 1) / r
Worked examples
Example 1: someone who turned 18 in 2020 and has never contributed.
2020–2022: 3 × $6,000 = $18,000
2023: $6,500
2024–2026: 3 × $7,000 = $21,000
Room in 2026: $45,500
If this person contributes $10,000 in March 2026 and withdraws $4,000 in August 2026, their remaining 2026 room is $35,500. The $4,000 comes back as room on 1 January 2027, on top of the 2027 limit.
Example 2: long-term growth. $7,000 a year for 20 years at 5% a year, starting from $0:
FV = 7,000 × (1.05^20 − 1) / 0.05 = $231,461.68
Contributions: $140,000
Tax-free growth: $91,461.68
For someone who was 18 or older and resident in Canada in 2009 and has never contributed, the full $109,000 of room is available in 2026.
Example 3: total room since 2009. Someone who was 18 or older in 2009, resident in Canada throughout and has never contributed has cumulative room of $109,000 in 2026: $20,000 (2009–2012) + $11,000 (2013–2014) + $10,000 (2015) + $16,500 (2016–2018) + $24,000 (2019–2022) + $6,500 (2023) + $21,000 (2024–2026).
Example 4: withdrawals and re-contributing. If you withdraw $15,000 in 2026, that $15,000 is added back to your room on 1 January 2027, along with the 2027 annual limit. Re-contributing it in 2026 without unused room would be an overcontribution, taxed at 1% a month on the excess until it's removed. The CRA's My Account shows your room as of 1 January, but it doesn't include transactions made since, so keep your own record.
Understanding your results
Available room: the maximum you can contribute in 2026 without penalty. If you have several TFSAs, this room is shared across all of them.
Over-contribution warning: any amount above your room is taxed at 1% a month for as long as it stays in the account.
Projected balance: fully tax-free when withdrawn. Withdrawals are not included in your income.
Investment losses don't restore room, and gains don't use it up. Room depends only on contributions and withdrawals.
TFSA vs RRSP, side by side
Take $1,000 of pre-tax income, a 30% marginal tax rate today, and 6% a year for 25 years (growth factor 4.2919):
RRSP: contribute the full $1,000 (the deduction offsets the tax). It grows to $4,291.87. Withdrawn at 30%, you keep $3,004.31. Withdrawn at 20%, you keep $3,433.50.
TFSA: pay tax first, leaving $700. It grows to $3,004.31, tax-free.
With equal tax rates the result is identical. The RRSP wins only if your rate at withdrawal is lower, and only if you invest the full pre-tax amount, including the refund.
Country notes
Residency: you only accumulate the annual limit for years you are a resident aged 18 or older. Contributions made while you're a non-resident are taxed at 1% a month.
US citizens in Canada: US tax rules may not treat a TFSA as tax-free. Get cross-border tax advice before opening one.
Comparable accounts: the Roth IRA (US) and the ISA (UK).
Tips and common mistakes
Re-contributing withdrawals in the same year. Room is restored only on 1 January of the next year.
Holding only cash. Investments inside a TFSA can grow tax-free.
Relying on CRA room figures mid-year. They don't include recent transactions.
Holding US dividend stocks. US withholding tax isn't recoverable in a TFSA.
Frequently asked questions
What is the TFSA limit for 2026?
The annual dollar limit is $7,000. If you were 18 or older and resident in Canada in 2009 and have never contributed, your total room in 2026 is $109,000.
When do withdrawals get added back?
On 1 January of the following year. If you re-contribute in the same calendar year without enough unused room, it counts as an over-contribution.
What is the penalty for over-contributing?
A tax of 1% per month on the highest excess amount in each month it remains in the account.
Should I use a TFSA or an RRSP?
A TFSA is flexible, and withdrawals are not taxed. An RRSP gives a deduction now but is taxed on withdrawal. If your tax rate will be lower in retirement, the RRSP often comes out ahead; if not, the TFSA usually does. Compare with the RRSP calculator.
What can I hold in a TFSA?
Cash, GICs, bonds, mutual funds and securities listed on a designated stock exchange, along with certain other qualified investments. Non-qualified or prohibited investments are taxed.
Does growth in my TFSA reduce my contribution room?
No. Investment earnings and losses don't change your room. Only contributions and withdrawals do.

Time Value of Money Calculator

Title tag
Time Value of Money Calculator: PV, PMT, FV | FigSumo (53 chars)
Meta description
Solve for any one of number of periods, interest rate, present value, payment or future value, like a financial calculator. Shows the equation used. (148 chars)
Country
global

1,066 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Time Value of Money Calculator
The time value of money is the idea that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar later, because today's dollar can earn interest. Every loan, savings plan, annuity and investment calculation rests on one equation that links five values: number of periods, interest rate, present value, payment and future value. This page explains that equation and gives you a quick tool for two of its most common uses: the monthly payment on a loan and the future value of regular monthly savings, at the same annual rate.
How to use this calculator
1. Loan balance: the amount borrowed (present value of the loan).
2. Annual rate: the yearly interest rate, used for both the loan and the savings.
3. Years: the period for both the loan term and the savings plan.
4. Monthly savings: a regular amount you save each month.
Results:
Loan payment (monthly): the fixed payment that repays the loan balance over the years entered.
Savings future value: what the monthly savings grow to by the end, with monthly compounding and deposits at the end of each month.
Net monthly (save − payment): monthly savings minus the loan payment. A negative figure means the loan payment is larger than your savings amount.
A typical use: "If I borrow this sum instead of saving for it, what would the payment be, and what would the same money grow to if I saved it instead?"
The formula
The general time-value-of-money equation, with payments at the end of each period, is:
PV × (1 + i)^n + PMT × ((1 + i)^n − 1) / i + FV = 0
n: number of periods
i: interest rate per period (annual rate ÷ periods per year)
PV: present value (money now)
PMT: regular payment each period
FV: future value (money at the end)
Cash you receive is positive and cash you pay out is negative. Given any four values, the fifth can be found. Solving for n or the payment has a closed form; solving for the rate needs a numerical method.
This tool uses two special cases:
Loan payment:  PMT = PV × i / (1 − (1 + i)^−n)            (FV = 0)
Savings FV:    FV  = PMT × ((1 + i)^n − 1) / i             (PV = 0)
with i = annual rate ÷ 12 and n = years × 12.
Worked examples
Example 1: $15,000 at 7% over 4 years, and $250 a month saved
Loan payment = 15,000 × (0.07 ÷ 12) ÷ (1 − (1 + 0.07 ÷ 12)^−48) = $359.19
Savings future value = 250 × ((1 + 0.07 ÷ 12)^48 − 1) ÷ (0.07 ÷ 12) = $13,802.31
Net monthly = 250 − $359.19 = −$109.19
Over four years you'd pay $17,241.30 on the loan, while $12,000.00 of savings would grow to $13,802.31. Borrowing now costs the interest; saving first earns it, but you wait four years.
Example 2: the other TVM questions, by hand
Present value: to have $50,000 in 8 years at 5% compounded monthly, you need $33,543.87 today: PV = 50,000 ÷ (1 + 0.05 ÷ 12)^96. The present value calculator does this directly.
Payment to reach a goal: to build $50,000 in 8 years from nothing at 5%, save $424.66 a month: PMT = FV × i ÷ ((1 + i)^n − 1).
Lump sum plus payments: $10,000 now plus $200 a month for 10 years at 6% grows to $50,969.84. The future value calculator handles the lump-sum part.
Understanding your results
Loan payment includes principal and interest only.
Savings future value assumes the rate is earned every month and deposits are made at the end of each month. Deposits at the start of each month would add one extra month of interest to each deposit.
One rate for both. In real life, borrowing rates are usually higher than savings rates. To compare realistically, run the calculator twice with each rate and read the relevant output from each run.
Key ideas
Compounding: interest earns interest. The more often it compounds, the faster money grows at the same nominal rate.
Discounting: the reverse of compounding; it converts future money into today's value.
Opportunity cost: the return you give up by using money one way rather than another. The discount rate you choose should reflect it.
Inflation: a separate effect that reduces buying power. Use a real rate (return minus inflation) to express results in today's money; see the inflation calculator.
Country notes
The maths is the same everywhere. Conventions differ: US and UK loans usually compound monthly, while Canadian fixed-rate mortgages are, by law, quoted with interest calculated yearly or half-yearly, not in advance (Interest Act, s.6), so monthly mortgage payments use an equivalent monthly rate. The Canadian mortgage calculator applies that rule.
Tips and common mistakes
Mismatched periods. Use a monthly rate with monthly periods.
Sign errors on financial calculators. Money paid out and money received need opposite signs, or the calculator returns an error.
Begin vs end mode. Leases and rent are usually paid at the start of a period; loans and most savings at the end.
Nominal vs effective rate. A 6% rate compounded monthly is an effective 6.17% a year.
Frequently asked questions
What is the time value of money?
The principle that money available now is worth more than the same amount in the future, because it can earn interest or returns in the meantime.
What are the five TVM variables?
Number of periods (N), interest rate per period (I/Y), present value (PV), payment (PMT) and future value (FV).
Why does the calculator use one rate for the loan and the savings?
It is a simple side-by-side view. For different rates, run it twice.
Is this the same as a financial calculator?
It uses the same equation. A full solver that finds any of the five values is planned; until then, the examples above show the other formulas.
How do I find the interest rate from a payment?
There is no closed formula, so it needs trial and error or a numerical solver. Use the interest rate calculator.
What discount rate should I use?
For personal decisions, the return you could reasonably earn elsewhere at similar risk, or your borrowing rate if you would otherwise borrow.

UK Capital Gains Tax Calculator

UK Capital Gains Tax Calculator 2026/27 | FigSumo (49 chars)

Estimate UK Capital Gains Tax on shares or residential property using the annual exempt amount, your Income Tax band and the rates for the year. (144 chars)

UK
