H1: UK Capital Gains Tax Calculator
Capital Gains Tax (CGT) is charged on the profit when you sell or give away an asset that has risen in value, such as shares outside an ISA, a second home or buy-to-let property, or business assets. This calculator estimates CGT for the 2026/27 tax year (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027) after the annual exempt amount, splitting your gains between the 18% and 24% rates based on your income.
How to use this calculator
1. Taxable income: your income for the year minus your Personal Allowance and any other Income Tax reliefs. On a £45,000 salary with the standard £12,570 allowance, that's £32,430.00.
2. Total gains: the sum of gains on disposals in the tax year (sale proceeds minus purchase cost and allowable costs such as fees, Stamp Duty and improvements).
3. Allowable losses: losses in the same year, plus any unused losses brought forward.
4. Asset type: residential property, other assets, or gains qualifying for Business Asset Disposal Relief.
Results: annual exempt amount used, gain taxed at 18%, gain taxed at 24%, total CGT and the effective rate.
2026/27 rates and allowance
Item
2026/27
Annual exempt amount (individuals)
£3,000
Rate on gains within the basic rate band
18%
Rate on gains above the basic rate band
24%
Business Asset Disposal Relief
18%
Trustees and personal representatives
24%
Residential property and other assets now use the same rates. The basic rate band is £37,700.
How it works
1. Gains − losses − £3,000 annual exempt amount = taxable gains.
2. Add taxable gains to taxable income.
3. The part of the gains that falls within the £37,700 basic rate band is taxed at 18%; the rest at 24%.
You can set the exempt amount and losses against the gains charged at the higher rate first, which minimises the tax.
Worked examples
Example 1: £45,000 salary and a £20,000 gain on shares
Taxable income £32,430.00; remaining basic rate band = 37,700 − 32,430 = £5,270.00
Taxable gains = 20,000 − 3,000 = £17,000
18% on £5,270.00 = £948.60
24% on £11,730.00 = £2,815.20
CGT = £3,763.80
Example 2: higher-rate taxpayer with a £10,000 gain
Taxable income £60,000 uses the whole basic rate band.
CGT = 24% × (10,000 − 3,000) = £1,680.00
Example 3: selling a business
A sole trader sells their business with a £100,000 qualifying gain. With Business Asset Disposal Relief at 18% (lifetime limit £1 million of gains), CGT = £17,460.00 after the annual exempt amount.
Example 4: a home that was let for part of the time
You owned a flat for 10 years, lived in it for 6, then let it out, and made a £150,000 gain. Private Residence Relief covers the years you lived there plus the final 9 months: 6.75 ÷ 10 of the gain, or £101,250.00. The remaining £48,750.00 is chargeable (letting relief now applies only if you shared occupancy with the tenant).
Example 5: sharing a gain with a spouse
Shares with a £20,000 gain are moved to joint names before sale (transfers between spouses and civil partners are free of CGT). Each partner has a £10,000 gain, less their own £3,000 exempt amount, so £7,000 is taxable each.
If both are basic-rate taxpayers with enough band left: 18% × 7,000 × 2 = £2,520.00
If one higher-rate partner sold alone: 24% × (20,000 − 3,000) = £4,080.00
Example 6: losses brought forward
A £10,000 gain this year and £12,000 of losses carried forward from earlier years: carried-forward losses are used only to bring the gain down to the £3,000 exempt amount. So £7,000 of the losses is used, no tax is due, and £5,000 of losses carries forward to later years. Losses must be reported to HMRC within four years of the end of the tax year they arose in to be usable.
What's exempt
Your main home, if Private Residence Relief applies in full.
ISAs and pensions: no CGT on gains inside them. See the ISA calculator.
UK government gilts, Premium Bonds, private cars, and most personal possessions worth £6,000 or less.
Gifts to your spouse or civil partner (no gain, no loss) and to charity.
Reporting and paying
UK residential property: report and pay any CGT within 60 days of completion using HMRC's online service.
Other assets: report on your Self Assessment return by 31 January after the tax year, or use the real-time CGT service if you don't file a return.
Keep records of purchase costs, fees and improvements.
Understanding your results
Effective rate = CGT ÷ total gains. It's lower than 18% for small gains because of the exempt amount.
Scottish taxpayers still use the UK basic rate band for CGT, because CGT isn't devolved.
Pension contributions and Gift Aid extend your basic rate band, which can move gains from 24% to 18%.
Tips and common mistakes
Wasting the annual exempt amount. It can't be carried forward; spread disposals across tax years where you can.
Not claiming losses. Losses must be reported within four years to be used.
Forgetting allowable costs like Stamp Duty, legal fees and improvements.
Missing the 60-day deadline for property.
Bed and breakfasting: shares bought back within 30 days are matched to the sale, so you can't crystallise a loss that way.
Frequently asked questions
What is the CGT allowance for 2026/27?
£3,000 for individuals.
What are the CGT rates for 2026/27?
18% within the basic rate band, 24% above it.
Do I pay CGT on my home?
Usually not, if it has been your only or main residence throughout.
How long do I have to pay CGT on property?
60 days from completion for UK residential property.
Can my spouse and I both use the allowance?
Yes. Transferring assets between spouses is tax-free, so couples can use two allowances and both basic rate bands.
Do I pay CGT on shares in an ISA?
No.

H1: UK Dividend Tax Calculator
Dividends from UK and overseas companies are taxed at their own rates, after a small tax-free dividend allowance. This calculator estimates the tax on your dividends for 2026/27 (6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027), taking account of your other income, the Personal Allowance and the bands your dividends fall into. It's useful for company directors who pay themselves in dividends and for investors with shares outside an ISA.
How to use this calculator
1. Salary and other income: employment income, self-employed profit, pensions and rental profit (non-savings income).
2. Savings interest (optional): taxed before dividends.
3. Dividends: total dividends received in the tax year.
4. Scottish taxpayer: for how your other income is taxed. Dividends themselves use UK-wide rates.
Results: dividend allowance used, dividends taxed at each rate, total dividend tax and the effective rate on dividends.
2026/27 rates
Band (taxable income)
Dividend rate
Dividend allowance
£500 at 0%
Basic rate band (up to £37,700 above the Personal Allowance)
10.75%
Higher rate (£37,701 to £125,140)
35.75%
Additional rate (above £125,140)
39.35%
The Personal Allowance is £12,570, reduced by £1 for every £2 of adjusted net income over £100,000.
How it works
Income is taxed in a fixed order: non-savings income first, then savings, then dividends on top. So dividends fall into whichever band your other income has reached.
1. Use the Personal Allowance against other income first (any unused allowance covers dividends).
2. The first £500 of dividends is taxed at 0%, but it still uses up band space.
3. Remaining dividends are taxed at 10.75%, 35.75% or 39.35% according to the band they fall in.
Worked examples
Example 1: £40,000 salary and £10,000 of dividends
Taxable salary = 40,000 − 12,570 = £27,430.00, leaving £10,270.00 of basic rate band
Dividends: £500 at 0%, then £9,500 at 10.75% (all within the remaining band)
Dividend tax = £1,021.25
Example 2: company director taking £12,570 salary and £50,000 dividends
The salary uses the Personal Allowance.
Dividends: £500 at 0%, £37,200 at 10.75% = £3,999.00, and the remaining £12,300 above the basic rate band at 35.75% = £4,397.25
Dividend tax = £8,396.25, an effective rate of 16.79% on the dividends
Directors should also consider employer and employee National Insurance on salary and Corporation Tax on company profits, which this calculator doesn't model.
Example 3: higher-rate taxpayer with £5,000 of dividends
Salary £60,000 means all dividends are in the higher rate band.
Tax = 35.75% × (5,000 − 500) = £1,608.75
Example 4: £100,000 salary and £20,000 of dividends
Adjusted net income is £120,000, so the Personal Allowance falls by (120,000 − 100,000) ÷ 2 = £10,000, to £2,570
Salary uses the basic rate band and part of the higher rate band; all dividends fall in the higher rate band
Dividend tax = 35.75% × 19,500 = £6,971.25
The dividends also cost £10,000 of Personal Allowance, which adds £4,000 of income tax on the salary at 40%. In total, the £20,000 of dividends increases the tax bill by about £10,971.25, an effective rate of 54.9%. Pension contributions that reduce adjusted net income below £100,000 can restore the allowance.
Example 5: £18,000 salary and £30,000 of dividends
Taxable salary £5,430, leaving £32,270 of basic rate band
Dividends: £500 at 0%, then £29,500 at 10.75%
Dividend tax = £3,171.25
Example 6: £30,000 salary and £15,000 of dividends
Taxable salary £17,430, leaving £20,270 of basic rate band
Dividends: £500 at 0% and £14,500 at 10.75%, all inside the basic rate band
Dividend tax = £1,558.75

Shares in an ISA
Dividends from shares held in an ISA or pension are tax-free and don't use the dividend allowance. Moving investments into an ISA (up to £20,000 a year) can remove the tax entirely; see the ISA calculator.
Paying dividend tax
Up to £10,000 of dividends: if you don't file a Self Assessment return, ask HMRC to change your tax code, or tell them through your personal tax account.
Over £10,000: you must file a Self Assessment return.
Self Assessment tax is due by 31 January after the tax year, with payments on account for the next year if your bill is over £1,000 and less than 80% of your tax is collected at source.
Understanding your results
The allowance isn't a band extension. The £500 at 0% still counts toward the basic rate limit.
Income above £100,000 reduces the Personal Allowance, which increases tax on both salary and dividends; the effective marginal rate in that range is higher than the headline rate.
High Income Child Benefit Charge and other income tests use total income including dividends.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting dividends sit on top of other income.
Assuming the allowance covers £500 of tax. It covers £500 of dividends.
Overlooking a spouse's allowance and bands. Holding shares jointly or in the lower earner's name can reduce tax (subject to settlements rules for family companies).
Ignoring ISA wrappers for investments.
Notes for US and Canadian readers
The UK system differs from both North American approaches. In the US, qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on taxable income, with ordinary dividends taxed as regular income. In Canada, eligible dividends from Canadian corporations are "grossed up" and then reduced by a dividend tax credit, which can make low-income dividend tax very small or even negative. UK residents receiving US or Canadian dividends may suffer withholding tax abroad, which can usually be credited against UK tax up to the treaty rate [VERIFY treaty rates].
Frequently asked questions
What is the dividend allowance for 2026/27?
£500.
What are the dividend tax rates for 2026/27?
10.75% basic, 35.75% higher and 39.35% additional rate.
Do I pay tax on dividends in an ISA?
No.
Do I pay National Insurance on dividends?
No. Dividends aren't subject to NI.
How do I pay dividend tax?
Through a tax code change for smaller amounts, or Self Assessment if dividends exceed £10,000 or you already file.
Do Scottish rates apply to dividends?
No. Dividends use UK-wide rates, although Scottish rates apply to your other income.

UK Income Tax Calculator (2026/27)

Title tag
UK Income Tax Calculator 2026/27 incl. Scotland | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Calculate 2026/27 UK Income Tax on salary, savings and dividends, with Scottish bands, the Personal Allowance taper and the savings and dividend allowances. (156 chars)
Country
UK
Status
new · tax year 2026/27 (6 April 2026 – 5 April 2027)
Body words
1,015 (minimum 1,000)
H1: UK Income Tax Calculator (2026/27)
UK Income Tax is charged on three kinds of income in a fixed order: earnings and pensions first, then savings interest, then dividends. Each kind has its own allowances and, for dividends, its own rates. This calculator applies the 2026/27 HMRC figures in that order. It shows how much of each band you use, the tax on each slice, and your effective and marginal rates. Scottish taxpayers get the Scottish bands for earnings.
How to use this calculator
1. Employment, self-employment and pension income: your total for the tax year.
2. Savings interest from bank accounts and bonds held outside ISAs.
3. Dividends from shares held outside ISAs and pensions.
4. Scottish taxpayer? Tick this if you live in Scotland.
5. Gross pension contributions under relief at source, and Gift Aid donations (optional): these extend your basic-rate band.
The formula
Adjusted net income (ANI)  = total income − gross relief-at-source pension contributions − grossed-up Gift Aid
Personal Allowance          = £12,570 − max(0, (ANI − £100,000) ÷ 2)       (zero at £125,140)
Order of taxation           = non-savings income → savings → dividends
Basic-rate band             = £37,700 (+ gross pension contributions / Gift Aid)
Non-savings income (England, Wales, NI): 20% on the first £37,700 of taxable income, 40% up to £125,140, 45% above. Scotland uses six bands: 19%, 20%, 21%, 42%, 45% and 48%.
Savings:
Starting rate for savings: up to £5,000 at 0%, reduced £1 for £1 by non-savings income above the Personal Allowance
Personal Savings Allowance: £1,000 for basic-rate taxpayers, £500 for higher-rate, £0 for additional-rate
Above these, savings are taxed at 20%, 40% or 45%
Dividends: the first £500 is taxed at 0%. Above that, the rate is 10.75% in the basic band, 35.75% in the higher band and 39.35% in the additional band.
Worked examples
Example 1: £60,000 salary, England.
Taxable income: 60,000 − 12,570 = £47,430
20% × 37,700 = £7,540.00
40% × (47,430 − 37,700) = 40% × 9,730 = £3,892.00
Income Tax: £11,432.00. Effective rate 19.05%; marginal rate 40%.
Add £5,000 of dividends: the salary already uses the whole basic-rate band, so the dividends fall in the higher band. £500 is covered by the dividend allowance, and £4,500 × 35.75% = £1,608.75 of dividend tax. Total tax is £13,040.75.
Example 2: £110,000 salary, England.
Personal Allowance: 12,570 − (110,000 − 100,000) ÷ 2 = £7,570
Taxable income: £102,430
20% × 37,700 = £7,540 · 40% × 64,730 = £25,892
Income Tax: £33,432. The marginal rate between £100,000 and £125,140 is effectively 60%.
A gross pension contribution of £10,000 under relief at source would bring adjusted net income back to £100,000 and restore the full allowance.
Scottish comparison, £40,000 salary: Scottish tax is £5,551.07, compared with £5,486.00 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland. See the take-home pay calculator for the full breakdown.
Understanding your results
Band usage chart: how much of each band your income fills, coloured by income type. This explains why the same dividend can be taxed at 10.75% for one person and 35.75% for another.
Effective rate: total Income Tax ÷ total income.
Marginal rate: the tax on your next £1 of the type you select. It includes the Personal Allowance taper.
What isn't included: National Insurance (see the take-home pay calculator), Capital Gains Tax, the High Income Child Benefit Charge, the Marriage Allowance and the Blind Person's Allowance.
Country notes
Scotland: Scottish rates apply to earnings, pensions and rental profit. Savings and dividends use the UK rates and bands.
Wales: Welsh rates of Income Tax currently match England and Northern Ireland.
Tax year: UK tax years run from 6 April to 5 April. For calendar-year systems, see the US and Canadian calculators.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting the Personal Allowance taper. Between £100,000 and £125,140 the effective rate is 60%.
Using rest-of-UK bands for a Scottish taxpayer. Scotland sets its own bands on earnings.
Mixing gross and net pension contributions. Relief-at-source contributions extend your basic rate band.
Leaving out savings and dividend income. They're taxed after earnings, at their own rates.
Assuming the tax code is right. Check it in your HMRC personal tax account.
Frequently asked questions
What are the UK Income Tax bands for 2026/27?
Outside Scotland: Personal Allowance £12,570; basic rate 20% on the next £37,700; higher rate 40% up to £125,140; additional rate 45% above. Scotland has six rates, from 19% to 48%.
How does the £100,000 taper work?
The Personal Allowance falls by £1 for every £2 of adjusted net income above £100,000, so it is gone at £125,140. Pension contributions and Gift Aid reduce adjusted net income and can bring back some or all of the allowance.
How much savings interest can I earn tax-free?
Basic-rate taxpayers can earn £1,000, and higher-rate taxpayers £500, under the Personal Savings Allowance. Additional-rate taxpayers get no allowance. People with low earnings may also get up to £5,000 under the starting rate for savings. Interest inside an ISA is always tax-free.
How are dividends taxed?
After the £500 dividend allowance, dividends are taxed at 10.75%, 35.75% or 39.35%, depending on which band they fall in once your other income is counted.
Do I need to file a Self Assessment return?
Many employees don't, because PAYE collects the tax. You may need to file if you have untaxed income such as self-employment, rental, or savings or dividends above the allowances. HMRC's online checker gives a definitive answer.
Why is my effective rate so much lower than my band?
Because the Personal Allowance and the lower bands apply first. At £60,000, the effective rate is about 19% even though the top slice is taxed at 40%.

UK Mortgage Calculator: Repayment & Interest-Only | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description
Work out monthly UK mortgage repayments in pounds, compare repayment and interest-only, model overpayments and see what happens when your fixed rate ends. (154 chars)
Country
UK
Status
rename (301)
Body words
1,232 (minimum 1,000)
H1: UK Mortgage Calculator
This calculator estimates monthly repayments on a UK mortgage in pounds sterling. Enter the property price, your deposit, the rate and the term. You can compare a repayment mortgage with interest-only, see how much an overpayment saves, and check what happens to the payment when an introductory fixed rate ends.
How to use this calculator
1. Property price and deposit. The calculator shows your loan-to-value (LTV). Lenders price deals in LTV bands, so a bigger deposit often gets a cheaper rate.
2. Interest rate and fixed period. Enter the initial rate and how long it lasts, for example 2 or 5 years. Then enter the rate you expect afterwards, usually the lender's standard variable rate (SVR) or a new deal. If you are unsure, leave the follow-on rate equal to the initial rate.
3. Term. The total length of the mortgage, commonly 25 to 35 years.
4. Repayment type. Choose repayment (capital and interest), interest-only, or part-and-part.
5. Overpayments (optional). Add a monthly or one-off overpayment. Many fixed-rate deals charge an early repayment charge (ERC) above a yearly overpayment limit. Enter your lender's limit if you know it, and the calculator will warn you when you go over it.
The formula
For a repayment mortgage with interest charged monthly:
M = P × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
M: monthly repayment
P: amount borrowed (price − deposit)
r: monthly rate = annual rate ÷ 12
n: number of monthly payments (term in years × 12)
For interest-only:
M = P × annual rate ÷ 12
The balance does not fall, and the full amount is still owed at the end of the term.
When the fixed period ends, the calculator takes the remaining balance and recalculates M with the new rate over the remaining months.
Some lenders calculate interest daily rather than monthly. This changes the payment by pennies, not pounds.
Worked examples
Example 1: repayment vs interest-only. Price £312,500, deposit £62,500 (20%), loan £250,000 (LTV 80%), 4.5%, 25 years.
r = 0.045 / 12 = 0.00375; n = 300
Repayment: £1,389.58 a month, with total interest over 25 years of £166,874.36
Interest-only: £250,000 × 0.045 ÷ 12 = £937.50 a month. That is £452.08 less each month, but after 25 years you still owe £250,000 and need a plan to repay it.
Longer term: the same loan over 35 years costs £1,183.14 a month, but total interest rises to £246,919.57.
Example 2: when the fix ends. The loan is fixed at 4.5% for 2 years, then moves to a follow-on rate of 6.5% (an illustrative figure; use your lender's actual rate).
After 24 payments of £1,389.58, the balance is £238,669.02
Recalculated over the remaining 276 months at 6.5%: £1,668.45 a month, a rise of £278.87
Seeing this rise in advance is the main reason to plan a remortgage before a fixed rate expires.
Overpaying: an extra £100 a month from the start on the 25-year, 4.5% loan clears it in 266 months instead of 300 (2 years 10 months sooner) and saves £21,870.77 in interest.
Understanding your results
Monthly repayment is the mortgage payment only. Buildings insurance, any service charge or ground rent, and council tax are separate.
LTV shows which pricing band you fall into. Moving from 90% to 85%, or from 80% to 75%, can unlock cheaper rates. Check real deals.
Total interest assumes rates follow what you entered. In reality, you will probably move to several different deals over the term.
Remaining balance at the end of the fix is the figure a remortgage would need to cover, plus any fees.
Common UK mortgage types
Fixed rate: the rate is fixed for a set period, often 2, 3 or 5 years, then reverts to the lender's follow-on rate unless you remortgage.
Tracker: the rate moves with a reference rate, usually the Bank of England Bank Rate, plus a set margin. Payments rise and fall with it.
Discount: a discount off the lender's standard variable rate for a period. The lender can change the SVR, so the payment can change.
Standard variable rate (SVR): the lender's own variable rate, typically what you move to after a deal ends.
Offset: savings held with the lender reduce the balance that interest is charged on. To model one, enter the loan minus your savings.
For a tracker or variable deal, run the calculator at a few different rates to see the range of payments you might face.
Country notes
England and Northern Ireland: use the stamp duty calculator to add Stamp Duty Land Tax to your upfront costs. Scotland charges Land and Buildings Transaction Tax and Wales charges Land Transaction Tax, both with different bands. Separate calculators for these are planned.
Affordability: lenders assess income, outgoings and stress-tested rates rather than a fixed salary multiple. Treat any multiple as a rough guide only.
For US or Canadian loans, use the US mortgage calculator or the Canadian mortgage calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Ignoring product fees. A lower rate with a £999 fee can cost more than a higher fee-free rate on a small loan.
Forgetting the deal period ends. Diarise remortgaging before you move onto the lender's SVR.
Comparing interest-only and repayment payments as like for like. Interest-only leaves the full loan to repay.
Overlooking early repayment charges. They often apply during the fixed period.
Leaving out Stamp Duty and legal costs. Budget for them alongside the deposit.
Frequently asked questions
What is the difference between repayment and interest-only?
On a repayment mortgage, every payment covers that month's interest plus some of the capital, so the debt reaches zero at the end of the term. On interest-only, you pay just the interest and must repay the whole loan at the end, for example from savings, investments or a sale.
How is LTV calculated?
Loan ÷ property value × 100. A £250,000 loan on a £312,500 property is an LTV of 80%.
What happens when my fixed rate ends?
Unless you switch to a new deal, most lenders move you to their standard variable rate, which is often higher. The calculator recalculates the payment on your remaining balance at the follow-on rate you enter.
Can I overpay my mortgage?
Most lenders allow some overpayment. Fixed-rate deals often limit how much you can overpay each year before an early repayment charge applies. Check your mortgage offer for the exact limit.
Does a longer term save money?
It lowers the monthly payment but increases total interest. In Example 1, stretching from 25 to 35 years cuts the payment by £206.44 a month but adds £80,045.21 of interest.
Is the rate the same as the APRC?
No. The APRC (annual percentage rate of charge) includes fees and the follow-on rate across the whole term, so you can compare deals. Use the initial rate and the follow-on rate here.
Does this include stamp duty or fees?
No. Arrangement fees, valuation and legal costs are separate. Stamp duty has its own calculator.

Example 5: checking a monthly payslip
On a Plan 2 loan with £3,000 of pay in a month, the deduction is 9% × (3,000 − 2,448) = £49.68. Payroll works on each pay period separately, so a one-off bonus month can trigger a larger deduction even if your annual pay is below the threshold. If that happens and your total income for the year is under the threshold, you can ask the Student Loans Company for a refund.
Interest and write-off
Interest is added from the first payment, whether or not you're repaying. Current rates (from GOV.UK):
Plan 1, Plan 4 and Plan 5: 4.1%
Postgraduate: 6%
Plan 2: 4.1% if you earn £29,385 or less, rising on a sliding scale to 6% at £52,885 or more
Rates are linked to RPI and change each September, with caps applied when market rates are higher. Remaining balances are written off after a set period, for example 30 years after the April you were first due to repay for Plan 2 and 40 years for Plan 5 [VERIFY write-off terms for each plan].
Will you repay in full? Many Plan 2 borrowers won't. A £45,000 Plan 2 balance at 6% accrues about £2,700.00 of interest a year, while someone earning £60,000 repays £2,755.35. If your repayments won't clear the balance before write-off, overpaying voluntarily may not save you money. If they will, overpaying cuts total interest.
Understanding your results
It works like a tax. For a basic-rate taxpayer on Plan 2, each extra £1 above the threshold loses 20% income tax, 8% National Insurance and 9% student loan: 37% in total.
Self-employed or extra income: HMRC collects repayments through Self Assessment on your total income above the annual threshold.
Two jobs: each employer deducts only if that job's pay is over the threshold; Self Assessment may top up.
Refunds: if your annual income ends up below the threshold but deductions were taken in high-paid months, you can ask for a refund.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the wrong plan. Thresholds differ by thousands of pounds.
Counting the balance when budgeting. The monthly repayment depends only on income.
Overpaying without checking write-off. It's money you might never have needed to repay.
Forgetting salary sacrifice reduces repayments because it lowers your pay. See the salary sacrifice calculator.
Frequently asked questions
How much will I repay on Plan 2?
9% of income above £29,385 a year (£2,448 a month).
Does my balance change my monthly repayment?
No. Repayments depend on income only.
When are student loans written off?
After a period that depends on your plan, for example 30 years for Plan 2 and 40 years for Plan 5.
What happens if I move abroad?
You must tell the Student Loans Company; repayments are based on overseas income thresholds.
Should I overpay my student loan?
Only if you're likely to repay in full before write-off. Otherwise, overpaying may not reduce what you'll pay in total.
Is a postgraduate loan repaid separately?
Yes, at 6% above £21,000, alongside any undergraduate plan.

UK Take-Home Pay Calculator 2026/27: Tax, NI & Loans | FigSumo (62 chars)

Work out 2026/27 take-home pay after Income Tax, National Insurance, student loan and pension, including Scottish rates and the £100,000 allowance taper. (153 chars)

H1: UK Take-Home Pay Calculator (2026/27)
Most employees in the UK pay Income Tax and National Insurance through PAYE, and many also repay a student loan and pay into a workplace pension. This calculator applies the 2026/27 rates from HMRC to your salary. It handles the separate Scottish bands, the withdrawal of the Personal Allowance above £100,000, and the three ways pension contributions are commonly taken. It then shows your take-home pay per year, month and week.
How to use this calculator
1. Annual salary before deductions, including any regular bonus you want counted.
2. Where you pay tax: England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Scotland. This depends on where you live, not where you work.
3. Student loan plan(s): Plan 1, 2, 4 or 5, and/or Postgraduate Loan. If you don't know which plan you are on, check your account with the Student Loans Company.
4. Pension: your contribution as a percent, and how it is taken. Choose net pay (taken before tax), relief at source (taken after tax, with basic-rate relief added by the provider) or salary sacrifice (reduces salary before tax and NI).
5. Tax code (optional): leave as 1257L unless your payslip shows something else.
The formula
Personal Allowance (PA)  = £12,570 − max(0, (adjusted net income − £100,000) ÷ 2)
Taxable income            = salary − pension (net pay / sacrifice) − PA
Income Tax                = bands applied to taxable income
NI (employee, cat. A)     = 8% × (earnings between £12,570 and £50,270) + 2% × earnings above £50,270
Student loan              = 9% × (earnings above plan threshold); Postgraduate Loan 6% above £21,000
Take-home                 = salary − pension − Income Tax − NI − student loan

Worked examples
Example 1: £40,000, England, Plan 2, no pension.
Taxable income: 40,000 − 12,570 = £27,430 → Income Tax 20% = £5,486.00
NI: 8% × (40,000 − 12,570) = £2,194.40
Student loan: 9% × (40,000 − 29,385) = £955.35
Take-home: £31,364.25 a year, £2,613.69 a month
Same salary in Scotland: 19% × 3,967 + 20% × 12,989 + 21% × 10,474 = £753.73 + £2,597.80 + £2,199.54 = £5,551.07 tax, so take-home is £31,299.18, £65.07 less than in England.
With a 5% pension (£2,000) by net pay arrangement: taxable income falls to £25,430, so tax is £5,086.00. NI and the student loan are unchanged, because a net pay pension doesn't reduce earnings for those. Take-home is £29,764.25. The £2,000 contribution cost £1,600 of take-home pay.
Example 2: £110,000, England, no student loan or pension.
Income is £10,000 over £100,000, so the PA falls by £5,000 to £7,570
Taxable income £102,430: 20% × 37,700 + 40% × 64,730 = £7,540 + £25,892 = £33,432
NI: 8% × 37,700 + 2% × 59,730 = £3,016 + £1,194.60 = £4,210.60
Take-home: £72,357.40 a year, £6,029.78 a month
Between £100,000 and £125,140, each extra £1 costs 40p in tax plus 20p from losing 50p of allowance. With NI, that is an effective 62% marginal rate. Pension contributions in this range recover allowance as well as saving tax.
Understanding your results
Monthly take-home assumes the same pay every month and a cumulative tax code. One-off bonuses, emergency tax codes or a mid-year start can make individual payslips differ.
Effective marginal rate: shown for your next £1. For a basic-rate taxpayer on Plan 2 above the threshold, it is 20% + 8% + 9% = 37%.
Pension method matters: salary sacrifice also saves NI. Relief-at-source schemes give basic-rate relief automatically; higher-rate taxpayers claim the extra relief through Self Assessment or by contacting HMRC.
Employer costs: your employer separately pays 15% NI above £5,000 of your earnings. It does not affect your take-home pay.
Country notes
Scotland: Scottish taxpayers pay Scottish Income Tax rates on non-savings, non-dividend income. NI and student loan rules are UK-wide.
Wales: Welsh rates are currently the same as England's.
For North America, see the US paycheck calculator and the Canadian take-home pay calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the wrong tax code. An emergency code can overtax you; check with HMRC.
Forgetting student loan deductions. Select your plan.
Ignoring pension contributions. They change both tax and take-home pay.
Using rest-of-UK rates in Scotland. Tick the Scottish taxpayer option.
Frequently asked questions
What is the Personal Allowance for 2026/27?
£12,570. It falls by £1 for every £2 of adjusted net income over £100,000, and reaches zero at £125,140.
How much National Insurance do employees pay?
Category A employees pay 8% on earnings between £12,570 and £50,270 a year, and 2% above that. Different NI categories apply in some cases, for example people over State Pension age, who pay no employee NI.
When does student loan repayment start?
When your income goes over your plan's threshold. In 2026/27 that is £26,900 for Plan 1, £29,385 for Plan 2, £33,795 for Plan 4 and £25,000 for Plan 5. You repay 9% of income above the threshold. The Postgraduate Loan is 6% above £21,000.
Does salary sacrifice increase take-home pay compared with other pension methods?
For the same pension contribution, it usually leaves you more take-home pay because it also saves employee NI. It can affect other things linked to salary, such as some benefits or mortgage affordability, so check before switching.
Why does my payslip show a different tax?
Your tax code may not be 1257L. You might have taxable benefits, an underpayment being collected, or a bonus in that month. Your payslip and your personal tax account show your actual code.
Is the Scottish rate based on where I work?
No, it is based on where you live. If you live in Scotland and work in England, you pay Scottish rates. Your tax code starts with "S".
What about the High Income Child Benefit Charge?
If you or your partner claim Child Benefit and one of you has adjusted net income over £60,000, a charge applies. It claws back 1% of the Child Benefit for every £200 over £60,000, and all of it at £80,000. This calculator doesn't include it.

H1: UK Workplace Pension Calculator
If you work in the UK, are aged 22 to State Pension age and earn more than £10,000 a year, your employer must automatically enrol you in a workplace pension and pay into it. This calculator shows how much you, your employer and the government put in each year and projects what your pension pot could grow to by retirement.
How to use this calculator
1. Annual salary: before tax.
2. Contribution basis: many schemes use "qualifying earnings" (pay between £6,240 and £50,270); some use your full salary or basic pay.
3. Your contribution (%) and employer contribution (%).
4. Tax relief method: relief at source, net pay arrangement or salary sacrifice. Your payslip or scheme documents say which.
5. Current pension pot, years to retirement, expected growth and annual charges.
Results: annual contributions (you, employer, tax relief), cost to your take-home pay, and the projected pot in today's money and future pounds.
Auto-enrolment minimums (2026/27)
Item

Workers earning between £6,240 and £10,000 can ask to join and get the employer contribution; those below £6,240 can ask to join, but the employer doesn't have to contribute.
How it works
Qualifying earnings = min(Salary, 50,270) − 6,240
Employer = Employer % × Qualifying earnings
Employee (gross) = Employee % × Qualifying earnings
Tax relief:
Relief at source: you pay 80% of your contribution from take-home pay and the provider claims 20% basic-rate relief from HMRC. Higher-rate taxpayers claim the extra through Self Assessment.
Net pay arrangement: the contribution is taken before Income Tax, so you get relief at your marginal rate automatically. Very low earners below the Personal Allowance get no relief this way.
Salary sacrifice: you also save National Insurance; see the salary sacrifice calculator.
Projection: the pot grows each year by the expected return minus charges, with contributions added. Results in today's money are deflated by an assumed inflation rate.
Worked examples
Example 1: £30,000 salary at the minimum
Qualifying earnings = 30,000 − 6,240 = £23,760.00
Employer 3% = £712.80
Your 5% = £1,188.00 gross. Under relief at source you pay £950.40 and HMRC adds £237.60.
Total going in: £1,900.80 a year
Kept up for 30 years with 5% annual growth after charges (and no pay rises), that builds a pot of about £126,286.96 from contributions of £57,024.00. In today's money, assuming 2.5% inflation, that's roughly £60,206.39.
Example 2: 5% + 5% on full salary
If your employer instead pays 5% and you pay 5% of your full £30,000, contributions are £3,000.00 a year, and the 30-year projection rises to £199,316.54, £73,029.58 more than the minimum. Check how your scheme defines pensionable pay.
Earning above £50,270
Qualifying earnings stop at £50,270, so at the minimum a high earner's employer pays 3% of £44,030.00, or £1,320.90. Many employers pay more, and some match extra employee contributions; it's worth asking.
Example 3: £45,000 salary at the minimum, qualifying earnings basis
Qualifying earnings = 45,000 − 6,240 = £38,760.00
Your 5% = £1,938.00 gross; under relief at source you pay £1,550.40
Employer 3% = £1,162.80
Total going in: £3,100.80 a year
Example 4: what charges cost
£3,000 a year for 30 years growing at 5% builds about £199,316.54. With 0.75% a year in charges (growth of 4.25%), the pot is about £175,456.59, £23,859.95 less. Check your scheme's annual management charge; auto-enrolment default funds are capped at 0.75% a year.

Understanding your results
Projections aren't guarantees. Investment returns vary, and charges reduce growth. A difference of 0.5% a year in charges makes a large difference over decades.
Tax-free cash: usually 25% of the pot can be taken tax-free from age 55 (rising to 57 in 2028); on a £126,286.96 pot that's £31,571.74. The rest is taxed as income when withdrawn.
State Pension is separate and based on your National Insurance record.
Annual allowance: £60,000 a year across all pensions, tapered for very high incomes.
Opting out
You can opt out within a month of being enrolled and get your contributions back, but you lose the employer contribution and tax relief. Employers must re-enrol you about every three years.
Tips and common mistakes
Opting out to boost take-home pay. You give up free money from your employer.
Forgetting old pensions. Use the government's Pension Tracing Service to find lost pots.
Not claiming higher-rate relief on relief-at-source schemes.
Ignoring charges and fund choice. The default fund suits many people, but check it.
Frequently asked questions
How much do I have to pay into a workplace pension?
At the minimum, 8% of qualifying earnings in total, with at least 3% from your employer.
Who gets auto-enrolled?
Workers aged 22 to State Pension age earning over £10,000 a year.
What are qualifying earnings?
Earnings between £6,240 and £50,270 a year in 2026/27.
Can my employer pay less than 3%?
Not if it uses qualifying earnings for auto-enrolment.
When can I take money from my pension?
From age 55 (57 from 2028), with 25% usually tax-free.
What happens to my pension if I change jobs?
It stays invested. You can leave it or transfer it to a new scheme.

US Capital Gains Tax Calculator 2026 | FigSumo (46 chars)

Estimate federal tax on short- and long-term capital gains with 2026 0%, 15% and 20% thresholds and the 3.8% NIIT. (114 chars)

US

1,029 (minimum 1,000)
H1: US Capital Gains Tax Calculator
When you sell an investment, a second home or other capital asset for more than you paid, the profit is a capital gain and is subject to federal income tax. The rate depends on how long you held the asset and your taxable income. This calculator estimates federal tax on short-term and long-term gains for 2026, including the 3.8% net investment income tax for higher earners.
How to use this calculator
1. Filing status: single, married filing jointly, married filing separately or head of household.
2. Taxable ordinary income: your taxable income excluding the gains (wages, interest and so on, after the standard or itemized deduction).
3. Short-term gains: net gains on assets held one year or less.
4. Long-term gains: net gains on assets held more than one year (include qualified dividends here; they're taxed at the same rates).
5. Modified adjusted gross income (MAGI): for the net investment income tax test.
Results: tax on long-term gains by rate band, tax on short-term gains, net investment income tax, total federal tax on gains and the effective rate on the gains.
How it works
Gain = Sale price − Selling costs − Cost basis (purchase price plus commissions and improvements).
Short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income at your marginal rate (10% to 37%).
Long-term gains are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%. They're "stacked" on top of your ordinary income: ordinary income fills the brackets first, and the gains use what's left.
2026 long-term capital gains thresholds (taxable income):
Filing status
0% up to
15% up to
20% above
Single
$49,450
$545,500
$545,500
Married filing jointly
$98,900
$613,700
$613,700
Head of household
$66,200
$579,600
$579,600
Married filing separately
$49,450
$306,850
$306,850
Net investment income tax (NIIT): 3.8% on the lesser of net investment income or MAGI above $200,000 (single, head of household), $250,000 (married filing jointly) or $125,000 (married filing separately). These thresholds aren't indexed for inflation.
Worked examples
Example 1: single, $60,000 ordinary taxable income, $20,000 long-term gain
Ordinary income already exceeds the $49,450 0% threshold, so all the gain is in the 15% band.
Tax = 15% × 20,000 = $3,000.00
If the same gain were short-term, it would be taxed at the 22% ordinary rate: $4,400.00, $1,400.00 more. Holding for more than a year can matter.
Example 2: single, $35,000 ordinary taxable income, $30,000 long-term gain
0% band: 49,450 − 35,000 = $14,450.00 of gain taxed at 0%
15% band: the remaining $15,550.00
Tax = $2,332.50
Example 3: married filing jointly, $500,000 ordinary taxable income, $200,000 long-term gain
15% on $113,700.00 (up to $613,700) and 20% on $86,300.00: $34,315.00
NIIT: MAGI about $700,000, so 3.8% × the lesser of $200,000 or $450,000 = $7,600.00
Total federal tax on the gain: $41,915.00
Example 4: selling a day too early
Single filer, $60,000 of ordinary taxable income, $10,000 gain:
Held one year or less (short-term): taxed as ordinary income at 22% = $2,200.00
Held more than one year (long-term): 15% = $1,500.00
Waiting until the holding period passes one year saves $700.00 here, if the price holds up in the meantime.
Example 5: harvesting a loss
The same filer also has a $4,000 loss on another holding. Selling it nets against the gain, cutting the long-term taxable gain to $6,000 and the tax to $900.00. Net losses beyond gains can offset up to $3,000 of ordinary income a year, with the rest carried forward. Buying the same security back within 30 days triggers the wash-sale rule and disallows the loss.
Special cases
Selling your home: up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for married couples filing jointly) is excluded if you owned and lived in the home for at least two of the five years before the sale. A couple selling for $620,000 a home with a basis of $280,000 has a $340,000 gain, fully excluded.
Collectibles (art, coins, precious metals) are taxed at up to 28%, and depreciation recapture on real estate (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain) at up to 25%. This calculator doesn't model those rates.
Losses: capital losses offset gains, and up to $3,000 of net loss a year ($1,500 married filing separately) offsets ordinary income, with the rest carried forward.
Wash sales: a loss is disallowed if you buy substantially identical securities within 30 days before or after the sale.
Inherited assets generally get a stepped-up basis to their value at death.
Understanding your results
Federal only. Most states tax capital gains as ordinary income; see the state income tax calculator.
Effective rate on gains is total tax ÷ total gains, useful for comparing scenarios.
Timing: spreading sales over two tax years, or selling in a low-income year, can keep more of the gain in the 0% band.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting cost basis adjustments such as reinvested dividends and commissions, which overstates the gain.
Counting from the wrong date. Long-term means held more than one year, counted from the day after purchase.
Ignoring NIIT once income passes the thresholds.
Assuming 0% means no tax anywhere. States may still tax the gain.
Frequently asked questions
What is the long-term capital gains rate for 2026?
0%, 15% or 20% depending on taxable income and filing status.
How long do I need to hold for long-term treatment?
More than one year.
Are short-term gains taxed differently?
Yes, at ordinary income rates.
What is the net investment income tax?
An extra 3.8% on investment income for people with MAGI above $200,000 (single) or $250,000 (married filing jointly).
Do I pay capital gains tax on my house?
Not on the first $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for couples) if you meet the ownership and use tests.
Can capital losses reduce my taxes?
Yes. They offset gains, then up to $3,000 of other income each year.

1,175 (minimum 1,000)
H1: US Estate Tax Calculator
This calculator estimates the US federal estate tax due on an estate that is larger than the federal exemption (the basic exclusion amount). Enter the taxable estate and the exemption that applies. For deaths in 2026, the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person (IRS, IR-2025-103). Very few estates owe federal estate tax, but for those that do, the tax on the amount above the exemption is 40%.
How to use this calculator
1. Taxable estate value: the gross estate (everything the person owned or controlled at death, including real estate, investments, business interests, retirement accounts and certain life insurance) minus allowable deductions: debts, funeral and administration expenses, bequests to a surviving spouse (the marital deduction) and to charity. Add back lifetime taxable gifts made after 1976, because they use up exemption.
2. Federal exemption: the basic exclusion amount for the year of death ($15,000,000 for 2026), plus any unused exclusion inherited from a spouse who died earlier (DSUE, "portability") if it was elected on that spouse's estate tax return.
Results: taxable amount above exemption, estimated federal estate tax (40%) and a note that the figure is simplified.
The formula
Amount above exemption = max(0, Taxable estate − Exemption)
Estimated estate tax   = 40% × Amount above exemption
The actual Form 706 computation applies graduated rates from 18% to 40% to the whole tax base and then subtracts the unified credit, which equals the tax on the exclusion amount. Because the exclusion is far above $1 million (where the 40% bracket starts), the result is the same as taxing only the excess at 40%. The calculator uses that shortcut.
Worked examples
Example 1: $18,000,000 taxable estate, death in 2026
Amount above exemption = 18,000,000 − 15,000,000 = $3,000,000.00
Estimated estate tax = 40% × $3,000,000.00 = $1,200,000.00
Example 2: a married couple with $28,000,000, using portability
The first spouse leaves everything to the survivor; the unlimited marital deduction means no tax at the first death, and the executor elects portability of the unused $15,000,000.
At the survivor's death (assuming 2026 values), the exemption is 2 × 15,000,000 = $30,000,000.00
Amount above = $0, so estimated tax: $0.00
Without the portability election, the survivor's exemption would be $15,000,000 and the estimated tax would be $5,200,000.00
Portability has to be elected on a timely filed Form 706 for the first spouse, even if no tax is due. This is the most common expensive mistake in this area.
Understanding your results
Taxable amount above exemption is the part of the estate exposed to tax.
Estimated federal estate tax is the 40% shortcut. The real figure can differ if there are credits (for example for foreign death taxes or state death taxes as a deduction) or valuation discounts.
Who pays: the estate, before assets pass to heirs. Heirs don't pay federal estate tax personally, and inherited assets generally receive a "stepped-up" basis for capital gains.
Filing: an estate tax return (Form 706) is due within 9 months of death if the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the filing threshold, with a 6-month extension available.
The exemption over time
The exclusion is indexed for inflation. It was $13,610,000 in 2024 and $13,990,000 in 2025 [VERIFY 2025 figure in Rev. Proc. 2024-40]. The 2025 tax law (the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") set it at $15,000,000 for 2026, indexed afterwards, replacing the scheduled drop that would otherwise have roughly halved it. Always use the figure for the year of death. The IRS estate tax page lists the amounts.
Gift tax and the annual exclusion
Gifts and estates share one lifetime exemption. Gifts up to the annual exclusion per recipient don't use it ($19,000 per recipient for 2025 [VERIFY 2026 annual exclusion in Rev. Proc. 2025-32]). Larger gifts are reported on Form 709 and reduce the exemption left at death.
State estate and inheritance taxes
Some states levy their own estate tax, often with much lower exemptions than the federal one, and a few levy inheritance tax on the people who receive assets [VERIFY current list of states and their exemptions with each state's revenue department]. This calculator covers federal tax only.
Canada and the UK
Canada has no estate tax. Instead, a person is generally treated as having sold their capital property at fair market value at death (a "deemed disposition"), and the resulting capital gains are taxed on the final return, unless the property passes to a spouse or partner. Provinces also charge probate fees. See the Canadian capital gains tax calculator.
United Kingdom charges Inheritance Tax at 40% above the £325,000 nil-rate band, with an extra residence nil-rate band of up to £175,000 when a home passes to direct descendants, tapered for estates over £2 million. Both bands are frozen until April 2030 [VERIFY]. Transfers between spouses and civil partners are exempt, and unused bands can pass to the survivor. From April 2027, most unused pension funds are due to be brought into the estate for IHT [VERIFY].
Tips and common mistakes
Using the wrong year's exemption. Check the year of death.
Forgetting life insurance. Policies you own are in your gross estate unless held in a properly structured trust.
Missing the portability election. File Form 706 for the first spouse to preserve the unused exemption.
Ignoring state tax. A state threshold can be far lower than the federal one.
Mixing up estate and income tax. Inherited IRAs and 401(k)s can also trigger income tax for the beneficiary.
Frequently asked questions
What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?
$15,000,000 per person, according to IRS release IR-2025-103. Married couples can effectively shelter up to $30,000,000 with portability.
What is the estate tax rate?
Graduated rates run from 18% to 40%, but because of the size of the exemption, any taxable excess is taxed at 40%.
Do heirs pay estate tax?
Not federally. The estate pays before distributing assets. Some states have inheritance taxes paid by recipients.
Is life insurance included in the estate?
If the deceased owned the policy or had "incidents of ownership", the death benefit is usually included in the gross estate.
Does the estate tax apply to non-US citizens?
Different rules apply. Non-resident non-citizens get a much smaller exemption on US-situated assets; transfers to a non-citizen spouse do not get the unlimited marital deduction.
Can I reduce estate tax?
Common legal approaches include lifetime gifts, charitable bequests and trusts. These are complex; take advice from an estate planning attorney.

H1: US Federal Income Tax Calculator (2026)
US federal income tax is progressive. Your income is split into slices, and each slice is taxed at its own rate. Your top bracket only applies to the dollars inside it. This calculator applies the 2026 brackets and standard deductions published by the IRS. It shows the tax due on each slice, the total tax, and your marginal and effective rates.
How to use this calculator
1. Tax year: 2026 is the default. Choose 2025 if you are preparing last year's return.
2. Filing status: single, married filing jointly, married filing separately or head of household.
3. Income: wages, self-employment profit, interest and other ordinary income. Enter long-term capital gains and qualified dividends separately, because they use different rates.
4. Adjustments: pre-tax contributions such as traditional 401(k) or deductible IRA contributions, if they aren't already removed from your W-2 wages.
5. Deductions: the standard deduction is applied automatically. Switch to itemized if your total is higher. Tick 65+ or blind for the additional standard deduction.
6. Credits: number of qualifying children for the child tax credit.
The formula
Taxable income  T = gross income − adjustments − (standard or itemized deduction)
Tax on T        = Σ  rate_i × (portion of T within bracket i)
Tax after credits = Tax on T − credits (not below zero for non-refundable credits)
Effective rate  = tax after credits ÷ gross income
Marginal rate   = rate of the bracket containing the last dollar of T

Married filing separately uses the single thresholds up to $256,225, then 35% to $384,350 and 37% above that.
2026 standard deduction: $16,100 single or MFS · $32,200 MFJ · $24,150 HoH. The additional amount for age 65+ or blindness is $1,650 per qualifying condition, or $2,050 if you are unmarried.
Long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%. The 0% rate applies while total taxable income is up to $49,450 (single) or $98,900 (MFJ). The 15% rate applies up to $545,500 (single) or $613,700 (MFJ).
Worked examples
Example 1: single, $90,000 salary, standard deduction.
Taxable income: 90,000 − 16,100 = $73,900
10% × 12,400 = $1,240.00
12% × (50,400 − 12,400) = $4,560.00
22% × (73,900 − 50,400) = $5,170.00
Total tax: $10,970
Marginal rate: 22%. Effective rate: 10,970 ÷ 90,000 = 12.19%
Only $23,500 of the income is taxed at 22%, and the first $16,100 is not taxed at all.
Example 2: married filing jointly, $150,000, two qualifying children.
Taxable income: 150,000 − 32,200 = $117,800
10% × 24,800 = $2,480 · 12% × 76,000 = $9,120 · 22% × 17,000 = $3,740
Tax before credits: $15,340 (effective 10.23%)
Child tax credit: 2 × $2,200 = $4,400
Tax after credits: $10,940, an effective rate of 7.29%
Understanding your results
Total federal income tax: your estimated liability for the year. Compare it with the federal tax withheld on your paystubs to see whether you can expect a refund or a balance due.
Bracket table: how much of your income falls in each bracket and the tax on it.
Marginal rate: use it to estimate the effect of a raise or a deduction. A $1,000 deduction at a 22% marginal rate saves about $220.
Effective rate: total tax ÷ income, which is always lower than the marginal rate.
Not included: state income tax, self-employment tax, the alternative minimum tax, net investment income tax and most credits other than the child tax credit. These are listed beside the result so you know they are missing.
Country notes
Canada: federal and provincial tax are calculated separately, and most credits are non-refundable credits at the lowest rate. See the Canadian income tax calculator.
UK: tax is based on the 6 April–5 April tax year, and the Personal Allowance is withdrawn above £100,000. See the UK income tax calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Applying your top rate to all income. Brackets are marginal; only income above each threshold is taxed at the higher rate.
Confusing deductions with credits. A $1,000 credit cuts tax by $1,000; a $1,000 deduction cuts it by your marginal rate.
Forgetting state and payroll taxes. This calculator covers federal income tax only.
Itemizing when the standard deduction is larger. Compare both.
Using last year's brackets. Thresholds are adjusted for inflation each year.
Frequently asked questions
Does moving into a higher bracket reduce my take-home pay?
Not because of the brackets. Only the dollars above a threshold are taxed at the higher rate, so the brackets alone never make a raise cost you money. Some credits and benefits shrink as income rises, and a few have hard income cut-offs, so check those separately.
What's the difference between marginal and effective tax rate?
The marginal rate applies to your next dollar of taxable income. The effective rate is your total tax divided by your income. In Example 1 they are 22% and 12.19%.
Should I itemize or take the standard deduction?
Itemize only if your allowable itemized deductions (for example mortgage interest, state and local taxes up to the cap, and charitable gifts) add up to more than your standard deduction. The calculator compares the two.
When are the 2027 brackets published?
The IRS normally announces the next year's inflation adjustments in the autumn. This page will add 2027 values once they are officially published.
How much is the 2026 child tax credit?
Up to $2,200 per qualifying child, of which up to $1,700 can be refundable. Income limits and eligibility rules apply.
Are capital gains taxed at these rates?
Short-term gains (assets held one year or less) are taxed as ordinary income. Long-term gains and qualified dividends use the 0%, 15% and 20% rates. Their thresholds are listed above.

Estimate 2026 take-home pay per paycheck after federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare and pre-tax 401(k) deductions, for any pay frequency. (146 chars)

H1: US Paycheck Calculator (2026)
Your offer letter quotes gross pay. Your bank account receives net pay. This calculator estimates the gap for the 2026 tax year: federal income tax, Social Security, Medicare and pre-tax retirement contributions, spread across your pay schedule. State and local income tax are not yet included (see Country notes), so add them from your state's figures if your state has one.
How to use this calculator
1. Gross pay: your annual salary, or an hourly rate with hours per week.
2. Pay frequency: weekly (52), bi-weekly (26), semi-monthly (24) or monthly (12).
3. Filing status: single, married filing jointly or head of household. This sets the standard deduction and the tax brackets.
4. Pre-tax deductions: traditional 401(k)/403(b) as a percent or an amount, plus health premiums and HSA contributions paid through payroll.
5. Other adjustments (optional): extra withholding from line 4(c) of your W-4, or deductions you expect to claim.
The formula
Annual gross                      G
Pre-tax retirement (401k etc.)    D401
Section 125 deductions (health)   D125
Federal taxable income            T = G − D401 − D125 − standard deduction
Federal income tax                = progressive brackets applied to T
Social Security (6.2%)            = 0.062 × min(G − D125, $184,500)
Medicare (1.45%)                  = 0.0145 × (G − D125)
Additional Medicare (0.9%)        = 0.009 × wages above $200,000 (withholding rule)
Net pay per period                = (G − D401 − D125 − taxes) ÷ periods per year
Traditional 401(k) contributions lower federal income tax but not Social Security and Medicare. Most Section 125 health premiums lower both.

Standard deduction: $16,100 single · $32,200 married filing jointly · $24,150 head of household. The 2026 Social Security wage base is $184,500.
Worked examples
Example 1: $75,000 salary, single, 5% to a 401(k), paid bi-weekly.
401(k): 5% × 75,000 = $3,750
Taxable income: 75,000 − 3,750 − 16,100 = $55,150
Federal income tax: 10% × 12,400 + 12% × 38,000 + 22% × 4,750 = 1,240 + 4,560 + 1,045 = $6,845
Social Security: 6.2% × 75,000 = $4,650; Medicare: 1.45% × 75,000 = $1,087.50; FICA total $5,737.50
Annual net: 75,000 − 3,750 − 6,845 − 5,737.50 = $58,667.50
Per paycheck (26): gross $2,884.62 − federal tax $263.27 − FICA $220.67 − 401(k) $144.23 ≈ $2,256.44. Per-period rounding can shift this by a cent.
Example 2: $210,000 salary, single, no pre-tax deductions.
Taxable income: 210,000 − 16,100 = $193,900 → federal tax $39,134 (top bracket reached: 24%)
Social Security stops at the wage base: 6.2% × 184,500 = $11,439
Medicare: 1.45% × 210,000 = $3,045
Additional Medicare: 0.9% × (210,000 − 200,000) = $90
Annual net $156,292; bi-weekly about $6,011.23
Once your wages for the year pass $184,500, the 6.2% Social Security deduction stops. This usually happens late in the year, so your last paychecks are larger.
Understanding your results
Net pay per period: an annualised estimate divided evenly. Your employer withholds using IRS Publication 15-T and your W-4, so individual paychecks can differ by a few dollars. Paychecks also change once you pass the Social Security wage base.
Marginal rate: the federal rate on your next dollar. In Example 1 it is 22% plus 7.65% FICA.
Withholding is not the final tax. Your final 2026 tax is settled on your return, filed in 2027. That return can include credits (such as the child tax credit) and deductions (such as the new temporary deductions for qualified tips and overtime) that payroll may not reflect.
Country notes
State and local tax: most states tax wages. A few do not, including Texas and Florida. State calculations are on our roadmap; each state's rules will be checked against that state's revenue department before launch.
Canada and UK: see the Canadian take-home pay calculator (CPP, EI, federal and provincial tax) and the UK take-home pay calculator (PAYE, National Insurance, student loans).
Tips and common mistakes
Comparing gross offers without benefits. Health premiums and 401(k) matches change take-home pay and total value.
Forgetting state and local taxes. They vary widely by location.
Ignoring pre-tax deductions. 401(k), HSA and Section 125 deductions lower taxable pay.
Not updating your W-4 after a life change.
Frequently asked questions
Why is my paycheck different from this estimate?
Employers use Publication 15-T withholding tables and your W-4 settings, including dependents, other income and extra withholding. Your paycheck may also include deductions this page doesn't know about, such as state tax, insurance or union dues.
Do 401(k) contributions reduce Social Security tax?
No. Traditional 401(k) deferrals reduce federal income tax withholding, but they are still subject to Social Security and Medicare. Roth 401(k) deferrals reduce neither.
What is the 2026 standard deduction?
$16,100 for single filers and married filing separately, $32,200 for married filing jointly, and $24,150 for heads of household. Additional amounts apply if you are 65 or older or blind.
When does the Additional Medicare Tax apply?
Employers must withhold an extra 0.9% on wages above $200,000 in a calendar year, regardless of filing status. The tax you actually owe is based on combined wages and filing status ($250,000 for married filing jointly) and is reconciled on your return.
Are tips and overtime tax-free in 2026?
Not entirely. Federal law created temporary deductions for 2025–2028: up to $25,000 for qualified tips, and up to $12,500 ($25,000 joint) for the overtime premium, with income limits. They are claimed on your return, and these amounts still have Social Security and Medicare taken out.
Does this include state income tax?
Not yet. It's planned for each state, with values checked against each state's revenue agency.
How do I convert an hourly wage?
Hourly rate × hours per week × 52 gives an annual figure. At $25/hour and 40 hours, that's $52,000 a year.

H1: US State Income Tax Calculator
On top of federal income tax, most US states tax income too, and the rules differ a lot: some have no income tax, some charge one flat rate, and others use graduated brackets with their own deductions and credits. This calculator estimates your state income tax for 2026 from your state, filing status and income, and shows your effective state tax rate.
How to use this calculator
1. State of residence. If you lived in more than one state during the year or work in a different state, see the notes below.
2. Filing status: most states follow your federal status.
3. Income: wages and other income. Many states start from federal adjusted gross income (AGI).
4. State deductions and exemptions: the calculator applies the state's standard deduction or personal exemption where it has one; you can override it.
5. Custom rate mode: enter a flat rate or your own brackets if you want to model a state from its tax form.
Results: state taxable income, state income tax, effective rate (tax ÷ income) and marginal rate.
How state income taxes work
States with no tax on wages: Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington and Wyoming. (Washington taxes some long-term capital gains; New Hampshire's tax on interest and dividends has been repealed [VERIFY].)
Flat-tax states apply one rate to taxable income. A growing number of states have moved to flat rates in recent years.
Graduated-tax states use brackets like the federal system, with each slice of income taxed at its own rate.
State taxable income = Income (often federal AGI) ± State adjustments − Deductions/exemptions
State tax = Σ (income in each bracket × bracket rate) − State credits
Worked examples
All rates below are for illustration; the calculator loads each state's verified 2026 values.
Example 1: a flat-rate state
$80,000 of income, a flat 4.95% rate and a $2,850 personal exemption (Illinois-style [VERIFY 2026 figures]):
Tax = (80,000 − 2,850) × 4.95% = $3,818.93
A flat 3.07% rate with no standard deduction (Pennsylvania-style [VERIFY]):
Tax = 80,000 × 3.07% = $2,456.00
Example 2: graduated brackets
A hypothetical state taxes 2% on the first $10,000, 4% to $40,000 and 6% above, with $70,000 of taxable income:
2% × 10,000 = $200.00
4% × 30,000 = $1,200.00
6% × 30,000 = $1,800.00
Tax = $3,200.00; effective rate 4.57%, marginal rate 6%
Example 3: $100,000 under three state models
Model

$0.00

$3,070.00
Flat 4.95%, $2,850 exemption

The gap between a no-tax state and a graduated one can be several thousand dollars a year, but sales and property taxes narrow it.
Example 4: credit for tax paid to another state
You live in State A (flat 5%) and work in State B, which taxes your $90,000 salary as a nonresident at 4%:
State B tax: 90,000 × 4% = $3,600.00
State A tax before credit: 90,000 × 5% = $4,500.00
Credit for tax paid to B: $3,600.00, so you owe A $900.00
Total state tax: $4,500.00, the higher of the two states' amounts, not both added together
Rules vary, and some neighbouring states have reciprocity agreements so only the home state taxes wages [VERIFY your states].
Multi-state situations
Moving during the year: you usually file part-year resident returns in both states, each taxing income earned while you lived there.
Living in one state and working in another: the work state may tax your wages as a nonresident, and your home state usually gives a credit for tax paid to the other state. Some neighbouring states have reciprocity agreements so you pay only your home state.
Remote work: a few states tax remote workers based on the employer's location ("convenience of the employer" rules) [VERIFY current states].
Understanding your results
Local income taxes are extra in some places, such as New York City, many Ohio and Pennsylvania municipalities, and Maryland counties. They aren't included yet.
Federal deduction: state income tax counts toward the federal SALT deduction if you itemize, subject to the cap [VERIFY 2026 cap]. At a 24% federal rate, deducting $3,200.00 could save up to $768.00 of federal tax.
Capital gains: most states tax them as ordinary income.
Retirement income: many states exempt Social Security and some exempt pension income.
Tips and common mistakes
Assuming no state tax means no tax. States without income tax often rely more on sales and property taxes.
Using federal taxable income when your state starts from AGI, or the other way round.
Forgetting the credit for taxes paid to another state.
Ignoring local taxes on your paycheck.
Notes for Canadian and UK readers
Canada has a similar two-level system: every province and territory charges its own income tax on top of federal tax, and residence on 31 December decides which province taxes the whole year's income. In the UK, income tax is national except in Scotland, which sets its own bands and rates on earnings; Wales has the power to vary rates but has so far matched England. See the UK income tax calculator.
Frequently asked questions
Which states have no income tax?
Alaska, Florida, Nevada, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas and Wyoming have no broad income tax, and New Hampshire and Washington don't tax wages.
What is a flat tax state?
A state that taxes all taxable income at a single rate.
Do I pay state tax where I live or where I work?
Generally your home state taxes all your income, and a work state may tax wages earned there, with a credit to avoid double taxation.
Is state income tax deductible on my federal return?
Yes, if you itemize, within the SALT cap.
Do states tax Social Security benefits?
Most don't; a handful do, often with exemptions [VERIFY current list].
How accurate is the estimate?
It uses each state's published 2026 brackets and standard deductions; state credits and special adjustments may change your final figure.

H1: VA Loan Calculator
VA home loans are mortgages guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans, active-duty service members, National Guard and Reserve members, and some surviving spouses. They usually need no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, but most borrowers pay a one-time VA funding fee. This calculator estimates the funding fee, the total loan amount when the fee is financed, and the monthly principal and interest payment.
How to use this calculator
1. Home price: the purchase price.
2. Down payment ($): optional; VA loans allow 0%. A down payment of 5% or 10% of the loan lowers the funding fee.
3. Interest rate: the annual rate from your lender.
4. Term (years): usually 30 or 15.
5. VA funding fee (%): use the rate from the table below that applies to you, or 0% if you're exempt.
Results: base loan, funding fee, total loan amount (base loan plus the financed fee) and monthly payment (principal and interest).
The formula
Base loan = Home price − Down payment
Funding fee = Base loan × Fee %
Total loan = Base loan + Funding fee
Monthly payment = L × r / (1 − (1 + r)^−n)
L: total loan amount
r: annual rate ÷ 12
n: years × 12
The calculator assumes the fee is financed. You can also pay it in cash at closing.

Other loan types: cash-out refinance 2.15% first use and 3.3% after; interest rate reduction refinance (IRRRL) 0.5%; loan assumption 0.5%; Native American Direct Loan 1.25% for purchase. These rates have been in effect since 7 April 2023. The fee applies to the loan amount, not the home price.
You don't pay the fee if you receive (or are eligible for but receive retirement or active-duty pay instead of) VA compensation for a service-connected disability, receive Dependency and Indemnity Compensation as a surviving spouse, have a pre-discharge rating before closing, or are an active-duty member who has received a Purple Heart.
Worked examples
Example 1: $350,000 home, no down payment, first use
Funding fee = 350,000 × 2.15% = $7,525.00
Total loan = $357,525.00
Monthly payment at 6.25% over 30 years = $2,201.34
Financing the fee adds $46.33 a month compared with $2,155.01 on $350,000. Over 30 years, total interest is $434,958.45.
Example 2: $400,000 home with 10% down
Base loan $360,000.00; fee at 1.25% = $4,500.00
Total loan $364,500.00; payment at 6% = $2,185.36
For comparison, a subsequent-use borrower with nothing down on $400,000 would pay a 3.3% fee: $13,200.00.
Example 3: second use, no down payment
The same $350,000 home with no down payment on a subsequent use:
Funding fee = 350,000 × 3.3% = $11,550.00
Total loan = $361,550.00
Monthly payment at 6.25% over 30 years = $2,226.13, $24.79 more than first use
Putting 5% down instead cuts the fee to 1.5% of the smaller loan: $4,987.50 on $332,500.
Example 4: an exempt veteran
Veterans receiving VA compensation for a service-connected disability, and some surviving spouses, don't pay the funding fee. For Example 1, that removes the $7,525 fee, and the payment at 6.25% falls to $2,155.01. Your Certificate of Eligibility shows whether you're exempt.
Understanding your results
Monthly payment is principal and interest only. Add property tax, homeowners insurance and any HOA dues for the full housing cost. VA lenders count these when checking affordability.
No PMI. A conventional loan with under 20% down usually needs private mortgage insurance; an FHA loan has mortgage insurance premiums. See the PMI calculator and the FHA loan calculator.
Residual income test. VA underwriting checks the money left over each month after major expenses, by family size and region, as well as debt-to-income.
VA loan basics
Eligibility: based on length and type of service. You need a Certificate of Eligibility (COE), which lenders can usually request for you.
Entitlement: with full entitlement there's no VA loan limit; if you have a VA loan already, remaining entitlement and county limits affect how much you can borrow with no down payment.
Primary residence: VA purchase loans are for homes you'll live in.
Seller concessions: VA limits seller concessions to 4% of the home's reasonable value; normal closing-cost credits don't count toward this limit.
Closing costs: only the funding fee can be financed into a purchase loan. Other closing costs must be paid at closing or covered by seller credits; see the closing cost calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the wrong fee rate. Check first use vs subsequent use and your down payment band.
Assuming the payment is the whole cost. Add taxes and insurance.
Missing an exemption. If you have a disability rating, the fee may be zero, and you may be eligible for a refund if a rating is later made retroactive.
Not comparing lenders. VA sets the fee, but rates, points and lender fees vary.
Frequently asked questions
What is the VA funding fee?
A one-time fee paid on most VA-backed loans, set as a percentage of the loan amount.
Can I roll the funding fee into the loan?
Yes. The calculator assumes you do.
Do VA loans need a down payment?
Usually not, though putting 5% or more down reduces the funding fee.
Do VA loans have mortgage insurance?
No monthly mortgage insurance; the funding fee takes its place.
Who is exempt from the funding fee?
Mainly veterans receiving or eligible for VA disability compensation, eligible surviving spouses, and Purple Heart recipients on active duty.
Can I use a VA loan more than once?
Yes. Subsequent use has a higher fee when you put down less than 5%.

VAT Calculator: Add or Remove VAT | FigSumo (43 chars)
Meta description
Add VAT to a net price or extract VAT from a gross price at 20%, 5% or any rate. Shows net, VAT and gross with the formula used. (128 chars)

1,027 (minimum 1,000)
H1: VAT Calculator
Value-added tax (VAT) is a consumption tax charged at each stage of the supply chain and borne by the final consumer. It's used in the UK, across the EU and in more than 170 countries. This calculator adds VAT to a net price or extracts the VAT from a gross price that already includes it.
How to use this calculator
1. Amount: the price you have.
2. VAT rate (%): the rate that applies. The UK standard rate is 20%.
3. Amount is: choose Excluding VAT to add VAT to a net price, or Including VAT to find the net price and VAT inside a gross price.
Results:
Excluding VAT: VAT amount and total including VAT
Including VAT: net (ex-VAT) and VAT amount
The formulas
Adding VAT:
VAT = Net × Rate
Gross = Net × (1 + Rate)
Removing VAT:
Net = Gross ÷ (1 + Rate)
VAT = Gross − Net
At 20%, the VAT inside a gross price is 1/6 of the gross (16.6667%), not 20% of it. This is the most common VAT mistake.
Worked examples
Example 1: adding 20% VAT to £100
VAT = 100 × 0.20 = £20.00
Gross = £120.00
Example 2: extracting VAT from £150
Net = 150 ÷ 1.20 = £125.00
VAT = £25.00
Taking 20% of £150 would give £30.00, which is wrong.
Example 3: the reduced rate
Home energy in the UK is charged at 5%. On a £80 net bill, VAT is £4.00, total £84.00.
Example 4: a quarterly VAT return
A VAT-registered business sells £30,000 (net) of standard-rated services in a quarter and buys £8,000 (net) of standard-rated supplies:
Output VAT: 30,000 × 20% = £6,000.00
Input VAT: 8,000 × 20% = £1,600.00
VAT to pay HMRC = £4,400.00
Example 5: removing 5% VAT
A £63.00 energy bill including 5% VAT: net = 63 ÷ 1.05 = £60.00, VAT £3.00.
VAT fractions
The VAT inside a VAT-inclusive price is rate ÷ (100 + rate):
Rate
Fraction of gross price
VAT in £100 gross

HMRC calls the 1/6 figure the "VAT fraction" and it's the quickest way to check a till receipt.
How VAT moves through the supply chain
A manufacturer sells goods to a retailer for £1,000 + VAT and charges £200.00 output VAT. The retailer sells them to consumers for £1,600 + VAT, charging £320.00. The retailer pays HMRC the difference between the VAT it charged and the VAT it paid: £120.00. Each business pays VAT only on the value it adds, and the consumer bears the full £320.00.
Understanding your results
Prices for consumers include VAT in the UK and EU. Business-to-business prices are often quoted ex-VAT ("+ VAT").
Rounding: HMRC allows VAT to be rounded to the nearest penny per line or invoice, so small differences are normal.
VAT vs sales tax: US sales tax is charged once at the final sale and is added at the till. See the sales tax calculator.
UK VAT rates and rules
Standard rate 20%: most goods and services.
Reduced rate 5%: for example home energy, children's car seats, some energy-saving installations.
Zero rate 0%: most food, children's clothes, books and newspapers. Zero-rated goods are still VAT-taxable (businesses can reclaim input VAT), unlike exempt items.
Exempt: for example most financial services, insurance, education and health services; no VAT is charged and input VAT generally can't be reclaimed.
Registration threshold: businesses must register when VAT-taxable turnover exceeds £90,000.00 in a rolling 12 months (from 1 April 2024) [VERIFY current threshold].
Flat Rate Scheme: small businesses can pay a fixed percentage of gross turnover instead of calculating input and output VAT; the percentage depends on the trade.
Since 1 January 2025, VAT applies to private school fees in the UK.
Other countries
EU: each member state sets its own rates, with a standard rate of at least 15%. Rates range up to 27% (Hungary) [VERIFY].
Canada: GST/HST is a value-added tax at 5% to 15% depending on the province; see the GST/HST calculator.
United States: no VAT; states and localities levy sales tax instead.
