https://figsumo.com/gfr-calculator
Title tag
eGFR Calculator (CKD-EPI 2021) | FigSumo (40 chars)
Meta description
Estimate kidney filtration rate (eGFR) from serum creatinine, age and sex with the race-free CKD-EPI 2021 equation. Discuss any result with a clinician. (152 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,091 (minimum 1,000)
H1: eGFR Calculator
Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) measures how well your kidneys filter blood. It's hard to measure directly, so labs estimate it (eGFR) from a blood test for creatinine, a waste product from muscle, along with your age and sex. This calculator uses the CKD-EPI 2021 creatinine equation, the race-free equation recommended in the US, to estimate eGFR and show the corresponding GFR category.
How to use this calculator
1. Age: 18 or older (the equation is for adults).
2. Sex: the equation uses different constants for men and women.
3. Serum creatinine: from your blood test, in mg/dL. If your lab reports µmol/L (common in Canada and the UK), divide by 88.4 to convert.
Results: eGFR in mL/min/1.73 m², the GFR category (G1 to G5), and a reminder that this isn't a diagnosis.
The formula (CKD-EPI 2021, creatinine)
eGFR = 142 × min(Scr/κ, 1)^α × max(Scr/κ, 1)^−1.200 × 0.9938^Age × 1.012 [if female]
Scr: serum creatinine (mg/dL)
κ: 0.7 for women, 0.9 for men
α: −0.241 for women, −0.302 for men
The result is standardised to a body surface area of 1.73 m². The 2021 equation removed the race coefficient used in earlier versions.
Worked examples
Example 1: man aged 45, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL
Scr/κ = 1.0 ÷ 0.9 = 1.111, so the min term is 1 and the max term is 1.111^−1.200
eGFR ≈ 95 mL/min/1.73 m² → G1 (normal or high)
The same creatinine at age 65 gives about 84: eGFR falls gradually with age.
Example 2: woman aged 60, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
eGFR ≈ 73 → G2 (mildly decreased) (counts as CKD only with other signs of kidney damage)
Example 3: man aged 70, creatinine 1.6 mg/dL
eGFR ≈ 46 → G3a (mildly to moderately decreased); if this persists for more than three months, it meets the definition of CKD
Converting µmol/L
A creatinine of 80 µmol/L is 80 ÷ 88.4 = 0.90 mg/dL. For a woman aged 52, that gives an eGFR of about 76.
GFR categories (KDIGO)
Category
eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)
Description
G1
90 or more
Normal or high
G2
60–89
Mildly decreased
G3a
45–59
Mildly to moderately decreased
G3b
30–44
Moderately to severely decreased
G4
15–29
Severely decreased
G5
under 15
Kidney failure
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is diagnosed when eGFR is below 60, or there are markers of kidney damage (such as albumin in the urine), for more than three months. A single eGFR of 60 to 89 without other signs isn't CKD.

The same creatinine gives a lower eGFR for a woman because women, on average, have less muscle and so produce less creatinine. Small rises in creatinine at the upper end make large differences: doubling from 1.5 to 3.0 mg/dL in a 50-year-old man takes eGFR from about 56 to 25.
Example 4: a lab report in µmol/L
A 35-year-old woman's result is 62 µmol/L. That's 62 ÷ 88.4 = 0.70 mg/dL, and the equation gives an eGFR of about 115 (G1). Many UK and Canadian lab reports show eGFR above 90 simply as "&gt;90".
Understanding your results
It's an estimate. Creatinine depends on muscle mass, diet (especially recent meat intake), hydration and some medicines. Very muscular people may show a falsely low eGFR; people with low muscle mass may show a falsely high one.
Cystatin C: a second blood marker that doesn't depend on muscle. Combining it with creatinine gives a more accurate estimate in many people.
Not for acute changes. eGFR equations assume stable kidney function; they're unreliable in acute kidney injury.
Medication dosing may use eGFR or creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault); your clinician or pharmacist decides which.
Ask about urine albumin. The urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (uACR) is the other half of CKD assessment.
eGFR and creatinine clearance
Some drug labels and dosing charts use creatinine clearance from the Cockcroft-Gault equation rather than eGFR:
CrCl (mL/min) = (140 − age) × weight (kg) ÷ (72 × Scr) [× 0.85 if female]
For a man aged 70, weighing 80 kg, with a creatinine of 1.2 mg/dL: (140 − 70) × 80 ÷ (72 × 1.2) = 64.8 mL/min. The calculator doesn't compute this, and it isn't interchangeable with eGFR, because it depends on body weight and isn't scaled to 1.73 m². Pharmacists choose which one applies to a given medicine.
Country notes
United States: the National Kidney Foundation and American Society of Nephrology recommended adopting CKD-EPI 2021 in 2021; most US labs report it.
Canada: most labs report creatinine in µmol/L; many have adopted CKD-EPI 2021 [VERIFY by province].
United Kingdom: NICE guidance (NG203) recommends the CKD-EPI creatinine equation; NICE advises not adjusting for ethnicity. Some UK labs still report the 2009 version [VERIFY].
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing units. Entering µmol/L as mg/dL gives a meaningless result.
Testing after a heavy meat meal or intense exercise, which can raise creatinine temporarily.
Reading one result in isolation. Trends over months matter more.
Frequently asked questions
What is a normal eGFR?
90 or above is normal in most adults; it declines slowly with age.
What eGFR indicates kidney disease?
Below 60 for more than three months, or any level with signs of kidney damage.
Why did the eGFR equation change in 2021?
To remove the race coefficient, which was considered inappropriate and could delay care.
Can I improve my eGFR?
Managing blood pressure, blood sugar, avoiding unnecessary NSAIDs and following medical advice can help preserve kidney function.
What's the difference between eGFR and creatinine clearance?
eGFR estimates filtration standardised to body size; creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault) estimates clearance in mL/min and is sometimes used for drug dosing.
Does high protein intake affect eGFR?
A large protein meal can raise creatinine briefly, lowering eGFR on that test.

Title tag
Fat Intake Calculator: Daily Fat in Grams | FigSumo (51 chars)
Meta description
Convert daily calories into a total fat range (20-35% of energy) and a saturated fat limit in grams, based on US dietary guidelines. (132 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,002 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Fat Intake Calculator
Fat is an essential nutrient. It supplies energy, helps you absorb vitamins A, D, E and K, and provides fatty acids your body can't make. It also has more than twice the calories of carbohydrate or protein, so portions add up quickly. This calculator turns your daily calories and a chosen percentage into a daily fat target in grams.
How to use this calculator
1. Daily calories: your maintenance calories or a weight-loss target. The TDEE calculator can estimate this.
2. Fat as % of calories: 10–70% (default 30%).
Results: daily fat intake in grams and calories from fat.
The formula
Fat (g) = Daily calories × Fat % ÷ 100 ÷ 9
Each gram of fat provides about 9 kcal.
Worked examples
Example 1: 2,000 kcal at 30%
2,000 × 0.30 = 600 kcal from fat
600 ÷ 9 = 67 g of fat a day
Example 2: 2,500 kcal at 35%
2,500 × 0.35 ÷ 9 = 97 g
Example 3: 1,800 kcal at 20%
40 g, the lower end of the recommended range.
Recommended ranges
Guideline
Total fat
Saturated fat
US (National Academies AMDR; Dietary Guidelines)
20–35% of calories
Less than 10%
Canada (Health Canada, same DRIs)
20–35%
Limit; replace with unsaturated fats
UK (government advice)
Average no more than 35% of food energy (COMA 1991)
No more than 11%
On 2,000 kcal, 20–35% is 44–78 g of total fat. Saturated fat under 10% is under 22 g in the US; the UK reference intake on labels is 20 g of saturated fat and 70 g of total fat for an adult.
Types of fat
Unsaturated fats (olive and rapeseed oils, nuts, seeds, avocado, oily fish) are linked with better heart health when they replace saturated fat.
Omega-3 fats (salmon, mackerel, sardines, walnuts, flaxseed) are recommended regularly; the NHS advises two portions of fish a week, one oily.
Saturated fat (butter, fatty meat, cheese, coconut and palm oil) raises LDL cholesterol.
Trans fats (partially hydrogenated oils) are the most harmful; the US and Canada have banned added partially hydrogenated oils.
Understanding your results
Very low fat (under 20%) can make it harder to get essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins.
Higher fat (over 35%) is common in low-carb diets; the type of fat matters more than the amount for heart health.
Your target is a daily average. Some days will be higher, some lower.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting cooking oil. A tablespoon of oil is about 14 g of fat (about 120 kcal).
Comparing grams of fat with grams of food. 100 g of cheese has about 30–35 g of fat, not 100 g.
Assuming "low fat" means low calorie. Some low-fat products add sugar.

Approximate fat in some everyday foods [VERIFY against current USDA FoodData Central or product labels]:

Most of the fat comes from oil, avocado, salmon and nuts, which are mainly unsaturated. To bring it closer to 67 g, the simplest change is the cooking oil or half the avocado.
Reading food labels in the US, Canada and UK
US Nutrition Facts: the % Daily Value for total fat is based on 78 g a day and for saturated fat on 20 g, both for a 2,000 kcal diet.
Canada Nutrition Facts table: the % Daily Value uses 75 g for fat and 20 g for saturated plus trans fat. Health Canada describes 5% DV or less as "a little" and 15% DV or more as "a lot".
UK front-of-pack labels: traffic-light colours show fat per 100 g. Food is "high" (red) in fat above 17.5 g per 100 g and "low" (green) at 3 g or less; for saturates, high is above 5 g and low is 1.5 g or less.
Labels give fat per serving, so multiply by the number of servings you actually eat before comparing with your target.
Frequently asked questions
How many grams of fat should I eat a day?
On a 2,000 kcal diet, about 44–78 g (20–35% of calories).
How do I convert fat percentage to grams?
Multiply calories by the percentage, then divide by 9.
Is a high-fat diet bad?
Not necessarily; what matters most is the type of fat and total calories.
How much saturated fat is too much?
Under 10% of calories in the US, and no more than 11% in the UK.
Do I need fat to lose weight?
Yes, some fat is essential; reducing it moderately can help lower calories.
What counts as a healthy fat?
Mainly unsaturated fats from plant oils, nuts, seeds and fish.

Healthy Weight Range Calculator by Height | FigSumo (51 chars)
Meta description
Find the weight range that corresponds to a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9 for your height, in kilograms or pounds, with the formula shown. (128 chars)

H1: Healthy Weight Calculator
A "healthy weight" for adults is usually defined as the weight range that gives a body mass index (BMI) of 18.5 to 24.9 for your height. This calculator shows that range in kilograms and pounds. It's a quick starting point; your ideal weight within or near that range depends on your build, muscle mass, age and health.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: metric (cm) or imperial (ft and in).
2. Height: without shoes.
Results: healthy weight range in kg and in lb.
The formula
BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)², so rearranging:
Lower weight = 18.5 × Height (m)²
Upper weight = 24.9 × Height (m)²
In pounds, divide the kilogram values by 0.45359237.
Worked examples
Example 1: 175 cm
Height² = 1.75² = 3.0625
Healthy range = 56.7 to 76.3 kg (124.9 to 168.1 lb)
Example 2: 5 ft 6 in
5 ft 6 in = 66 in = 167.6 cm
Healthy range = 114.6 to 154.3 lb
Example 3: 162 cm
Healthy range = 48.6 to 65.3 kg

Each range is 18.5 × height² to 24.9 × height², the same calculation the tool does. For heights between rows, enter your exact height above.
Where the 18.5 and 24.9 limits come from
The cut-offs were set by the World Health Organization in the late 1990s, based on studies linking BMI to the risk of ill health and death across large populations. The US National Institutes of Health adopted them in 1998, and Canada and the UK use the same values. They describe risk across a population, not a precise threshold for one person, which is why a weight a little above or below the range isn't automatically a problem.
Example 4: 6 ft 2 in
74 in = 188.0 cm
Healthy range = 144 to 194 lb (65.4 to 88.0 kg)
Under NICE's lower thresholds for some ethnic groups, overweight starts at BMI 23, which is 179 lb at this height.
Adult BMI categories
BMI
Category
Under 18.5
Underweight
18.5 to 24.9
Healthy weight
25 to 29.9
Overweight
30 or more
Obesity
These categories apply to adults aged 20 and over (18 and over in the UK). Children and teens use BMI-for-age percentiles instead; see the BMI calculator.
Understanding your results
BMI is a screening tool. It doesn't measure body fat directly or show where fat is stored. Muscular people can have a high BMI without excess fat, and some people within the healthy range carry fat around the waist that raises health risks.
Waist size adds useful information. Keeping your waist to less than half your height is a simple guide used by NICE in the UK: for a 175 cm person, a waist under 87.5 cm. Try the waist-to-height ratio calculator.
Ethnicity: NICE recommends lower BMI thresholds for people of South Asian, Chinese, other Asian, Middle Eastern, Black African or African-Caribbean family background, with overweight starting at 23 and obesity at 27.5. At 175 cm, a BMI of 23 corresponds to 70.4 kg.
Older adults: some research suggests slightly higher BMIs may be associated with lower risk in older age; discuss targets with your doctor.
Pregnancy: BMI ranges don't apply during pregnancy; see the pregnancy weight gain calculator.
If you're outside the range
Being outside the healthy range doesn't mean you're unhealthy, and being inside it doesn't guarantee good health. If you're above the range, even a 5% to 10% weight loss can improve blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol for people with excess weight. If you're below it, talk to a doctor about possible causes and whether you need to gain weight. The calorie deficit calculator and TDEE calculator can help with planning.
Country notes
United States: the CDC uses the categories above for adults 20+, and BMI-for-age percentiles for ages 2 to 19.
Canada: Health Canada's guidelines use the same adult BMI categories and recommend using waist circumference with BMI.
United Kingdom: the NHS uses the same categories, plus the lower thresholds for some ethnic groups and the waist-to-height ratio.
Tips and common mistakes
Measuring height with shoes on, which shifts the range.
Treating the top of the range as a goal when your doctor may suggest a different target.
Using adult ranges for children.
Frequently asked questions
What is a healthy weight for my height?
The range that gives a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9; this calculator shows it for your height.
Is BMI accurate?
It's a reasonable population screening tool but doesn't account for muscle, bone or fat distribution.
Does the range differ for men and women?
Adult BMI ranges are the same for both sexes.
What is a healthy weight for someone 5 ft 6 in?
About 115 to 154 lb.
Is the healthy range different for older people?
The standard categories still apply, but clinicians may consider other factors.
Should I aim for the middle of the range?
Not necessarily. Health markers, fitness and how you feel matter more than a specific number.

H1: Ideal Weight Calculator
"Ideal body weight" formulas were developed for clinical use, mainly to dose certain medicines, not as personal weight goals. They give a single number for your height and sex. This calculator uses the Robinson formula (1983); this page also explains the other common formulas and how they compare with the healthy BMI range, which is usually a better guide for setting a goal.
How to use this calculator

2. Units: metric (cm) or imperial (ft and in).
3. Height: without shoes.
Results: ideal weight (Robinson formula) in kg and lb.
The formulas

Understanding your results
One number isn't a target. Different formulas give different answers, and none accounts for muscle mass, frame size, age or ethnicity.
Healthy range: a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9 is the standard adult guide; see the healthy weight calculator.
Frame size: people with a large frame may sit toward the upper end of a range; see the body type calculator.
Body composition: two people of the same weight can have very different body fat. The body fat calculator and lean body mass calculator give a fuller picture.
Where ideal body weight is used
In hospitals, ideal body weight (often the Devine formula) is used to calculate doses of some drugs, set ventilator tidal volumes and estimate kidney function in certain equations. For people with obesity, clinicians may use an "adjusted body weight" (ideal weight plus 40% of the excess). These uses are clinical decisions, not something to calculate for yourself.
Adjusted body weight, for reference
For a man of 175 cm who weighs 100 kg, the Devine ideal weight is 70.5 kg, so the adjusted body weight is 70.5 + 0.4 × (29.5) = 82.3 kg. Clinicians use figures like this only for specific drugs and calculations; it isn't a recommended weight.
Setting a personal goal
If you want to change your weight, a goal based on health markers is more useful than a formula. For many people with excess weight, losing 5% to 10% of current weight brings measurable health benefits. Use the calorie deficit calculator to plan a gradual change, and talk to your doctor if you have health conditions.
Country notes
The formulas use inches and kilograms because they came from US clinical practice. The NHS, Health Canada and the CDC all use BMI ranges rather than ideal-weight formulas for public health advice. NICE recommends lower BMI thresholds for some ethnic groups (overweight from 23).
Tips and common mistakes
Treating the result as the only healthy weight.
Using it for children. These formulas are for adults.
Comparing results from different formulas as if one were "correct".
Frequently asked questions
What is my ideal weight?
Formulas give a single estimate, but a healthy weight is a range: BMI 18.5 to 24.9 for adults.
Which ideal weight formula is most accurate?
None is clearly best. Robinson and Miller tend to give lower values for tall people than Hamwi.
Why do the formulas start at 5 feet?
They were built as a base weight at 5 feet plus an amount per inch.
Does muscle change my ideal weight?
Muscular people may be healthy above the formula weight; the formulas don't consider body composition.
Is ideal weight the same for men and women?
No, the formulas use different constants by sex, while BMI ranges are the same.
Why do doctors use ideal body weight?
For dosing certain medications and some clinical calculations.

Lean Body Mass Calculator

Title tag
Lean Body Mass Calculator: Boer, James & Hume | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Estimate lean body mass from height, weight and sex using the Boer, James and Hume formulas, or from a known body-fat percentage. (129 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,032 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Lean Body Mass Calculator
Lean body mass (LBM) is everything in your body that isn't fat: muscle, bone, organs, skin and water. Knowing it helps you track whether weight changes come from fat or muscle, set protein targets, and use equations such as Katch-McArdle that estimate metabolic rate from lean mass. This calculator works out lean body mass and fat mass from your weight and body fat percentage.
How to use this calculator
1. Units and weight.
2. Body fat %: from a body composition scan (DEXA), bioimpedance scale, skinfold measurement or a circumference estimate such as the body fat calculator.
Results: lean body mass and fat mass in kg and lb.
The formula
Fat mass = Weight × Body fat % ÷ 100
Lean body mass = Weight − Fat mass = Weight × (1 − Body fat % ÷ 100)
Worked examples
Example 1: 80 kg at 22% body fat
Fat mass = 80 × 0.22 = 17.6 kg
Lean body mass = 62.4 kg (137.6 lb)
Example 2: 150 lb at 30% body fat
Fat mass = 45.0 lb; LBM = 105.0 lb
Example 3: tracking a weight change
The person in Example 1 loses 6 kg, of which an estimated 4.5 kg is fat and 1.5 kg lean. New weight 74 kg; fat mass 13.1 kg; body fat about 17.7%. Monitoring lean mass shows whether a diet is preserving muscle.
Example 4: 65 kg at 32% body fat
Fat mass = 65 × 0.32 = 20.8 kg
Lean body mass = 44.2 kg (97.4 lb)
That's close to the Boer estimate of 46.1 kg for a 65 kg, 165 cm woman (below), which shows the formula is reasonable for someone of average build.
Estimating LBM without body fat %
When body fat isn't known, formulas estimate LBM from height and weight. The Boer formula (1984):
Men:   LBM = 0.407 × Weight (kg) + 0.267 × Height (cm) − 19.2
Women: LBM = 0.252 × Weight (kg) + 0.473 × Height (cm) − 48.3
For a man of 80 kg and 180 cm, that's 61.4 kg; for a woman of 65 kg and 165 cm, 46.1 kg. These are population averages and less accurate than a measured body fat percentage.
Comparing estimation formulas
For a man of 80 kg and 180 cm, three published formulas give:
Formula
Men
Result
Boer (1984)
0.407W + 0.267H − 19.2
61.4 kg
James (1976)
1.1W − 128(W ÷ H)²
62.7 kg
Hume (1966)
0.32810W + 0.33929H − 29.5336
57.8 kg
W is weight in kg and H height in cm. The spread of about 4.9 kg is typical, and it's why a measured body fat percentage gives a better answer when you have one. The James formula is known to give implausible results at high body weights, so it's rarely used for people with obesity.
Fat-free mass index
Lean mass is easier to compare between people when it's scaled by height, like BMI: FFMI = LBM (kg) ÷ height (m)². For 62.4 kg of lean mass at 1.80 m, FFMI = 19.3. Higher values mean more lean mass for your height, but there's no single official healthy range, so use it to track your own trend.
Using lean body mass
Metabolic rate: the Katch-McArdle equation estimates BMR = 370 + 21.6 × LBM (kg). With 62.4 kg of LBM, that's about 1,718 kcal a day. See the BMR calculator.
Protein: some sports nutritionists set protein per kg of lean mass; at 1.6 g/kg of LBM, 62.4 kg of LBM suggests about 100 g a day. See the protein calculator.
Medication dosing: some anaesthetic and other drugs are dosed on lean body weight; that's a clinical decision.
Understanding your results
Accuracy depends on the body fat estimate. Home scales and tape methods can be several percentage points off, which changes LBM by a few kilograms.
LBM isn't the same as muscle. It includes bone, organs and water, so it changes with hydration.
Typical body fat ranges vary by age and sex, and different organisations publish different ranges. Use trends over time rather than a single reading.
Strength training and adequate protein help preserve lean mass when losing weight, and build it over time.
Measurement tips
Measure at the same time of day under similar conditions (for example, morning, before eating).
Bioimpedance readings change with hydration, recent exercise and food.
DEXA scans are among the more accurate widely available methods, but they're not available everywhere and involve a small dose of radiation.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing kg and lb. Use one unit throughout.
Comparing results from different devices.
Assuming all weight loss is fat. Rapid weight loss often includes water and some lean tissue.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
There's no national guideline for lean body mass itself in any of the three countries; health services use BMI and waist measurements for screening. In the US, body-composition DEXA scans are widely sold direct to consumers at private clinics and gyms. In Canada and the UK, DEXA is mainly used for bone density testing through the public health system, and body-composition scans are usually private and paid for. Home bioimpedance scales are sold everywhere; treat their readings as estimates.
Frequently asked questions
What is lean body mass?
Your total weight minus fat mass.
How do I calculate lean body mass?
Weight × (1 − body fat % ÷ 100).
What is a healthy lean body mass?
There's no single healthy figure; it depends on height, sex and age. What matters is having enough muscle for strength and function.
Is lean body mass the same as muscle mass?
No. LBM includes muscle, bone, organs and water.
How can I increase lean body mass?
Resistance training with enough protein and calories.
Why use LBM for calorie estimates?
Lean tissue uses more energy than fat, so equations based on LBM can be more accurate for people with very high or low body fat.

Title tag
Macro Calculator: Protein, Carbs & Fat in Grams | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Split your daily calories into protein, carbohydrate and fat grams using ranges you choose, with presets based on dietary guideline ranges. (139 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,037 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Macro Calculator
Macronutrients, or "macros", are the three nutrients that supply calories: carbohydrate, protein and fat. This calculator estimates your daily calorie needs and splits them into grams of each macro using one of three preset ratios. It's useful for meal planning, tracking food in an app, or checking whether your current diet is roughly balanced.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: metric (kg, cm) or imperial (lb, ft and in).
2. Age, sex, weight and height: used to estimate your basal metabolic rate (BMR).
3. Activity level: sedentary, light (1–3 days a week), moderate (3–5 days), active (6–7 days) or very active (hard exercise daily).
4. Macro split:
Balanced: 40% carbohydrate, 30% protein, 30% fat
High protein: 30% carbohydrate, 40% protein, 30% fat
Low carb: 20% carbohydrate, 35% protein, 45% fat
Results: daily calories (TDEE) and grams of carbohydrate, protein and fat, with a chart.
How it works
Step 1: BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor equation)
Men:   BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age + 5
Women: BMR = 10 × weight (kg) + 6.25 × height (cm) − 5 × age − 161
Step 2: TDEE. BMR × activity factor (1.2, 1.375, 1.55, 1.725 or 1.9).
Step 3: grams.
Carbohydrate g = TDEE × carb % ÷ 4
Protein g      = TDEE × protein % ÷ 4
Fat g          = TDEE × fat % ÷ 9
Carbohydrate and protein provide about 4 kcal per gram; fat about 9 kcal per gram. Alcohol (7 kcal per gram) isn't included.
The calories are your maintenance estimate. The calculator doesn't subtract a deficit for weight loss; use the calorie deficit calculator for a target and apply the same percentages to it.
Worked examples
Example 1: woman, 35, 65 kg, 165 cm, moderate activity, balanced split
BMR = 650 + 1,031.25 − 175 − 161 = 1,345.25 kcal
TDEE = 1,345.25 × 1.55 = 2,085 kcal
Carbohydrate: 2,085.14 × 0.40 ÷ 4 = 209 g
Protein: × 0.30 ÷ 4 = 156 g (about 2.4 g per kg of body weight)
Fat: × 0.30 ÷ 9 = 70 g
With the high-protein split, protein would be 209 g, or 3.2 g per kg. That's well above what most people need (see below).
Example 2: man, 40, 90 kg, 180 cm, light activity, low carb
BMR = 1,830.00 kcal; TDEE = 2,516 kcal
Carbohydrate 126 g, protein 220 g (2.4 g/kg), fat 126 g
Understanding your results
TDEE is an estimate. Mifflin-St Jeor is among the more accurate prediction equations for adults, but individuals can differ by 10% or more. Track your weight for two to four weeks and adjust.
Check protein per kilogram. Percentage splits can give very high or low protein. A common range is 0.8 g/kg for general health up to about 1.6–2.0 g/kg for strength training. The protein calculator works per kilogram directly.
Fat floor. Very low fat intakes make it harder to get essential fatty acids and fat-soluble vitamins. All three splits here give 30% or more of calories from fat.
Grams are targets, not exact requirements. Hitting within 5–10 g most days is plenty for most goals.
Official guidance on macro ranges
The US National Academies set Acceptable Macronutrient Distribution Ranges (AMDRs) for adults:
Macro
AMDR (% of calories)
Carbohydrate
45–65%
Protein
10–35%
Fat
20–35%
The calculator's presets are higher in protein and lower in carbohydrate than the AMDRs. The low-carb split (20% carbohydrate, 45% fat) falls outside both ranges, which is common in diets designed for weight loss but worth knowing. For Example 1, carbohydrate within the AMDR would be 235–339 g a day.
Country notes
US: the Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020–2025 use the AMDRs and recommend limiting saturated fat to under 10% of calories.
Canada: Health Canada uses the same Dietary Reference Intakes as the US.
UK: government advice suggests carbohydrate should provide about 50% of energy (SACN 2015), total fat no more than 35% and saturated fat no more than 11% of food energy (COMA 1991).
Choosing a split
Balanced: a good default for most people who exercise.
High protein: may help with fullness and preserving muscle during weight loss, but check grams per kg.
Low carb: some people find it easier to control appetite; endurance athletes usually need more carbohydrate.
The best split is one you can stick to. Total calories matter most for weight change, and protein matters most for muscle.
Tips and common mistakes
Using maintenance calories when you want to lose weight.
Choosing "active" when you exercise moderately. Overestimating activity is the most common reason calorie targets don't work.
Ignoring fibre. Aim for whole grains, fruit, vegetables and legumes within your carbohydrate grams.
Forgetting cooking oils and drinks when tracking.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate my macros?
Work out your daily calories, multiply by each macro's percentage, then divide by 4 for carbohydrate and protein, or 9 for fat.
What macro ratio is best for weight loss?
A calorie deficit drives weight loss; higher protein (around 1.2–1.6 g/kg) can help preserve muscle and keep you full.
Why does fat have fewer grams?
Fat has more than twice the calories per gram (9 vs 4).
Do I count fibre as carbohydrate?
Yes, nutrition labels in the US and Canada include fibre in total carbohydrate; UK labels list it separately.
How accurate is TDEE?
It's a population-based estimate; adjust it based on your weight trend.
Is a high protein diet safe?
For healthy adults, intakes up to about 2 g/kg are generally considered safe. People with kidney disease should get medical advice.
Should I change macros on rest days?
Some people do, but keeping the same targets daily is simpler and works for most goals.

Title tag
One Rep Max (1RM) Calculator: Epley & Brzycki | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Estimate your one-rep max from a weight and rep count with the Epley and Brzycki formulas, plus a percentage table for training loads. (134 chars)
Country
global

Body words
640 (minimum 600)
H1: One Rep Max Calculator
Your one-rep max (1RM) is the heaviest weight you can lift once with good form. Testing it directly is tiring and carries some risk, so most lifters estimate it from a heavier set of several reps. This calculator uses the Epley formula to turn a set of 1 to 12 reps into an estimated 1RM, which you can use to plan training loads.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: metric or imperial.
2. Weight lifted: the load for the set, in kg or lb.
3. Repetitions: how many full reps you completed with good form (1–12).
Result: estimated one-rep max in kg and lb.
The Epley formula
1RM = w × (1 + r ÷ 30)
w = weight lifted
r = reps completed
If you enter 1 rep, the calculator returns the weight itself. Estimates become less reliable above about 10 reps, which is why entries are capped at 12.
Worked examples
Example 1: 100 kg for 5 reps
1RM = 100 × (1 + 5 ÷ 30) = 116.7 kg (257.2 lb).
The Brzycki formula (w × 36 ÷ (37 − r)) gives 112.5 kg for the same set, so formulas differ by a kilogram or two at low reps.
Example 2: 185 lb for 8 reps
1RM = 185 × (1 + 8 ÷ 30) = 234.3 lb.
Using your 1RM: training percentages
Programs often prescribe loads as a percentage of 1RM. For an estimated 1RM of 116.7 kg:
% of 1RM
Load (kg)
Typical reps

80%

75%

75.8

60%

Rep counts at each percentage vary between people and exercises; treat them as a guide.
Understanding your results
It's an estimate. Accuracy is best with sets of 3 to 6 reps taken close to failure.
Exercise matters. Formulas fit compound lifts (squat, bench press, deadlift) better than isolation or machine exercises.
Formulas diverge at high reps. For 60 kg × 10 reps, Epley gives 80.0 kg and Brzycki 80.0 kg.
Training status matters. Endurance-trained lifters can usually do more reps at a given percentage than strength athletes.
Safety tips
Warm up with gradually heavier sets before your working set.
Use a spotter or safety bars for bench press and squats.
Stop the set when form breaks down; count only clean reps.
Beginners don't need to test a true 1RM; estimates are enough to set loads.
Tips and common mistakes
Counting reps with poor form, which inflates the estimate.
Using a set that wasn't close to failure. If you could have done three more reps, the estimate will be low.
Mixing units. Enter the weight in the unit you selected.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate my one-rep max?
Multiply the weight by (1 + reps ÷ 30), using the Epley formula.
Which 1RM formula is most accurate?
Epley and Brzycki are the most widely used and agree closely at low reps; no single formula is best for everyone.
How many reps should I use?
A set of 3 to 6 reps near failure gives the most reliable estimate.
Should I test my real 1RM?
Experienced lifters sometimes test it with a spotter; it isn't necessary for most training.
How often should I recalculate?
Every 4 to 8 weeks, or after a training block.
Does it work for bodyweight exercises?
Not directly; you'd need to include body weight in the load.

Title tag
Ovulation Calculator: Fertile Window Dates | FigSumo (52 chars)
Meta description
Estimate your fertile window and likely ovulation day for the next cycles from your last period and average cycle length. (121 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,087 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Ovulation Calculator
Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg. It usually happens about 14 days before your next period, and pregnancy is most likely from sex in the few days before and on the day of ovulation. This calculator estimates your ovulation date and fertile window from the first day of your last period and your usual cycle length.
How to use this calculator
1. First day of last period (LMP): the first day of full bleeding, not spotting.
2. Average cycle length: the number of days from the first day of one period to the first day of the next (21–45; default 28). Average your last three to six cycles if they vary.
Results:
Estimated ovulation date
Fertile window: five days before ovulation to one day after
Next period (estimate)
How it works
Ovulation   = LMP + (cycle length − 14) days
Fertile window = ovulation − 5 days to ovulation + 1 day
Next period = LMP + cycle length
The method assumes the luteal phase (the time from ovulation to your next period) is 14 days. That is an average; it typically ranges from about 11 to 17 days. Sperm can survive up to five days in the reproductive tract, and the egg lives about 12 to 24 hours, which is why the window starts five days before ovulation.
Worked examples
Example 1: 28-day cycle, LMP 1 September 2026
Ovulation: day 14 → 15 September 2026
Fertile window: 10 September 2026 to 16 September 2026
Next period: 29 September 2026
Example 2: 32-day cycle, same LMP
Ovulation: day 18 → 19 September 2026
Fertile window: 14 September 2026 to 20 September 2026
Next period: 3 October 2026
Example 3: 24-day cycle
Ovulation: day 10 → 11 September 2026; window 6 September 2026 to 12 September 2026
Longer cycles move ovulation later; the first half of the cycle changes length, not the second.
Looking several cycles ahead
If the 28-day cycle in Example 1 stays regular, later cycles follow the same pattern. Enter each new period start date to update the estimate:
Period starts
Estimated ovulation
Fertile window

13 October
8 October to 14 October
27 October 2026

3 December to 9 December

16 February 2027

Real cycles drift by a few days, so treat dates further ahead as rough planning only.
Understanding your results
The most fertile days are the two or three days before ovulation and the day itself.
Dates are estimates. Ovulation can shift from cycle to cycle because of stress, illness, travel, breastfeeding or hormonal conditions.
Irregular cycles: if your cycle varies by more than about seven days, a calendar estimate is unreliable. Ovulation predictor kits or temperature tracking work better.
Not contraception. Calendar-based estimates are not a reliable way to avoid pregnancy.
Confirming ovulation
Ovulation (LH) tests: detect the hormone surge 24 to 36 hours before ovulation.
Cervical mucus: becomes clear, slippery and stretchy near ovulation.
Basal body temperature: rises by about 0.2–0.5 °C after ovulation, so it confirms ovulation has happened rather than predicting it.
Using ovulation tests with this calculator
Many test makers suggest starting LH tests about 17 days before your next period is due, which gives a couple of days' margin before the estimated ovulation date. For a 28-day cycle, that's 11 days after the first day of your last period (12 September 2026 in Example 1); for a 32-day cycle, 15 days after it. Test at the same time each day and keep testing until you see a positive result. If you never see a surge over several cycles, mention it to a doctor.
Things that can change ovulation timing
Coming off hormonal contraception: cycles can take a few months to settle.
Breastfeeding: often delays the return of ovulation after birth, but not reliably enough to use as contraception.
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and thyroid conditions: can cause irregular or absent ovulation.
Low body weight or very intensive training: can suppress ovulation.
Perimenopause: cycles become less predictable in the years before periods stop.
If your cycles are regularly shorter than 21 days or longer than 35, a calendar estimate won't be reliable, and it's worth a check-up.
Country notes
US: ACOG and the Office on Women's Health provide guidance on fertility awareness.
UK: the NHS advises that couples having regular unprotected sex every two to three days don't need to time sex to ovulation.
Canada: the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (SOGC) gives similar advice.
In the US, ACOG advises seeing a doctor if you haven't conceived after 12 months of trying, or after 6 months if you're 35 or over. The NHS advises seeing a GP after a year of trying, or sooner if you're 36 or over or know of a fertility problem.
Tips and common mistakes
Counting from the last day of your period. Use the first day.
Assuming everyone ovulates on day 14. That's only true for a 28-day cycle with a 14-day luteal phase.
Using one unusual cycle. Average several cycles.
Frequently asked questions
When am I most fertile?
In the two to three days before ovulation and on ovulation day.
Can I get pregnant outside the fertile window?
It's less likely but possible, because ovulation dates vary.
How long does ovulation last?
The egg survives 12 to 24 hours after release.
Can I ovulate twice in a cycle?
More than one egg can be released within 24 hours (leading to non-identical twins), but not days apart in a typical cycle.
Does the pill affect this calculator?
Hormonal contraception usually stops ovulation; the calculator isn't meaningful while you're using it.
What if my cycles are irregular?
Use ovulation tests and talk to your doctor, especially if cycles are shorter than 21 or longer than 35 days.

Running Pace Calculator: Pace, Time or Distance | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description

H1: Pace Calculator
Pace is the time it takes to cover one kilometre or one mile. Runners use it to plan races and training; walkers and cyclists use speed more often. This calculator turns a distance and a finish time into pace per kilometre, pace per mile, and speed in km/h and mph.
How to use this calculator
1. Distance unit: kilometres or miles.
2. Distance: for example 5 for a 5K, or 26.2 miles.
3. Time: hours, minutes and seconds.
Results: pace in min/km, pace in min/mi, speed in km/h and speed in mph.
Formulas
Pace (min per km) = total time in minutes ÷ distance in km
Speed (km/h)      = distance in km ÷ time in hours
Pace per mile     = pace per km × 1.609344
A mile is exactly 1.609344 km. The decimal part of the pace is converted to seconds (× 60).
Worked examples
Example 1: 5 km in 28:00
Pace = 28 ÷ 5 = 5.6 minutes = 5:36 min/km
Per mile: 9:01 min/mi
Speed: 10.71 km/h (6.66 mph)
Example 2: marathon (42.195 km) in 3:30:00
210 minutes ÷ 42.195 = 4.977 minutes = 4:59 min/km (8:01 min/mi)
Speed 12.06 km/h
Example 3: 3.1 miles in 25:10
Pace = 8:07 min/mi, or 5:03 min/km

To estimate a finish time yourself, multiply pace by distance.
Using pace in training
Easy runs are usually 1 to 2 minutes per km slower than 5K race pace; you should be able to hold a conversation.
Tempo runs are "comfortably hard", near the pace you could hold for an hour.
Intervals are run at or faster than 5K pace with recovery between.
Heart rate is another way to set effort; see the target heart rate calculator.
Understanding your results
GPS watches drift. Tree cover and tall buildings can add or remove distance, so pace on a watch may not match a measured course.
Hills and wind slow pace without meaning lower fitness.
Treadmill pace often feels easier than outdoor pace; a 1% incline is commonly used to compensate.
Country notes
The US and UK mostly use miles for road races (though 5K and 10K are metric distances everywhere), while Canada uses kilometres. Track events are metric worldwide.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering 1:30 as 1.30 hours. Use the separate hours and minutes fields.
Using the wrong unit. A 10-mile run entered as 10 km gives a pace 1.6 times too fast.
Planning an even pace on a hilly course. Aim for even effort instead.
Quick check
A 5 km parkrun in 27:30 is a pace of 5.5 min/km, or 5:30 per km.
A 10-mile run at 9:00 per mile takes 1 hour 30 minutes.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate my running pace?
Divide your time by distance.
What is a good 5K pace?
It depends on age and experience; many recreational runners finish in 25 to 35 minutes, or 5:00 to 7:00 per km.
How do I convert min/km to min/mile?
Multiply by 1.609344.
What pace do I need for a sub-4-hour marathon?
About 5:41 per km or 9:09 per mile.
Is pace or speed better?
Runners mostly use pace; cyclists use speed.
How do I convert pace to speed?
Speed in km/h = 60 ÷ pace in min/km.

Title tag
Period Calculator: Next Period Dates | FigSumo (46 chars)
Meta description
Predict your next period start dates for the coming months from your last period, cycle length and period length. (113 chars)
Country
global
Status

1,025 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Period Calculator
A period calculator predicts when your next period is likely to start and end, based on your last period and your usual cycle. It's useful for planning travel, sport and events, for noticing when a period is late, and for keeping a simple record to discuss with a doctor.
How to use this calculator
1. First day of last period: the first day of bleeding (not spotting).
2. Average cycle length: days from the first day of one period to the first day of the next (21–45; default 28).
3. Period length: how many days you usually bleed (2–10; default 5).
Results: next period start, next period end (estimate) and following period start.
How it works
Next period start      = last period start + cycle length
Next period end        = next start + (period length − 1)
Following period start = next start + cycle length
The end date subtracts one day because the start day counts as day 1 of bleeding.
Worked examples
Example 1: 28-day cycle, 5-day period, last period began 3 September 2026
Next period: 1 October 2026, ending about 5 October 2026
Following period: 29 October 2026
Estimated ovulation in that cycle: about 17 September 2026 (see the ovulation calculator)
Example 2: 33-day cycle, 6-day period, same start date
Next period: 6 October 2026, ending about 11 October 2026
Following period: 8 November 2026
Example 3: working out an average from several cycles
Suppose your last five cycles were 27, 31, 29, 33, 30 days long. The calculator takes a single average, so add them up and divide: 150 ÷ 5 = 30 days. With a last period starting on 3 September 2026, the next is predicted for 3 October 2026.
Because your cycles ranged from 27 to 33 days, a realistic window is 30 September 2026 to 6 October 2026. Run the calculator with your shortest and longest cycle as well as the average to see that window.
Example 4: 24-day cycle, 4-day period
Next period: 27 September 2026, ending about 30 September 2026
Following period: 21 October 2026
Shorter cycles mean periods come around more often: about 15 a year at 24 days, compared with 13 at 28 days.
What's a typical cycle?
Cycle length: in adults, cycles commonly last 21 to 35 days, and many people's cycles vary by a few days from month to month. In the first few years after periods begin, cycles of up to 45 days are common.
Period length: usually 2 to 7 days.
Blood loss: most people lose less than 80 ml per period; heavy bleeding means needing to change products every one to two hours, passing large clots or bleeding longer than 7 days.
Understanding your results
Predictions are estimates. Stress, illness, travel, weight changes, exercise, breastfeeding and some medicines can shift a period by days or weeks.
A late period can mean pregnancy; a home test is reliable from the first day of a missed period.
Using several months of data gives a better average cycle length.
When to see a doctor
Contact a doctor or nurse if you have:
periods that stop for more than three months (and you aren't pregnant)
cycles shorter than 21 days or longer than 35 days (adults)
very heavy or painful periods that affect daily life
bleeding between periods, after sex or after menopause
Country notes
US: the Office on Women's Health (HHS) and ACOG publish guidance on menstrual health.
UK: the NHS covers periods, heavy periods and PMS.
Canada: the SOGC runs "Your Period" educational resources.
Tips and common mistakes
Counting from the end of a period. Start from day 1 of bleeding.
Assuming 28 days. Only a minority of cycles are exactly 28 days.
Treating predictions as contraception. Period predictions don't reliably show safe days.
What to track
A note of a few details each month makes the predictions better and gives a doctor useful information:
Start date of each period (day 1 of full flow)
Number of bleeding days and which days are heaviest
Product changes on heavy days, as a rough measure of flow
Pain, mood changes or headaches, and on which days of the cycle they happen
Anything unusual: spotting between periods, a missed period, clots
Three to six months of records show your true average cycle and how much it varies.
Premenstrual symptoms
Many people notice symptoms such as bloating, breast tenderness, irritability or low mood in the week or two before a period. These usually ease once bleeding starts. Knowing when your next period is due helps you plan around them. If symptoms are severe enough to affect work, relationships or daily life, speak to a doctor: premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) is a recognised condition with effective treatments.
Period apps and this calculator
Period-tracking apps use the same basic method but average your cycle automatically as you log dates. This calculator doesn't store anything, so you'll need to work out your average and re-enter it. If you use an app, check its privacy policy, since cycle data is sensitive health information.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate my next period?
Add your average cycle length to the first day of your last period.
What counts as day 1?
The first day of full flow.
Is a 35-day cycle normal?
Yes, cycles from 21 to 35 days are typical for adults.
Why is my period late?
Stress, illness, weight change, exercise, contraception or pregnancy are common reasons.
Can I use this with irregular periods?
It will give an estimate, but it will be less reliable; tracking several months helps.
Does hormonal contraception change my cycle?
Yes; bleeds on the pill are withdrawal bleeds, so predictions may not apply.

Pregnancy Week Calculator: How Far Along Am I? | FigSumo (56 chars)
Meta description
Find how many weeks and days pregnant you are today from your last period or due date, with trimester and key milestone dates. (126 chars)

H1: Pregnancy Week Calculator
"How far along am I?" is one of the first questions in pregnancy. Doctors and midwives count pregnancy from the first day of your last menstrual period (LMP), not from conception, so at conception you're already about two weeks pregnant. This calculator works out your gestational age today, your estimated due date and your trimester.
How to use this calculator
Enter the first day of your last menstrual period. The date must be today or earlier.
Results:
Gestational age in weeks and days, as of today
Estimated due date
Trimester
How it works
Gestational age (days) = today − LMP
Weeks = days ÷ 7 (rounded down); days = the remainder
Due date = LMP + 280 days (40 weeks)
This is Naegele's rule, which assumes a 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14. If your cycles are longer or shorter, your dating scan may move the due date.
The calculator shows trimesters as weeks 1–12, 13–26 and 27 onwards. Sources differ slightly: ACOG counts the third trimester from week 28, and the NHS describes the first trimester as weeks 1 to 12.
Worked examples
Example 1: LMP 1 June 2026, checked on 14 October 2026
Days since LMP: 135
Gestational age: 19 weeks, 2 days
Due date: 8 March 2027
Second trimester (weeks 13–26)
Example 2: LMP 10 March 2026, checked on 14 October 2026
218 days = 31 weeks, 1 day
Due date: 15 December 2026
Understanding your results
"20 weeks, 3 days" means you've completed 20 weeks and are 3 days into week 21.
Due dates are estimates. Only about 4% of babies arrive on the due date [VERIFY]; most are born between 37 and 42 weeks.
Your scan date takes priority. A first-trimester ultrasound measuring the baby (crown-rump length) is the most accurate way to date a pregnancy; if it differs from your LMP date by more than a set amount, your care team will use the scan date.
IVF pregnancies are dated from the embryo transfer date, not LMP.

For an LMP of 1 June 2026, each completed week falls on a Monday, the same weekday as the LMP:

How many months pregnant am I?
Care teams count in weeks, but people often think in months. Forty weeks is a little over nine calendar months, so there's no exact conversion. A rough guide: weeks 1–13 cover months 1–3, weeks 14–27 months 4–6, and weeks 28–40 months 7–9.
Country notes
US: ACOG defines early term as 37w0d–38w6d, full term 39w0d–40w6d, late term 41w0d–41w6d and post-term 42w0d onward.
UK: the NHS offers a dating scan at 10 to 14 weeks and an anomaly scan at 18 to 21 weeks.
Canada: the SOGC recommends first-trimester ultrasound dating where available.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the date of conception. Use the first day of your last period.
Ignoring irregular cycles. If your cycles are long, your due date may be later.
Changing dates after the scan. Once your care team sets your due date, stick to it.
What the trimesters cover
First trimester (to week 12 or 13): the main organs form. Nausea, tiredness and breast tenderness are common. Most early miscarriages happen in this period, which is one reason many people wait until after the dating scan to share news.
Second trimester (to week 26 or 27): nausea often eases. The anatomy scan checks the baby's development, and many people first feel movement between about 16 and 24 weeks; it's often earlier in a second pregnancy.
Third trimester (to birth): the baby gains most of its weight. Antenatal appointments become more frequent, and your care team will ask about the baby's movements. Contact your maternity unit or doctor straight away if movements slow down or change; don't wait for the next appointment.
Gestational age is the measure your care team uses on scan reports and maternity notes, so quoting weeks and days in that format, such as 19+2, avoids confusion. UK maternity notes typically write it that way, and US and Canadian charts often write 19w2d.
Frequently asked questions
How many weeks pregnant am I?
Count the days since the first day of your last period and divide by 7.
Why is pregnancy 40 weeks?
It's counted from your last period, about two weeks before conception; the baby's actual age is about 38 weeks at the due date.
How accurate is the due date?
It's an estimate; most babies arrive within two weeks either side.
When does the second trimester start?
Around week 13 or 14, depending on the source.
What if I don't know my LMP?
A dating ultrasound can estimate gestational age.
Is this calculator right for IVF?
Not exactly; IVF dating uses the transfer date and embryo age.

Pregnancy Weight Gain Calculator (IOM Guidelines) | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description

H1: Pregnancy Weight Gain Calculator
Gaining a healthy amount of weight in pregnancy supports your baby's growth and lowers the risk of complications for both of you. How much is "healthy" depends mainly on your weight before pregnancy. This calculator uses your pre-pregnancy BMI to show the total weight gain recommended for a single baby by the US Institute of Medicine (IOM, now the National Academy of Medicine), and gives a rough figure for where you might be by your current week.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: metric or imperial.
2. Pre-pregnancy weight: your weight before you became pregnant (or at your first appointment if you don't know it).
3. Height.
4. Current pregnancy week (1–42).
Results:
Pre-pregnancy BMI
Total recommended gain for a full-term pregnancy, in kg and lb
Approximate gain by your current week (a simple mid-range estimate)
How it works
Step 1: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)².
Step 2: the IOM (2009) range for one baby:
Pre-pregnancy BMI
Total gain
Weekly rate, 2nd and 3rd trimesters
Under 18.5 (underweight)
12.5–18 kg (28–40 lb)
about 0.5 kg (1 lb)
18.5–24.9 (healthy weight)
11.5–16 kg (25–35 lb)
about 0.4 kg (1 lb)
25–29.9 (overweight)
7–11.5 kg (15–25 lb)
about 0.3 kg (0.6 lb)
30 or more (obese)
5–9 kg (11–20 lb)
about 0.2 kg (0.5 lb)
Step 3: gain by week. The calculator takes the middle of your range and scales it by week ÷ 40. This is a simplification: in practice most weight is gained after the first trimester. The IOM assumes 0.5 to 2 kg in the first trimester, then the weekly rates above.
Worked examples
Example 1: 65 kg, 165 cm, week 20
BMI = 65 ÷ 1.65² = 23.9 (healthy weight)
Recommended total gain: 11.5–16 kg (25–35 lb)
Calculator's by-week estimate: 13.75 × 20 ÷ 40 = 6.9 kg
IOM pattern for comparison: 0.5–2 kg by week 13 plus 0.35–0.50 kg a week for 7 weeks = about 2.9–5.5 kg
Example 2: 90 kg, 165 cm, week 30
BMI = 33.1 (obese)
Recommended total gain: 5–9 kg
By-week estimate: 7 × 30 ÷ 40 = 5.3 kg
Example 3: 50 kg, 165 cm, week 28
BMI = 50 ÷ 1.65² = 18.4 (underweight)
Recommended total gain: 12.5–18 kg (28–40 lb)
By-week estimate: 15.25 × 28 ÷ 40 = 10.7 kg
Example 4: 150 lb, 5 ft 4 in, week 36
150 lb = 68.0 kg; 5 ft 4 in = 162.6 cm
BMI = 25.7 (overweight)
Recommended total gain: 7–11.5 kg (15–25 lb)
By-week estimate: 9.25 × 36 ÷ 40 = 8.3 kg (18.4 lb)
A BMI just over 25 moves the recommended range down by several kilograms, so check that your pre-pregnancy weight and height are accurate.
Where the weight goes
At full term, a typical gain is made up of roughly:
Component
Approximate weight
Baby
3.5 kg
Placenta
0.7 kg
Amniotic fluid
0.8 kg
Uterus
0.9 kg
Breast tissue
0.4 kg
Blood volume
1.5 kg
Other fluid
1.5 kg
Fat stores
3–4 kg
These are approximate averages from obstetric textbooks [VERIFY]; individual pregnancies vary.
Understanding your results
Ranges, not targets. Gaining a little above or below the range isn't automatically a problem; your midwife or doctor will look at the trend.
Too little gain is linked to a higher risk of a small baby and preterm birth.
Too much gain is linked to gestational diabetes, high blood pressure, a large baby, caesarean birth and retaining weight after birth.
Twins or more: the ranges above are for one baby. The IOM gives provisional ranges for twins (for example 17–25 kg for a healthy BMI), which this calculator doesn't show.
Morning sickness can mean little or no gain, or a small loss, in the first trimester.
Eating in pregnancy
You don't need to "eat for two". Most guidance suggests no extra calories in the first trimester, about 340 extra kcal a day in the second and about 450 in the third (US). The NHS says extra energy is only needed in the last three months, about 200 kcal a day. Focus on nutrient-rich foods, take folic acid (400 micrograms a day until 12 weeks) and vitamin D, and avoid alcohol.
Country notes
US: ACOG endorses the IOM 2009 guidelines.
Canada: Health Canada uses the same IOM ranges and BMI categories.
UK: NICE doesn't set official weight gain targets; midwives usually weigh you at booking and focus on healthy eating and activity. Many UK clinicians still refer to the IOM ranges.
Tips and common mistakes
Using your current weight instead of pre-pregnancy weight.
Dieting to lose weight during pregnancy. Not recommended unless advised by your care team.
Comparing week-by-week with friends. Patterns vary; the trend matters most.
Ignoring rapid gain. Sudden swelling or fast weight gain can be a sign of pre-eclampsia; contact your maternity unit.
Frequently asked questions
How much weight should I gain during pregnancy?
It depends on your pre-pregnancy BMI: 11.5–16 kg (25–35 lb) for a healthy BMI, less if you were overweight, more if underweight.
How much should I gain in the first trimester?
About 0.5 to 2 kg for most people.
Is it safe to lose weight while pregnant?
Generally no, unless your doctor recommends it.
How much weight do I lose after birth?
About 5 to 6 kg straight away (baby, placenta, fluid), with more over the following weeks.
Does BMI work in pregnancy?
Use pre-pregnancy BMI only; BMI during pregnancy isn't meaningful.
What if I'm expecting twins?
Gain ranges are higher; ask your care team.
How much extra should I eat?
Typically none in the first trimester and modest amounts later.

Protein Calculator: Grams of Protein per Day | FigSumo (54 chars)

Estimate daily protein in grams from body weight, from the 0.8 g/kg adult RDA upward for active people, with the share of calories it represents. (145 chars)

H1: Protein Calculator
Protein builds and repairs muscle and other tissues, and makes enzymes and hormones. How much you need depends mostly on your body weight and how active you are. This calculator gives a daily protein target in grams based on your weight and goal, along with the calories that protein provides.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: metric (kg) or imperial (lb).
2. Body weight.
3. Goal:
General health: 0.8 g per kg
Active / endurance: 1.2 g per kg
Strength / muscle gain: 1.6 g per kg
High intake: 2.0 g per kg
Results: daily protein (grams), calories from protein and the guideline used.
How it works
Protein (g/day) = body weight (kg) × grams per kg
Calories from protein = protein g × 4
Weights in pounds are converted with 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg.
0.8 g/kg is the Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for adults set by the US National Academies, used in the US and Canada. It's the amount that meets the needs of nearly all healthy adults, not an optimal figure for athletes. The higher settings reflect sports nutrition position stands, which suggest 1.2–2.0 g/kg for active people.
Worked examples
Example 1: 70 kg, active
70 × 1.2 = 84 g a day
Calories from protein: 336 kcal
At the RDA (0.8 g/kg), the same person needs 56 g.
On a 2,200 kcal diet, 84 g is about 15% of calories.
Example 2: 180 lb, strength training
180 lb = 81.65 kg
× 1.6 = 131 g a day (523 kcal)
Example 3: a day that reaches 84 g

Understanding your results
Spread it out. Muscle protein synthesis responds best to about 0.3–0.4 g/kg per meal over three to four meals. For 70 kg, that's 21–28 g per meal.
More isn't always better. Benefits for muscle growth tend to plateau around 1.6 g/kg for most people; intakes above 2 g/kg are rarely needed.
Weight loss: higher protein (1.2–1.6 g/kg or more) helps preserve muscle in a calorie deficit and can help with fullness.
People with obesity: basing the target on your actual weight can overestimate needs. Some dietitians use a goal or adjusted weight instead.
Older adults: some experts recommend 1.0–1.2 g/kg for people over 65 to help limit muscle loss.

Country notes
US and Canada: RDA 0.8 g/kg for adults; 71 g a day during pregnancy (or 1.1 g/kg) [VERIFY current DRI table].
UK: the Reference Nutrient Intake (RNI) is 0.75 g/kg a day for adults, about 56 g for men and 45 g for women.
Nutrition labels in all three countries list protein per serving or per 100 g.
Protein on food labels
US: the Nutrition Facts label lists protein in grams. A % Daily Value, based on 50 g a day, is only required when a protein claim is made or the food is for young children.
Canada: the Nutrition Facts table lists protein in grams but gives no % Daily Value for it.
UK: labels list protein per 100 g, and the reference intake for an average adult is 50 g a day.
These label figures are general reference amounts. Your own target from the calculator may be higher, especially if you train regularly.
Tips and common mistakes
Counting all of a food's weight as protein. 100 g of chicken has about 31 g of protein, not 100 g.
Relying on supplements. Food sources also provide fibre, vitamins and minerals; powders are a convenience, not a requirement.
Ignoring kidney disease. People with chronic kidney disease may need to limit protein; ask your doctor.
Forgetting plant proteins. Beans, lentils, tofu, nuts and whole grains all count.
Frequently asked questions
How much protein do I need a day?
At least 0.8 g per kg of body weight for most adults, more if you're very active or training for strength.
How much protein to build muscle?
About 1.6 g/kg is a widely used target for people doing resistance training.
Can I eat too much protein?
Healthy adults tolerate up to about 2 g/kg well; very high intakes offer little extra benefit.
Should I use lean body mass?
Some people do, especially with high body fat. See the lean body mass calculator.
Is plant protein as good as animal protein?
A varied plant diet can meet needs; some plant proteins are lower in certain amino acids, so mix sources.
Do I need protein right after a workout?
Total daily intake matters most; a meal with protein within a few hours of training is enough.

Target Heart Rate Calculator

Title tag
Target Heart Rate Calculator by Age | FigSumo (45 chars)
Meta description
Find your estimated maximum heart rate and moderate and vigorous target zones by age, as described by the CDC and American Heart Association. (141 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,033 (minimum 1,000)
H1: Target Heart Rate Calculator
Your target heart rate zone is the range of beats per minute (bpm) that gives a moderate to vigorous workout. Exercising in this zone improves heart and lung fitness without pushing to your limit. This calculator estimates your maximum heart rate from your age and gives a target zone of 50% to 85%, using either a simple percentage of maximum or the Karvonen method if you enter your resting heart rate.
How to use this calculator
1. Age (1–120).
2. Resting heart rate (optional): your pulse when fully at rest, ideally first thing in the morning before getting up (30–120 bpm).
Results: estimated maximum heart rate, target zone low and high, and the method used.
How it works
Maximum heart rate:
Max HR = 220 − age
Without resting heart rate (percent of max):
Low = 0.50 × Max HR;  High = 0.85 × Max HR
With resting heart rate (Karvonen, heart rate reserve):
HRR  = Max HR − Resting HR
Low  = Resting HR + 0.50 × HRR
High = Resting HR + 0.85 × HRR
The Karvonen method personalises the zone: two people of the same age with different resting heart rates get different targets.
Worked examples
Example 1: age 40, no resting heart rate
Max HR = 220 − 40 = 180 bpm
Target zone: 90–153 bpm
Moderate intensity (50–70%): 90–126 bpm; vigorous (70–85%): 126–153 bpm
Example 2: age 40, resting heart rate 60
HRR = 180 − 60 = 120
Low = 60 + 0.50 × 120 = 120 bpm
High = 60 + 0.85 × 120 = 162 bpm
Example 3: age 65, resting heart rate 72
Max HR 155; Karvonen zone 114–143 bpm (percent-of-max gives 78–132)
Example 4: comparing 220 − age with Tanaka at 60
220 − 60 = 160 bpm; Tanaka: 208 − 0.7 × 60 = 166 bpm
50–85% zone: 80–136 bpm with 220 − age, or 83–141 bpm with Tanaka
The difference grows with age, which is why the choice of formula matters more for older exercisers. The calculator currently uses 220 − age.

Understanding your results
220 − age is a rough estimate. Real maximum heart rates vary by 10 to 12 bpm or more either way. The Tanaka formula (208 − 0.7 × age) is an alternative that tends to be more accurate for older adults; for a 40-year-old it gives 180 bpm.
Moderate vs vigorous. The American Heart Association describes moderate intensity as about 50–70% of maximum and vigorous as about 70–85%. The CDC uses slightly higher bands (64–76% moderate, 77–93% vigorous), so the boundary between "moderate" and "vigorous" depends on the source.
Talk test. At moderate intensity you can talk but not sing; at vigorous intensity you can say only a few words without pausing for breath.
Medicines matter. Beta blockers and some other drugs lower heart rate, so zones based on age won't apply. Ask your doctor.
Five-zone training model
Many fitness watches and coaching plans split effort into five zones by percentage of maximum heart rate. For a 40-year-old with an estimated maximum of 180 bpm:
Zone

Heart rate
Typical use
Zone 1
50–60%

Zone 2

The calculator's 50–85% range covers zones 1 to 4. Brands label zones slightly differently, so check your device's settings before comparing numbers.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US: the American Heart Association publishes target heart rate tables using 220 − age and 50–85%.
Canada: Heart & Stroke and the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines describe intensity mainly with the talk test and perceived effort rather than heart rate numbers.
UK: the NHS describes a normal adult resting heart rate as 60 to 100 bpm and recommends the talk test for judging moderate and vigorous activity.
Measuring your heart rate
Find your pulse on the inside of your wrist or the side of your neck.
Count beats for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 (or 30 seconds × 2).
Chest-strap monitors are more accurate than wrist-based optical sensors during intense exercise.
How much exercise?
US, Canadian and UK guidelines all recommend adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days.
Tips and common mistakes
Measuring resting heart rate after coffee or exercise. Measure on waking.
Chasing the top of the zone every session. Most training should be at easy to moderate intensity.
Ignoring warning signs. Stop and seek help if you have chest pain, severe breathlessness, dizziness or an irregular heartbeat.
Frequently asked questions
What is a good target heart rate?
For most adults, 50% to 85% of maximum heart rate.
How do I calculate my maximum heart rate?
The common estimate is 220 minus your age.
What is a normal resting heart rate?
For adults, 60 to 100 bpm; fit people often have lower rates.
What is the Karvonen formula?
It uses your heart rate reserve (max minus resting) to set the target zone.
Is it dangerous to exceed my max heart rate?
The estimate isn't a hard limit, but if you feel unwell, slow down. Talk to a doctor before vigorous exercise if you have heart disease.
Which zone burns the most fat?
Lower intensities use a higher proportion of fat, but higher intensities burn more total calories.

TDEE Calculator

https://figsumo.com/tdee-calculator
Title tag
TDEE Calculator: Total Daily Energy Expenditure | FigSumo (57 chars)
Meta description
Estimate total daily energy expenditure from BMR and activity level, and see how many calories a chosen weekly weight change implies. (133 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
1,010 (minimum 1,000)
H1: TDEE Calculator
Total daily energy expenditure (TDEE) is the number of calories you burn in a day, including everything from breathing to exercise. Eat about this many calories and your weight should stay roughly the same. This calculator estimates your TDEE from your age, sex, height, weight and activity level, and shows calorie targets for gradual weight loss and gain.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: metric or imperial.
2. Age, sex, weight and height.
3. Activity level:
Sedentary: little or no exercise (× 1.2)
Light: exercise 1–3 days a week (× 1.375)
Moderate: 3–5 days a week (× 1.55)
Active: 6–7 days a week (× 1.725)
Very active: hard daily exercise or a physical job (× 1.9)
Results: BMR, TDEE (maintenance), weight-loss target (TDEE − 500) and weight-gain target (TDEE + 500), with a chart splitting BMR and activity.
How it works
BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor):
Men:   BMR = 10W + 6.25H − 5A + 5
Women: BMR = 10W + 6.25H − 5A − 161
W = weight in kg, H = height in cm, A = age in years.
TDEE = BMR × activity factor.
TDEE has four parts: BMR (usually 60–70% of the total), the thermic effect of food (about 10%), exercise, and non-exercise activity such as walking, standing and fidgeting (NEAT). The activity factor bundles the last three.
Worked examples
Example 1: man, 30, 80 kg, 180 cm, moderate activity
BMR = 800 + 1,125 − 150 + 5 = 1,780 kcal
TDEE = 1,780 × 1.55 = 2,759 kcal
Activity adds 979 kcal
Weight loss (−500): 2,259 kcal; weight gain (+500): 3,259 kcal
The same man at each activity level:
Activity
TDEE (kcal)
Sedentary
2,136
Light
2,448
Moderate
2,759
Active
3,071
Very active
3,382
Example 2: woman, 55, 70 kg, 160 cm, sedentary
BMR = 700 + 1,000 − 275 − 161 = 1,264 kcal
TDEE = × 1.2 = 1,517 kcal; −500 target 1,017 kcal
Example 3: woman, 35, 150 lb, 5 ft 5 in, light activity
150 lb = 68.0 kg; 5 ft 5 in = 165.1 cm
BMR = 10 × 68.0 + 6.25 × 165.1 − 5 × 35 − 161 = 1,376 kcal
TDEE = 1,376 × 1.375 = 1,892 kcal; −500 target 1,392 kcal
Example 4: how TDEE falls as weight drops
If the man in Example 1 loses 10 kg, his BMR falls by 10 × 10 = 100 kcal to 1,680 kcal, and his moderate-activity TDEE falls to 2,604 kcal, 155 kcal less than before. A 2,259 kcal target that was 500 below maintenance at 80 kg is only 345 below at 70 kg, which is one reason weight loss slows. Recalculate as your weight changes.
Understanding your results
It's an estimate. Mifflin-St Jeor predicts resting energy within about 10% for most adults, and activity factors add more uncertainty.
Test and adjust. Eat at your TDEE for two to three weeks and track your weight. If it's rising, your real TDEE is lower; if it's falling, it's higher.
500 kcal a day below TDEE is roughly 0.45 kg (about 1 lb) a week using the old 7,700 kcal per kg rule. In practice, weight loss slows over time as your body adapts and you get lighter; the NIH Body Weight Planner models this.
Don't go too low. Very low-calorie diets (under about 800 kcal a day) should only be followed under medical supervision. Many guidelines suggest not going below about 1,200 kcal (women) or 1,500 kcal (men) without advice.
Weight gain: a surplus of 250–500 kcal with resistance training favours muscle over fat.
Choosing an activity level
Most people overestimate their activity. An office worker who goes to the gym three times a week is usually "light" to "moderate", not "active". Fitness trackers can help, but their calorie estimates can be off by 20% or more.
Country notes
US: Dietary Guidelines for Americans list estimated calorie needs from about 1,600 to 2,400 for adult women and 2,000 to 3,000 for adult men, depending on age and activity.
UK: reference intakes on labels are based on 2,000 kcal for women and 2,500 kcal for men.
Canada: Health Canada uses the same Dietary Reference Intakes (energy equations) as the US.
From TDEE to macros
Once you've chosen a calorie target, you can split it between protein, carbohydrate and fat. For 2,259 kcal at 30% protein, 40% carbohydrate and 30% fat:
Protein: 2,259 × 0.30 ÷ 4 = 169 g
Carbohydrate: 2,259 × 0.40 ÷ 4 = 226 g
Fat: 2,259 × 0.30 ÷ 9 = 75 g
The macro calculator does this split for you with other ratios.
Tips and common mistakes
Counting exercise twice: choosing a high activity level and also adding workout calories from a tracker.
Using outdated weight. Recalculate after every 5 kg change.
Expecting linear weight loss. Water and glycogen cause day-to-day swings; look at weekly averages.
Frequently asked questions
What is TDEE?
Total daily energy expenditure: your BMR plus calories from digestion and activity.
What's the difference between BMR and TDEE?
BMR is energy at complete rest; TDEE includes everything you do in a day. See the BMR calculator.
How do I lose weight with TDEE?
Eat below it; about 500 kcal less a day is a common starting point.
How accurate is TDEE?
It's an estimate; adjust based on your weight trend over several weeks.
Which BMR formula does this use?
Mifflin-St Jeor, recommended by the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics for healthy adults.
Should I eat back exercise calories?
Not if you've already chosen an activity level that includes your exercise.
Does TDEE change with age?
Yes; BMR falls by about 5 kcal a day per year of age in the formula, and muscle loss with age lowers it further.

Waist-to-Height Ratio Calculator | FigSumo (42 chars)

Calculate your waist-to-height ratio and compare it with the NHS guide of keeping your waist below half your height. (116 chars)

H1: Waist-to-Height Ratio Calculator
Waist-to-height ratio (WHtR) compares the size of your waist with your height. It's a simple way to check for excess fat around the middle (central or abdominal fat), which is linked to type 2 diabetes, heart disease and high blood pressure. The UK's National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends it alongside BMI, with one easy rule: keep your waist to less than half your height.
How to use this calculator
1. Units: centimetres or inches.
2. Waist: measured as described below.
3. Height: without shoes.
Results: your waist-to-height ratio, its health risk category, and the waist size that would equal half your height.
How to measure your waist
NICE and the NHS describe the method:
1. Find the bottom of your ribs and the top of your hips.
2. Wrap a tape measure around your middle at a point halfway between them (for many people, this is just above the belly button).
3. Breathe out naturally and measure. Don't pull the tape tight or hold your stomach in.
NICE's own worked example: a 38 in waist and a 67 in height (5 ft 7 in) give 0.57.
Use the same tape and the same point each time to track change.
The formula
WHtR = waist ÷ height
Both measurements must be in the same unit, so the result has no units and is the same in centimetres or inches.
NICE categories (adults)
Ratio
Category
Under 0.4
Below NICE's healthy range ("take care" in Ashwell's chart; may reflect low weight)
0.4 to 0.49
Healthy central adiposity, no increased health risk
0.5 to 0.59
Increased central adiposity, increased health risk
0.6 or more
High central adiposity, further increased health risk
NICE says these classifications can be used for adults with a BMI under 35, of both sexes and all ethnicities, including people with high muscle mass. The "under 0.4" band isn't part of the NICE classification.
Worked examples
Example 1: waist 84 cm, height 175 cm
84 ÷ 175 = 0.48 → healthy
Half of height: 87.5 cm, so this waist is comfortably below it.
Example 2: waist 38 in, height 64 in (5 ft 4 in)
38 ÷ 64 = 0.59 → increased health risk
Half of height is 32 in, so reducing the waist by 6 in would bring the ratio to 0.5.
Example 3: waist 101 cm, height 162 cm
0.62 → high health risk
Example 4: man, 6 ft (72 in), waist 40 in
40 ÷ 72 = 0.56 → increased health risk
Half of height is 36 in, so a 4 in smaller waist would bring the ratio to 0.5.
Example 5: tracking a change
A woman 168 cm tall reduces her waist from 92 cm to 86 cm. Her ratio falls from 0.55 to 0.51, moving from the increased-risk band into the healthy band.

A waist between the 0.4 and 0.5 columns for your height is in NICE's healthy range.
Why waist-to-height ratio?
It accounts for height. A 90 cm waist means something different on someone 160 cm tall than on someone 190 cm tall.
It detects central fat that BMI misses. People with a "healthy" BMI can still carry risky abdominal fat.
One cut-off for everyone. Unlike waist circumference alone, the 0.5 threshold works across sexes and ethnic groups in research.
Predicts risk well. Studies have found WHtR predicts cardiometabolic risk at least as well as BMI or waist size alone.
Understanding your results
A ratio of 0.5 or more doesn't mean you have a disease; it means your risk is higher and it may be worth discussing with a doctor, especially with other risk factors such as high blood pressure or a family history of diabetes.
Changes over time matter. Losing even a few centimetres from your waist reduces risk.
Pregnancy: WHtR isn't meaningful during pregnancy.
Children: NICE applies the same bands to children and young people aged 5 and over. The NHS has a separate waist-to-height calculator for children.
Country notes
UK: NICE guideline NG246 (overweight and obesity management, 2025; the waist-to-height recommendations date from 2022) advises adults with a BMI under 35 to measure their own WHtR and to seek advice if it shows increased risk.
US: the CDC and NIH use waist circumference: higher risk above 40 in (102 cm) for men and 35 in (88 cm) for most women.
Canada: Obesity Canada and Health Canada guidance use waist circumference with similar cut-offs.
Tips and common mistakes
Measuring at the belt line. Many people wear trousers below the natural waist.
Measuring after a large meal.
Mixing units. Use centimetres for both or inches for both.
Frequently asked questions
What is a healthy waist-to-height ratio?
Between 0.4 and 0.49 for adults.
How do I calculate my waist-to-height ratio?
Divide your waist measurement by your height, in the same units.
Is waist-to-height ratio better than BMI?
It's a useful addition: it shows fat distribution, which BMI doesn't.
What does a ratio over 0.5 mean?
Increased health risk from central fat; over 0.6 is high risk.
Does it work for men and women?
Yes, the same thresholds apply.
How can I reduce my waist size?
A combination of a calorie deficit, regular physical activity and less alcohol helps reduce abdominal fat.

Area Calculator: Square, Circle, Triangle & More | FigSumo (58 chars)
