H1: Age Calculator
How old are you, exactly? This calculator gives your age in completed years, as years, months and days, and as a total count of days, between your date of birth and any other date. Use it for forms, eligibility checks, milestones or simply curiosity.
How to use this calculator
1. Date of birth: pick or type the date (YYYY-MM-DD).
2. Calculate age as of: the date you want the age on. It's set to 1 January 2026 by default; change it to today, a future date (how old will I be on…?) or a past one.
Results: age in years, years, months and days, and total days, with a breakdown table.
The as-of date must be on or after the birth date.
How age is calculated
Age is counted in completed units, the way it's used legally and on official forms:
1. Years: the number of full birthdays reached by the as-of date.
2. Months: full months since the last birthday.
3. Days: remaining days since the last "monthiversary".
4. Total days: the calendar difference between the two dates, including every leap day in between.
Because months have 28 to 31 days, the months-and-days figure depends on where the count starts; that's why two tools can differ by a day in edge cases, while total days always agree.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
Born 15 June 1990, age on 1 January 2026:
Last birthday: 15 June 2025 → 35 years
15 June to 15 December = 6 months; 15 December to 1 January = 17 days
35 years, 6 months, 17 days, or 12,984 days in total (1,854 weeks, about 311,616 hours)
Example 2: a different as-of date
Born 10 March 1985, age on 15 October 2026: 41 years, 7 months, 5 days, or 15,194 days.
Example 3: "How old will I be?"
Want to know your age on a retirement date or at a child's graduation? Enter that future date as the as-of date.
Age rules worth knowing
Birthdays on 29 February: in non-leap years, many jurisdictions treat the legal birthday as 28 February or 1 March; the rule varies by country and purpose [VERIFY for your jurisdiction].
"Age next birthday", used by some insurers, is your completed age plus one.
East Asian age reckoning, where a baby is one at birth, is different: South Korea standardised on international age for legal purposes in June 2023.
Full retirement age for US Social Security, UK State Pension age and CPP eligibility all depend on exact birth date; see the retirement calculator.
Common uses
Checking age limits for school entry, driving, voting or alcohol.
Pension and benefits eligibility.
Insurance quotes and travel visas.
Calculating a pet's or a building's age.
Counting days for a milestone such as 10,000 days old (about 27 years and 4 months).
Understanding your results
Total days counts the as-of date but not the birth date (the same as subtracting dates).
Time zones and birth times are ignored; the calculation is by calendar date.
For a plain day count between any two dates, use the day counter; to add or subtract days, use the date calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Leaving the as-of date at its default when you want today's age.
Typing dates in the wrong order (MM/DD vs DD/MM); the picker uses year-month-day.
Rounding up: someone who is 17 years and 11 months is 17, not 18.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate my exact age?
Enter your birth date and today's date.
How many days old am I?
The "total days" result shows it.
Does it account for leap years?
Yes; every 29 February between the dates is counted.
Can I calculate age on a future date?
Yes. Set the as-of date in the future.
Why does my age in months and days differ from another site?
Months have different lengths, so methods vary at month ends. The years and total days should match.
What if I was born on 29 February?
The calculator uses calendar arithmetic; check local rules for legal purposes.

Base64 Encode and Decode Online | FigSumo (41 chars)

Encode text to Base64 or decode Base64 back to text in your browser, with UTF-8 support and URL-safe variant. Nothing is uploaded. (130 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
604 (minimum 600)
H1: Base64 Encoder and Decoder
Base64 turns any data into plain text made of 64 safe characters (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, + and /). It's how email attachments travel, how small images are embedded in web pages and CSS, and how many APIs pass binary data inside JSON. This tool encodes text to Base64 or decodes Base64 back to readable text, entirely in your browser.
How to use this tool
1. Text: paste the text to encode, or the Base64 string to decode.
2. Mode: "Encode to Base64" or "Decode from Base64".
Result: the Base64 output or the decoded text. Text is handled as UTF-8, so accents, non-Latin scripts and emoji work. If the input isn't valid Base64, you'll see "Could not decode".
How Base64 works
1. Convert the text to bytes (UTF-8).
2. Take the bytes three at a time: 3 bytes = 24 bits.
3. Split the 24 bits into four 6-bit groups (values 0–63).
4. Map each value to a character: 0–25 → A–Z, 26–51 → a–z, 52–61 → 0–9, 62 → +, 63 → /.
5. If the last group has only one or two bytes, pad the output with = signs.
Every 3 bytes become 4 characters, so encoded data is about 33% larger than the original.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
"Hello, Figsumo!" → SGVsbG8sIEZpZ3N1bW8h
Example 2: three letters, step by step
"Man" in ASCII is 77, 97, 110 → binary 01001101 01100001 01101110 → 6-bit groups 19, 22, 5, 46 → TWFu.
Example 3: padding
"Ma" → TWE= (one = for a missing byte); "M" → TQ== (two).
Example 4: non-English text
"café" → Y2Fmw6k=. The é takes two bytes in UTF-8, which is why the output is longer than for "cafe".
Example 5: an HTTP Basic auth header
"user:pass" → dXNlcjpwYXNz. Anyone can decode this, which is why Basic authentication must only be used over HTTPS.
Where you'll see Base64
Email (MIME): attachments are Base64 encoded.
Data URIs: data:image/png;base64,iVBOR… embeds an image directly in HTML or CSS.
JSON Web Tokens (JWT): the header and payload are base64url encoded; decode them to inspect claims.
API keys and certificates: PEM files (-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----) contain Base64.
Variants
Variant
Characters 62, 63
Padding
Standard (RFC 4648) — this tool
+ /
=
base64url (URLs, JWT)
- _
Often omitted
MIME
+ /
=, with line breaks every 76 characters
To decode base64url here, replace - with + and _ with /, and add = until the length is a multiple of 4.
Base64 is not encryption
Base64 is reversible by anyone, with no key. Never use it to hide passwords or personal data. For secrets, use proper encryption; for strong passwords, use the password generator.
Privacy
Encoding and decoding run in your browser. The text you paste isn't sent to FigSumo's servers.
Tips and common mistakes
Stray spaces or line breaks inside pasted Base64 can cause decode errors; leading and trailing spaces are trimmed.
Missing padding from base64url strings.
Decoding binary files as text gives garbled characters; that data was an image or file, not text.
Confusing Base64 with URL encoding. For query strings, use the URL encoder.
Practice
A 300-byte file becomes exactly 400 Base64 characters.
Frequently asked questions
What is Base64 used for?
Sending binary data through text-only channels such as email, JSON and HTML.
Is Base64 secure?
No. It's an encoding, not encryption.
Why does Base64 end with = or ==?
Padding, when the input length isn't a multiple of 3 bytes.
Why is the output longer than the input?
Every 3 bytes become 4 characters (about 33% more).
Does it support emoji and accents?
Yes, via UTF-8.
Can I encode an image?
Not yet; this tool handles text.

H1: Bra Size Calculator
A bra that fits depends on two measurements: the band (around your ribcage, just under the bust) and the bust (around the fullest part). This calculator uses both, in inches, to suggest a US bra size, and shows the difference that sets the cup.
How to measure
You'll need a soft tape measure. Wear a non-padded bra or none.
1. Underbust: wrap the tape snugly around your ribcage directly under the bust, keeping it level and exhaling normally.
2. Bust: measure loosely around the fullest part of the bust, tape level across the back.
Stand straight and look in a mirror to check the tape isn't riding up at the back.
How to use this calculator
1. Underbust (in): default 32.
2. Bust (in): default 36.
Results: suggested US size (band and cup) and cup difference in inches.
How the size is worked out
band = underbust, rounded to the nearest inch
cup difference = bust − underbust, rounded to the nearest inch
Each inch of difference is one cup size:

US and UK bands use the same numbers in inches, but cup letters diverge after DD, so a US 34G is roughly a UK 34F. Brands vary; this table is a common guide, not a standard [VERIFY against brand charts].
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
Underbust 32, bust 36: band 32, difference 4 in → 32D.
Example 2: a larger cup
Underbust 34, bust 39: difference 5 in → 34DD (US and UK).
Example 3: an odd band measurement
Underbust 31 in: bands are usually sold in even sizes, so try both 30 and 32. Going up a band usually means going down a cup to keep the same volume (see sister sizes below).
Sister sizes
Cup volume is tied to the band: a 32D, 34C and 36B hold about the same volume. If the cup fits but the band is loose, go down a band and up a cup (34C → 32D). If the band is tight, go up a band and down a cup.
Signs of a good fit
Band: level all round, firm on the loosest hook when new (it will stretch). It should provide most of the support.
Cups: no gaping or spilling over the edge.
Centre gore: lies flat against the breastbone on underwired styles.
Straps: stay put without digging in.
Understanding your results
A calculation is a starting point. Shape, brand, style (plunge, balconette, sports) and fabric all change fit.
Some fitters still use the older "plus four" method, adding 4–5 in to the underbust for the band, which tends to give a looser band and smaller cup letter than this method.
Bodies change with weight, pregnancy, breastfeeding and age; re-measure every year or so.
Tips and common mistakes
Pulling the tape too tight on the bust, or too loose on the band.
Measuring over a padded bra.
Sticking with one size across brands. Try the sister sizes too.
Assuming D is "large". Cup letters are relative to band size.
Frequently asked questions
How do I find my bra size?
Measure underbust and bust; the difference sets the cup.
What does 32D mean?
A 32-inch band with about a 4-inch difference between bust and band.
Is DD the same as E?
In UK sizing, E comes after DD. In US sizing, DDD (often labelled F) comes after DD.
What is a sister size?
A size with the same cup volume on a different band, such as 34C and 32D.
Can I measure in centimetres?
Convert to inches first (divide by 2.54), or use the unit converter.
How often should I re-measure?
Every 6–12 months, or after weight change or pregnancy.

H1: BTU Calculator
BTU (British thermal unit) per hour is how air conditioners, heat pumps and heaters are rated. Buy a unit that's too small and it runs constantly without keeping up; too large and it cycles on and off, wastes energy and leaves the room damp. This calculator estimates the capacity a room needs from its length, width, ceiling height and how demanding its conditions are.
How to use this calculator
1. Room length (ft) and room width (ft): inside wall to wall (default 14 × 12).
2. Ceiling height (ft): default 8.
3. Climate factor: mild, average, or cold / sunny.
Results: estimated BTU/hr and room volume (ft³).
How room AC sizing works
The most widely used guide for room air conditioners is ENERGY STAR's chart, which sizes by floor area for an 8 ft ceiling:

Then adjust:

Higher ceilings mean more air to cool, so scale up proportionally (a 10 ft ceiling is 25% more volume than 8 ft).
Worked examples
Example 1: a bedroom
14 × 12 ft = 168 ft² (volume 1,344 ft³) → 6,000 BTU/hr. Very sunny: 6,600. With four people regularly using it: 6,000 + 2 × 600 = 7,200.
Example 2: a kitchen-diner
20 × 16 ft = 320 ft² → 8,000 BTU/hr, plus 4,000 for the kitchen = 12,000 BTU/hr.
Example 3: converting units
6,000 BTU/hr is about 1.76 kW of cooling. One "ton" of cooling is 12,000 BTU/hr, so a 2-ton system delivers 24,000 BTU/hr.
Heating vs cooling
Heating needs depend far more on climate, insulation and how warm you want the room compared with outside. Rough rules of thumb range from about 20 BTU/hr per ft² in mild climates with good insulation to 50–60 in cold climates with poor insulation [VERIFY for your climate zone]. For whole-house systems, installers in the US and Canada should carry out a Manual J load calculation; in the UK, heating engineers do a room-by-room heat-loss survey.
Understanding your results
It's an estimate. Windows, insulation, appliances and orientation matter.
Round to the nearest available unit size, usually the next size up if you're between two.
Portable units are often rated under a newer standard (SACC) that gives lower BTU figures than the older ASHRAE rating; compare like with like.
Running cost: use the electricity calculator with the unit's wattage.
Tips and common mistakes
Oversizing. A unit that's too big cools quickly without removing humidity, leaving the room clammy.
Ignoring open-plan spaces. Include connected areas without doors.
Measuring outside walls instead of the room's interior.
Forgetting heat sources such as computers, TVs and cooking.
Frequently asked questions
How many BTUs do I need for a 12 × 12 room?
144 ft² sits in the 100–150 band: about 5,000 BTU/hr, more if very sunny.
What does BTU stand for?
British thermal unit: the heat needed to raise one pound of water by 1 °F.
How many BTUs per square foot?
Roughly 20–40 BTU/hr per ft² for cooling, depending on room size.
Is a bigger air conditioner better?
No. It short-cycles and doesn't dehumidify well.
How do I convert BTU to kW?
Multiply BTU/hr by 0.000293.
What's a ton of air conditioning?
12,000 BTU/hr.

Title tag
Concrete Calculator: Slabs, Footings, Columns | FigSumo (55 chars)
Meta description
Calculate concrete volume in cubic yards or cubic metres for slabs, footings, columns and steps, plus bags of premix needed with waste allowance. (145 chars)
Country

641 (minimum 600)
H1: Concrete Calculator
Ordering concrete is a balance: too little and you're left with a cold joint halfway through the pour; too much and you're paying for waste. This calculator converts a slab's length, width and depth into the cubic yards a ready-mix supplier needs, plus cubic feet for working out bagged concrete.
How to use this calculator
1. Length (ft) and width (ft): the slab's outline (default 12 × 10).
2. Depth (in): thickness in inches (default 4).
Results: cubic yards (highlighted) and cubic feet, with a chart splitting the volume into whole cubic yards and leftover cubic feet.
The formula
ft³ = length × width × (depth ÷ 12)
yd³ = ft³ ÷ 27
Depth is divided by 12 to turn inches into feet; there are 27 ft³ in a cubic yard (3 × 3 × 3).
Worked examples
Example 1: the default patio
12 × 10 × (4 ÷ 12) = 40 ft³ = 1.48 yd³. Adding 10% for waste and uneven ground: order 1.63 yd³, which most suppliers will round to the nearest quarter or half yard.
Example 2: in bags
Bagged mix yields roughly 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb bag and 0.45 ft³ per 60 lb bag (check the bag). For 40 ft³: 67 × 80 lb or 89 × 60 lb bags, before waste. At that volume, ready-mix delivery is usually easier.
Example 3: a two-car garage
24 × 24 ft at 5 in deep = 8.89 yd³.
Example 4: fence post footings (round)
Not yet built in; work it out by hand. A 12 in diameter hole 3 ft deep: π × 0.5² × 3 = 2.36 ft³ each. Four posts: 9.42 ft³ = 0.35 yd³ (bagged mix is the practical choice).
Example 5: metric
A 4 m × 3 m slab, 100 mm thick: 4 × 3 × 0.1 = 1.2 m³. Enter the dimensions in feet and inches to use the calculator, or work in metres directly as shown.
Planning the pour
Waste allowance: 5–10% for flat, well-prepared ground; more for irregular shapes or soft subgrade.
Sub-base: most slabs sit on 4 in or so of compacted gravel; see the gravel calculator.
Thickness at edges: thickened edges or footings add volume; calculate them separately and add.
Minimum orders: many ready-mix suppliers charge a short-load fee under a few cubic yards [VERIFY with local suppliers].
Reinforcement: mesh or rebar is set by the job and local code, not by volume.
Concrete in the US, Canada and UK
US: ready-mix is ordered in cubic yards; bags in pounds.
Canada: suppliers usually quote cubic metres (1 yd³ ≈ 0.7646 m³); bags in kilograms.
UK: ready-mix in cubic metres; bags of 20–25 kg, with yields printed on the bag.
Understanding your results
The whole yards / extra feet chart helps when a supplier sells in whole or half yards.
Results assume a rectangle with a uniform depth. For L-shapes, split into rectangles and add the volumes.
Uneven ground is the biggest cause of shortfalls: a slab meant to be 4 in that averages 4.5 in needs 12.5% more.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering depth in feet. The depth box is inches.
Skipping the waste allowance.
Measuring the top of the forms rather than the excavated depth.
Forgetting footings and thickened edges.
Frequently asked questions
How much concrete do I need for a 10 × 10 slab, 4 in thick?
33.33 ft³, or 1.23 yd³.
How many cubic feet are in a cubic yard?
27.
How many 80 lb bags make a cubic yard?
About 45, at 0.60 ft³ per bag.
How thick should a patio be?
Commonly 4 in; driveways 4–6 in. Check local code.
Should I order extra?
Yes, typically 5–10%.
Can it do round columns?
Not yet; use πr²h as shown above.

H1: Date Calculator
What date is 30 days from now? When does a 90-day notice period end? This calculator adds or subtracts a number of days from any start date and tells you the resulting date and the day of the week it falls on.
How to use this calculator
1. Start date: default 1 January 2026.
2. Days: how many days to move (a whole number of 0 or more).
3. Operation: "Add days" or "Subtract days".
Results: the result date (YYYY-MM-DD) and its day of the week.
How it works
The calculator moves forward or back one calendar day at a time, so month lengths (28–31 days) and leap years are handled automatically. The start date itself counts as day 0: adding 1 day to a Monday gives Tuesday.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
1 January 2026 + 30 days = 31 January 2026, a Saturday.
Example 2: a 90-day deadline
15 October 2026 + 90 days = 2027-01-13, a Wednesday. A return window, probation period or visa allowance is often counted this way; check whether your contract counts the first day.
Example 3: counting back
A due date of 15 October 2026 minus 280 days (40 weeks) = 2026-01-08, the date pregnancy is conventionally counted from. For pregnancy dates, use the due date calculator.
Example 4: crossing February
2 March 2026 + 30 days = 2026-04-01, because March has 31 days.
Example 5: a milestone
1,000 days after 15 October 2026 is 2029-07-11 (Wednesday).
Calendar facts that affect date maths
Leap years: every year divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400. 2000 was a leap year; 2100 won't be.
Weeks: adding a multiple of 7 days always lands on the same weekday.
Months aren't fixed lengths, so "1 month" from 31 January has no single answer; that's why this tool counts days.
ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD) avoids the US (MM/DD) vs UK and Canadian (DD/MM) confusion: 03/04 is 4 March in the US and 3 April in the UK.
Business days and legal deadlines
The calculator counts calendar days, including weekends and holidays. Many deadlines use business days instead:
US federal holidays, Canadian statutory holidays and UK bank holidays differ, and some vary by state, province or nation (Scotland has different bank holidays from England).
Courts and tax authorities have their own rules for deadlines that fall on a weekend; the IRS, for example, moves a due date to the next business day.
Check the rule that applies before relying on a date for anything legal or financial.
Understanding your results
Day 0 is the start date. Some contracts count the start as day 1; subtract one from the days if so.
For the number of days between two dates, use the day counter.
Time zones don't change calendar arithmetic, but a deadline at midnight in one zone may already have passed in another; see the time zone calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Off-by-one errors: decide whether the first or last day counts.
Mixing up date formats when typing.
Assuming 30 days = 1 month.
Forgetting public holidays for working-day deadlines.
Frequently asked questions

Yes; it counts calendar days.
Does it handle leap years?
Yes.
How do I count back from a date?
Choose "Subtract days".
Can I add months or years?
Not yet. Use 365 days for a year (366 if it spans 29 February).
How do I find the days between two dates?
Use the day counter.

2. To date: default 31 December 2026.
Results: days between, weeks (approximate, to two decimals) and direction (forward if the "to" date is later, backward if earlier, with the number of days shown as positive).
How it's counted
Days between = the "to" date minus the "from" date. The start date isn't counted, but the end date is, which is the same as counting nights. From Monday to Tuesday is 1 day.
Including both ends: if you need to count both the first and last day (for example, a hotel's days of stay or a 7-day course from Monday to Sunday), add 1 to the result.
Worked examples

Example 3: days since
4 July 2026 to 15 October 2026 = 103 days.
Example 4: a leap year
1 January 2028 to 1 January 2029 = 366 days, because 2028 includes 29 February.
Example 5: counting backwards
Put the later date first and the counter shows the same number of days with the direction "Backward".
Where day counts matter
Notice periods and cooling-off periods: often counted in calendar days.
Interest: many loans and savings accounts accrue daily; the number of days determines the interest. US Treasury bills, UK gilts and Canadian money markets each use specific day-count conventions (actual/360, actual/365) [VERIFY for your product].
Residency and visa rules: the UK Statutory Residence Test, US Substantial Presence Test and Canadian 183-day rule all count days present, with specific rules for partial days.
Pregnancy, medication courses and training plans.

Title tag
What Day of the Week Was It? Calculator | FigSumo (49 chars)
Meta description
Find the day of the week for any date in the past or future, from 1583 onward in the Gregorian calendar, and see how the calculation works. (139 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
602 (minimum 600)
H1: Day of the Week Calculator
Which day of the week were you born on? What day does a holiday fall on next year? Enter any date and this calculator tells you the weekday, along with the date in standard ISO format.
How to use this calculator
1. Date: pick or type a date (default 4 July 2026).
Results: the day of the week and the ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD).
How it works
The calculator uses the Gregorian calendar, which most of the world uses for civil dates, and counts days from a known reference to find the weekday. You can do the same by hand with Zeller's congruence:
h = (d + ⌊13(m + 1) ÷ 5⌋ + K + ⌊K ÷ 4⌋ + ⌊J ÷ 4⌋ + 5J) mod 7
d: day of the month
m: month (3 = March … 14 = February; January and February count as months 13 and 14 of the previous year)
K: year within the century (year mod 100)
J: century (⌊year ÷ 100⌋)
h: 0 = Saturday, 1 = Sunday, 2 = Monday … 6 = Friday
Worked examples
Example 1: 4 July 2026
d = 4, m = 7, K = 26, J = 20: 4 + ⌊104 ÷ 5⌋ (20) + 26 + 6 + 5 + 100 = 161; 161 mod 7 = 0 → Saturday. That's the 250th anniversary of the US Declaration of Independence.
Example 2: the Moon landing
20 July 1969 was a Sunday.
Example 3: the millennium
1 January 2000 was a Saturday.
Example 4: Christmas 2026
25 December 2026 is a Friday.
Shortcuts for mental calculation
Same date, next year: the weekday moves forward one day, or two if a 29 February falls in between. 15 October 2026 is a Thursday, so 15 October 2027 is a Friday.
Doomsday rule: certain easy dates share a weekday each year: 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10, 12/12, the last day of February, and 9/5 and 5/9 (and 7/11, 11/7). In 2026 they're all Saturdays.
The calendar repeats every 28 years within a century (when no century non-leap year intervenes); the full Gregorian cycle is 400 years.
Weekday names
The English names come from Old English and Norse: Sunday (Sun), Monday (Moon), Tuesday (Tiw), Wednesday (Woden), Thursday (Thor), Friday (Frigg) and Saturday (Saturn).
Week conventions
US and Canada: calendars usually start the week on Sunday.
UK, Europe and ISO 8601: the week starts on Monday, and week 1 is the week containing the year's first Thursday. 15 October 2026 is in ISO week 42 and is day 288 of the year.
Understanding your results
Historical dates: Britain and its colonies switched from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar in September 1752, skipping 11 days. For dates before a country's switch, a Gregorian weekday may not match contemporary records.
ISO format avoids MM/DD vs DD/MM confusion.
Tips and common mistakes
Typing DD/MM in a US-format field (or vice versa).
Forgetting the January/February adjustment in Zeller's formula.
Applying Gregorian rules to old Julian dates.
Practice
1 January 2000 was a Saturday; Christmas Day 2026 is a Friday.
Frequently asked questions
What day of the week was I born?
Enter your birth date.
What day is 4 July 2026?
Saturday.
What day is Christmas 2026?
Friday.
Does the week start on Sunday or Monday?
Sunday in the US and Canada; Monday in the UK and under ISO 8601.
Can I check dates before 1752?
Yes, but results use the Gregorian calendar.
What is the doomsday rule?
A mental method using dates that share a weekday each year.

Density Calculator: Mass, Volume or Density | FigSumo (53 chars)

H1: Density Calculator
Density is how much mass is packed into a given volume. It explains why a steel bolt sinks while a log floats, and it's used to identify materials, convert between weight and volume, and estimate the load of a delivery. Enter a mass and a volume and this calculator gives the density in kilograms per cubic metre and grams per cubic centimetre.
How to use this calculator
1. Mass (kg): default 2.5.
2. Volume (L): litres, default 1.
Results: density in kg/m³ and in g/cm³ (which equals kg/L and g/mL).
The formula
ρ = m ÷ V
ρ (rho): density
m: mass
V: volume
Rearranged: m = ρ × V, and V = m ÷ ρ.
The calculator converts litres to cubic metres (1 L = 0.001 m³), so density in kg/m³ is mass ÷ (volume ÷ 1,000). Dividing by 1,000 again gives g/cm³.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
2.5 kg in 1 L = 2,500 kg/m³ = 2.5 g/cm³, close to glass or granite. In US units that's about 156.1 lb/ft³.
Example 2: is it gold?
A ring weighs 10.5 g and displaces 0.66 mL of water: 10.5 ÷ 0.66 = 15.91 g/cm³. That's within the typical range for 18-carat gold alloys (about 15–16 g/cm³ [VERIFY by alloy]) and well below pure gold's 19.3. Displacement on small items is imprecise, so an assay is the reliable test.
Example 3: mass from density
An oak board 0.75 m × 0.3 m × 20 mm has a volume of 0.0045 m³. At about 600–750 kg/m³ (oak varies), it weighs roughly 2.7 kg at 600 kg/m³.
Example 4: aluminium sheet
2 litres (0.002 m³) of aluminium at 2,700 kg/m³ weighs 5.4 kg.

Multiply density by volume.

Density divided by the density of water.

Title tag
Dew Point Calculator from Temperature & Humidity | FigSumo (58 chars)
Meta description
Calculate dew point from air temperature and relative humidity, or humidity from dew point, using the Magnus approximation. (123 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
658 (minimum 600)
H1: Dew Point Calculator
The dew point is the temperature air must cool to before water vapour starts condensing into dew, fog or condensation on a window. Unlike relative humidity, which changes as the air warms and cools during the day, the dew point tracks the actual amount of moisture in the air, which makes it the better guide to how muggy it feels. Enter the air temperature and relative humidity to find it.
How to use this calculator
1. Air temperature (°F): default 75.
2. Relative humidity (%): between 1 and 100 (default 55).
Result: the dew point in °F, to one decimal place.
The formula
The calculator uses the Magnus approximation, accurate to a few tenths of a degree for everyday temperatures:
γ = (a × T) ÷ (b + T) + ln(RH ÷ 100)
Td = (b × γ) ÷ (a − γ)
T: air temperature in °C (the calculator converts from °F first)
RH: relative humidity in %
a = 17.27, b = 237.7 °C: Magnus constants
Td: dew point in °C, converted back to °F
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
75 °F with 55% humidity → dew point 57.7 °F: comfortable.
Example 2: in Celsius, step by step
24 °C at 60% RH:
(17.27 × 24) ÷ (237.7 + 24) = 1.5838
ln(0.60) = −0.5108, so γ = 1.0730
Td = 237.7 × 1.0730 ÷ (17.27 − 1.0730) = 15.7 °C
Example 3: a sticky summer day
90 °F at 70% → 78.9 °F: oppressive.
Example 4: dry indoor air
68 °F at 40% → 42.8 °F. A window colder than that will fog up.
Example 5: saturated air
At 100% humidity, the dew point equals the air temperature (60 °F → 60.0 °F), which is when fog forms.

Why it matters
Condensation and mould: surfaces colder than the dew point get wet. Keeping indoor humidity at roughly 30–50% (US EPA guidance) limits condensation on windows and walls.
Frost: when the dew point is below freezing, moisture forms frost instead of dew.
Painting and coatings: many paints shouldn't be applied unless the surface is several degrees above the dew point (often 5 °F / 3 °C); check the product sheet.
Weather forecasting: fog, cloud base and thunderstorm potential depend on dew point.
Heat stress: a high dew point stops sweat from evaporating; see the heat index calculator.
Understanding your results
The dew point can't be higher than the air temperature.
Relative humidity alone can mislead: 90% at 40 °F is dry air in absolute terms, while 50% at 95 °F is very humid.
Magnus constants vary slightly by source; results can differ by a few tenths from other tools.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering humidity as a decimal (use 55, not 0.55).
Entering °C in the °F box; convert first with the unit converter.
Confusing dew point with wet-bulb temperature, which lies between the dew point and the air temperature.
Frequently asked questions
What is a comfortable dew point?
Below about 60 °F (16 °C).
Can dew point be higher than temperature?
No. At 100% humidity they're equal.
What's the difference between dew point and humidity?
Dew point measures actual moisture; relative humidity is moisture relative to the maximum the air can hold at that temperature.
Why do my windows get condensation?
The glass is colder than the room's dew point.
What dew point causes fog?
Fog forms when air cools to its dew point.
Can I use Celsius?
Not yet; convert to °F first, or use the formula with °C directly.

H1: Dice Roller
Need dice for a board game, a tabletop RPG or a classroom probability lesson and can't find any? This roller throws as many dice as you like with any number of sides, and shows each roll, the total and the average.
How to use the dice roller
1. Number of dice: at least 1 (default 2).
2. Sides per die: 2 or more (default 6). Use 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 or 20 for standard polyhedral dice, 2 for a coin flip, or 100 for percentile rolls.
3. Press Calculate to roll; press again to re-roll.
Results: total, the individual rolls, and the average per die.
How it works
Each die is rolled independently:
roll = 1 + floor(random × sides)
Every face has an equal 1 ÷ sides chance. The total is the sum of all rolls; the average is the total ÷ number of dice.
The maths of dice
Expected value
The average roll of a fair die with s sides is (s + 1) ÷ 2:
d6: 3.5
d20: 10.5
3d6: 3 × 3.5 = 10.5

Is it fair?
The roller uses your browser's pseudo-random number generator, which is unbiased for practical purposes and has no memory: a six last roll doesn't make a six less likely next time. Physical dice can be slightly biased by manufacturing; precision casino dice are made to tight tolerances. For anything involving money, follow the venue's or regulator's rules.
Tips and common mistakes
Expecting results to "even out" quickly. Streaks are normal in short runs.
Confusing the average per die with the total.
Using a d6 roll for a d20 game. Set the sides to match.

7, with a 1 in 6 chance.
Can I roll a d20?
Yes; set sides to 20.
Is the roller random?
Yes, for games and teaching. Each roll is independent.
Can I add a modifier like +3?
Not yet; add it to the total yourself.
How many dice can I roll?
As many as you need for a game; very large numbers just make a long list.

H1: Download Time Calculator
How long will a file take to download (or upload)? Enter its size and your connection speed and this calculator gives the time. It's handy for planning large game downloads, video uploads, cloud backups or file transfers before a deadline.
How to use this calculator
1. File size (MB): in megabytes (default 850). For gigabytes, multiply by 1,000 (a 50 GB game = 50,000 MB).
2. Download speed (Mbps): megabits per second, the figure your provider advertises or a speed test reports (default 100).
Results: download time in minutes and seconds, and the same in seconds.
The formula
time (seconds) = file size (MB) × 8 ÷ speed (Mbps)
The × 8 converts bytes (B, used for file sizes) to bits (b, used for connection speeds). The calculator uses decimal megabytes (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes) and assumes the full speed is available.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
850 MB × 8 = 6,800 megabits ÷ 100 Mbps = 68 seconds (1 min 8 s)
Example 2: a 50 GB game
50,000 MB × 8 ÷ 100 Mbps = 4,000 s = 66.7 minutes. At a more realistic 90 Mbps actual throughput: 74.1 minutes.
Example 3: streaming-quality video
A 7 GB 4K film on a 25 Mbps connection: 37.3 minutes.
Example 4: uploading
Upload speeds are often much lower. A 2 GB video upload at 20 Mbps takes about 13.3 minutes. Enter your upload speed in the speed box.
Bits, bytes and units
Unit
Meaning
b (bit)
Smallest unit; speeds use bits
B (byte)
8 bits; file sizes use bytes
Mbps
Megabits per second
MB/s
Megabytes per second = Mbps ÷ 8
1 GB
1,000 MB (decimal)
1 GiB
1,024 MiB (binary), about 1,073.74 decimal MB
Steam and some browsers show download rates in MB/s: 12.5 MB/s equals 100 Mbps. Operating systems may report file sizes in binary units (Windows labels GiB as "GB"), so a file can look about 7% bigger or smaller depending on the tool.
Why real downloads are slower
Protocol overhead: TCP/IP and encryption use some bandwidth, often 5–10%.
Wi-Fi: walls, distance and interference cut speeds well below your plan.
Server limits: the source may cap speed per user.
Shared connections: other devices streaming or updating.
Peak times: busier networks in the evening.
Run a speed test first and use the measured figure for a better estimate.
Typical connection speeds
Broadband plans range from under 10 Mbps on older DSL to 1,000 Mbps (1 Gbps) or more on fibre. The US FCC's benchmark for broadband is 100 Mbps download and 20 Mbps upload (set in 2024), and Ofcom defines UK "superfast" broadband as at least 30 Mbps [VERIFY current definitions].
Tips and common mistakes
Confusing MB and Mb. A 100 Mbps connection downloads 12.5 MB per second, not 100.
Entering GB as MB. 5 GB is 5,000 MB.
Using the advertised "up to" speed; measured speeds are more realistic.
Forgetting upload speed for backups and video uploads.
Frequently asked questions
How long does 1 GB take at 100 Mbps?
About 80 seconds (1,000 × 8 ÷ 100).
What's the difference between Mbps and MB/s?
Mbps is megabits; MB/s is megabytes. Divide Mbps by 8 to get MB/s.
Why is my download slower than the estimate?
Overhead, Wi-Fi, server limits and other users on your network.
Can I use this for uploads?
Yes, enter your upload speed.
Does it use 1,000 or 1,024?
Decimal units (1 MB = 1,000,000 bytes).
How do I convert GB to MB?
Multiply by 1,000.

H1: Electricity Cost Calculator
How much does it cost to run a space heater, a gaming PC or a window AC unit? This calculator turns an appliance's voltage and current into its power draw, the energy it uses over a period, and what that costs at your electricity rate.
How to use this calculator
1. Voltage (V): 120 V for standard US and Canadian outlets, 240 V for large US appliances and 230 V in the UK (default 120).
2. Current (A): from the appliance label or a plug-in meter (default 12).
3. Hours of use: how long it runs (default 2).
4. Electricity rate (per kWh): from your bill (default 0.16).
Results: power in watts, energy used in kilowatt-hours, and estimated cost.
The formulas
power (W) = voltage (V) × current (A)
energy (kWh) = power (W) × hours ÷ 1,000
cost = energy (kWh) × rate
A kilowatt-hour is 1,000 watts for one hour, the unit utilities bill in.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default (a space heater)
120 V × 12 A = 1,440 W
1,440 × 2 h ÷ 1,000 = 2.88 kWh
2.88 × $0.16 = $0.46
Run daily for a month (30 days), that's $13.82; all year, $168.19.
Example 2: a TV
A 100 W TV used 5 hours a day for a year at $0.16/kWh costs about $29.20.
Example 3: a UK kettle
A 3 kW kettle boiling for 15 minutes a day uses 0.75 kWh, about 20.2p a day at 27p/kWh. (Enter 230 V and 13 A for a similar result, since 230 × 13 ≈ 3,000 W.)
Example 4: charging an EV
Adding 60 kWh to a battery at $0.16/kWh costs $9.60 (plus roughly 10% charging losses). At about 3.3 miles per kWh, a typical figure for many EVs, that's around 200 miles [VERIFY per vehicle].
Example 5: standby power
A device drawing 15 W on standby uses 131.4 kWh a year if left on standby around the clock: about $21.02 at $0.16/kWh.
Where to find the numbers
Watts are printed on most labels and chargers. If you have watts, enter the voltage and divide watts by voltage for amps (1,500 W ÷ 120 V = 12.5 A).
Your rate is on your bill as cents or pence per kWh. Include delivery charges if they're per kWh.
Average residential rates are roughly 17–18¢/kWh in the US, vary widely across Canadian provinces (Quebec is among the lowest), and are set by the Ofgem price cap in Great Britain [VERIFY current rates].

Multiply by the voltage.

Engine Displacement and Horsepower Estimator | FigSumo (54 chars)
Meta description
Calculate engine displacement from bore, stroke and cylinders, and estimate airflow-based horsepower at a given RPM and volumetric efficiency. (142 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
632 (minimum 600)
H1: Engine Displacement & Horsepower Estimator
An engine's displacement is the total volume its pistons sweep in one revolution of the crankshaft. Together with engine speed and how efficiently the engine fills and burns that volume, it sets how much power is possible. This calculator works out displacement from bore, stroke and number of cylinders, and estimates horsepower.
How to use this calculator
1. Bore (in): cylinder diameter (default 3.5).
2. Stroke (in): distance the piston travels (default 3.2).
3. Cylinders: default 4.
4. RPM: engine speed for the power estimate (default 6,000).
5. Volumetric efficiency (%): how fully the cylinders fill with air (default 85).
Results: estimated horsepower and displacement (L).
Displacement formula
displacement (in³) = π ÷ 4 × bore² × stroke × cylinders
litres = in³ × 0.016387
cc = in³ × 16.387
For metric dimensions in millimetres, displacement (cc) = π ÷ 4 × bore² × stroke × cylinders ÷ 1,000.
Horsepower from displacement
Power depends on how much pressure combustion produces on average over each cycle, the brake mean effective pressure (BMEP):
hp = BMEP (psi) × displacement (in³) × RPM ÷ 792,000      (four-stroke)
The 792,000 combines 33,000 ft·lbf/min per hp, 12 in per ft and two revolutions per power stroke. Typical BMEP for a naturally aspirated petrol engine at peak power is around 130–190 psi; turbocharged engines reach 250 psi or more [VERIFY typical ranges].
Airflow: volumetric efficiency feeds the air demand: CFM = in³ × RPM × VE ÷ 3,456.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default four-cylinder
One cylinder: π ÷ 4 × 3.5² × 3.2 = 30.79 in³
× 4 = 123.2 in³ = 2.02 L (2,018 cc)
At 6,000 rpm with BMEP 150 psi: 150 × 123.2 × 6,000 ÷ 792,000 ≈ 140 hp
With a high-performance BMEP of 190 psi: about 177 hp
Airflow at 85% VE: about 182 CFM
Example 2: a classic V8
Bore 4.00 in, stroke 3.48 in, 8 cylinders → 349.8 in³ (5.73 L): the well-known "350" small-block.
Example 3: metric "square" engine
Bore and stroke both 86 mm, 4 cylinders: π ÷ 4 × 8.6² × 8.6 × 4 = 1,998 cc (about 2.0 L).
Bore, stroke and character
Oversquare (bore > stroke): revs higher, common in performance engines.
Undersquare (stroke > bore): more low-down torque, common in diesels.
Square: bore equals stroke.
Understanding your results
Displacement is exact from the dimensions; horsepower is an estimate that depends heavily on BMEP.
Crank vs wheel horsepower: manufacturers quote crank (brake) power; drivetrain losses of roughly 10–20% reduce power at the wheels.
Torque and horsepower are linked: hp = torque (lb·ft) × RPM ÷ 5,252. See the horsepower calculator.
Gross vs net: US ratings before 1972 were often gross (without accessories), inflating figures compared with today's SAE net ratings.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing inches and millimetres.
Using the radius for bore.
Counting a V8 as 4 cylinders per bank without multiplying.
Assuming peak power at redline. Peak often comes a little below it.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US enthusiasts still describe classic V8s by cubic inches, while current US, Canadian and UK brochures give litres or cubic centimetres. In the UK, engine size has a direct cost for older cars: vehicle excise duty for cars registered before 1 March 2001 is charged by engine size, with a lower rate for engines up to 1,549 cc.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate engine displacement?
π/4 × bore² × stroke × number of cylinders.
How many cc is a 2.0 L engine?
About 2,000 cc.
How many cubic inches is 5.7 L?
About 350 in³ (5.7 ÷ 0.016387).
Can you calculate horsepower from displacement alone?
Not exactly; you also need RPM and BMEP (or a dyno test).
What is volumetric efficiency?
How much air the cylinders actually take in compared with their swept volume.
What is BMEP?
The average effective pressure on the piston over a cycle, a measure of how hard the engine works.

H1: Fuel Cost Calculator
Planning a road trip or comparing commuting costs? This calculator works out how much fuel a journey uses and what it costs, from the distance, your vehicle's fuel economy and the price of fuel.
How to use this calculator
1. Trip distance (mi): one way, or double it for a round trip (default 120).
2. Fuel economy (mpg): US miles per gallon (default 28). Use a real-world figure from your trip computer or fill-up records if you have it.
3. Price per gallon ($): default 3.75.
Results: trip fuel cost and gallons used.
The formula
gallons = distance ÷ mpg
cost = gallons × price per gallon
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
120 mi ÷ 28 mpg = 4.29 gallons × $3.75 = $16.07
Example 2: a weekend round trip, shared
450 miles each way in a car averaging 32 mpg, with fuel at $3.40: 900 ÷ 32 = 28.12 gallons = $95.62, or $31.88 each for three people.
Example 3: Canada (metric)
A 500 km trip in a car using 7.5 L/100 km needs 500 × 7.5 ÷ 100 = 37.5 L. At $1.55 a litre: $58.12. Until metric mode is added, convert with the fuel economy calculator.
Example 4: the UK
A 200-mile journey at 45 mpg (UK gallons) uses 20.2 litres; at £1.40 a litre that's £28.29. UK mpg figures use the 4.546 L imperial gallon, so don't enter them as US mpg without converting (UK mpg × 0.8327 = US mpg).
Example 5: yearly running cost
Driving 12,000 miles a year at $3.75: 28 mpg costs $1,607.14; 35 mpg costs $1,285.71, saving $321.43 a year.
What affects real-world fuel use
Speed: fuel use rises sharply above about 50 mph. The US DOE estimates each 5 mph over 50 is like paying an extra 30¢ or so per gallon [VERIFY current figure].
Aggressive driving: hard acceleration and braking can cut highway mileage by 15–30%.
Load and roof racks: extra weight and drag.
Tyre pressure: under-inflation increases rolling resistance.
Air conditioning and short trips: cold engines and AC use more fuel.
Idling burns fuel for zero miles.
Fuel prices in the US, Canada and UK
US: sold by the gallon; prices vary by state, largely because of state fuel taxes. Check AAA or the EIA for averages.
Canada: sold by the litre in cents per litre, with provincial taxes and carbon-pricing differences.
UK: sold by the litre in pence per litre, with fuel duty and VAT making up a large share.
Understanding your results
The result is fuel only. For the full cost of driving (wear, insurance, depreciation), the IRS standard mileage rate or HMRC approved mileage rates give a broader per-mile figure; see the mileage reimbursement calculator.
Rated vs real mpg: EPA and WLTP ratings are lab-based; most drivers see somewhat lower figures.
Electric vehicles: use the electricity calculator with kWh per mile.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting the return trip.
Using UK mpg as US mpg (UK figures look about 20% better).
Using the best-case rated mpg for a mountainous or high-speed trip.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate fuel cost for a trip?
Distance ÷ mpg × price per gallon.
How many gallons will I use?
Distance divided by mpg.
How do I split fuel costs?
Divide the total by the number of people.
Can I use litres and kilometres?
Not yet. Convert as in Example 3, or multiply L/100 km by distance ÷ 100.
Does this include tolls or parking?
No; add them separately.
What's the difference between US and UK mpg?
UK gallons are about 20% larger, so UK mpg figures are higher for the same car.

H1: Fuel Economy Calculator
Your car's trip computer and the official rating are estimates. The most reliable way to know your real fuel economy is to measure it from a fill-up. Enter the miles driven and the gallons used, and this calculator gives miles per gallon and the metric equivalent, litres per 100 kilometres.
How to measure your fuel economy
1. Fill the tank completely and note the odometer reading (or reset the trip meter).
2. Drive normally until you need fuel again.
3. Fill up completely again and note the gallons added (on the receipt) and the miles driven since the last fill.
4. Enter both numbers.
For the most accurate figure, average over several tanks.
How to use this calculator
1. Miles driven: default 300.
2. Gallons used: US gallons (default 10.5).
Results: fuel economy in mpg and litres per 100 km.
The formulas
mpg = miles ÷ gallons
L/100 km = (gallons × 3.785411784) ÷ (miles × 1.609344) × 100
The two measures are inverses: mpg is distance per unit of fuel (higher is better), while L/100 km is fuel per unit of distance (lower is better). A shortcut: L/100 km = 235.215 ÷ US mpg.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
300 ÷ 10.5 = 28.57 mpg, or 8.23 L/100 km. In UK mpg that's 34.31, and in km per litre, 12.15.
Example 2: a highway tank
412 miles on 13.2 gallons = 31.21 mpg (7.54 L/100 km).
Example 3: Canada
A rating of 7.5 L/100 km equals about 31.4 US mpg.
Why mpg can mislead
Fuel used falls less and less as mpg rises. Over 1,000 miles:

40.0

25.0
50
20.0
Going from 20 to 25 mpg saves 10 gallons; going from 40 to 50 saves only 5. That's why fuel-per-distance measures (L/100 km, or gallons per 100 miles, which US window stickers also show) make comparisons clearer.

Title tag
GDP Growth Projection Calculator | FigSumo (42 chars)
Meta description
Project GDP forward at a constant growth rate, or find the compound annual growth rate between two GDP figures. (111 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
623 (minimum 600)
H1: GDP Growth Calculator
Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of finished goods and services produced in an economy over a period. This calculator projects how GDP grows at a steady annual rate: enter a starting value, a growth rate and a number of years to see the future GDP, the total increase and the growth multiple. It works just as well for a business's revenue or a city's output.
How to use this calculator
1. Starting GDP ($): any currency amount (default 1,000,000).
2. Annual growth rate (%): real or nominal, as you choose (default 3). Negative rates model contraction.
3. Years: default 5.
Results: future GDP, total growth and growth multiple (future ÷ starting).
The formula
future GDP = starting GDP × (1 + g)ⁿ
g: annual growth rate as a decimal
n: number of years
This is compound growth: each year's growth builds on the last.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
1,000,000 × 1.03⁵ = $1,159,274.07; total growth $159,274.07; multiple 1.159.
Example 2: a decade at 2.5%
The growth multiple is 1.025¹⁰ = 1.280, a 28.0% increase.
Example 3: doubling time
At 2% a year, an economy doubles in ln 2 ÷ ln 1.02 = 35.0 years. The rule of 70 gives a quick estimate: 70 ÷ 2 = 35 years.
Example 4: backing out a growth rate
If an economy grows from $21.4 trillion to $27.0 trillion in 5 years, the compound annual growth rate is (27.0 ÷ 21.4)^(1/5) − 1 = 4.76% (nominal). Figures are illustrative.
How GDP is measured
The expenditure approach, used for headline figures in the US, Canada and UK:
GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
Component
Meaning
C
Household consumption
I
Business investment and housing
G
Government spending on goods and services
X − M
Exports minus imports
Illustration: C 15.0, I 3.8, G 3.4, X 2.4, M 3.0 (trillions) → GDP = 21.6 trillion.
The income approach adds wages, profits, rents and taxes less subsidies; the output approach sums value added by each industry. In principle all three give the same total.
Real vs nominal GDP
Nominal GDP is measured at current prices.
Real GDP removes inflation, so it measures changes in volume.
Real growth ≈ (1 + nominal growth) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1. With 5% nominal growth and 3% inflation, real growth is 1.94%. Use real rates to compare living standards over time; see the inflation calculator.
Who publishes GDP
US: Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), quarterly at an annualised rate.
Canada: Statistics Canada, monthly and quarterly.
UK: Office for National Statistics (ONS), monthly and quarterly (UK quarterly growth is usually reported as a non-annualised rate).
That last point matters: a US "2% growth" quarter means about 0.5% that quarter, while a UK "0.5%" quarter is roughly the same pace.
Understanding your results
Constant growth is a simplification. Real economies have recessions and recoveries.
GDP per capita divides by population and better reflects living standards.
Currency comparisons between countries need exchange rates or purchasing power parity.
Tips and common mistakes
Mixing real and nominal rates in the same projection.
Comparing annualised and non-annualised quarterly rates.
Using simple growth (rate × years) instead of compounding.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate GDP growth?
(New GDP ÷ old GDP) − 1, or use this calculator to project forwards.
What is the GDP formula?
C + I + G + (X − M).
What's the difference between real and nominal GDP?
Real GDP is adjusted for inflation.
What is the rule of 70?
70 ÷ growth rate ≈ years to double.
Can I use this for company revenue?
Yes; it's compound growth for any amount.
Can growth be negative?
Yes; enter a negative rate.

Title tag
Golf Handicap Index Calculator (World Handicap System) | FigSumo (64 chars)
Meta description
Estimate a Handicap Index from your score differentials using World Handicap System rules, with course rating and slope rating inputs. (134 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
682 (minimum 600)
H1: Golf Handicap Calculator
A golf handicap lets players of different abilities compete fairly. Under the World Handicap System (WHS), used in the US, Canada, the UK and most golfing countries since 2020, each round produces a score differential that measures how well you played relative to the course's difficulty. This calculator works out that differential for a round, and shows how differentials build into a Handicap Index.
How to use this calculator
1. Score: your adjusted gross score for 18 holes (default 92).
2. Course rating: the expected score for a scratch golfer from your tees, printed on the scorecard (default 72.1).
3. Slope rating: how much harder the course plays for a bogey golfer, from 55 to 155; 113 is average (default 125).
4. Course par: default 72.
Results: score differential and score vs par.
The formula
score differential = (113 ÷ slope rating) × (adjusted gross score − course rating − PCC)
113: the slope of a course of standard difficulty
PCC (playing conditions calculation): an adjustment from −1 to +3 applied by your golf authority when conditions are unusually hard or easy. The calculator assumes 0.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
(113 ÷ 125) × (92 − 72.1) = 18.0; you finished +20 against par.
Example 2: an easier course
Score 85, rating 70.2, slope 118: (113 ÷ 118) × (85 − 70.2) = 14.2.
Example 3: from differentials to a Handicap Index
Your Handicap Index is the average of the lowest 8 of your most recent 20 differentials. Suppose your best eight are 15.8, 16.1, 16.4, 16.9, 17.2, 17.5, 17.9, 18.0. Their average is 17.0: your Handicap Index.
Example 4: Course Handicap
Before a round, convert your index to strokes for the tees you're playing:
Course Handicap = Handicap Index × (slope ÷ 113) + (course rating − par)
With index 17.0, slope 131, rating 73.4 and par 72: 21.11, rounded to 21 strokes.
Adjusted gross score
For handicap purposes, your score on any hole is capped at net double bogey: par + 2 + any handicap strokes you receive on that hole. One disastrous hole won't wreck your differential. Until you have an index, the maximum is par + 5 per hole.
Fewer than 20 rounds
New players can get an index after 54 holes (any combination of 9- and 18-hole rounds). With fewer than 20 differentials, a sliding scale applies: for example, the lowest one with an adjustment for 3 rounds, rising to the lowest 8 at 20 [VERIFY the full table with your national association].
Who runs handicaps
US: the USGA, through state and regional associations (GHIN).
Canada: Golf Canada.
UK: England Golf, Scottish Golf, Wales Golf and Golf Ireland, under the R&A.
Only an official index from your association is valid for competitions; this calculator is for estimates and tracking.
Understanding your results
Lower differentials are better. A scratch golfer averages around 0 on their best rounds.
Differentials reflect your better rounds, since the index averages the best 8 of 20; typical scores run a few shots above your index.
The maximum Handicap Index is 54.0.
Slope matters: the same score on a harder (higher slope) course gives a lower differential.
Tips and common mistakes
Using par instead of course rating in the formula.
Forgetting the net double bogey cap.
Using the wrong tees' ratings.
Mixing 9-hole and 18-hole scores without the official 9-hole method.
Frequently asked questions
How is a golf handicap calculated?
Average the lowest 8 of your last 20 score differentials.
What is a score differential?
(113 ÷ slope) × (adjusted score − course rating − PCC).
What is a slope rating?
A measure of how much harder a course is for a bogey golfer than for a scratch golfer.
What is net double bogey?
The maximum hole score for handicap purposes: par + 2 + strokes received.
How many rounds do I need?
Scores from 54 holes to get an initial index.
Is the index the same as my course handicap?
No; the course handicap adjusts the index for the tees you play.

H1: GPA Calculator
Your grade point average (GPA) is a credit-weighted average of your course grades, used by US and Canadian colleges and many high schools for honours, scholarships, graduate admissions and academic standing. This calculator gives your term GPA from your courses' grade points and credit hours.
How to use this calculator
1. Course grade (4.0 scale): enter the grade points for each course (for example A = 4.0, A− = 3.7, B+ = 3.3).
2. Course credits: credit hours for each course.
3. Leave a course's credits blank or at 0 to skip it.
Results: term GPA (two decimals), credit hours, and a table showing each course's quality points.
The formula
GPA = Σ(grade points × credits) ÷ Σ credits
Each course's grade points × credits are its quality points. Courses with more credits count more.

Example 2: cumulative GPA

Example 3: what you need
To graduate with 3.50 over 90 credits, starting from 3.20 over 60, you'd need (3.50 × 90 − 3.20 × 60) ÷ 30 = 4.10 in the last 30 credits, which is above 4.0 and so impossible on this scale. Raising a GPA late is hard because earlier credits carry weight.
Weighted vs unweighted GPA
US high schools often report a weighted GPA that adds points for honours, AP or IB courses (for example +0.5 or +1.0), so it can exceed 4.0. Colleges often recalculate on their own scale. This calculator is unweighted unless you enter the boosted points yourself.
Canada and the UK
Canada: scales vary by university: 4.0 or 4.33 at many, a 9-point scale at York and a 12-point scale at McMaster. Many report percentages too.
UK: universities award degree classifications (First, 2:1, 2:2, Third) based on weighted module marks, not GPA. Some institutions now also report a GPA alongside, on a 4.25 scale [VERIFY current UK GPA scheme]. US graduate schools usually convert UK results themselves.
Understanding your results
Pass/fail and withdrawn courses usually don't count in GPA; check your school's rules.
Repeated courses may replace or average the earlier grade.
Rounding: schools may truncate rather than round (3.696 → 3.69).
Tips and common mistakes
Averaging grades without weighting by credits.
Entering percentages instead of grade points.
Mixing scales (4.0 vs 4.3).
Including pass/fail courses.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate GPA?
Multiply each grade's points by its credits, add them up, and divide by total credits.
What is a good GPA?
Many scholarships and honours programmes set minimums around 3.0–3.5; competitive graduate programmes often look for 3.5 or higher.
What's a 3.7 GPA as a letter grade?
A−.
How do I calculate cumulative GPA?
Combine total quality points and total credits across all terms.
Can GPA be above 4.0?
Yes, on weighted or 4.3 scales.
How many courses can I enter?
Three at present; combine more by hand as in Example 2.

H1: Grade Calculator
How does a final exam change your course grade? Enter your current grade and how much of the course it covers, then your exam score and the exam's weight, and this calculator returns your weighted overall grade.
How to use this calculator
1. Current grade (%): your average so far (default 88).
2. Current weight (%): the share of the course that grade represents (default 70).
3. Final exam score (%): your actual or expected exam result (default 92).
4. Final exam weight (%): the exam's share of the course (default 30).
Results: weighted course grade and the weight total used. If the weights don't add up to 100, the calculator divides by their total, so 60% + 20% is treated as the 80% of the course completed so far.
The formula
course grade = (current × current weight + exam × exam weight) ÷ (current weight + exam weight)
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
(88 × 70 + 92 × 30) ÷ 100 = 89.2%
Example 2: what do you need on the final?
To finish with 90% when you have 88% on 70% of the course and the exam is worth 30%:
needed = (target − current × current weight) ÷ exam weight
       = (90 − 88 × 0.70) ÷ 0.30 = 94.67%
For a 93%, you'd need 104.67%. Above 100% means the target isn't reachable on the exam alone. (A dedicated mode for this is planned.)
Example 3: the worst case
Score 0 on the final and you'd finish with 88 × 0.70 = 61.6%. Your grade can't fall below this.
Example 4: several weighted parts
Homework 85% (20% of the grade), midterm 78% (30%), final 92% (50%): 85 × 0.2 + 78 × 0.3 + 92 × 0.5 = 86.4%.
Example 5: points-based classes
If your course uses points rather than weights, divide total points earned by total points possible. Two categories with weights 25 and 15 and scores of 90% and 80% give (90 × 25 + 80 × 15) ÷ 40 = 86.25%; enter them as "current" and "exam" to see the same result.

The calculator divides by the total you enter.

Only with extra credit.

It's in your syllabus; 20–40% is common.

H1: Gravel Calculator
Whether you're laying a path, a driveway or a drainage bed, gravel is sold by volume (cubic yards) or by weight (tons). This calculator converts the area and depth you want to cover into both, so you can compare quotes from suppliers that price either way.
How to use this calculator
1. Area length (ft) and area width (ft): default 15 × 10.
2. Depth (in): default 4.
Results: estimated gravel in tons and cubic yards, with a note on the density assumed.
The formulas
volume (ft³) = length × width × depth ÷ 12
cubic yards = ft³ ÷ 27
tons = ft³ × 100 lb ÷ 2,000
The tonnage assumes about 100 lb per cubic foot (1.35 tons per cubic yard), a typical figure for loose gravel. Actual densities run from about 95 to 110 lb/ft³ depending on stone type, size and moisture; ask your supplier for theirs.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
15 × 10 × (4 ÷ 12) = 50 ft³ = 1.85 yd³ ≈ 2.5 tons
Example 2: a parking pad
A 40 ft × 12 ft parking pad topped up 3 in deep is 120 ft³ = 4.44 yd³ ≈ 6.00 tons. Allowing 15% for compaction: 6.90 tons.
Example 3: bagged gravel
Bags are often 0.5 ft³. A 15 × 10 ft area at 2 in deep needs 50 bags, which is why bulk delivery is cheaper for anything bigger than a small bed.
Example 4: metric (UK, Canada)
6 m × 3 m at 100 mm deep = 1.8 m³. At about 1.6 tonnes per m³, that's roughly 2.88 tonnes. UK merchants often sell 850 kg "jumbo" bulk bags.
How deep should gravel be?
Use
Typical depth
Decorative top layer
2 in (5 cm)
Footpath
2–3 in on a compacted base
Patio or shed base
4 in compacted sub-base
Driveway
4–6 in sub-base plus 2 in top layer (often more on soft ground)
French drain
Per design; often 12 in+
These are common practice, not engineering specifications.
Types of gravel
Crushed stone (#57, MOT Type 1 in the UK): angular, compacts well; for bases and driveways.
Pea gravel: small and rounded; comfortable underfoot but shifts, so edge it.
River rock: larger rounded stones for decoration and drainage.
Decomposed granite: fine, packs into a firm path.
Understanding your results
Compaction: crushed base can compact 10–20%; order extra for driveways and sub-bases.
Waste: add 5–10% for uneven ground and edges.
Weight limits: a pickup truck bed or trailer may not carry what the volume suggests. A ton of gravel is only about 0.74 yd³.
The chart splits volume and weight for reference only.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering depth in feet (the box is inches).
Ignoring compaction for base layers.
Assuming all stone weighs the same.
Skipping landscape fabric under decorative gravel, which lets weeds through.
Quick check
One cubic yard is about 0.765 m³.
Frequently asked questions
How much gravel do I need for a 10 × 10 area?
At 4 in deep, about 33 ft³ (1.23 yd³), or 1.67 tons.
How many tons are in a cubic yard of gravel?
About 1.35 at 100 lb/ft³; 1.3–1.5 depending on the stone.
How deep should a gravel driveway be?
Often 4–6 in of base plus a 2 in top layer.
Can I enter metres?
Not yet; convert, or use the metric example above.
Should I order extra?
Yes, 5–10% plus compaction for base layers.
What's the difference between tons and tonnes?
A US short ton is 2,000 lb (907 kg); a metric tonne is 1,000 kg.

Heat Index Calculator (Feels-Like Temperature) | FigSumo (56 chars)

Calculate the heat index from temperature and relative humidity with the NWS Rothfusz regression, in °F or °C, with risk levels. (128 chars)

618 (minimum 600)
H1: Heat Index Calculator
The heat index, or "feels like" temperature in hot weather, combines air temperature and humidity to estimate how hot it feels to the human body. When humidity is high, sweat evaporates more slowly, so the body cools less efficiently and heat illness becomes more likely. Enter the temperature and relative humidity to get the heat index.
How to use this calculator
1. Air temperature (°F): measured in the shade (default 92).
2. Relative humidity (%): 0 to 100 (default 65).
Result: the heat index in °F. Below 80 °F the calculator returns the air temperature, because humidity has little effect on how hot it feels at those temperatures.
The formula
The US National Weather Service uses the Rothfusz regression, fitted to Steadman's apparent-temperature tables:
HI = −42.379 + 2.04901523T + 10.14333127R − 0.22475541TR
     − 0.00683783T² − 0.05481717R² + 0.00122874T²R
     + 0.00085282TR² − 0.00000199T²R²
T: air temperature (°F)
R: relative humidity (%)
The NWS applies small corrections at very low or very high humidity; this calculator doesn't yet, so results in those conditions can differ by a degree or two.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
92 °F at 65% humidity → 108.3 °F (42.4 °C): "Danger" level.
Example 2: a warm, moderate day
85 °F at 50% → 86.5 °F: slightly above the air temperature.
Example 3: dry heat
100 °F at 40% → 109.3 °F.
Example 4: tropical humidity
95 °F at 75% → 128.0 °F: "Extreme danger".
What the numbers mean
NWS risk bands for prolonged exposure or strenuous activity:
Heat index (°F)
Level
Possible effects
80–90
Caution
Fatigue possible
90–103
Extreme caution
Heat cramps and heat exhaustion possible
103–124
Danger
Heat cramps or exhaustion likely; heat stroke possible
125+
Extreme danger
Heat stroke highly likely
The heat index is calculated for shade. Direct sunshine can add up to about 15 °F to the felt temperature.
Canada and the UK
Canada uses the humidex, based on temperature and dew point and reported in °C. A humidex of 40 °C+ is classed as "great discomfort" by Environment and Climate Change Canada.
The UK doesn't use a heat index for public warnings; the UK Health Security Agency and Met Office issue Heat-Health Alerts based on forecast temperatures.
To convert, 33 °C = 91.4 °F; use the unit converter.
Staying safe in heat
Drink water regularly; don't wait until you're thirsty.
Limit strenuous activity during the hottest hours.
Wear light, loose clothing and rest in shade or air conditioning.
Check on older people, young children and people with health conditions, who are most at risk.
Never leave children or pets in parked cars.
Heat stroke (confusion, hot skin, collapse) is a medical emergency: call 911 in the US or Canada, or 999 in the UK.
Tips and common mistakes
Using a sun-exposed thermometer, which reads high.
Entering humidity as a decimal (use 65, not 0.65).
Confusing heat index with dew point. Dew point measures moisture; see the dew point calculator.
Frequently asked questions
What is the heat index?
The apparent temperature combining air temperature and humidity.
When is the heat index dangerous?
From about 103 °F, the NWS "Danger" threshold.
Why does humidity make it feel hotter?
Sweat evaporates less, so the body cools less.
Does the heat index apply in the sun?
It's calculated for shade; sun can add up to about 15 °F.
What is the humidex?
Canada's equivalent, reported in °C.
Why does it show the air temperature below 80 °F?
The formula isn't intended for cooler conditions.

H1: Height Converter
Height is given in feet and inches in the US and, informally, in Canada and the UK, but in centimetres on passports, medical records and most of the world's forms. This converter switches between the two.
How to use this converter
1. Convert: "Centimeters → feet & inches" or "Feet & inches → centimeters".
2. Enter height (cm), or feet and inches.
Results:
cm → ft & in: feet and inches (to 0.1 in) and total inches.
ft & in → cm: centimetres (to 0.1 cm).
The formulas
1 inch = 2.54 cm (exact)
total inches = cm ÷ 2.54
feet = whole part of (total inches ÷ 12)
inches = total inches − 12 × feet
cm = (feet × 12 + inches) × 2.54
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
175 cm ÷ 2.54 = 68.90 in → 5 ft 8.9 in
Example 2: feet and inches to centimetres
5 ft 9 in = 69 in × 2.54 = 175.3 cm. 6 ft = 182.9 cm.
Example 3: 160 cm
160 ÷ 2.54 = 62.99 in → 5 ft 3.0 in (almost exactly 5 ft 3 in).
Example 4: 5 ft 4 in
64 in × 2.54 = 162.6 cm.

Average heights
Average adult heights differ by country and over time. Typical recent figures are about 5′9″ (175 cm) for men and 5′3½″ (161 cm) for women in the US, and around 5′9½″ (176–178 cm) and 5′4″ (163–164 cm) in Canada and the UK [VERIFY latest national surveys].
Predicting a child's adult height
A common rough method is the mid-parental height:
boy: (mother's height + father's height + 13 cm) ÷ 2
girl: (mother's height + father's height − 13 cm) ÷ 2
With a father of 178 cm and a mother of 165 cm: a boy's target is about 178.0 cm and a girl's 165.0 cm, with a typical range of about ±8.5 cm. Nutrition, health and genetics all play a part; growth charts from a paediatrician are more informative. (This calculator doesn't yet include the prediction.)
Measuring height accurately
Stand barefoot on a hard floor with heels, buttocks and shoulders against a wall.
Look straight ahead; place a flat object (a book) on your head at a right angle to the wall.
Mark the wall and measure from the floor.
You're slightly taller in the morning; the spine compresses during the day by up to about 1 cm.
Understanding your results
Rounding: 5 ft 8.9 in is often rounded to 5′9″ in everyday use.
Height for BMI: the BMI calculator accepts either unit system.
Forms: passports and driving licences may require whole centimetres or inches.
Tips and common mistakes
Typing 5.9 to mean 5 ft 9 in. 5.9 ft is 5 ft 10.8 in. Use the separate feet and inches boxes.
Using 2.5 cm per inch (it's 2.54).
Measuring with shoes on.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US driver's licences print height in feet and inches, as many Canadian provincial licences do alongside or instead of centimetres. UK passports and driving licences don't show height at all, but NHS records and clinic forms use centimetres. In all three countries, children's growth charts plot height in centimetres, with inches as a secondary scale on some US charts.

Horsepower Calculator
URL
https://figsumo.com/horsepower-calculator
Title tag
Horsepower Calculator from Torque and RPM | FigSumo (51 chars)
Meta description
Convert torque and engine speed into horsepower with hp = torque × RPM ÷ 5,252, or solve for torque. Also converts hp to kW. (124 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
624 (minimum 600)
H1: Horsepower Calculator
Horsepower measures how fast an engine can do work. Torque, the twisting force at the crankshaft, tells you how hard it pulls. The two are tied together by engine speed: horsepower is torque multiplied by RPM, scaled by a constant. Enter torque and RPM and this calculator gives the horsepower.
How to use this calculator
1. Torque (lb·ft): at a given engine speed, from a dyno sheet or manufacturer spec (default 250).
2. Engine speed (RPM): the speed at which that torque is produced (default 5,500).
Result: horsepower, to one decimal place.
The formula
hp = torque (lb·ft) × RPM ÷ 5,252
Where 5,252 comes from: one horsepower is 33,000 ft·lbf per minute (James Watt's figure for a working horse), and one revolution is 2π radians, so 33,000 ÷ 2π ≈ 5,252.
A consequence: on any dyno chart plotted in lb·ft and hp, the torque and power curves cross at 5,252 rpm.
Metric equivalent
kW = torque (N·m) × RPM ÷ 9,549
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
250 × 5,500 ÷ 5,252 = 261.8 hp (about 195.2 kW, or 265.4 PS).
Example 2: finding torque
An engine makes 300 hp at 6,000 rpm. Torque at that speed = 300 × 5,252 ÷ 6,000 = 262.6 lb·ft.
Example 3: a turbo-diesel (metric)
400 N·m at 3,000 rpm → 400 × 3,000 ÷ 9,549 = 125.7 kW (168.5 hp).
Example 4: an electric motor
EVs are usually rated in kW: a 150 kW motor is about 201 hp. Electric motors produce peak torque from zero rpm, which is why they feel quick off the line.
Horsepower units
Unit
Equals
Used in

UK and Canadian brochures often quote both PS and kW; US ratings use SAE net horsepower.
Torque vs horsepower
Torque gets the car moving and pulling a load: high torque at low RPM makes towing easy.
Horsepower sets the top speed and how quickly you can accelerate at high speed.
Gearing multiplies torque at the wheels, which is why a lower gear gives stronger acceleration.
Understanding your results
Peak power and peak torque occur at different RPMs. Use torque at the same RPM you're calculating for.
Crank vs wheel: dyno figures at the wheels are 10–20% lower than crank ratings because of drivetrain losses.
Gross vs net: pre-1972 US ratings were gross and higher than today's SAE net ratings.
For an estimate from engine size, see the engine displacement calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using N·m with the 5,252 constant. Convert first (1 lb·ft = 1.3558 N·m) or use 9,549 for kW.
Mixing peak torque with peak-power RPM.
Comparing PS and hp directly (1 PS = 0.986 hp).
Quick check
A 150 kW electric motor is 150 ÷ 0.7457 = 201.2 hp.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US and Canadian car ads quote SAE net horsepower. UK ads usually quote PS or bhp, and electric cars are often rated in kW, so convert before you compare models.
Frequently asked questions
How do I convert torque to horsepower?
Multiply torque by RPM and divide by 5,252.
Why 5,252?
It's 33,000 ft·lbf/min divided by 2π.
How many watts in a horsepower?
About 745.7 for mechanical horsepower.
What's the difference between hp and PS?
PS is metric horsepower, about 1.4% smaller.
How do I convert kW to hp?
Divide by 0.7457 (or multiply by 1.341).
Why do torque and horsepower curves cross at 5,252 rpm?
At that speed, the formula makes hp equal to torque.

Rounding rules at work
US: the Department of Labor allows employers to round clock times to the nearest 5, 6 (tenth of an hour) or 15 minutes, provided rounding averages out and doesn't consistently underpay workers.
Canada and the UK: employment standards don't set a rounding rule in the same way, but employees must be paid for all time worked and at least the minimum wage on average for the pay period [VERIFY provincial rules].

Overtime
US (FLSA): non-exempt employees earn 1.5× their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek; some states (such as California) add daily overtime.

Understanding your results
Repeating decimals: 20 min is 0.3333…; four decimal places keep pay calculations accurate to the cent for normal hours.

Tips and common mistakes
Treating 7:45 as 7.45 hours. Minutes are sixtieths, not hundredths.
Entering 90 minutes in the minutes box; use 1 hour 30 minutes.
Rounding each day and then summing, which can shift weekly totals.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US and Canadian timesheets usually show the 12-hour clock with AM and PM, so check that a shift from 10:00 PM to 6:00 AM is entered as crossing midnight. UK employers use 12- and 24-hour formats, and many rotas are written as 22:00–06:00. Overtime rules differ: US federal law sets overtime by the week, Canadian rules are provincial, and UK law has no general overtime premium.

IP Subnet Calculator (IPv4 and IPv6) | FigSumo (46 chars)

Calculate network and broadcast addresses, usable host range, subnet mask and wildcard for any IPv4 or IPv6 address and prefix length. (134 chars)
Country

626 (minimum 600)
H1: IP Subnet Calculator
Setting up a home lab, configuring a router or studying for a networking exam? This calculator takes an IPv4 address and a CIDR prefix length and returns the network address, subnet mask, broadcast address, usable host range and number of addresses.
How to use this calculator
1. IPv4 address: four numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots (default 192.168.1.10).
2. CIDR prefix (/n): 0 to 32, the number of leading 1 bits in the mask (default 24).
Results: network address, subnet mask, broadcast address, first host, last host, total addresses and usable host addresses.
How subnetting works
An IPv4 address is 32 bits. The prefix length splits it into a network part (the first n bits) and a host part (the remaining 32 − n bits).
mask = n ones followed by (32 − n) zeros
network = address AND mask
broadcast = network OR (NOT mask)
total addresses = 2^(32 − n)
usable hosts = total − 2         (network and broadcast reserved)
Special cases: a /31 has 2 usable addresses (point-to-point links, RFC 3021) and a /32 is a single host.
Worked examples
Example 1: a home network (the default)
192.168.1.10/24:

Example 2: a /20
10.0.5.77/20 → network 10.0.0.0, mask 255.255.240.0, broadcast 10.0.15.255, hosts 10.0.0.1 – 10.0.15.254, 4,096 addresses (4,094 usable).
Example 3: a small office segment
172.16.40.200/27 → network 172.16.40.192, mask 255.255.255.224, broadcast 172.16.40.223, hosts 172.16.40.193 – 172.16.40.222 (30 usable).
Example 4: a point-to-point link
203.0.113.9/30 → network 203.0.113.8, hosts 203.0.113.9 and 203.0.113.10, broadcast 203.0.113.11: exactly two usable addresses, the traditional choice for a router-to-router link.

These aren't routed on the public internet; home routers use them behind NAT. 100.64.0.0/10 is reserved for carrier-grade NAT, and 169.254.0.0/16 is link-local (often a sign that DHCP failed).
Understanding your results
Any address in the subnet gives the same network and broadcast; the calculator works out which subnet the address belongs to.
Cloud providers reserve extra addresses: AWS reserves 5 per subnet, so a /24 VPC subnet has 251 usable [VERIFY current provider docs].
Binary view: the mask 255.255.240.0 is 11111111.11111111.11110000.00000000. The binary calculator helps you check.
Tips and common mistakes
Assigning the network or broadcast address to a device.
Overlapping subnets when planning; each subnet's range must be distinct.
Confusing the mask with the wildcard (inverse) mask used in Cisco ACLs: 0.0.0.255 for a /24.
Typing a leading zero like 192.168.01.10, which some systems read as octal.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
Subnetting rules are the same everywhere because IPv4 and CIDR are international standards. Regional internet registries hand out public address space: ARIN covers the US and Canada, and RIPE NCC covers the UK and Europe. Home routers sold in all three countries usually default to a 192.168.x.0/24 or 10.0.0.0/24 network, which the calculator's default reproduces.
Frequently asked questions
How many hosts are in a /24?
254 usable out of 256.
What is a subnet mask?
A 32-bit value marking the network part of an address.
What does /24 mean?
The first 24 bits are the network; 8 bits are for hosts.
Why are two addresses unusable?
The network and broadcast addresses are reserved.
What is a /31 used for?
Point-to-point links, with two usable addresses.
Does it support IPv6?
Not yet.
