H1: Love Calculator
The love calculator is a game: type two names and it returns a "compatibility" percentage. It's for fun at parties, on a first date or in a classroom lesson on how algorithms work. It doesn't (and can't) measure real compatibility.
How to use it
1. First name: default Alex.
2. Second name: default Jordan.
3. Press Calculate.
Result: a compatibility score between 13% and 98%.
How the score is made
The calculator joins the two names, ignores capital letters and spaces, and runs the result through a simple hashing function, a recipe that turns text into a large number. It then maps that number onto the range 13–98.
Because the recipe is fixed:
The same pair always gets the same score. Alex and Jordan get 28% every time, however you capitalise them ("alex" and "JORDAN" also give 28%).
Order matters. Jordan and Alex give 60%, because the letters are combined in a different sequence.
Tiny changes swing the score. Adding a surname or using a nickname gives a completely different number.
There's no randomness and no psychology involved; it's a demonstration of how a hash function behaves.
Famous couples
Names
Score
Romeo + Juliet
93%
Elizabeth + Darcy
77%
Alex + Jordan
28%
Literature's most tragic couple outscores one of its happiest, which says everything about how seriously to take the result.
Ideas for using it
Party game: everyone tests their name with a celebrity; the highest score picks the next song.
Classroom: show that the same input always gives the same output, then change one letter and see the "avalanche" effect. It's a gentle introduction to how hashing is used for passwords and data checks.
Icebreaker: test team members' names with "pizza" or "Mondays".
What really predicts relationship satisfaction
Research on couples points to things a name can't capture: how partners handle conflict, shared values, kindness and trust, and commitment over time. The Gottman Institute's research, for example, emphasises how partners respond to each other's bids for attention [VERIFY specific findings before citing]. If you're looking for relationship support, professional counselling services exist in the US, Canada and the UK.
Privacy
Names are processed in your browser to create the score. FigSumo doesn't need or keep them.
Want it on your site?
You can embed the same game on a blog or event page with the love calculator widget.
Tips
Try full names and nicknames for a different result.
Swap the order for a second opinion.
Don't base decisions on it. It's a toy.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
Love calculators are an old schoolyard and magazine game in all three countries, and there's no regional version: the score depends only on the letters typed. Names with accents (Chloé, Zoë) are treated as they're typed, so "Chloe" and "Chloé" can give different scores. If you're comparing friends' names, spell them the same way each time.
Make it a game
Try each pair both ways round. The current version gives different scores for different name orders, which is part of the fun.
Use nicknames and full names and see which "matches" better.
Frequently asked questions
Is the love calculator accurate?
No. It's a game based on a hash of the letters, not on anything about the people.
Why does the same pair always get the same score?
The calculation is deterministic: the same letters always give the same number.
Does the order of the names matter?
Yes. Swapping them usually changes the score.
Why is the lowest score 13%?
The game keeps scores between 13% and 98% so nobody gets a flat zero or a perfect 100.
Does capitalisation matter?
No; names are converted to lower case first.
Are names stored?
No; the score is calculated in your browser.

H1: Mass Calculator
Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. If you know what something is made of (its density) and how big it is (its volume), you can work out its mass without a scale: useful for shipping estimates, lifting plans, engineering and science homework.
How to use this calculator
1. Density (kg/m³): for the material (default 7,850, typical carbon steel).
2. Volume (m³): the object's volume in cubic metres (default 0.01).
Result: mass in kilograms.
Volume in litres? Divide by 1,000 (10 L = 0.01 m³). In cubic centimetres? Divide by 1,000,000.
The formula
m = ρ × V
m: mass (kg)
ρ: density (kg/m³)
V: volume (m³)
Worked examples
Example 1: the default steel block
7,850 × 0.01 = 78.5 kg (about 173.1 lb).
Example 2: a steel ball
A solid steel ball 10 cm across has radius 0.05 m: V = 4/3 × π × 0.05³ = 0.000524 m³; mass = 4.11 kg. See the volume calculator for other shapes.
Example 3: water in a tank
A tank 2 m × 1.5 m filled to 0.4 m holds 1.2 m³ of water. At 1,000 kg/m³, that's 1,200 kg, more than a tonne; check floor loading before installing.
Example 4: an aluminium sheet
A 2.4 m × 1.2 m sheet, 3 mm thick: volume 0.00864 m³ × 2,700 = 23.33 kg.

Weight = mass × gravitational acceleration (9.80665 m/s² standard on Earth). The 78.5 kg block weighs 769.8 N on Earth but only about 127.2 N on the Moon (g ≈ 1.62 m/s²), while its mass stays 78.5 kg.
In everyday language in the US, Canada and the UK, "weight" in pounds or kilograms usually means mass. Use the weight converter for kg ↔ lb.

Understanding your results
Hollow objects: subtract the hollow volume, or the mass will be far too high.
Loose materials (sand, gravel, grain) need bulk density, which includes air gaps.
Precision: results are only as good as the density figure; real materials vary by a few percent.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering litres as cubic metres (1,000 times too heavy).
Mixing g/cm³ and kg/m³. 7.85 g/cm³ = 7,850 kg/m³.
Ignoring hollow sections and holes.
Treating newtons and kilograms as the same.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US engineers and fabricators often work in pounds and cubic inches. Steel's density is about 0.284 lb/in³ (7,850 kg/m³), so a 1 in × 2 in × 36 in steel bar weighs about 20.4 lb. Canadian and UK workshops use kg and m³ (or g/cm³), which avoids conversion. The UK spelling "aluminium" and the US "aluminum" are the same metal at about 2,700 kg/m³.

Multiply them: m = ρ × V.
What's the difference between mass and weight?
Mass is matter; weight is the force of gravity on it.

About 1,000 kg.
How do I convert g/cm³ to kg/m³?
Multiply by 1,000.
Does mass change on the Moon?
No, only weight does.

About 7,850 kg/m³ for common carbon steel.

Worked examples

How the rates are used
US employees: reimbursements at or below the IRS rate under an accountable plan are tax-free. Unreimbursed employee mileage is no longer deductible for most employees (the suspension was made permanent).

Canada: allowances at or below the CRA rates are generally tax-free to employees. Self-employed people deduct a business-use share of actual vehicle costs instead.
UK: payments up to AMAP are tax- and NIC-free. If your employer pays less, you can claim Mileage Allowance Relief on the difference.

Tips and common mistakes
Claiming commuting miles.
Using one US rate for the whole of 2026.
Forgetting the tier in Canada and the UK once you pass 5,000 km or 10,000 miles.
Using the rates as fuel cost. They cover fuel, wear, insurance and depreciation; for fuel only, use the fuel cost calculator.

73¢/km for the first 5,000 km and 67¢/km after that, in the provinces.
What is the HMRC mileage rate?
45p per mile for the first 10,000 business miles and 25p after.
Is mileage reimbursement taxable?
Not if it's at or below the official rate and properly documented.
Can I claim my commute?
Generally no.
Do I need a mileage log?
Yes; it's the main evidence for any claim.
Disclaimer
This page is general information, not tax advice. Rules depend on your circumstances; check with the IRS, CRA or HMRC, or a qualified tax adviser.

Title tag
Molarity Calculator: Moles, Volume, Concentration | FigSumo (59 chars)
Meta description
Solve for molarity, moles, solute mass or solution volume, with molar mass lookup for common compounds and dilution (C1V1 = C2V2). (130 chars)
Country
global

Body words
612 (minimum 600)
H1: Molarity Calculator
Molarity is the most common way chemists express concentration: the number of moles of a substance dissolved per litre of solution. Enter the amount in moles and the solution volume in litres, and this calculator returns the molarity in mol/L (M).
How to use this calculator
1. Amount (mol): moles of solute (default 0.5).
2. Volume (L): total volume of the solution, not just the solvent (default 1).
Result: molarity in mol/L.
Have grams instead of moles? Divide the mass by the molar mass first (see the molecular weight calculator).
The formula
M = n ÷ V
n = mass (g) ÷ molar mass (g/mol)
M: molarity (mol/L)
n: moles of solute
V: solution volume (L)
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
0.5 mol in 1 L = 0.5 M
Example 2: from grams (sodium chloride)
5.844 g of NaCl (molar mass 58.44 g/mol) is 0.1000 mol. Dissolved and made up to 250 mL (0.250 L): 0.1000 ÷ 0.250 = 0.4000 M.
Example 3: how much to weigh out
To make 500 mL of 0.1 M glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆, 180.16 g/mol): moles needed = 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.05 mol; mass = 0.05 × 180.16 = 9.008 g.
Example 4: dilution
To make 250 mL of 0.1 M solution from a 2.0 M stock: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂, so V₁ = 0.1 × 250 ÷ 2.0 = 12.5 mL of stock, topped up to 250 mL with water.
Preparing a solution correctly
1. Weigh the solute.
2. Dissolve it in less water than the final volume.
3. Transfer to a volumetric flask and add water up to the mark.
4. Mix thoroughly.
Adding solute to exactly 1 L of water gives slightly more than 1 L of solution, so the concentration would be a little low.
Related concentration units
Unit
Definition
Molarity (M)
mol solute per L solution
Millimolar (mM)
0.001 M; 0.25 M = 250 mM
Molality (m)
mol solute per kg solvent (doesn't change with temperature)
Mass percent (% w/w)
g solute per 100 g solution
% w/v
g solute per 100 mL solution
ppm
mg per kg (≈ mg/L for dilute water solutions)
Normality (N)
equivalents per L (e.g. 1 M H₂SO₄ = 2 N for acid–base)
Understanding your results
Temperature: volume changes with temperature, so molarity does too, slightly. Molality avoids this.
Significant figures: report to the precision of your measurements (see the rounding calculator).
Ionic compounds dissociate: 0.1 M CaCl₂ gives 0.1 M Ca²⁺ and 0.2 M Cl⁻.
Tips and common mistakes
Using mL as L. 250 mL is 0.250 L.
Using solvent volume instead of final solution volume.
Forgetting water of hydration in the molar mass (CuSO₄·5H₂O is 249.69 g/mol, not 159.61).
Mixing molarity and molality.
Safety
Follow your lab's safety rules and the substance's safety data sheet (SDS). Always add concentrated acid to water, not water to acid.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
UK GCSE and A-level papers write concentration as mol dm⁻³, which is identical to mol/L or M in US and Canadian textbooks (1 dm³ = 1 L). UK courses also use "g dm⁻³" for mass concentration.
Frequently asked questions
What is molarity?
Moles of solute per litre of solution.
How do I calculate molarity from grams?
Convert grams to moles with the molar mass, then divide by litres.
What does 1 M mean?
One mole of solute per litre of solution.
How do I dilute a solution?
Use C₁V₁ = C₂V₂.
What's the difference between molarity and molality?
Molarity uses litres of solution; molality uses kilograms of solvent.
Can I enter millilitres?
Not yet; divide by 1,000 to get litres.

H1: Molecular Weight Calculator
Molecular weight (molar mass) is the mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole. It's the bridge between grams, which you weigh, and moles, which chemical equations count. This calculator finds the molar mass from a measured sample: enter its mass and the number of moles it contains.
How to use this calculator
1. Sample mass (g): default 18.
2. Amount (mol): default 1.
Result: molecular weight in g/mol.
To find the molar mass from a chemical formula instead, add up the atomic weights, as shown below.
The formulas
From a sample:
M = mass (g) ÷ amount (mol)
From a formula:
M = Σ (number of atoms of each element × atomic weight)
Standard atomic weights (common elements)
Element
Symbol
Atomic weight
Hydrogen
H
1.008
Carbon
C
12.011
Nitrogen
N
14.007
Oxygen
O
15.999

22.990

32.06

35.45

Values follow IUPAC conventional atomic weights; some elements are officially given as ranges because natural isotope mixes vary.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
18 g ÷ 1 mol = 18 g/mol, close to water.
Example 2: water from its formula
H₂O = 2 × 1.008 + 15.999 = 18.015 g/mol
Example 3: glucose
C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6 × 12.011 + 12 × 1.008 + 6 × 15.999 = 180.156 g/mol. Carbon makes up 40.00% of its mass.
Example 4: brackets
Ca(OH)₂ = 40.078 + 2 × (15.999 + 1.008) = 74.092 g/mol. Multiply everything inside the brackets by the subscript.
Example 5: identifying an unknown
0.100 mol of an unknown gas has a mass of 4.40 g: 4.40 ÷ 0.100 = 44.0 g/mol, which matches carbon dioxide (CO₂ = 44.009 g/mol).
Example 6: sulfuric acid
H₂SO₄ = 98.072 g/mol.
Terminology
Molar mass (g/mol): mass of one mole; what this calculator gives.
Molecular weight / relative molecular mass (Mr): the same number without units, relative to 1/12 of a carbon-12 atom.
Molecular mass (Da or u): mass of a single molecule; numerically equal to molar mass.
Formula weight: used for ionic compounds like NaCl (58.44 g/mol) that don't form discrete molecules.
One mole contains 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant, exact since 2019).
Understanding your results
Hydrates include their water: CuSO₄·5H₂O is 249.69 g/mol.
Precision depends on your mass and mole measurements; weigh carefully.
To turn molar mass into concentration, use the molarity calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Forgetting subscripts outside brackets.
Using mass numbers (O = 16) when atomic weights are needed for precise work.
Leaving out water of crystallisation.
Confusing grams and moles in the inputs.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
Spelling: US textbooks write "sulfur"; UK schools now use "sulfur" too, following IUPAC, though older British books say "sulphur". Canadian texts generally use "sulfur". Enter the symbol S either way.
Terminology: US and Canadian high-school chemistry often says "molar mass" (g/mol). UK GCSE and A-level use "relative formula mass" (Mr, no units) and "relative molecular mass" for molecules. The numbers are the same: water is 18.02 g/mol, or Mr = 18.
Rounding in exams: UK exam boards usually give relative atomic masses to one decimal place (Cl = 35.5) in their data sheets, so your answer may differ slightly from the calculator's, which uses more precise values. Use the values your exam provides.
Frequently asked questions
What is molecular weight?
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol.
How do I calculate molar mass from a formula?
Multiply each element's atomic weight by its number of atoms and add them.
What is the molar mass of water?
About 18.015 g/mol.
Is molar mass the same as molecular weight?
Numerically yes; molar mass has units of g/mol.
What is Avogadro's number?
6.02214076 × 10²³ per mole.
Can I type a chemical formula?
Not yet; add atomic weights as shown above.

A layer of mulch keeps soil moist, suppresses weeds and evens out soil temperature. To order the right amount, you need the bed's area and the depth you want. This calculator converts length, width and depth into cubic yards (how bulk mulch is sold in the US and Canada) and cubic feet (how bags are labelled).

2. Depth (in): default 3.

The formulas
ft³ = length × width × depth ÷ 12
yd³ = ft³ ÷ 27
bags = ft³ ÷ bag size (ft³), rounded up
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
20 × 8 × (3 ÷ 12) = 40 ft³ = 1.48 yd³. In bags: 20 × 2 ft³ bags or 14 × 3 ft³ bags.
Example 2: a round bed

Entering depth in feet.

Ohm's Law Calculator

Title tag
Ohm's Law Calculator: Voltage, Current, Resistance | FigSumo (60 chars)
Meta description
Enter any two of voltage, current, resistance and power to find the other two, using V = I × R and P = V × I, with units from milli to mega. (140 chars)
Country
global
Status

Body words
606 (minimum 600)
H1: Ohm's Law Calculator
Ohm's law links the three basic quantities of an electrical circuit: voltage (V), current (I) and resistance (R). Know any two and you can find the third. This calculator solves for whichever value you leave blank and also gives the power the circuit uses.
How to use this calculator
1. Enter exactly two of:
Voltage (V)
Current (A)
Resistance (Ω)
2. Leave the one you want to find blank. By default, voltage is blank, current is 2 A and resistance is 10 Ω.
Results: voltage, current, resistance and power (W).
The formulas
V = I × R
I = V ÷ R
R = V ÷ I
P = V × I = I² × R = V² ÷ R
V: voltage in volts, the electrical "pressure"
I: current in amperes (amps), the flow of charge
R: resistance in ohms (Ω), the opposition to flow
P: power in watts
A handy memory aid is the triangle with V on top and I × R below: cover the one you want to find.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
I = 2 A, R = 10 Ω → V = 20 V, P = 40 W
Example 2: current through a resistor
12 V across 220 Ω: I = 12 ÷ 220 = 0.0545 A (54.5 mA), dissipating 0.6545 W. A standard ¼ W resistor is fine.
Example 3: an LED resistor
A red LED drops about 2 V and needs 20 mA. From a 5 V supply, the resistor must drop 3 V: R = 3 ÷ 0.020 = 150 Ω (use the next standard value up, 150 Ω), dissipating 0.06 W.
Example 4: a heater
A 120 V heater drawing 12.5 A has a resistance of 120 ÷ 12.5 = 9.6 Ω and uses 1,500 W.
Example 5: a UK kettle
A 3,000 W kettle on 230 V draws 13 A and has a resistance of about V² ÷ P = 17.63 Ω.
Unit prefixes
Prefix
Factor
Example
milli (m)
0.001
20 mA = 0.020 A
micro (µ)
0.000001
50 µA
kilo (k)
1,000
4.7 kΩ = 4,700 Ω
mega (M)
1,000,000
1 MΩ
Convert to base units before entering values.
Where Ohm's law applies
It holds for resistors and conductors at a steady temperature (ohmic devices). It doesn't directly describe:
LEDs and diodes, whose current rises sharply above a threshold voltage.
Filament bulbs, whose resistance increases as they heat up.
AC circuits with capacitors or motors, where impedance replaces resistance.
For series and parallel combinations, use the resistor calculator; for long cable runs, the voltage drop calculator.
Safety
Household voltages (120 V in North America, 230 V in the UK) can kill. Use these calculations for design and learning; leave mains wiring to a licensed electrician, and follow the NEC (US), the Canadian Electrical Code or BS 7671 (UK).
Tips and common mistakes
Filling in all three boxes; leave one blank.
Forgetting prefixes: 220 kΩ is 220,000 Ω.
Ignoring power ratings: a resistor dissipating more than its rating overheats.
Applying Ohm's law to LEDs without a series resistor.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
North American outlets supply about 120 V and the UK about 230 V, so the same 1,500 W heater draws 12.5 A in Toronto or Texas and 6.52 A in London. That's one reason UK plugs carry fuses (commonly 3 A or 13 A).
Frequently asked questions
What is Ohm's law?
V = I × R.
How do I calculate current?
Divide voltage by resistance.
How do I calculate resistance?
Divide voltage by current.
How do I calculate power?
Multiply voltage by current.
What unit is resistance measured in?
Ohms (Ω).
Does Ohm's law work for AC?
For purely resistive loads, yes; otherwise use impedance.

H1: Password Generator
Strong, unique passwords are the simplest defence against account takeovers. This generator creates random passwords from the character types you choose, from 4 to 128 characters long, in your browser.
How to use the generator
1. Password length: 4 to 128 (default 16).
2. Uppercase (A–Z), Lowercase (a–z), Numbers (0–9), Symbols: include or exclude each set. Symbols are ! @ # $ % ^ & * ( ) - _ = + [ ] { }.
3. Press Calculate for a new password, then copy it into your password manager.
Result: the generated password.
How strong is it?
Strength is measured as entropy, the number of guesses an attacker would need, expressed in bits:
entropy (bits) = length × log₂(number of possible characters)
With all four sets there are 26 + 26 + 10 + 18 = 80 possible characters.
Password
Entropy
4-digit PIN
13.3 bits
8 characters, all sets
50.6 bits
12 characters, all sets
75.9 bits
16 characters, letters and digits only
95.3 bits
16 characters, all sets (default)
101.2 bits
6-word diceware passphrase
77.5 bits
Each extra bit doubles the work. Even at a trillion guesses a second, exhausting half the space of a 16-character password would take on the order of 4.5e+10 years. Length matters more than symbols: a longer password with letters and digits beats a short one with every character type.
Why random beats clever
People pick predictable patterns: words with capital first letters, numbers at the end, "!" for a symbol, letter swaps like "@" for "a". Cracking tools try these first. A randomly generated password has no pattern to exploit.
Good password habits
Use a password manager to generate, store and fill passwords, so you only need to remember one strong master passphrase.
Never reuse passwords. A breach at one site then exposes the others.
Turn on multi-factor authentication (MFA), ideally with an authenticator app or passkey rather than SMS.
Check for breaches with a service such as Have I Been Pwned.
Change a password when there's a breach or sign of compromise, not on a fixed schedule; that's the current advice of NIST in the US and the UK's NCSC.
What the authorities recommend
NIST SP 800-63B (US): at least 8 characters for user-chosen passwords (15 when it's the only authentication factor), allow at least 64, and block known-breached passwords. No forced composition rules or periodic resets [VERIFY current revision numbers].
NCSC (UK): "three random words" for memorable passwords, plus a password manager.
Canadian Centre for Cyber Security: passphrases of at least 4 words / 15 characters, or complex passwords of 12+ characters.
Privacy
Passwords are generated on your device and aren't sent to FigSumo. Don't share them over email or chat.
Tips and common mistakes
Making it memorable by editing it. Changing a random password back into something familiar weakens it.
Excluding all but one set to fit a site's rules; increase the length instead.
Sites with odd symbol rules: turn symbols off and add four or more characters.
Saving passwords in a plain document.
Frequently asked questions
How long should my password be?
At least 12–16 characters; longer for important accounts.
Are symbols necessary?
They help, but length helps more.
Is it safe to generate passwords online?
This generator runs in your browser; use a password manager to store the result.
What is password entropy?
A measure in bits of how hard a password is to guess.
What's a passphrase?
Several random words, easier to remember and type.
How often should I change passwords?
When there's a reason to suspect compromise.

Title tag
Resistor Color Code Calculator (4, 5 and 6 Band) | FigSumo (58 chars)
Meta description
Decode resistor colour bands into resistance and tolerance, or find the bands for a value. Covers 4, 5 and 6-band resistors. (124 chars)
Country

622 (minimum 600)
H1: Resistor Color Code Calculator
Resistors combine in two basic ways. In series, current flows through one after another and the resistances add. In parallel, current splits between them and the combined resistance is lower than the smallest one. Enter two resistor values and choose a configuration to get the equivalent resistance.
How to use this calculator
1. R1 (Ω) and R2 (Ω): default 100 and 220.
2. Configuration: "Parallel (R1 ∥ R2)" or "Series (R1 + R2)".
Result: equivalent resistance in ohms.
The formulas
Series:
R = R1 + R2 + …
Parallel:
1 ÷ R = 1 ÷ R1 + 1 ÷ R2 + …
For two resistors: R = (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2)
Worked examples
Example 1: parallel (the default)
(100 × 220) ÷ (100 + 220) = 22,000 ÷ 320 = 68.75 Ω
Example 2: series
100 + 220 = 320 Ω
Example 3: three in parallel
Add a 470 Ω: 1 ÷ (1/100 + 1/220 + 1/470) = 59.98 Ω. For more than two, combine two at a time with the calculator: first 100 ∥ 220 = 68.75, then 68.75 ∥ 470.
Example 4: equal resistors
Two 1 kΩ in parallel = 500 Ω (half of one). n equal resistors in parallel give R ÷ n.
Example 5: a voltage divider
1 kΩ and 2.2 kΩ in series across 9 V: the voltage across the 2.2 kΩ is 9 × 2,200 ÷ 3,200 = 6.188 V. See the Ohm's law calculator for current and power.
Why use series or parallel?
Series: to make a value you don't have (100 + 220 = 320), or to share a high voltage across several resistors.
Parallel: to make a lower value, or to share power dissipation so each resistor runs cooler.

Standard values
Resistors come in preferred series. E12 (±10%): 10, 12, 15, 18, 22, 27, 33, 39, 47, 56, 68, 82 and their multiples of ten. E24 (±5%) adds values in between. Choose the nearest standard value, or combine two.

Tolerance adds up: two ±5% resistors in series give a total that's still within ±5%.
Parallel results are always below the smallest resistor.

Tips and common mistakes
Adding parallel resistors directly.
Forgetting the reciprocal at the end of the parallel formula.
Mixing kΩ and Ω in the inputs (4.7 kΩ = 4,700).
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
US and Canadian electronics texts write "color code" and UK texts "colour code", but the bands are an international standard (IEC 60062) and the values are the same. UK schools and some datasheets use the "R" notation, where 4R7 means 4.7 Ω and 2K2 means 2.2 kΩ, because a printed decimal point is easily lost.
Check: 2.2 kΩ and 4.7 kΩ in parallel give 2.2 × 4.7 ÷ (2.2 + 4.7) = 1.499 kΩ.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate resistors in series?
Add the values.
How do I calculate resistors in parallel?
1 ÷ (1/R1 + 1/R2), or (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2) for two.
Is parallel resistance always lower?
Yes, lower than the smallest resistor.
What is 100 Ω in parallel with 220 Ω?
68.75 Ω.
How do I read a resistor colour code?
First two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier, the fourth is tolerance.
Can I calculate more than two resistors?
Combine them two at a time.

H1: Roman Numeral Converter
Roman numerals still appear on clock faces, book chapters, film copyright dates, monarchs' names, Super Bowl titles and tattoos. This converter turns ordinary (Arabic) numbers from 1 to 3,999 into Roman numerals, and Roman numerals back into numbers.
How to use this converter
1. Direction: "Arabic number → Roman" or "Roman → Arabic number".
2. Value: a whole number from 1 to 3,999, or a Roman numeral (capitals or lower case).
Result: the Roman numeral or the number.

The rules
1. Add symbols written from largest to smallest: VI = 5 + 1 = 6; LXX = 70.
2. Subtract a smaller symbol placed before a larger one, in six standard pairs only:

3. Don't repeat a symbol more than three times in a row (so 4 is IV, not IIII), and never repeat V, L or D.
How the conversion works
To go from a number to Roman, the converter repeatedly takes the largest value from the list M, CM, D, CD, C, XC, L, XL, X, IX, V, IV, I that still fits and subtracts it. To go back, it reads left to right, adding each value and treating the six subtractive pairs as single units.
Worked examples
Example 1: 2026
2026 = 1000 + 1000 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1 → MMXXVI
Example 2: 1999
1000 (M) + 900 (CM) + 90 (XC) + 9 (IX) → MCMXCIX
Example 3: the largest
3,999 = MMMCMXCIX
Example 4: Roman to Arabic
XLIV → XL (40) + IV (4) = 44
Example 5: historic dates

Why stop at 3,999?
Standard Roman numerals have no symbol above M, and four Ms in a row breaks the three-repeat rule. Historically, a bar over a numeral (a vinculum) multiplied it by 1,000: V̄ = 5,000. There's also no Roman symbol for zero; medieval scholars wrote "nulla".
Where you'll see them
Monarchs and popes: Charles III, Elizabeth II, Leo XIV.
Super Bowl: Super Bowl LX (60) was played in February 2026.
Film and TV credits: copyright years such as MMXXVI.
Clocks: many clock faces use IIII instead of IV for visual balance, a tradition, not an error.
Outlines and book front matter: chapters, appendices and preface pages (i, ii, iii).
Tips and common mistakes
Invalid subtractions: 99 is XCIX, not IC; 49 is XLIX, not IL.
Too many repeats: 40 is XL, not XXXX.
Mixing up D and C, or L and C, when reading old inscriptions.
Tattoo dates: convert each part separately (day, month, year) and double-check before committing to ink.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
Film and TV copyright dates in the US and UK traditionally use Roman numerals, such as MMXXVI for 2026.
Super Bowl numbers (US) and monarchs' names (UK: Charles III, Elizabeth II) are the most familiar modern uses.
Clocks: many clock faces in all three countries show IIII for 4 rather than IV, a long-standing design tradition. The converter uses the standard subtractive form, IV.
Outlines and prefaces: US and Canadian book prefaces often number pages i, ii, iii in lower-case Roman numerals; the values are the same.
Practice
1,987 = M + CM + LXXX + VII = MCMLXXXVII
CDXLIV = 400 + 40 + 4 = 444

MMXXVI.

IV (clock faces sometimes use IIII).

MCMXCIX.

MMMCMXCIX (3,999).

No.

Yes; the converter accepts both.

Title tag
Roofing Calculator: Roof Area, Squares and Bundles | FigSumo (60 chars)
Meta description

H1: Roofing Calculator
Roofing materials are sold by the "square", which is 100 square feet of roof surface. A roof's real surface is larger than the footprint of the house because it slopes. This calculator adjusts the footprint for pitch, adds a waste allowance, and tells you the area and the number of squares to order.
How to use this calculator
1. Roof length (ft) and roof width (ft): the horizontal footprint the roof covers, including overhangs (default 40 × 30).
2. Pitch rise (in per 12 in run): for example 6 for a 6/12 roof (default 6).
3. Waste factor (%): extra for cuts, starter rows, ridges and mistakes (default 10).
Results: roof area with waste (ft²) and roofing squares, plus a chart splitting the sloped surface and the waste allowance.
The formulas
pitch factor = √(1 + (rise ÷ 12)²)
sloped area = length × width × pitch factor
area with waste = sloped area × (1 + waste ÷ 100)
squares = area with waste ÷ 100
The pitch factor comes from the Pythagorean theorem: for each 12 in of horizontal run, the roof surface runs along the hypotenuse of a 12-by-rise triangle.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
Pitch factor for 6/12 = √1.25 = 1.1180
Sloped area = 40 × 30 × 1.1180 = 1,341.64 ft²
With 10% waste = 1,476 ft² = 14.76 squares
Asphalt shingles commonly come 3 bundles per square: about 45 bundles
Example 2: steeper roof, with overhangs
A 42 × 32 ft house with 1 ft overhangs all round (44 × 34 ft footprint), 8/12 pitch (factor 1.2019), 15% waste for a hip roof: 1,798 ft² sloped, 2,068 ft² with waste, 20.68 squares.
Example 3: metric pitch
A 10 m × 8 m footprint at a 35° pitch, common in the UK: factor = 1 ÷ cos 35° = 1.2208, so about 97.7 m² of roof.

The formula works for any roof with a single pitch throughout, whether gable or hip, because every face shares the same slope. For roofs with sections at different pitches, calculate each section separately and add.
Waste allowance
Simple gable: about 10%.
Hip roofs, valleys, dormers: 15–20%.
Patterned or architectural shingles: follow the manufacturer's guidance.
What else to order
Underlayment: synthetic rolls often cover 4–10 squares each [VERIFY product].
Starter strip, ridge cap and drip edge: measured in linear feet along eaves, rakes and ridges.
Ice and water shield: many US and Canadian codes require it along eaves in cold climates.
Nails: typically 4–6 per shingle; high-wind areas require more.
Understanding your results
Measure the footprint including overhangs; building plans or aerial measurements help.
The chart is area, not cost.
Local codes (the IRC in the US, the National Building Code of Canada, UK Building Regulations) set minimum slopes for each roofing material.
Tips and common mistakes
Using the house's floor area without overhangs.
Ignoring pitch: a 12/12 roof has 41% more surface than its footprint.
Under-ordering waste on complex roofs.
Working on a roof without fall protection. Steep or high roofs are a job for professionals.
Frequently asked questions
What is a roofing square?
100 square feet of roof surface.
How do I calculate roof area from pitch?
Multiply the footprint by √(1 + (rise ÷ 12)²).
How many bundles are in a square?
Usually 3 for standard asphalt shingles.
How much waste should I add?
10% for simple roofs; 15–20% for complex ones.
What does 6/12 pitch mean?
The roof rises 6 inches for every 12 inches of horizontal run.
How do I measure pitch?
Hold a level 12 in horizontally against a rafter and measure the vertical rise.

H1: Shoe Size Converter
Shoe sizes differ between the US, UK and Europe, and between men's, women's and children's ranges, which makes buying shoes online across borders tricky. This converter maps US men's sizes to European (EU) sizes and back, and the tables below cover UK and women's sizes too.
How to use this converter
1. Convert: "US men's → EU" or "EU → US men's".
2. Shoe size: whole or half sizes (default 10).
Result: the approximate size in the other system.
Size systems at a glance
US: based on the length of the shoe's last in thirds of an inch, with separate men's and women's scales (women's is about 1.5 sizes larger for the same foot).
UK: also in thirds of an inch but starts from a different zero; UK men's is usually ½ to 1 size smaller than US men's. UK sizes are unisex.
EU (Paris points): steps of ⅔ cm along the last; one scale for everyone.
Mondopoint (JP/ski boots): the foot length in millimetres.

Worked examples

Measure your foot
The most reliable way to buy across systems is by length:
1. Stand on a sheet of paper against a wall, heel touching the wall.
2. Mark the tip of your longest toe; measure heel to mark in centimetres.
3. Measure both feet in the evening, when feet are largest, and use the longer one.
4. Compare with the brand's chart, which often lists foot length (or Mondopoint) for each size.
Allow about 1–1.5 cm of room beyond your toes for most shoes; running shoes often need a thumb's width.
Children's sizes
Children's US and UK sizes run on separate scales that restart after 13 (US 13C → youth 1). EU sizes continue on the same scale, so EU is often the simplest system for kids. Measure every few months; children's feet grow quickly.
Width
US widths run from narrow (A/B) through medium (D for men, B for women) to wide (E, EE, 4E). UK widths use letters such as E, F, G and H. EU sizing rarely specifies width; look for "wide fit" ranges.
Understanding your results
Every conversion is approximate. There's no single international standard everyone uses.
Half sizes don't always exist in EU sizing.
Fit varies by style: boots, trainers, heels and sandals of the same nominal size fit differently.
Tips and common mistakes
Confusing UK and US sizes; UK numbers are smaller.
Using men's conversions for women's shoes.
Measuring in the morning.
Ignoring width.
Frequently asked questions

About 43–44.
How do UK and US sizes compare?
UK is usually ½–1 size smaller than US men's and about 2 sizes smaller than US women's.
How do I convert women's to men's sizes?
Subtract about 1.5 from the US women's size.
What's the most accurate method?
Measure foot length in centimetres and use the brand's chart.
Are EU sizes unisex?
Yes.

Use the chart above; a UK direction is planned.

H1: Sleep Calculator
Waking up at the end of a sleep cycle, rather than in the middle of deep sleep, can leave you feeling less groggy. This calculator works backwards from the time you need to get up and suggests when to go to bed, based on 90-minute sleep cycles plus time to fall asleep.
How to use this calculator
1. Wake-up time (HH:MM): in 24-hour format (default 07:00).
2. Sleep cycles (90 min each): 3 to 6 (default 5).
Results: suggested bedtime and time in bed (hours).
How it works
time in bed = cycles × 90 minutes + 15 minutes
bedtime = wake-up time − time in bed
The 15 minutes is a typical time to fall asleep.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
Wake at 07:00 with 5 cycles: 5 × 90 + 15 = 465 minutes (7.75 h, shown as 7.8) → bed at 23:15.
Example 2: options for a 07:00 alarm

What happens in a sleep cycle
Each night you pass through roughly four to six cycles, each lasting about 80–110 minutes:
1. N1 (light sleep): a few minutes of drifting off.
2. N2: body temperature drops, heart rate slows; most of the night is spent here.
3. N3 (deep, slow-wave sleep): hardest to wake from; important for physical recovery. More of it happens early in the night.
4. REM sleep: vivid dreams and memory processing; REM periods lengthen towards morning.
Ninety minutes is an average. Your cycles vary from night to night and through the night, so treat the suggested bedtime as a guide, not a precise target.
How much sleep do you need?
Recommendations from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the US CDC and the UK NHS are broadly similar:
Age
Recommended per day
Teenagers (13–18)
8–10 hours
Adults (18–60)
7 or more hours
Adults (61–64)
7–9 hours
65+
7–8 hours
Five cycles (7.5 h of sleep) fits most adults; four cycles (6 h) falls short of the 7-hour minimum.
Tips for better sleep
Keep a consistent schedule, including weekends.
Get morning daylight and limit bright screens in the hour before bed.
Avoid caffeine late in the day (its effects can last 6 hours or more) and heavy meals or alcohol close to bedtime.
Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet.
If you can't sleep after about 20 minutes, get up and do something calm until you feel sleepy.
When to get help
Persistent trouble sleeping, loud snoring with gasping, or severe daytime sleepiness can signal conditions such as insomnia or sleep apnoea. Talk to a doctor (a GP in the UK).
Understanding your results
Times are 24-hour: 23:15 is 11:15 pm.
Falling asleep takes longer for some people; move the bedtime earlier if you usually need 30 minutes.
Naps: a 20-minute nap avoids deep sleep; a 90-minute nap covers a full cycle.
Frequently asked questions
What time should I go to bed to wake up at 7 am?
Around 23:15 for five cycles, or 21:45 for six.
How long is a sleep cycle?
About 90 minutes on average (80–110).
Is it better to sleep 6 or 7.5 hours?
7.5 hours meets adult recommendations; 6 doesn't.
Why add 15 minutes?
It's a typical time to fall asleep.
Can I enter 12-hour times?
Use 24-hour format (07:00, 23:30).
Does this work for shift workers?
Yes; enter your actual wake-up time.
Disclaimer
This calculator gives general sleep-timing suggestions, not medical advice. If you have ongoing sleep problems, speak to a healthcare professional.

H1: Speed Calculator
Average speed is distance divided by time. This calculator takes a distance in miles and a time in hours and minutes and returns your average speed in miles per hour and kilometres per hour. Use it for road trips, cycling and running splits, or physics homework.
How to use this calculator
1. Distance (mi): default 26.2 (a marathon).
2. Hours and Minutes: the elapsed time (default 0 h 45 min).
Results: average speed in mph and km/h.
The formulas
speed = distance ÷ time
distance = speed × time
time = distance ÷ speed
km/h = mph × 1.609344
Time must be in hours: 45 minutes = 0.75 h.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
26.2 mi ÷ 0.75 h = 34.93 mph (56.22 km/h). That's a car on a suburban road, not a runner.
Example 2: a marathon runner
26.2 mi in 4 h 0 min → 6.55 mph (10.54 km/h), a pace of about 9:10 per mile. Pace (time per mile) is the inverse of speed: 60 ÷ mph minutes per mile.
Example 3: how far will I get?
Driving at an average of 65 mph for 2.5 hours covers 65 × 2.5 = 162.5 miles.
Example 4: how long will it take?
300 miles at an average of 70 mph takes 300 ÷ 70 = 4.29 h ≈ 4 h 17 min, before stops.
Example 5: the fastest human
Usain Bolt's 100 m world record of 9.58 s is an average of 10.44 m/s, or 23.35 mph.

about 340 m/s, 761 mph
Ships and aircraft use knots: 20 knots = 37.04 km/h.
Average speed vs average of speeds
If you drive 60 miles at 30 mph and another 60 miles at 60 mph, your average speed is not 45 mph. Total time is 2 h + 1 h = 3 h, so the average is 120 ÷ 3 = 40 mph. Always divide total distance by total time.
Speed limits in the US, Canada and UK
US: limits are in mph and set by states; rural interstates are often 65–75 mph, with some at 80 or more.
Canada: limits are in km/h; most highways are 100–110 km/h.
UK: limits are in mph: 70 mph on motorways and dual carriageways, 60 mph on single carriageways for cars, 30 mph in built-up areas (20 mph is the default in Wales since 2023).
Understanding your results
Average, not maximum: traffic, stops and hills mean your top speed was higher.
Moving time vs elapsed time: fitness trackers often show both; use the one that matches your question.
Precision: results show two decimals.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering 1.30 for 1 hour 30 minutes. Use the separate hours and minutes boxes.
Averaging speeds instead of dividing total distance by total time.
Mixing kilometres and miles.
Practice
10 km in 50 minutes is 10 ÷ (50/60) = 12 km/h, or about 7.46 mph.
At 12 km/h, a half marathon (21.1 km) takes about 1 h 45 min.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate average speed?
Divide total distance by total time.
How do I convert mph to km/h?
Multiply by 1.609344.
How do I find time from speed and distance?
Divide distance by speed.
How do I calculate running pace?
Divide time by distance (minutes per mile).
What is 100 km/h in mph?
About 62.1 mph.
Can I enter kilometres?
Not yet; divide km by 1.609344 to get miles.

Understanding your results

Stair Calculator: Rise, Run and Stringer Length | FigSumo (57 chars)

H1: Stair Calculator
Building or replacing a staircase starts with simple arithmetic: how many steps fit the height between floors, how tall each riser is, and how far the stairs will run. This calculator takes the total rise and your target step sizes and returns the number of risers, the exact riser height, the total run and an approximate stringer length.
How to use this calculator
1. Total rise (in): finished floor to finished floor (default 108, a 9 ft rise).
2. Target riser height (in): the step height you'd like (default 7.5).
3. Target tread depth (in): the horizontal depth of each step (default 10).
Results: number of steps (risers), actual riser height, total run and approximate stringer length.
The formulas
risers = total rise ÷ target riser, rounded to the nearest whole number
actual riser = total rise ÷ risers
treads = risers − 1        (the top floor acts as the last step)
total run = tread depth × treads
stringer ≈ √(riser² + tread²) × risers
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
108 ÷ 7.5 = 14.4 → 14 risers
108 ÷ 14 = 7.714 in each (about 7 ¹¹⁄₁₆ in)
13 treads × 10 in = 130 in run (10 ft 10 in)
Stringer ≈ 176.82 in. The straight-line diagonal from bottom to top is 169.01 in; the calculator's figure includes one extra step's diagonal to allow for the top connection.
Stair angle ≈ 37.6°
Example 2: comfort check
A common rule of thumb is 2 × riser + tread ≈ 24–25 in. Here: 2 × 7.714 + 10 = 25.43 in. That's a little short; a 10.5 in or 11 in tread would feel more natural if space allows.
Example 3: metric
A UK or Canadian rise of 2,700 mm with 180 mm target risers and 250 mm treads: 15 risers of 180.0 mm, a 3,500 mm run, and a pitch of 35.8°. Convert to inches (÷ 25.4) to use the calculator, or work it by hand like this.

US (IRC)
Canada (NBC, dwellings)
England (Approved Document K, private stair)

7¾ in (196 mm)
200 mm

10 in (254 mm)

Local amendments apply, so check with your building department or local authority before you build.
Terms
Rise / riser: vertical height of one step.
Run / tread / going: horizontal depth of one step (the "going" excludes the nosing overhang).
Nosing: the front edge that overhangs the riser below, typically ¾–1¼ in.
Stringer: the sloped board that supports the treads.
Headroom: vertical clearance above the stair's pitch line.
Understanding your results
Every riser must be equal. Even small differences trip people; codes limit variation to ⅜ in (9.5 mm) in the US.
Measure finished heights, including flooring on both levels.
Stringer stock length: buy the next standard length up from the stringer figure and allow for the cut at top and bottom.
Tips and common mistakes
Counting treads as risers. There's one fewer tread than risers.
Ignoring flooring thickness, which changes the first and last riser.
Forgetting the landing on long flights; codes limit the total rise of a single flight.
Leaving out the nosing when checking tread depth.
Frequently asked questions
How many stairs do I need for a 9 ft rise?
About 14 risers of 7.7 in.
What is the maximum riser height?
7¾ in under the US IRC; 200 mm in Canada and 220 mm for English private stairs.
What is a comfortable stair angle?
About 30–37°.
Why is there one fewer tread than riser?
The upper floor forms the last step.
How long should my stringer be?
Roughly the diagonal of the total rise and run, plus a little for the cuts.
Does it check building codes?
Not yet; compare your results with the table above.

H1: Tile Calculator
Ordering tile means working out how many pieces cover the floor or wall, plus extra for cuts, breakage and future repairs. This calculator takes the area to cover, the tile size and a waste allowance, and tells you how many tiles to buy.
How to use this calculator
1. Area to cover (ft²): from the square footage calculator if needed (default 120).
2. Tile size (in): the side of a square tile (default 12 for 12 × 12 in).
3. Waste (%): extra for cuts and breakage (default 10).
Results: tiles needed (rounded up) and tile area (ft² per tile).
The formulas
tile area (ft²) = (tile size in ÷ 12)²
area with waste = area × (1 + waste ÷ 100)
tiles = area with waste ÷ tile area, rounded up
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
12 in tiles are 1 ft² each. 120 × 1.10 = 132 ft² → 132 tiles. In boxes of 10, that's 14 boxes.
Example 2: smaller tiles
Same floor with 6 in tiles (0.25 ft² each) → 528 tiles.
Example 3: rectangular tiles
Not yet built in: divide by the tile's area. 12 × 24 in tiles cover 2 ft² each, so 132 ÷ 2 = 66 tiles.
Example 4: a metric bathroom (UK, Canada)
11 m² with 30 × 30 cm tiles (0.09 m² each) and 10% waste → 135 tiles.
Example 5: a backsplash
30 ft² of 3 × 6 in subway tiles (0.125 ft² each) with 15% waste → 276 tiles.

Keep a few spare tiles after the job. Dye lots vary, and an exact match later can be impossible.
Grout lines
The calculation ignores grout joints, which slightly reduces the number of tiles needed (a ⅛ in joint on 12 in tiles is about 2%). The waste allowance usually covers the difference. Common joint widths are 1/16–⅛ in for rectified wall tiles and ⅛–¼ in for floors.
Other materials
Thinset or adhesive: coverage depends on trowel notch size; check the bag (often 40–95 ft² per 50 lb bag for floor tile [VERIFY product]).
Grout: depends on tile size, joint width and depth; manufacturers publish calculators.
Underlayment, membranes and trim: measure separately.
Understanding your results
Tiles are rounded up, so you never under-order a whole tile.
Order full boxes; most suppliers won't split them.
The chart compares the coverage area with the waste buffer.
Tips and common mistakes
Using nominal sizes: a "12 × 12" tile may actually be 11¾ in. For large areas, use the actual size.
Forgetting waste for patterns.
Buying from different dye lots. Check the lot number on every box.
Tiling under fixed cabinets. Usually unnecessary; subtract that area.
Quick check
12 m² plus 10% waste is 13.2 m² of tile.
Frequently asked questions
How many tiles do I need for 100 ft²?
With 12 × 12 in tiles and 10% waste, 110.
How much extra tile should I buy?
Usually 10%, more for diagonal or herringbone layouts.
How many 12 × 24 tiles are in a square foot?
Each covers 2 ft², so half a tile per ft².
Should I count grout lines?
Not usually; the waste allowance covers them.
Can I use metric sizes?
Not yet. Convert to inches and ft², or use the metric example above.
How many tiles are in a box?
It varies; check the box's coverage in ft² or m².

H1: Time Calculator
Adding up durations in your head goes wrong as soon as minutes pass 60. This calculator adds or subtracts two lengths of time given in hours and minutes and returns the result in hours and minutes, plus the total in minutes.
How to use this calculator
1. First time: hours and minutes (default 2 h 45 min).
2. Second time: hours and minutes (default 1 h 30 min).
3. Operation: Add or Subtract.
Results: total time in hours and minutes and total minutes. If you subtract a longer time from a shorter one, the result is shown as negative.
How it works
total minutes = (h₁ × 60 + m₁) ± (h₂ × 60 + m₂)
hours = total minutes ÷ 60 (whole part)
minutes = total minutes mod 60
Working in minutes avoids the carry-over errors that happen with base-60 arithmetic.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
2 h 45 min + 1 h 30 min = 165 + 90 = 255 minutes = 4 h 15 min.
Example 2: subtracting
1 h 30 min − 2 h 45 min = −1 h 15 min (−75 minutes).
Example 3: a playlist or project
Adding several durations (1 h 12 min, 58 min, 2 h 5 min and 47 min) two at a time gives 5 h 2 min (302 minutes). Add the first two, then add the next to the result, and so on.
Example 4: time remaining
An 8-hour shift with 5 h 50 min already worked leaves 2 h 10 min.
Example 5: doubling a recipe time
Some processes scale with quantity: 3 h 45 min twice over is 3 h 45 + 3 h 45 = 7 h 30 min. (Most cooking times don't double when you double the quantity.)
Base-60 arithmetic by hand
Add the minutes and the hours separately, then carry:
  2 h 45 min
+ 1 h 30 min
= 3 h 75 min → 75 min = 1 h 15 min → 4 h 15 min
To subtract, borrow 60 minutes from the hours when needed:
  5 h 10 min − 2 h 40 min → 4 h 70 min − 2 h 40 min = 2 h 30 min

To turn hours and minutes into a decimal for payroll, use the hours calculator.
Where time arithmetic comes up
Timesheets and billing: totalling hours across a week.
Travel: adding legs and layovers (check time zones with the time zone calculator).
Video and audio editing: summing clip lengths.
Fitness: total training time across sessions.
Cooking and baking: chaining prep, proving and baking times.
Understanding your results
Results can exceed 24 hours; this is a duration calculator, not a clock.
For the time between two clock times (09:15 to 17:40), use the time duration calculator.
Negative results mean the second time is longer than the first.
Tips and common mistakes
Treating minutes as decimals. 1.30 hours isn't 1 h 30 min.
Forgetting to carry when minutes exceed 59.
Mixing clock times and durations.
Frequently asked questions

Convert both to minutes, add, then convert back.
What is 2 h 45 min + 1 h 30 min?
4 h 15 min.
Can I subtract time?
Yes; choose Subtract.
Can the result be more than 24 hours?
Yes.
Can I add seconds?
Not yet; use fractions of a minute or convert to minutes.
How do I add more than two times?
Add them two at a time.

H1: Time Card Calculator
This calculator turns a clock-in time, a clock-out time and an unpaid break into the hours you actually worked, both as a decimal (for payroll) and in hours and minutes. It handles overnight shifts that finish after midnight.
How to use this calculator
1. Clock in (HH:MM): 24-hour format (default 09:00).
2. Clock out (HH:MM): default 17:30. If it's earlier than clock-in, the shift is treated as ending the next day.
3. Unpaid break (min): default 30.
Results: hours worked (decimal, two places) and time on clock (hours and minutes, after the break).
The formula
minutes worked = clock out − clock in (+ 1,440 if past midnight) − break
decimal hours = minutes worked ÷ 60
Worked examples
Example 1: the default day
09:00 to 17:30 is 8 h 30 min, minus a 30-minute break = 8 h 0 min = 8.00 hours. At $18.50 an hour, that's $148.00.
Example 2: a night shift
22:00 to 06:15 with a 45-minute break: 8 h 15 min − 45 min = 7 h 30 min (7.50 hours).
Example 3: a week with overtime (US)
Daily totals of 8, 8, 8.5, 9.25 and 8.75 hours make 42.50 hours. Under the FLSA, non-exempt employees get time and a half after 40 hours: 2.50 overtime hours. At $20/hour: 40 × $20 + 2.50 × $30 = $875.00. (The calculator handles one shift at a time; add days together for the week.)
Breaks and overtime rules
United States
Federal law (FLSA) doesn't require meal breaks, but short breaks of 5–20 minutes that an employer allows must be paid. Bona fide meal periods (usually 30 minutes or more) where you're fully relieved of duty can be unpaid.
Overtime: 1.5× the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states, including California, also require daily overtime (over 8 hours) and mandate meal and rest breaks.
Canada
Rules are set by each province (and federally for federally regulated industries). Most require a 30-minute break after about 5 hours, often unpaid.
Overtime thresholds are commonly 8 hours a day and/or 40 or 44 hours a week, at 1.5× [VERIFY province].
United Kingdom
Workers over 18 are entitled to a 20-minute rest break if they work more than 6 hours a day; it doesn't have to be paid.
There's no statutory overtime rate, but average pay for all hours must meet the National Minimum Wage / National Living Wage.
Rounding
US employers may round clock times to the nearest 5, 6 or 15 minutes if it averages out over time and doesn't systematically underpay. Record exact times where you can.
Understanding your results
Decimal hours are what payroll multiplies by your rate; 8 h 15 min is 8.25, not 8.15. See the hours calculator.
Gross pay only: for take-home pay after tax, use the US paycheck calculator or the UK take-home pay calculator.
Breaks longer than the shift produce an error.
Tips and common mistakes
Using 12-hour times without am/pm. Enter 17:30, not 5:30.
Deducting paid breaks. Only subtract unpaid time.
Missing overnight shifts on paper timesheets; the calculator adds a day automatically.
Rounding each shift to the nearest hour.
Frequently asked questions
How do I calculate hours worked?
Clock-out minus clock-in, minus unpaid breaks.
How do I calculate an overnight shift?
Enter the times as normal; if clock-out is earlier, the calculator adds 24 hours.
What is 8 hours 15 minutes in decimal?
8.25.
Are breaks paid?
It depends on the jurisdiction and the length of the break.
When does overtime start in the US?
After 40 hours in a workweek under federal law.
Can I calculate a whole week?
Calculate each day and add the decimal hours.

How long is it from 08:15 to 12:45? From 21:30 to 06:10 the next morning? This calculator gives the duration between two clock times in hours and minutes, and in total minutes.

duration = end − start            (in minutes)
if negative, add 1,440 (24 hours)
Worked examples

1. Count up from the start to the next full hour.
2. Count whole hours to the last full hour before the end.
3. Add the remaining minutes.

H1: Time Zone Converter
Scheduling a call between Toronto and London, or checking when a flight lands in Vancouver? This calculator converts a time from one UTC offset to another and shows the equivalent UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).
How to use this calculator
1. Local time (HH:MM): 24-hour format (default 14:00).
2. From UTC offset (hours): the offset of the starting location (default −5).
3. To UTC offset (hours): the offset of the destination (default +1).
Fractional offsets work: enter −3.5 for Newfoundland or 5.5 for India.
Results: converted time and UTC time.
How it works
UTC = local time − from offset
converted time = UTC + to offset
Results wrap around midnight. Check whether the converted time falls on the previous or next day.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
14:00 at UTC−5 → UTC 19:00 → 20:00 at UTC+1. That's 2 pm in New York (winter) and 8 pm in Paris (winter).
Example 2: crossing midnight backwards
09:00 in Pakistan (UTC+5) → UTC 04:00 → 00:00 in New York during summer time (UTC−4), on the previous day.
Example 3: Toronto to London in summer
09:00 in Toronto (EDT, UTC−4) → UTC 13:00 → 14:00 in London (BST, UTC+1). In winter, enter −5 and 0: the gap is still five hours, except during the weeks when only one side has changed its clocks.
Example 4: half-hour zones
Noon in St John's, Newfoundland (UTC−3:30 standard) → 16:30 in Paris (UTC+1).

Daylight saving time
Offsets change during summer time, and countries switch on different dates:
US and Canada: second Sunday in March to first Sunday in November.
UK and EU: last Sunday in March to last Sunday in October.
For a few weeks each spring and autumn, the gap between North America and Europe is an hour shorter than usual. This calculator uses the offsets you enter, so pick the ones in force on the date in question.
UTC vs GMT
UTC is the international time standard, kept by atomic clocks. GMT is a time zone (the UK in winter) that's equal to UTC for everyday purposes. Aviation and IT systems use UTC (sometimes written "Z" or "Zulu").
Understanding your results
Day changes aren't labelled yet. If the converted time is earlier than the original when moving east, or later when moving west, it's on a different day.
For flight durations, convert departure and arrival to the same zone first, then use the time duration calculator.
Tips and common mistakes
Using standard offsets in summer.
Getting the sign wrong: west of Greenwich is negative.
Forgetting half-hour and 45-minute zones (Nepal is +5:45).
Scheduling across a DST changeover week.
Frequently asked questions
How do I convert time zones?
Subtract the source offset to get UTC, then add the destination offset.
What's the UTC offset for Eastern Time?
−5 in winter, −4 in summer.
Is GMT the same as UTC?
Effectively, for everyday use.
Does the calculator handle daylight saving?
Enter the offset in force on the date; it doesn't adjust automatically.
What time is it in London when it's noon in Vancouver?
20:00 in winter (−8 → 0) and 20:00 in summer (−7 → +1).
Can I enter half-hour offsets?
Yes, as decimals such as 5.5.

Title tag
Tire Size Calculator: Compare Two Tire Sizes | FigSumo (54 chars)
Meta description
Decode tire sizes like 225/45R17 and compare overall diameter, width, sidewall height and speedometer difference between two sizes. (131 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
615 (minimum 600)
H1: Tire Size Calculator
The code on a tyre's sidewall, such as 225/45R17, describes its size. This calculator converts the three key numbers into the tyre's overall diameter, sidewall height and revolutions per mile, which you need when changing wheel or tyre sizes.
How to use this calculator
1. Section width (mm): the first number (default 225).
2. Aspect ratio (%): the second number, sidewall height as a percentage of width (default 45).
3. Wheel diameter (in): the number after "R" (default 17).
Results: overall diameter (in), sidewall height (each, in) and revolutions per mile.
Reading a tyre size
225/45R17 94W
225: section width in millimetres
45: aspect ratio (sidewall = 45% of 225 mm = 101.25 mm)
R: radial construction
17: wheel (rim) diameter in inches
94: load index; W: speed rating (up to 168 mph / 270 km/h)
LT (light truck) and P (passenger) prefixes appear on some US tyres.
The formulas
sidewall (in) = width × aspect ÷ 100 ÷ 25.4
diameter (in) = rim + 2 × sidewall
circumference = π × diameter
revolutions per mile = 63,360 ÷ circumference
(63,360 is the number of inches in a mile.)
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
Sidewall = 225 × 0.45 ÷ 25.4 = 3.99 in
Diameter = 17 + 2 × 3.99 = 24.97 in
Circumference = 78.45 in → 808 revolutions per mile
Example 2: plus-sizing to 245/40R18
Diameter = 25.72 in, 2.98% larger than 225/45R17. Your speedometer, calibrated for the original size, would read 60 mph when you're actually doing about 61.8 mph.
Example 3: a truck tyre
265/70R17: diameter 31.61 in, 638 revolutions per mile.
Changing tyre sizes safely
Keep the overall diameter within about 3% of the original to limit speedometer error and avoid problems with ABS, traction control and transmission shift points; many manufacturers and tyre retailers recommend this [VERIFY with your vehicle maker].
Check clearance at full steering lock and suspension compression.
Match or exceed the original load index and speed rating.
Use the same size on each axle (all four on AWD vehicles).
Tyre placard: the recommended sizes and pressures are on the driver's door jamb.
Speedometer error
If a new tyre is larger, each revolution covers more ground, so the speedometer reads low. If it's smaller, the speedometer reads high. Actual speed = indicated speed × (new diameter ÷ old diameter).
Regional notes
US: tyres carry a DOT code showing manufacture date (the last four digits: week and year).
Canada: winter tyres bearing the three-peak mountain snowflake are mandatory in Quebec from 1 December to 15 March, and required on many BC highways from 1 October to 30 April.
UK: the legal minimum tread depth for cars is 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the tread.
Understanding your results
Actual diameter varies slightly between brands and with tread wear and pressure.
Revolutions per mile from a manufacturer's spec sheet may differ by 1–2% from this geometric figure because a loaded tyre deforms.
Tips and common mistakes
Treating the aspect ratio as a height in mm. It's a percentage of the width.
Mixing up width (mm) and rim (in).
Ignoring load index when choosing a larger wheel with a lower-profile tyre.
Frequently asked questions
What does 225/45R17 mean?
225 mm wide, sidewall 45% of the width, radial, for a 17-inch wheel.
How tall is a 225/45R17 tyre?
About 24.97 in.
How much can tyre diameter change?
Usually within about 3% of the original.
Will bigger tyres affect my speedometer?
Yes; it will read lower than your true speed.
How do I calculate revolutions per mile?
63,360 ÷ (π × diameter in inches).
Can I compare two sizes?
Run the calculator for each and compare diameters.

H1: Unit Converter
Converting between metric and imperial units comes up constantly in North America and the UK: recipes in grams, road signs in miles, weather in Celsius or Fahrenheit. This converter handles the everyday conversions for length, weight and temperature using exact defined factors.
How to use this converter

Length: meters, kilometers, feet, inches, miles

How it works
Length and mass convert through a base unit: the value is multiplied by the "from" unit's size in meters (or kilograms) and divided by the "to" unit's size. Temperature uses formulas because the scales have different zero points.

Quick mental conversions

US, Canada and UK usage
United States: customary units for almost everything outside science and medicine; Fahrenheit for weather.
Canada: metric officially, but height in feet and inches and body weight in pounds are common; cooking and construction often mix both.
United Kingdom: metric for most trade, but road distances and speeds in miles, pints for beer and milk, and body weight often in stones (1 st = 14 lb). See the weight converter.
US vs UK volumes differ: a US gallon is 3.785 L and a UK gallon 4.546 L.

Pounds here are avoirdupois pounds, the everyday kind. Troy pounds for precious metals differ.
Mass vs weight: the kilogram and pound here are masses; on Earth they're used interchangeably for weight.
Tips and common mistakes
Picking units from different categories.
Converting temperature differences with the full formula. A change of 10 °C is a change of 18 °F (no +32).
Rounding too early in multi-step conversions.
Using 2.2 for pounds per kilogram in precise work (it's 2.20462…).
Kitchen check
A US cup is about 236.6 mL; the metric cup used in Canada is 250 mL.

About 2.20462.
Can I convert cups or liters?
Not yet; volume is a planned category.

It's where the two formulas give the same number.

Title tag
URL Encode and Decode Online | FigSumo (38 chars)
Meta description
Percent-encode text for use in URLs or decode encoded strings, using encodeURIComponent rules, entirely in your browser. (120 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
669 (minimum 600)
H1: URL Encoder and Decoder
URLs can only contain a limited set of characters. Spaces, accented letters, emoji and symbols with special meaning (such as &, = and ?) must be percent-encoded to travel safely in a web address or query string. This tool encodes text for use in a URL, or decodes percent-encoded text back to readable form, in your browser.
How to use this tool
1. Text: paste the text or the encoded string (default "figsumo calculators").
2. Mode: "URL-encode" or "URL-decode".
Result: the encoded or decoded text. Malformed sequences (such as a lone % sign) show an error when decoding.
How percent-encoding works
Each character that isn't allowed is converted to its UTF-8 bytes, and each byte is written as % followed by two hexadecimal digits.
Space → %20
é (two UTF-8 bytes, C3 A9) → %C3%A9
👍 (four bytes) → %F0%9F%91%8D
Characters left unchanged by this tool: letters A–Z and a–z, digits 0–9, and - _ . ! ~ * ' ( ). Everything else, including / ? & = # + :, is encoded, which makes the output safe to drop into a single query-string value or path segment.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
"figsumo calculators" → figsumo%20calculators
Example 2: reserved characters
"a&b=c/d?e" → a%26b%3Dc%2Fd%3Fe. Without encoding, the & and = would split the value into separate parameters.
Example 3: accents and percent signs
"café 50%" → caf%C3%A9%2050%25
Example 4: building a search link
To link to a search for "mortgage & tax", encode the term and add it to the URL: https://example.com/search?q=mortgage%20%26%20tax.
Example 5: decoding a tracking link
utm_campaign=spring%20sale%202026 decodes to "spring sale 2026".
Reserved and unreserved characters
Type
Characters
Notes
Unreserved (never need encoding)
A–Z a–z 0–9 - _ . ~
Safe anywhere
Reserved (have meaning)
: / ? # [ ] @ ! $ & ' ( ) * + , ; =
Encode when used as data
Everything else
spaces, %, ", <, >, non-ASCII
Always encode
%20 or +?
In HTML form submissions (application/x-www-form-urlencoded), spaces are often written as +. In paths and most modern APIs, %20 is used. This tool encodes spaces as %20 and doesn't convert + to a space when decoding; replace + with %20 first if you're decoding form data.
Common uses
Query-string values in links and API calls.
UTM tracking parameters in marketing links.
Redirect URLs passed inside another URL (?next=%2Fdashboard).
Debugging: reading encoded text in server logs and analytics.
Encoding is not encryption
Anyone can decode percent-encoded text. Never put passwords or personal data in URLs: they're stored in browser history, server logs and analytics. For a different encoding used for binary data, see the Base64 tool.
Privacy
Encoding and decoding run in your browser; the text isn't sent to FigSumo.
Tips and common mistakes
Double encoding: encoding an already encoded string turns %20 into %2520.
Encoding a whole URL with this tool also encodes :// and /; encode only the parts that are data.
Decoding + as a space in form data.
Notes for US, Canada and UK users
Percent-encoding is an international standard (RFC 3986), so it works the same in every country. Differences you'll notice are in the text itself: French Canadian place names such as Trois-Rivières or Montréal contain accented letters that become two-byte UTF-8 sequences (è is %C3%A8, é is %C3%A9), and the pound sign £ becomes %C2%A3. The dollar sign is plain ASCII, but it's a reserved character in some contexts and may be encoded as %24.
Checking an encoded link
1. Decode it here and read the result: you should see the address, path and parameters you expect.
2. Look for double encoding, such as %2520, which is an encoded %20. It usually means a link was encoded twice.
3. Make sure the domain at the start of the decoded link is the one you intend to visit.
Frequently asked questions
What is URL encoding?
Replacing unsafe characters with % and their hex byte values.
What does %20 mean?
A space.
Why does my URL have %2F?
It's an encoded forward slash (/).
Is URL encoding the same as Base64?
No. They're different encodings for different purposes.
What is %25?
An encoded percent sign.
Does it support emoji?
Yes, via UTF-8.

Voltage Drop Calculator

Title tag
Voltage Drop Calculator for Copper and Aluminium Wire | FigSumo (63 chars)
Meta description
Estimate voltage drop from wire size, length, current and material, for single-phase and three-phase circuits. Confirm against local electrical code. (149 chars)
Country
global
Status
keep
Body words
718 (minimum 600)
H1: Voltage Drop Calculator
Every wire has some resistance, so the voltage at the far end of a cable is a little lower than at the panel or battery. Too much drop makes motors run hot, lights dim and electronics misbehave. This calculator estimates the voltage drop on a two-wire circuit from the current, cable length, wire resistance and system voltage.
How to use this calculator
1. Current (A): the load current (default 15).
2. One-way wire length (ft): distance from source to load, not the round trip (default 100).
3. Wire resistance (Ω / 1,000 ft): from a wire table for your conductor size and material (default 1.02, roughly 10 AWG copper at 20 °C).
4. System voltage (V): default 120.
Results: voltage drop, drop percentage and voltage at load.
The formula
voltage drop = 2 × length × (resistance per 1,000 ft ÷ 1,000) × current
drop % = voltage drop ÷ system voltage × 100
The factor 2 accounts for current flowing out and back. For balanced three-phase circuits, use √3 (1.732) instead of 2.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
2 × 100 × 0.00102 × 15 = 3.06 V, 2.55%, leaving 116.94 V at the load.
Example 2: a smaller wire
Same run with 12 AWG copper (about 1.588 Ω/1,000 ft at 20 °C): 4.76 V (3.97%), over the 3% guideline.
Example 3: a 240 V run
30 A over 150 ft with 1.02 Ω/1,000 ft at 240 V: 9.18 V (3.82%).
Example 4: a 12 V DC system
A 10 A load 20 ft from a battery on wire of 1.0 Ω/1,000 ft drops 0.40 V, or 3.33%. Low-voltage systems need much thicker wire for the same percentage drop.
Example 5: the UK (mV/A/m)
UK cable tables give voltage drop in millivolts per amp per metre (for the circuit, both conductors). 2.5 mm² twin and earth is about 18 mV/A/m [VERIFY in BS 7671 Appendix 4]. At 16 A over 25 m: 18 × 16 × 25 ÷ 1,000 = 7.2 V (3.13%) of 230 V.
Example 6: maximum resistance for 3%
For 15 A over 100 ft at 120 V and a 3% limit, the wire's resistance must be at most 0.03 × 120 ÷ (2 × 0.1 × 15) = 1.200 Ω per 1,000 ft.
Wire resistance (copper, approx. at 20 °C)
AWG
Ω per 1,000 ft

2.525

0.999

0.628

Resistance rises about 0.4% per °C, so wire at 75 °C has about 20% more resistance. The NEC's Chapter 9, Table 8 lists values at 75 °C. Aluminium has about 1.6 times the resistance of copper of the same size.
Recommended limits
US (NEC): informational notes recommend no more than 3% on a branch circuit and 5% total for feeder plus branch. These are recommendations, not mandatory rules, though local codes may adopt them.
Canada (CEC): sets voltage drop limits, generally 3% for branch circuits and 5% overall [VERIFY current edition].
UK (BS 7671): 3% for lighting and 5% for other uses on circuits supplied from the public network.
Understanding your results
Use the one-way distance; the calculator doubles it.
AC reactance in large cables adds a little to the drop; this simple method uses resistance only.
Continuous loads and motor starting currents can cause larger momentary drops.
Safety
Voltage drop is one design check; conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection and installation method also decide wire size. Mains wiring should be designed and installed by a qualified electrician to the NEC, CEC or BS 7671.
Tips and common mistakes
Entering the round-trip length (doubles the result).
Using resistance per foot instead of per 1,000 ft.
Ignoring temperature on long, heavily loaded runs.
Frequently asked questions
What is an acceptable voltage drop?
3% on a branch circuit and 5% total are common guidelines.
How do I reduce voltage drop?
Use thicker wire, shorten the run or raise the system voltage.
Why multiply by 2?
Current flows out on one conductor and back on the other.
What about three-phase?
Use 1.732 in place of 2.
Where do I find wire resistance?
Manufacturer data or NEC Chapter 9, Table 8.
Does it work for DC?
Yes, for two-wire DC circuits.

US: pounds and ounces are used for body weight, food labels (alongside grams) and shipping. Note that a US "ton" is the 2,000 lb short ton.
Canada: metric is official, and groceries are priced per kg and per 100 g, but many people still give their body weight in pounds, and doctors' offices may record either. Store flyers often show both, such as "$4.39/lb ($9.68/kg)".
UK: food is sold in grams and kilograms, but body weight is often given in stones and pounds, and babies' birth weights in pounds and ounces. Pub and road signs keep some imperial units, but weight on packaging is metric.
The legal definition is the same in all three countries: since the 1959 international yard and pound agreement, 1 lb is exactly 0.45359237 kg.
Check the price example: $4.39 per lb × 2.20462 lb per kg = $9.68 per kg.
Frequently asked questions
How many pounds are in a kilogram?
About 2.2046.
How do I convert pounds to kilograms?
Multiply by 0.45359237.
How many pounds are in a stone?
14.
What is 70 kg in stones?
About 11 stone.
How many grams are in an ounce?
About 28.35.

Not yet; convert stones to pounds (× 14) first.

Wind Chill Calculator (NWS Formula) | FigSumo (45 chars)

Calculate wind chill from air temperature and wind speed using the 2001 NWS/Environment Canada formula, in °F or °C. (116 chars)
Country

H1: Wind Chill Calculator
Wind chill is how cold it feels on exposed skin when wind strips away the thin layer of warm air around your body. It's why a breezy 20 °F day can feel like single digits. Enter the air temperature and wind speed to get the wind chill temperature used by US and Canadian weather services.
How to use this calculator
1. Air temperature (°F): default 20.
2. Wind speed (mph): measured at about 33 ft (10 m), as in forecasts (default 15).
Results: wind chill in °F and a note on whether the formula applies. It's defined for temperatures at or below 50 °F and winds of at least 3 mph; outside that range the calculator returns the air temperature.
The formula
The 2001 wind chill index, adopted jointly by the US National Weather Service and the Meteorological Service of Canada:
WC = 35.74 + 0.6215T − 35.75V^0.16 + 0.4275T·V^0.16
T: air temperature (°F)
V: wind speed (mph)
The metric version (used in Canada):
WC = 13.12 + 0.6215T − 11.37V^0.16 + 0.3965T·V^0.16
with T in °C and V in km/h.
Worked examples
Example 1: the default
20 °F with a 15 mph wind → 6.2 °F.
Example 2: a bitter day
0 °F with 20 mph → -22.0 °F. Frostbite on exposed skin is possible within about 30 minutes.
Example 3: extreme cold
−10 °F with 30 mph → -39.4 °F: frostbite in 10 minutes or less.
Example 4: Canada (metric)
−20 °C with a 30 km/h wind → wind chill -32.6, reported by Environment Canada as a unitless index that equals what that temperature would feel like in calm conditions.
Example 5: a UK winter day
2 °C with a 20 mph wind (about 32 km/h) → about -4.1 °C. The Met Office's "feels like" temperature uses a related approach.

Staying safe in the cold
Dress in layers: a wicking base layer, an insulating middle layer and a windproof outer shell.
Cover exposed skin: hat, gloves or mittens (warmer than gloves) and a face covering.
Stay dry; wet clothing loses insulation quickly.
Watch for frostbite: numbness and white or greyish-yellow skin. Warm the area gradually; don't rub it.
Watch for hypothermia: shivering, confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness. It's a medical emergency (911 in the US and Canada, 999 in the UK).
Understanding your results
Wind chill affects people and animals, not objects. A car or a pipe can't get colder than the air temperature, though wind cools them faster.
Sunshine can make it feel up to about 10–18 °F warmer; the formula assumes no sun.
Use forecast wind speeds at standard height; ground-level gusts vary.
Tips and common mistakes
Applying the formula above 50 °F.
Using gust speeds instead of sustained wind.
Entering km/h in the mph box; divide km/h by 1.609 first.
Frequently asked questions
What is wind chill?
How cold it feels on exposed skin, given temperature and wind.
When does wind chill apply?
At 50 °F (10 °C) or colder with winds of at least 3 mph (5 km/h).
Can wind chill freeze water?
No. Water freezes only when the air temperature is at or below 32 °F (0 °C).
What is a dangerous wind chill?
Below about −18 °F (−28 °C), frostbite can occur in 30 minutes.
Does Canada use the same formula?
Yes, in metric units.
Can I enter Celsius?
Not yet; convert first with the unit converter.

What the calculator does
Visitors enter the length and width of a slab in feet and its depth in inches. The tool returns the volume in cubic yards and cubic feet:
Volume (ft³) = length (ft) × width (ft) × depth (in) ÷ 12
Volume (yd³) = ft³ ÷ 27
Ready-mix suppliers in the US and Canada sell by the cubic yard, so the cubic-yard figure is the one to quote when ordering.
Examples
A 12 × 10 ft patio, 4 in deep: 40.00 ft³ = 1.48 yd³. With a 10% allowance for spillage and uneven ground, order about 1.63 yd³.
A 20 × 20 ft garage slab, 6 in deep: 200.00 ft³ = 7.41 yd³.

How the score is made
There's no science here. The calculator:
1. Joins the two names, lower-cases them and removes spaces.
2. Turns the letters into a number with a simple hash (a repeatable scrambling formula).
3. Maps that number to a score between 13% and 98%.
So the same pair always gets the same score, capital letters don't matter ("alex" and "JORDAN" also give 28%), and nothing is random. The order of names does change the result in the current version: Jordan first and Alex second gives 60%.
Be clear it's a game
A compatibility percentage from two names has no meaning for real relationships. If you embed it, label it as entertainment, for example "Just for fun!", especially on sites with younger visitors. It works best as an icebreaker, a party game or a social media prompt.

1. Paste the code on a draft page and try sin(30) in Deg mode (0.5) and Rad mode.
2. Check the keypad at your column width on a phone.
3. Make sure your site's content security policy allows frames from figsumo.com.
Frequently asked questions
Is the scientific calculator widget free?
Yes. No account or key is needed.
Does it work on phones and tablets?
Yes; the keypad is touch-friendly. Use a width of 320–360 px for narrow mobile layouts.
Can students use it offline?
No, it needs an internet connection to load.
Does it support graphing or fractions?
No. For fractions, link to the fraction calculator.
Can I set it to radians by default?
Not yet; visitors can switch modes with the Deg/Rad buttons.

Appendix C: QA summary
Pages: 241 of 241 non-merge/remove rows in on-page-seo.csv present (/money 109, /health 29, /math 44, /everyday 54, /embed 5).
Body words: minimum 600, median 1,007, mean 868, total 209,322. No page is below its minimum (1,000 for finance, tax and health pages; 600 for math, everyday and embed pages).
Finance and health pages: 134, shortest 1,001 words. Other pages: shortest 600 words.
Worked examples: 211 pages built from Python sources were re-run (calc_check.py) and every computed value appears in the final copy. The 30 launch-pack pages were re-run with examples.py and spot-checked. An arithmetic scan of 506 inline 'a op b = c' expressions found one rounding error (pregnancy weight gain 5.25 kg shown as 5.2), now corrected, and one 1-cent inconsistency in the Canada take-home example, now corrected. The other flags were chained equations that check out.
Duplicates: no repeated paragraph of 12+ words across pages, apart from two shared formula blocks (Navy body-fat equation on the body-fat and army body-fat pages; Mifflin-St Jeor on the BMR and TDEE pages). These are intentional.
Links: every related-calculator link and inline link points to a URL in the sheet, except /methodology (211 links) and /privacy (3), which are site pages still to be created. One dead link (/us/take-home-pay-calculator) was changed to /us/paycheck-calculator.
[VERIFY] flags: 198 on 108 pages (Appendix A).
Structure: every page has a how-to-use section, examples, tips, 5–8 FAQs, related calculators and sources. Every finance and health page has a disclaimer.
Calculator fixes: 14 pages carry a 'FIX' requirement (Appendix B). The copy describes the corrected behaviour or flags the limitation, so the tool must match before publishing: BTU, engine horsepower, bra size, shoe size, password generator, mileage reimbursement, z-score, pace rounding, pregnancy weight gain, and the five embed widgets.
